Each row says whether it is unread against the caller's own read state and carries the position that marks it read; the answer counts the unread mentions and replies over the newest 100 of each. `?kind=` (`mention`, `reply` or `reaction`) narrows it, `?unread=true` answers the unread rows alone, whole, `?cursor=` and `?limit=` page it. See [what a reader keeps](../concepts/chatlet.md#what-a-reader-keeps) |
| `GET` | `/chatlet/threads` | The threads the caller follows, newest reply first, each with its root (carrying the thread line) and its two newest replies: the threads they started, replied or were named in, and those they followed by hand, less those they unfollowed. `?cursor=`, `?limit=` (default 20, at most 50) |
| `GET` | `/chatlet/saved` | The messages the caller saved for later, newest save first, each with its message, or `gone` where it was taken back, erased, pruned or is in a room they may no longer read. `?cursor=`, `?limit=` |
| `GET` | `/chatlet/sent` | What the caller said, newest first, in every room they may still read; a message they took back is left out. `?cursor=`, `?limit=` |
| `GET` | `/chatlet/channels/{channel_id}/reach` | Whom a draft would reach if sent now, by the post's own routing, published nowhere: `?body=` (the words, read for `@handle` and `@channel` as the post reads them) and `?reply_to=` (a reply's thread). Answers the room, the thread, `reach.recipients` (each `{handle, reason}`), `mentions`, `collective`, and `quiet` when it would reach no agent (`no_agent`, or `addressed_to_people` when it names only people). An archived room, or one the caller may not post in, is refused as the post would be |
| `GET` | `/chatlet/channels/{channel_id}/links` | Every link the room's messages carried, newest first, each with who shared it, when, and the message it came from; a taken-back message's are left out. `?cursor=`, `?limit=` (messages a page reads) |
| `GET` | `/chatlet/channels/{channel_id}/messages/{message_id}` | One message, read in place: with its thread's root and the two replies just before it when it is a reply. A message not in that room answers `404`, as a room the caller may not read does |
| `GET` | `/chatlet/search` | The rooms the caller may read **ranked** against `?q=`: keyword only, over the engine's own chat index. `?channel_id=` and `?author=` narrow it, `?limit=` (default 20, at most 40) |
| `GET` | `/chatlet/room-names` | The name of every room the caller may read, joined or not, archived included: each room's `id`, `name`, `kind` and `archived`, live rooms first, at most 1000 with `truncated` where rooms were left out. A direct conversation has no name and is not here |
| `GET` | `/chatlet/rooms` | Every named room the caller may read, joined or not, archived included, each with its member count, whether the caller is in it and when it was last active: the `chat_rooms` question |
| `POST` | `/worklet/items` `/doclet/pages` | **File an item, write a page**, and the rest of the [write surface](#the-human-write-surface): the same tools a seat and your own assistant hold, as the person you signed in as. Guarded; the item routes are absent on a company that does not run Worklet, the page routes on one that does not run Doclet |
| `PATCH` | `/worklet/items/{key}` | Change an item, and its `/comments`, `/rank`, `/depend`, `/relate`, `/restore` and `/purge` beside it. See [below](#the-human-write-surface) for every route and the authority each takes |
| `GET` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/{collection}` `/{collection}/{doc}` `/{collection}/query` `/history` `/schema` `/state` | **An artifact's datastore, read**: a collection's documents, one document, a query over its field index, the store's history, its schema and the caller's own per-viewer state, each decided per artifact and shaped by the collection's read rule (see [below](#artifactsiddata-an-artifacts-datastore-auth-gated)) |
| `POST` `PUT` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/writes` `/undo` `/state` `/schema` | **An artifact's datastore, written**: one atomic batch of ops, an undo, a per-viewer state key, a schema change. `Idempotency-Key` required; each answers the verdict the applier wrote |
| `GET` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/export.csv` | One collection as CSV, to an editor of the artifact |
| `POST` | `/auth/login` | **Sign in.** Login or address, password, and a second factor where one is held. **Unguarded**, and throttled on the login **as typed** from the caller's source: a failure costs the next attempt a wait, never a lockout (see [below](#a-failure-costs-a-wait-never-a-lockout)). Every failure answers one code after the same argon2id derivation (see [below](#every-failed-sign-in-is-one-refusal)). A node that cannot read the identity estate or record the session answers `503`, and **every `503` under `/auth` carries a `Retry-After`**. A write whose outcome nobody can establish (the second factor's spend, the session's own start) is that `503` with the `op_id`, and **never a session**. A success answers `{person, login, seat?, expires_at, position, status}`; `status` is `signed_in`, or, where the company requires a second factor (its default) and the person holds none, `second_factor_enrolment_required`: the session may only enrol one (see [A required second factor is enrolled before anything else](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#a-required-second-factor-is-enrolled-before-anything-else)). `POST /auth/invite/{id}` and a password `POST /auth/step-up` answer the same shape, restricted on the same rule |
| `GET` | `/auth/config` | What a sign-in page needs before anybody has signed in: `{min_password_length, second_factor}`. `min_password_length` is the company's `sign_in.min_password_length` held within this node's limit, never below the engine's twelve (the floor for every password a person sets); `second_factor` is `required` or `optional` from the company's `sign_in.require_second_factor` held within this node's limit (unset is `required`). Password sign-in is always served. **Unguarded**, with **no user list and no count of people** |
| `GET` | `/auth/invite/{id}` | **Renders an invitation and never spends it** (mail prefetchers, scanners and preview cards follow links). **Unguarded**: holding the link is the credential, the **secret** it carries after the id, presented in the `X-Crewlet-Invite-Secret` header and never in the URL. The link a person follows is the dashboard's screen, `<api.external_url>/dashboard#/invite/<id>.<secret>`, whose fragment no browser sends to a server; the screen calls this route with the two halves apart. Answers the address it is for; who sent it (`invited_by`: a person by their seat's chart name, absent for a machine, a Tier A token or a service account, whose coloned login, `token:founder`, the holder would not recognise); the password floor; the `seat` redeeming it binds (**always present**: `{handle, name}` as the chart calls it now, or `{}` where the company no longer holds it as a human seat, which the redemption refuses as a link that no longer works); a `login` **proposed** from the address in the person grammar (`jane.doe@example.com` → `jane.doe`, `jane@example.com` → `jane.example`) for the form to pre-fill; and `signed_in_as`, the login of the session the browser already holds (absent for none), because redeeming ends that session and the form says so first. Absent, redeemed, expired and a missing or wrong secret are one `410` in the same bytes, so a guessed secret against a leaked id does not say the id exists. An id nobody issued or a secret that is not the link's is a **failed attempt**, counted on the audit trail's per-minute failure row (`iam_login_failures`) under its source; that count climbing shows someone walking ids or secrets. It meets no [curve](#a-failure-costs-a-wait-never-a-lockout): the secret is 256 bits nobody walks, and a curve keyed on the address would let a stranger there hold it shut for everybody else. A link that **proved itself** and is spent (redeemed, expired, its address enrolled) is the same `410` and is not counted. A node whose identity rows cannot **vouch** for a link that does not open (behind the identity log, or holding a record it could not apply) answers `503 identity_unavailable` instead, for an id it does not hold and a wrong secret alike, and counts nothing: the link may have been issued through a peer |
| `POST` | `/auth/invite/{id}` | Redeems it, conferring exactly the grants and seat whoever issued it decided; a link spent or aged out between the form and the post is `410 invite_spent`. **Unguarded**. Body `{secret, login, name, password}`: `secret` is the half of the link after the id, checked as the view checks it; `login` is **required** (what they sign in with, the name a lead finds them by, and the `by jane.doe` in every trail reason; the view proposes one). An absent login, or one outside a person's grammar (dotted, `jane.doe`), is `400` naming the rule; a login somebody already holds is `409`, without saying who. The redemption is **one record** (the person, their address, their login, the seat the invitation binds and the spent link), so every refusal writes nothing: a seat removed or made an agent's since the issue is `410`; one a person holds since (only a retained record or a restore leaves that) is `409` saying the seat is taken, naming nobody. Only a person holding the seat refuses it, not an older open invitation on the same seat. Only a record that could not land is `503`. **Retry until it lands**: a redeemer told their login is taken posts another. A link whose address somebody is already enrolled under is `410`, like a redeemed one. A browser that already holds a session has it **ended** as `POST /auth/logout` ends it, before the new one opens, and its cookie is replaced; every sign-in that opens a fresh session does the same (`POST /auth/login`, `POST /auth/token`). The company's **first person** redeems exactly this way: a Tier A token issues their invitation into a human seat the company declares (see [How the first person exists](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#how-the-first-person-exists)) |
| `GET` | `/auth/session` | **Who you are**: your id, login, seat, kind, stage and grants; your own `name` as your directory row holds it (absent for a Tier A token, which has no row, and where this node cannot read or open it, which never fails the answer); for a session cookie its `expires_at` and its `lineage` (the id a listing of your sessions names it by, so a client can tell which is this browser); `reauth_at`, the instant your proof of identity stops counting for a [step-up](#some-gestures-ask-how-recently-you-proved-who-you-are) gesture, with `step_up_due` saying whether the next one will ask you to confirm it; and `status`: `signed_in`, or `second_factor_enrolment_required` for a session that may only enrol a second factor, which is one of the routes such a session reaches |
| `POST` | `/auth/token` | Exchanges a **Tier A bearer** (presented as `Authorization: Bearer`, never a cookie) for a one-hour session cookie. The session **is the token**: it names the token's login, and every request re-composes it from the entry this node holds now (the entry's permissions under this node's `api.auth.admin` posture, the seat the identity directory binds the token to, stepped up by construction as the bearer is). Removing or renaming the entry ends it on the next request. It answers to the token's **id**, not its value: a new value under the same id leaves the sessions the old value opened working until their hour ends, so to cut a leaked value's sessions off at once, rotate by giving the token a **new id** (see [Identity and access](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#the-three-credential-shapes-meet-at-one-frame)). `POST /auth/logout` from it closes it as it closes a person's, and `POST /auth/logout/all` from it and `crewlet iam invalidate-all` end it too. A refused bearer here is answered as on every guarded route: `401`, counted on the audit trail's per-minute failure row, never slowed or refused on its address (see [A bearer is its own protection](#a-bearer-is-its-own-protection)) |
| `POST` | `/auth/step-up` | Confirm who you are on a session that is already valid. The only route here that is **both guarded and throttled** (unbounded retries against a known person would be a password oracle). It answers a **fresh session cookie** and **ends the session it replaces** first (a close that does not land is `503` with a `Retry-After` and opens nothing; a presented session no longer live is `401`). The replacement keeps the replaced session's absolute deadline. **Only a person confirms**: a machine token is `403 token_refused`, the answer the authority table gives a token wherever a person must be present, and a session that is no person's (exchanged from a Tier A token, or a service account's) is `403 forbidden` saying why, as `POST /auth/password` answers it |
| `POST` | `/auth/totp` | Enrol a second factor, replacing any you hold. **Two requests**: the first answers a seed and stores nothing, the second presents a code derived from it (the only evidence the authenticator app works). Needs a proof inside `step_up`, the second-factor reset's window; an older one is `403 step_up_required` naming it (`reason`, `window`) as every step-up refusal does. **Never through a machine token**: `403 token_refused`, whatever its owner may do. **Never by a principal that is no person** (a session exchanged from a Tier A token, a service account): `403 forbidden` saying why, as `POST /auth/password` answers it, never `step_up_required`. A factor nobody can confirm is stored is `503` with its `op_id`, never "enrolled". The second leg answers `{"status": "enrolled"}` and, through a session that could only enrol a second factor, **replaces that session**: the restricted one is ended first, a whole one opens keeping its absolute deadline and its proof instant (the password's: the enrolment's code proves a seed, not who holds it, so it opens no fresh step-up window), its cookie is on the response and it is answered beside the status as `session` (the sign-in's own shape, `status: signed_in`). Such a session enrols only while its person holds **no** second factor, decided in the write's own snapshot, so one that has come to hold one since is `403 second_factor_required` and nothing is stored: a password alone never replaces a factor. The seed is sealed under your own key before it is stored, and opened only to check a code |
| `POST` | `/auth/totp/recovery` | Issue ten fresh single-use codes, retiring the old set. Answered **once**, in the clear; only their hashes are stored, so a lost set is regenerated, not recovered. Needs a proof inside `step_up`, refused as `POST /auth/totp` is, a machine token and a non-person principal included. Issued only beside an authenticator app: a person who holds none is refused `409 invalid` and issued nothing; the first set comes with the first enrolment. A set nobody can confirm is stored is `503` with its `op_id`, and the codes are not shown |
| `POST` | `/auth/logout` | End **this** session. The cookie is cleared whatever the write did. It ends the session behind **either** cookie name, the one this deployment issues and the other a browser may still hold from before `api.external_url` moved to https (which the guard no longer authenticates), and clears both. Only a session this node's rows still hold is closed and announced as `iam_session_ended`: a cookie past its deadline, revoked, or naming a session a record already ended is cleared and nothing is written, and a node that cannot read its rows records the close without announcing it. **Unguarded**, so a node that cannot read its identity estate cannot answer `503 identity_unavailable` before the sign-out runs and leave the cookie set. It verifies every bearer the browser holds itself, and the origin check still judges it |
| `POST` | `/auth/logout/all` | End **every** session you hold, by bumping your own revocation epoch, the one move that is immediate on every node. A revocation nobody can confirm is `503` with its `op_id`, not a claim that your other sessions ended |
| `GET` | `/auth/reset/{id}` | **Says whose password a reset link sets, and never spends it.** The same route opens a person's **first password link**, which `POST /iam/people` hands back when an administrator creates them on their seat: the same kind of credential, opened and spent identically. **Unguarded**: the link is the credential, its **secret** presented in the `X-Crewlet-Reset-Secret` header and never in the URL; the link a person follows is the dashboard's screen, `<api.external_url>/dashboard#/reset/<id>.<secret>`. Answers `{login, expires_at, min_password_length, first}`: `first` is `true` when the person holds no password yet, so the screen asks them to choose one rather than a new one and warns of no sessions ending; it is derived from what the person holds, not stored on the link, so a reset link issued to somebody whose first link lapsed unspent is a first password too. Every way a link fails to open (an id that is no link, a secret that is not its link's, a link spent, revoked, ended by a counter or aged out, a person suspended, retired or removed since) is one `410 reset_spent` in the same bytes, and only a link that did **not** prove itself is a failed attempt on the per-minute failure row (method `reset`). A node whose identity rows cannot vouch for a link that does not open is `503 identity_unavailable` instead, counting nothing, as the invitation's view is. It meets no [curve](#a-failure-costs-a-wait-never-a-lockout) |
| `POST` | `/auth/reset/{id}` | **Sets a new password from a reset link, once.** **Unguarded**. Body `{secret, password}`, the password held to the floor (`422 invalid`, naming the rule). One record sets it, spends the link with every other the person held and moves their revocation epoch (every session and machine token they held ends), judged by the link again in that record's own snapshot, so a link spent from another tab in between is the same `410 reset_spent`. Answers `{status: "password_set", login}` and **no session**: the person signs in next, where a second factor they hold still applies. A first password link is spent by the same record, and for somebody who never held a password it has nothing to end. Each spend is its own operation, so a second one (another tab, or a retry of a spend whose answer was lost) finds the link spent and is `410 reset_spent`, never a `password_set` for a password nothing set; the password the first spend set is the one that works. Issued by an administrator: `POST /iam/people/{id}/password-reset`, or, for a person's first password, the create itself (`POST /iam/people`) |
| `POST` | `/auth/password` | **Change your own password.** Takes `{current_password, new_password, code}`; the proof is a step-up's, taken in this request, so no step-up is asked first. The current password is verified on the step-up's terms: on the throttle's curve for the login you are signed in as, a wrong one the `401 sign_in_refused` every failed sign-in answers, with `field: current_password` and a `detail` saying so. **`code` is asked of anybody who holds a second factor**, the current code from their authenticator app or one of their recovery codes, exactly as a step-up asks it: absent, `401 second_factor_required`, which changes nothing and counts as no attempt; wrong or already spent, `401 sign_in_refused`, counted on the person's own curve as well as the pair's (a wait past five seconds is `429` with a `Retry-After`); right, it is spent. (Without it, somebody holding your session cookie and password but not your authenticator could end every session you held and lock you out.) Somebody who holds no second factor sends no `code`. The new password is held to the password floor (`422 invalid`, naming the rule). Needs a person present: a machine token is `403 token_refused`, and a session exchanged from a Tier A token, which is no person's, is `403 forbidden`. **One record** sets the password and moves the person's revocation epoch, ending every session and machine token they held and every outstanding reset link; this browser is then handed a new session, proved now and answered in the sign-in's own shape. A change this node has not applied yet is `202` with `status: password_changed` and no session (sign in again with the new password); one that finds the password changed by somebody else since it was verified is `409 stale` with the cookie cleared, because that change ended this session too. See [Changing your own password ends everything else](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#changing-your-own-password-ends-everything-else) |
| `POST` | `/auth/logout/{lineage}` | End **one named** session, e.g. a laptop you left somewhere, from the browser you are using. Whether you may end it is the authority table's, the same rule as `DELETE /iam/people/{id}/sessions`: your **own** on no proof at all (a session exchanged from a Tier A token counts the token's other sessions as its own), and **anybody else's** on `admin`, a proof inside `step_up` and a person present. A refusal is the table's own envelope: `403 unauthorized` naming `admin`, `403 step_up_required`, or `403 token_refused` for a machine token. A lineage nobody holds answers `ended`, as a session already over does (ended by a record, past its absolute deadline, revoked or invalidated), with nothing written or announced; "nobody holds it" is **proved** against the identity log's end, so a node whose rows have not applied every record the log holds (behind, or holding one it could not apply) does not say it, since a session opened through a peer is a row it may still be missing. That node, and one that cannot read its rows at all, answers `503 identity_unavailable` with a `Retry-After` and writes nothing, because the owner the caller is checked against is one of those rows (unlike `POST /auth/logout`, whose lineage comes off the cookie's own signature). A close nobody can confirm is `503` with its `op_id`; asking again is a fresh close, and one that finds the first had landed answers `ended` |
| `GET` | `/viewer` | **Who is asking.** The caller's `login`; the `grants` they carry **on this node**, the effective set (every app an admin holds spelled out, unknown names dropped, and `admin` only where this node's `api.auth.admin` serves it); the seat the identity directory binds them to, its `handle`, `name` and `kind`, all empty for a credential nobody is bound through; and `owner`, the name the caller's own record (inbox, pins, priorities, personal views) is kept under: the seat for a person, or for a token or service account the directory binds to one, and the login for a credential bound to none. `acts` names the tools [`/operator/act`](#operatoract--the-dashboards-write-surface) would serve this caller (the catalogue's writes the authority table can admit them to before any object is named, a write asking a step-up the caller has yet to make among them), always an array; a node that cannot yet decide `acts` answers `503` rather than an empty list. `project` is where a create of theirs that names no project files, `""` for a caller bound to no seat or a seat whose team owns no project; `space` is where a page of theirs that names no container lands, by the same rule. A credential bound to no seat (a Tier A token's session, a service account bound to none) is an **ordinary state**, not an error: a pipeline's token acts under its own login, and binding it to a seat is a directory row. A person always holds a human seat, so is never answered unbound. `config_writer` is whether the caller's credential may change the company document: false for an anonymous caller and for every credential a [managed document's](../concepts/configuration.md#managed-configuration) `api.auth.company_writers` does not list (a person's session, a machine token and a lead's among them); it says nothing about authority, which `admin` or a lead's subtree still decides. `config_managed_by` is the Tier A token ids that alone may change it when another system manages it, empty when nothing does and for an anonymous caller. `assistant` is whether [Ask Crewlet](#ask-crewlet) is available to the caller on this node, `{available, reason?, model, notice, can_assign, reads_images}`, every member but `reason` always sent. `model: {key, label}` is the model Ask Crewlet is assigned (`assistant.model` and the model its entry names), null where none; `can_assign` is whether the caller holds the company document's write, through which it is assigned (a step-up may still be asked). `reason` is the first reason it is not available: `no_model` (none assigned, or this node does not serve Ask Crewlet), `model_problem` (the assigned model is one no helper can run on), `not_a_person` (a machine token, a service account or a Tier A token's session), `no_permission`, or `model_not_ready`, checked last so only a person Ask Crewlet would answer learns it: the model is known unusable right now, read from what the node already holds and never by calling a model (its plan spent until a reset, its harness signed out or with nothing that signs it in, or unable to start). With that reason `notice` is `{code, message, hint?, retry_at?}` (null for any other), the [turn error](#how-a-turn-fails-on-the-model) a question would have failed with, in the same words, and the hint an administrator or anybody else is given. `reads_images` is whether a question's images are handed to the assigned model, which its harness decides ([Big tasks and images](../guides/assistant.md#big-tasks-and-images)); where false the dashboard takes no image. `chat_vendors` names the vendor chat a company talks on, to a holder of `chatlet` (see the [`viewer`](#queries) question) |
| `GET` | `/home/board` | **Your own Home board**, the [`home_board`](#queries) question: the widgets you placed on the dashboard's Home and how you arranged them, kept under your seat so they follow you to every browser. About the caller alone, so everybody's; served where the node reaches the coordination store. Its write is [`save_home_board`](#saving-your-home-board) |
| `GET` | `/stream/snapshot` | Dashboard initial-state bundle, served from the in-memory projection (REST fallback for the WebSocket) |
| `WS`  | `/ws/stream` | Live dashboard stream: agents, events, LLM invocations, health |
| `GET` | `/dashboard` | Dashboard shell (`/` and `/dashboard/` redirect here; `/static/{path}` serves its assets) |
| `POST` | `/webhooks/jira` | Receive Jira Data Center webhooks (Cloud arrives via `/webhooks/forge`) |
| `POST` | `/webhooks/slack/{handle}` | Receive Slack Events API deliveries for one seat's app |
| `GET` | `/webhooks/slack-oauth` | OAuth install landing: finishes an install the Agents tab began |
| `GET` | `/webhooks/mcp-oauth` | Where a vendor sends the browser back after an MCP server's or an integration's sign-in: finishes the sign-in its signed state names (see [below](#get-webhooksmcp-oauth)) |
| `GET` | `/webhooks/mcp-oauth/client-metadata.json` | The engine's OAuth client metadata document, the client id a `cimd` sign-in is made as (see [below](#get-webhooksmcp-oauthclient-metadatajson)) |
| `POST` | `/webhooks/github` | Receive GitHub webhooks, HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body |
| `POST` | `/webhooks/github/{handle}` | The same route addressed to one seat, where that seat's own [GitHub App](../integrations/github.md#one-github-app-per-agent) delivers |
| `GET` | `/webhooks/github-app` | Landing page for the per-agent GitHub App flow: converts the one-time creation code, or reports an install (see [below](#get-webhooksgithub-app)) |
| `POST` | `/webhooks/gitlab` | Receive GitLab webhooks |
| `POST` | `/webhooks/confluence` | Receive Confluence Data Center webhooks, HMAC-signed. Cloud arrives on the two routes below instead |
| `POST` | `/webhooks/confluence/{event}` | Receive one Confluence **Cloud** event, authenticated by the shared token the registered URL carries: `X-Crewlet-Token` first, `?token=` as the fallback (Cloud honours no registration field for a header) |
| `POST` | `/webhooks/datadog` | Receive a Datadog monitor alert, authenticated by a constant-time comparison of `X-Crewlet-Token`. Datadog signs nothing, so the token is the whole check: an unset one answers `503`, and so does one shorter than 26 characters (see [Datadog](../integrations/datadog.md#verification-is-weaker-here-and-that-is-the-providers-ceiling)) |
| `POST` | `/webhooks/forge` | Receive Forge events (FIT-verified) |
| `POST` | `/otlp/{token}/v1/{signal}` | Engine-fronted OTLP receiver for [sandbox](../concepts/code-sandbox.md) telemetry (per-run token in the path). Mounted where `CREWLET_SANDBOX_OTEL_RECEIVER_URL` is set, or, for a node's own `direct` boxes, where it runs seats: it binds `api.port` and forwards to `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`, on a node without `ingress` to its own host's loopback alone, as the bridge is |
| `GET` `POST` `DELETE` | `/mcp/{token}` | The [tool bridge](../concepts/code-sandbox.md#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box): one running seat's tool surface, served over streamable-HTTP MCP to the seat's executor (its harness's run in a box) by the node holding the seat, to which the node the call reaches relays it over the broker. Per-run token in the path; all three verbs because the transport uses them. A call is admitted under any `Host`, a proxy's or tunnel's public name on the node's loopback included. `401` for a token that is forged or names a run that is over (a run's token has no expiry of its own: the run's end ends it), and for a request on a job's other token once its box has said which session it started (a job whose launch continues a session is handed one token per session its box may start: see [Which session the box started](../concepts/code-sandbox.md#which-session-the-box-started)). `503` with a `Retry-After` while no node can answer for the run's seat, after waiting up to two seat-lease lifetimes for one, and at once where the node a call was relayed to let the seat go before serving it, or where a request opening an MCP session reached the run's session just as it ended on the node that held it. `502` when the seat's holder took the call and stopped answering before it wrote a status. Mounted only on a node that has a bridge: one given `CREWLET_MCP_BRIDGE_URL`, or one that runs seats and binds `api.port`, for its own `direct` boxes. A node without `ingress` mounts it on `api.port` beside its probes and serves it to its own host's loopback alone, answering any other caller `404 no_route` (see [Probes on a node without ingress](#probes-on-a-node-without-ingress)); on any other node the route is absent |
| `GET` `POST` `DELETE` | `/mcp/{token}/server/{server}` | One of the seat's MCP servers, served apart from the engine's own tools at `/mcp/{token}` so the run's harness can keep its tools out of each request ([the tool bridge](../concepts/code-sandbox.md#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box)): that server's tools alone, under the name the company gives it, with what the company says the server is for as its MCP instructions. Every call is the run's, decided and recorded as one at `/mcp/{token}` is. Same token, transport, routing and refusals as `/mcp/{token}`; `400` for a server the run's session does not serve |
| `GET` | `/mcp/{token}/steer/notes?after={seq}` | The run's [notes](../concepts/code-sandbox.md#notes-to-a-running-run): the notes waiting for its turn past the cursor, `{"notes": [{seq, id, inbox, message}]}`, held up to ten seconds while none waits and answered at once when one arrives. `503` with a `Retry-After` once the node is stopping (`draining`) or the run's session has ended here (`unavailable`), the held poll included: its notes wait for the session's next opening. Same token, routing and refusals as the bridge; `404` for a run that has nothing to steer |
| `POST` | `/mcp/{token}/steer/read` | Record the notes the run's harness put in front of its model, `{"ids": [...]}` (one to twenty: a turn's ten notes and up to ten more meant for the job alone; at most 64 KiB): `204`, or `503` with a `Retry-After` when the record could not be written; when the run's session ended here as the read reached it or before it was recorded; while the run's tools are closed here, its seat leaving the node or a person having stopped it; once the run's record takes no read of its job any more, its completion having claimed the run; or where it names a waiting note sealed under a key this node does not hold (a node that holds the key records it: `unavailable`). The notes it did not record wait |
| `POST` | `/mcp/{token}/skill` | Record that the run's harness loaded one of the skills it was handed as its own, `{"skill": "<name>"}` (at most 4 KiB), naming the skill as the harness listed it: recorded as a `load_tool_skill` call on the run's record, which unlocks the tools a required skill covers. `204` whether or not the name is one of the run's skills; `404` for a run handed none. The plugin of an OpenCode run posts here; a Claude Code run's hook reports the same load as a call of the bridge's `skill_loaded` tool, which is never listed. Same token, routing and refusals as the bridge |
| `POST` | `/operator/mcp` | Worklet, Doclet and Chatlet, served over MCP to **your** AI assistant. **Always needs a credential**, which for an assistant is a [machine token](#post-iamcredentials-mints-a-machine-token) acting as you: it files and moves work (see [below](#operatormcp--your-own-assistant)). The catalogue is built per request: `503 no_active_revision` until this node has met its first company, never empty after that. Pausing, resuming and steering a seat and answering a parked run concern the fleet's own records, so every company is served them whatever backends it runs. Stateless: no session, so any node answers any request, and a `GET` or `DELETE` is answered `405` |
| `POST` | `/operator/act/{tool}` | The same catalogue's writes, one tool per request, **as the principal your request resolves to**: the dashboard's write surface. Any credential the guard resolved; every tool is decided by the authority table, and the `Idempotency-Key` header is required (see [below](#operatoract--the-dashboards-write-surface)). Answers `503 no_active_revision` before the first company, as `/operator/mcp` does, and `404 unknown_tool` for a tool the company's catalogue does not serve |
| `GET` `HEAD` | `/git/{repo}/info/refs` | A git client's advertisement of a repository the engine hosts, on a node whose roles name `gitlet`. git's protocol, a person's credential as the Basic password; a push only with one that resolves to a person. **Always needs a credential**, never on `api.public` (see [Gitlet](#gitlet-git-and-gitlet)) |
| `POST` | `/git/{repo}/git-upload-pack` | A clone's or a fetch's request (same) |
| `POST` | `/git/{repo}/git-receive-pack` | A push (same) |
| `GET` `HEAD` | `/box/git/{repo}/info/refs` | A **box's** advertisement of a repository it was given, on a node whose roles name `gitlet`. git's protocol, a box's own credential as the Basic password: a **coding box's** (user name `run` and its run's token, admitted by the run's row; see [Coding boxes](../concepts/gitlet.md#coding-boxes)) or a **check's box's** (user name `check` and its check's token, admitted by its attempt's row to fetch one commit over protocol v2 and shown no ref; see [Check boxes](../concepts/gitlet.md#check-boxes)); never a person's credential, and published on `api.public` beside a coding box's other two edges. **A node that serves none of Gitlet says why only to a token this fleet signed**: any other request (no credential, a person's, or a token that does not verify under the user name presenting it) is answered the box's `401` challenge, the one Gitlet's admission answers, whatever the reason; a signed one is told the `404` or `503` a person's `/git/` request is ([git's smart HTTP](#gits-smart-http)) |
| `POST` | `/box/git/{repo}/git-upload-pack` | A box's clone or fetch (same) |
| `POST` | `/box/git/{repo}/git-receive-pack` | A coding box's push (same); a check's box pushes nothing |
| `GET` | `/box/gitlet/{repo}/tree` | A **check's box's** listing of a directory of the commit its check measures (`path` or `path_b64`, `recursive`, `cursor`), on a node whose roles name `gitlet`, with the credential its git presents: user name `check` and its check's token as the Basic password, admitted by its attempt's row. Reads that one commit and no other: no revision is a parameter, and one named is `400`. Answered as the box's git is where a node serves none of Gitlet (see [Check boxes](../concepts/gitlet.md#check-boxes)) |
| `GET` | `/box/gitlet/{repo}/blob` | A check's box's read of one file's lines of its commit: `path` (or `path_b64`), `start_line`, `end_line`, `cursor` (same) |
| `GET` | `/box/gitlet/{repo}/diff` | A check's box's diff of its commit from the base its attempt was queued with: `paths` (repeated) for the stat of those, or `file` (or `file_b64`) for one file's patch, `renames`, `cursor` (same) |
| `GET` | `/atlas` | The company's [atlas](../concepts/atlas.md), a page of its entries at a time. **Needs the `atlas` permission** (see [The atlas](#the-atlas)) |
| `GET` | `/atlas/map` | The atlas drawn as its lanes: every lane, its groups, the entries of the open groups and the relations drawn at rest, or every relation between them (same) |
| `GET` | `/atlas/facets` | How many entries each filter value leaves (same) |
| `GET` | `/atlas/log` | The atlas's own log, newest first, paged: what changed, when and in whose voice (same) |
| `GET` | `/atlas/activity` | The log counted a day at a time over its last two weeks, for the company and for each entry, with each entry's last change (same) |
| `GET` | `/atlas/work` | How many open Worklet tasks name each entry, for a caller who also holds `worklet` (same) |
| `GET` | `/atlas/named` | The entries a list of ids names, as rows: what a task's linked entries are drawn from (same) |
| `GET` | `/atlas/{id}` | One entry in full: its facts with their sources, relations, use, the agents holding accounts at it, its open signals, and what relies on it (same) |
| `GET` | `/atlas/{id}/trace` | What depends on one entry, or what it depends on, hop by hop (same) |
| `GET` | `/atlas/{id}/log` | One entry's own lines of the log, newest first (same) |
| `GET` | `/atlas/{id}/work` | The open and recently finished Worklet tasks that name one entry, for a caller who also holds `worklet` (same) |
| `GET` | `/gitlet/repos` | The repositories the engine hosts, paged, at the caller's freshness. **Always needs a credential** (see [The code reads](#the-code-reads)) |
| `GET` | `/gitlet/repos/{name}` | One repository in detail (same) |
| `GET` | `/gitlet/repos/{name}/pushes` | One repository's push history, newest first in landing order, each push naming who made it (a person by credential and seat, a seat by its handle and the turn behind its push) and how its pack was built (same) |
| `GET` | `/gitlet/repos/{name}/readers` | Who read a `visibility: unit` repository's contents over a range of company days: every credential and the person it acted as, and every seat, with how often and how many bytes, paged. **An admin's** (see [below](#get-gitletreposnamereaders)) |
| `POST` | `/gitlet/repos/{name}/verify` | Begin a check of this Gitlet node's copy of one repository against its rows, `?repair=true` to repair what it finds (in place, or by a rebuild): `200` with its report where the check ends within a quarter of a second, else `202`, the check running on (see [below](#post-gitletreposnameverify)) |
| `GET` | `/gitlet/repos/{name}/verify/{id}` | A check begun above: running, done with its report, or failed with why and what it found (see [below](#get-gitletreposnameverifyid)) |
| `POST` | `/assistant/proposals/{id}/approve` | Approve one of **your own** Ask Crewlet proposals. A proposal whose turn read through an app you no longer hold is not sent: it settles `failed` with the refusal `access_withdrawn`, and the turn ends. Needs your session cookie and a matching `Origin` only (an assistant grant is refused before routing), `Content-Type: application/json`, the `Idempotency-Key` header, and `{"protocol_version": 3, "digest": "sha256:..."}` echoing the digest the card showed, with an optional `page_context`: the screen you decided from, as it is now, which the resumed turn runs on (the actions it accepts, the draft as the change left it). A turn you asked without a page never gains one this way, and a `page_context` the screen's own rules refuse is `400 invalid_body` before anything is decided. Refusals: `404 not_found` (not yours, or no such proposal), `409 proposal_already_decided` (with its `state`), `410 proposal_expired`, `409 proposal_digest_mismatch` (nothing sent), `409 proposal_stale` (the record moved since it was shown), `403 step_up_required` (nothing recorded; confirm it is you and send the same request again), `503 unavailable` with `"outcome": "unknown"` and the `op_id` to retry under for a decision nobody can confirm, and `503 unavailable` without `outcome` for a condition of the node, which recorded nothing: its `detail` says what happened in a sentence, with a `Retry-After` exactly where waiting clears it. A server write is sent in process as you, once, under the proposal's own operation key, and `202` answers its state (`applied`, `failed` or `unknown`), the turn and where its continuation streams. An `unknown` proposal is retried by approving it again: the same write, never a second one |
| `POST` | `/assistant/proposals/{id}/decline` | Decline one of your proposals: the same body, header and refusals as the approval; nothing is sent, and Ask Crewlet is told. `200` with the proposal's state |
| `PUT` | `/assistant/actions/{id}` | A page claiming (`{"state": "applying"}`), then reporting, a page action you approved (the report may carry `page_context`, the screen as the action left it, read as the approval's is), or a view change (`confirm: none`: a filter, a range, a lens) the turn sent to the page at once, recorded as a proposal it approved itself; the report of a view change settles it and resumes nothing. The claim succeeds once across your tabs; another tab is `409 action_already_claimed`. A claim must name the revision the screen is at for that action (its `action_revisions` entry, else `source_revision`): one whose screen moved since the action was prepared is `409 proposal_stale`, and nothing is applied. The report (`applied`, `stale`, `blocked`, `invalid`, `no_handler`, with the page's `revision`) is the page's own statement, which Ask Crewlet reads as client-reported; its `revision`, `reason` and `receipt` are each one short line, at most 256 bytes, and a longer one is `400 invalid_body`. `Idempotency-Key` is optional: a claim sent again under its key is the same claim |
| `POST` | `/assistant/audit/conversations/{id}/read` | An administrator's **compliance read** of somebody else's Ask Crewlet conversation (`assistant.conversation.audit_read`: admin, a recent proof, a person present, never Ask Crewlet). Body `{"protocol_version": 3, "reason": "..."}`, the reason required, at most 500 characters. The read is recorded first, beside your name and reason, and the conversation's owner is shown it; then `200` answers the transcript and an `assistant_conversation_read` audit record names you, the owner and the reason |
| `POST` | `/assistant/audit/conversations/{id}/files/{file}/read` | The same **compliance read** of one file the conversation keeps, same verb and body: the read is recorded beside the conversation first, the `assistant_conversation_read` audit record names the file as well (`file_id`), and `200` answers the file with every header of [the owner's download](#ask-crewlet). A file the conversation does not keep is `404 not_found`, and the read stays on its record. Absent on a node with no object store |

> **Auth.** Every route needs a credential, reads included. Three shapes reach
> every route: a **session cookie** from signing in (`__Host-crewlet_session` on
> https, `crewlet_session` on plain http; only the name the deployment issues is
> read, since a sibling host can plant the bare name); `Authorization: Bearer`
> with a **Tier A token**, the deployment's machine credential from
> `api.auth.tokens`; and `Authorization: Bearer` with a
> **[machine token](#post-iamcredentials-mints-a-machine-token)** (`cwl_pat_…`),
> a directory member's (person's or service account's) token, acting as its
> owner. The two bearers are told apart by the value's shape, which picks how it
> is checked and admits nothing by itself. All three resolve to the same
> principal. **When a request carries a header and a cookie, the header
> decides**: a browser sends its cookie unasked, so a *wrong* header stays
> anonymous instead of being upgraded by the cookie. `/ws/stream` reads the same
> two: a browser cannot set a header on a WebSocket, so the dashboard sends its
> cookie and any other client sets the header. **No route reads a credential off
> its URL**, the socket included: `?token=…` authenticates nobody (URLs land in
> proxy logs and history). Never guarded: `/health`, `/ready`, `/webhooks/*`,
> `/otlp/*`, `/mcp/*`, `/box/git/*`, `/box/gitlet/*`, the dashboard shell (`/`,
> `/dashboard`, `/dashboard/`, `/favicon.ico`, `/static/*`), and `/auth/config`,
> `/auth/login`, `/auth/logout`, `/auth/invite/*` and `/auth/reset/*` (a login
> cannot require a login). That is an **exact list, not a `/auth/` prefix**: the
> same surface ends sessions and enrols second factors, and a prefix would leave
> those with no credential. See
> [Configuration § Auth](../concepts/configuration.md#auth).
>
> **A git client is answered in git's terms.** On `/git/*` only, the token may
> also arrive as the **password** of `Authorization: Basic` (the user name is
> ignored), because a git client answers a Basic challenge from its credential
> helper or a prompt. Basic is accepted nowhere else: a browser caches it and
> replays it to every route of the origin. A refused git request answers `401`
> with `WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="crewlet",
> charset="UTF-8"` and a `text/plain` body git prints (`authentication
> required: use a Crewlet API token as the password (crewlet gitlet
> credential)` — the helper that answers git's prompt with the token, see
> [`crewlet gitlet credential`](cli.md#crewlet-gitlet-credential)),
> never the JSON below, which git shows as nothing. A git request with no
> credential is the protocol's normal first step, logged at debug as
> `api_auth_challenge`; a credential presented and refused is
> `api_auth_failed`, a warning, as on every route.
>
> **A token that is present and wrong is refused even where reads are open**:
> `/ws/stream` answers `401` rather than serving you as anonymous (which is how
> a revoked token goes on appearing to work). A browser presents only its
> session cookie, so a dashboard whose session ended gets `401` and sends its
> reader to sign in.
>
> **`GET /ws/stream` without an `Upgrade` header** answers `401` for a refused
> credential and `426 Upgrade Required` for an accepted one. This pairing is a
> contract: a browser learns nothing about why a WebSocket handshake failed (no
> status, no close frame), so the dashboard re-asks over plain HTTP to tell
> "nobody is signed in" (sends the reader to sign in) from "the engine is down".
> The same re-ask reads a `503 identity_unavailable` (the node cannot read its
> identity estate yet) and dials again when its `Retry-After` says, and a `409
> reader_changed` (a handshake made for a reader the browser's cookie is no
> longer) and hands the tab to whoever it is.
>
> **`api.auth.admin` clamps a person exactly as it clamps a token.** On a node
> whose posture is `refuse`, every principal composed there loses `admin` and
> keeps every app. The posture is applied when the request is resolved, not
> stored, so a restart that changes it takes effect on the next request,
> including for somebody already signed in.
>
> **A person whose seat is gone is `403 seat_unavailable`, naming the seat**,
> and so is a Tier A token the identity directory binds to one (both bindings
> resolve against the company this node runs). Their credential is valid and
> signing in again changes nothing, so `401` would loop a browser through
> sign-in. `/auth/*` is the exception, since its subject is a person's own
> credential, not their seat: ending a session, re-proving identity and enrolling
> a second factor keep working, so an offboarded person can still sign out.
>
> **The guard is always mounted**, with or without Tier A. An API built without
> `api.auth` configuration has no token, so every guarded route (all but the
> exemptions above) answers `401`. No process serves this surface without a
> guard.
>
> **A cross-site write is refused by its `Origin`** with `403 csrf_origin`,
> whatever credential it carries, or none. The match is `api.external_url`'s own
> origin plus every `api.auth.allowed_origins` entry. Reads are never refused for
> theirs, nor are the server-to-server edges (`/webhooks/*`, `/otlp/*`, `/mcp/*`,
> `/box/git/*`, `/box/gitlet/*`), which carry a credential of their own. The
> sign-in routes are judged like every other write although no credential guards
> them (`POST /auth/login`, `/auth/invite/{id}` and `/auth/reset/{id}`): a
> sign-in posted from another page is how an attacker leaves a victim's browser
> signed in as somebody the attacker controls. See
> [Identity and Access § A cross-site write is refused by its Origin](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#a-cross-site-write-is-refused-by-its-origin).
>
> **A permitted origin may send exactly the request headers the routes read,
> and read exactly the response headers a client acts on.** The preflight
> answers a closed set and never echoes what the browser asked for, so a page on
> an `api.auth.allowed_origins` entry can make every request the dashboard can;
> the browser refuses a request carrying a header the preflight did not allow,
> and hides every response header not exposed:
>
> | Request header a permitted origin may send | Read by |
> |---|---|
> | `Authorization` | the guard: the bearer token |
> | `Content-Type` | every route that takes a body |
> | `Idempotency-Key` | [`/operator/act`](#operatoract--the-dashboards-write-surface), which requires it, and `/worklet`, `/doclet/pages`, `/chatlet` and `/iam`, which make a retry the same write by it |
> | `If-Match`, `If-None-Match` | `/config` and its entities, a work item, a page, a project file, an artifact's publish and `/setup`'s forced disconnect; see [Conditional requests](#conditional-requests) |
> | `X-Summary` | a `/config` write's revision summary |
> | `X-Crewlet-Invite-Secret`, `X-Crewlet-Reset-Secret` | `GET /auth/invite/{id}` and `GET /auth/reset/{id}`: a link's secret, kept out of the URL |
>
> | Response header a permitted origin's script may read | What a client does with it |
> |---|---|
> | `ETag` | writes it back as `If-Match`, or revalidates with it as `If-None-Match` |
> | `Retry-After` | waits that many seconds before asking again |
> | `Accept-Patch` | resends a refused `PATCH /config` in a format it names |
> | `Allow` | uses a method an `OPTIONS` or a `405` lists |
> | `Content-Disposition` | saves a downloaded project file under its name |
> | `Location` | reads a started verification of a Gitlet node's copy (`POST /gitlet/repos/{name}/verify`'s `202`) at [`GET /gitlet/repos/{name}/verify/{id}`](#get-gitletreposnameverifyid) |
>
> `Content-Type`, `Content-Length` and `Cache-Control` are readable unlisted, as
> every CORS-safelisted header is. Not offered: `X-Crewlet-Reader`, which stays
> same-origin (only the dashboard sends it, from this process's origin, to say
> which person a tab was opened for); headers only a browser or proxy sets
> (`Origin`, `Upgrade`, `Accept-Encoding`, `X-Forwarded-For`); the webhook
> routes' vendor headers (no page calls `/webhooks/*`); the MCP transport's
> session headers (`/operator/mcp` and `/mcp/` are reached by programs); and
> `Last-Event-ID`, which [Ask Crewlet's stream](#the-turns-stream) resumes by
> (the stream answers only a person's own browser session and no answer allows
> another origin credentials, so only the dashboard on this origin opens it). A
> gate in `internal/api/auth` fails on any header a route reads or sets that is
> neither offered here nor withheld for a stated reason.
>
> **And it may use every method a route serves**: `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`,
> `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` and `OPTIONS`, the last for `OPTIONS /config`,
> whose `Allow` and `Accept-Patch` say what the document takes. Every method but
> the first three is preflighted, and the preflight names exactly the methods the
> routes are registered with (a gate holds it to them), so an omitted method is
> refused by the browser. See
> [Configuration § Auth](../concepts/configuration.md#auth).
>
> **A request that says who it is for is served only to them.**
> `X-Crewlet-Reader: <principal id>` (the `person` `GET /auth/session` answers)
> names the principal a request is made FOR; the dashboard sends it on every
> request a tab makes. A guarded route serves it only when its credential
> resolves to that principal; anybody else is `409 reader_changed`, written by
> the guard before any handler runs, so nothing is read, written or audited and
> no `Idempotency-Key` is scoped. This stops a window left open beside a sign-in
> as somebody else (whose cookie moved under it) from making or retrying the last
> person's change as the new one; the dashboard hands that tab to the new person.
> It holds under `/auth/*` too, so a **Sign out everywhere** pressed on the last
> person's Account ends nobody's sessions; an unguarded route never reads it. A
> request naming no reader (scripts, assistants, the command line) is decided as
> before, as are nobody (`401`) and a node that cannot tell (`503`): there is no
> principal to hold the name against. The value is compared as an id; one that is
> not an id names nobody the credential is. It is not a credential and widens
> nothing.
>
> **A socket's handshake names its reader in its URL**, since a browser sets no
> header on a WebSocket: `/ws/stream?reader=<principal id>`. The guard reads
> `reader` on a WebSocket upgrade only, and only where the request carries no
> `X-Crewlet-Reader` (on any other request a URL is never a second way to say who
> it is for), and holds it to the credential like the header, so a handshake for
> somebody else is `409 reader_changed` before the stream is served. A browser
> reports that as a bare 1006, so the dashboard reads the `409` off its
> plain-HTTP re-ask of the path (above). The principal id is not a secret (every
> `GET /auth/session` answer carries it) but a proxy's or balancer's access log
> of `/ws/stream` records it; the engine's own logs name the path alone.
>
> **Every `/webhooks/*` route fails closed.** They are exempt from the bearer
> token because each verifies its provider's signature; a route whose secret is
> not configured answers `503` with `Retry-After` rather than accepting the
> delivery. The sender retries and the delivery flows once the secret is set;
> nothing is discarded, and nothing unsigned is ever recorded, published, or
> shown on the dashboard.

Plus the surfaces whose reads are as sensitive as their writes: [`/config/*`](#config--live-config-management-auth-gated), [`/secrets/*`](#secrets--the-companys-credentials-auth-gated), [`/setup/*`](#setting-an-integration-up), `/operator/*` — [`/operator/mcp`](#operatormcp--your-own-assistant) and [`/operator/act`](#operatoract--the-dashboards-write-surface) — and Gitlet's `/git/*` and `/gitlet/*`. Which credentials a company has not configured yet is a map of what to attack, and so is the company's shape. So is a repository, the company's source, which even a clone needs a credential to read, and so are the code reads, which name every repository and who pushed to it.

### Every failed sign-in is one refusal

`POST /auth/login` answers `401 sign_in_refused` for every way it can fail (a login nobody holds, a wrong password, a person suspended, a person removed, a second factor that does not check out), and each spends the same argon2id derivation first.

**Both halves are needed.** Distinct codes would make the equal work pointless, and a missing derivation would make the single code pointless: a miss is verified against a dummy verifier at the same cost as a real one, because otherwise the *absence* of that cost is the answer. Every derivation waits for a slot of the node's verify cap, first come first served; a request that goes away while waiting is answered `503` and counts as no attempt. Nothing is padded: what still separates the arms is the directory read before the derivation, and a stored verifier written at another cost than this build's; see
[Identity and Access](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#a-sign-in-endpoint-is-not-a-roster).

So this surface is not a roster: a caller cannot learn who works here, nor test a list of addresses against it.

The exceptions are specific, and each discloses nothing the caller did not already have:

| Code | Why it is safe to be specific |
|---|---|
| `throttled` | `429` with a `Retry-After`: the seconds until this attempt is admitted. Keyed on the subject **as typed** from the caller's source, never on the source alone nor on what it resolved to, so a name nobody holds climbs the curve like a real one and a stranger learns only that they failed recently from where they are. Keyed on the resolved person it would be an oracle ("this account exists and I can slow it down"), which is why the one curve that is, a second factor's, is reached only past the password |
| `second_factor_required` | Reached only past the first factor, so it discloses nothing to a stranger; without it a client cannot tell "your password is wrong" from "now type your code", which are different screens. `POST /auth/step-up` answers it, a `401`, to a right password with no code from a person who holds a second factor. It is also the `403` a session that may only enrol a second factor meets at `POST /auth/totp` once its person holds one (enrolled since, from another session): a password alone never enrols over a factor; sign in again with it |
| `second_factor_enrolment_required` | A `status` on a successful sign-in, and a `403` from every guarded route but three for the session it opened; reached only past the password. The deployment requires a second factor and this person holds none: the session may read `GET /auth/session`, enrol one at `POST /auth/totp` and re-confirm the password at `POST /auth/step-up`, and sign out at `POST /auth/logout` (no guard stands before it); enrolling replaces it with a whole session. Its own code rather than `step_up_required`, because no fresher password changes the answer |
| `invite_spent` | Read by somebody holding the link, which is evidence it was issued to them. One code for redeemed, withdrawn and expired, and for a secret that is not the link's (same bytes as an id nobody issued), because the remedy is the same and distinguishing them would say "already used" to somebody whose link merely aged out, or reveal which ids exist to somebody guessing secrets |
| `reset_spent` | A password reset link's `410`, for `invite_spent`'s reasons: one code for spent, revoked, expired, a person the reset no longer reaches, and a wrong secret (same bytes as an id nobody issued). Ask an administrator for a new one |

### A failure costs a wait, never a lockout

The sign-in routes are throttled by a **curve**, not a ceiling. Each failure doubles the wait before the next attempt on the same key (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, then 30 seconds, never more), and a correct credential after the wait always succeeds. A wait of up to five seconds is served inside the request; a longer one is `429 throttled` with a `Retry-After` naming it. There is no lockout, because an outsider could cause one: keyed on a login it would shut that person out for as long as anybody kept typing their name.

One key: the login or address **as typed** (an address folded the way the directory folds one), from one source: the client's address as the trusted proxies resolve it, an IPv6 client by its `/64`. It has no allowance, so the first failure already costs a second, and it catches a run at one account. A success clears that pair and nothing else (clearing more was a bypass: anybody holding an account could sign in as themselves between guesses at somebody else's and wipe every record). An attempt still being checked counts as a failure against its pair until it resolves, so concurrent guesses at one account are served one after another along the curve.

**A second factor also climbs the person's own curve.** Otherwise somebody holding a password could guess the six digits from every address they have, each a fresh pair (a `/48` of IPv6 is 65,000 of them, enough to find a code in about an hour). So once the password has proved itself, the code is also decided on a curve keyed on the person the login resolved to, the same 1-to-30-second doubling: every address's wrong codes climb it together, and a wait past five seconds is `429 throttled`. It is keyed on the resolved person only here, because it is reached only past the password. The code that completes the sign-in lifts it, and the wrong code that takes the curve to its ceiling is announced as `iam_second_factor_throttled`, once per climb, because somebody holding that person's password is guessing at their code, and the password is what to rotate.

**No address is ever refused on its own.** A source-only curve is one anybody sharing the address holds shut for everybody else: one stranger's failure every twenty-five seconds, at any name, kept every sign-in from that office or proxy at `429`. So one password tried against many names from one address meets no curve; it is bounded by cost (every name tried is an argon2id derivation under the node's verify cap), by the password floor and blocklist, and shown by the audit trail's per-minute failure count, which names the source. A credential that names nobody (an invitation link) meets no curve, and every refusal of one is still counted.

The window is fifteen minutes, and **each node keeps its own curve**: nothing is written to the coordination store, so a sign-in never waits on a round trip. On a fleet of N nodes serving sign-ins, a guesser spread across all of them by a load balancer is admitted up to N times as often as on one node: still one guess per node every thirty seconds at the ceiling, each an argon2id verification, against a password of at least twelve characters not on the blocklist, with a second factor behind it for a person who holds one. A node holds a pair under a keyed digest, never what was typed. See [identity and access](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#a-failure-costs-a-wait-never-a-lockout)
for why the curve is not shared.

#### A bearer is its own protection

Every guarded route compares the bearer it is handed (a Tier A token, a machine token or a session cookie), and whether it matched is the whole answer. No curve stands in front: a bearer names nobody until compared, so a curve could only be keyed on the address, and a refusal decided on an address is one anybody sharing it holds shut for everybody else, the break-glass Tier A token included. What protects a bearer is its value: 32 bytes of `crypto/rand` in a machine token, an HMAC under the fleet's keyring in a session cookie, and at least 26 characters in a Tier A value, which `crewlet validate` refuses shorter. Every refused bearer on a guarded route still counts as a failed attempt in the audit trail's per-minute count by source, so a spray is seen; it is never answered `429`, however many requests the address has in flight. An unguarded route (`/health`, `/ready`, the dashboard's shell and assets, the webhooks, the sign-in routes) never compares a bearer: the request is anonymous there.

**Every source is the proxy's unless you say otherwise.** Behind a proxy that is not in [`api.trusted_proxies`](../getting-started/configuration.md#tier-a), every caller shares the proxy's address and so one curve per login (a stranger guessing at somebody's login puts that person's own sign-in behind the same wait), and every audit row names the proxy. `crewlet validate` warns when `api.external_url` is `https` and no proxy is trusted, and every node start logs the same warning as `config_advisory`, because the engine never terminates TLS itself.

### Which permission a route needs

Holding a credential is not the same as being allowed to use it here. Every route and socket question declares who may ask it: **everybody**, one of the [permissions](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#access-admin-and-one-permission-per-app) (`admin`, `worklet`, `doclet`, `artifacts`, `chatlet`, `gitlet`, `atlas`), or a verb of the authority table that the answer decides record by record. A principal that does not carry what it declares is refused, a Tier A token included, whose declared permissions are read through the node's `api.auth.admin` posture on every request.

**`403`, not `401`**: `401` means *present a credential*, `403` means *the one you presented does not carry what this needs*. A person using one app meets the second on opening a screen of the other, so it must not tell them to go and get a new credential.

**A `403` says which rule refused, and what would have admitted you.** Beside `"error": "unauthorized"` it carries two detail fields wherever the authority table made the refusal: every question, the policy every `/config/*` and `/iam/*` route is mounted with, and the snapshot mirrors. The code is the table's own mapping on every surface, the WebSocket's frames included: `unauthorized`, `step_up_required` for a stale proof, `token_refused` for a machine token where a person must be present. No route spells one of those codes itself:

```json
{
  "error": "unauthorized",
  "message": "…",
  "reason": "no_grant",
  "grants": ["worklet"]
}
```

`reason` is the authority table's word for the deciding rule: `no_grant`, `not_self`, `not_lead`, `not_author`, `stage`, `seat_refused`, `seat_only` (a person or token asking for a verb only an agent seat takes), `unseated` (a credential the identity directory binds to no seat asking for a verb made as one; bind it to a human seat, `crewlet iam bind`), `token_refused` (a [machine token](#post-iamcredentials-mints-a-machine-token) on a gesture that needs a person present, answered under the code `token_refused` rather than `unauthorized`), `assist_refused` and `assist_scope` (a request Ask Crewlet made on a verb its row keeps from it, or a write through a read grant: see
[Every row says what Ask Crewlet may do with it](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#every-row-says-what-ask-crewlet-may-do-with-it)), `unnamed`, and `step_up` on the one refusal the caller clears themselves ([below](#some-gestures-ask-how-recently-you-proved-who-you-are)). `grants` are the **least** that would have admitted this caller for this object: any **one** of them, added to what the caller holds, would. A Worklet row names `["worklet"]`, a relation the caller does not hold names `["admin"]`, a lead missing the app names the app, and a question either app answers names both. An empty `grants` is an answer, not an omission: no permission would (a seat-only verb, a verb made as a seat asked by a credential bound to none, or a relation the org chart does not hold). The [human write surface](#the-human-write-surface) answers its own refusals `403 forbidden` in its tools' wording instead.

The `message` follows the `reason` and names a permission only where one is the remedy. `no_grant` names the permissions in `grants` ("You don't have the access this needs (Worklet)"); a refused relation (`not_self`, `not_lead`, `not_author` or `unnamed`) says what the rule asked and names `grants` as what would admit you anyway, or says no access would. Every other reason says what clears it, whatever `grants` holds: `role`, a share of an artifact below the role the verb asks (every route answering it names `role`, the role to ask the owner for), that its owner can share it with you at a higher one (the admin path admits whatever the shares say, but the share is what to ask for); `unseated`, a credential bound to a human seat (`crewlet iam bind`); `stage`, an account an admin activates (`crewlet iam activate`); `seat_refused` and `seat_only`, that the verb is a person's or an agent's; `ceiling`, that the person an agent is working for could not do it either; `assist_refused`, that Ask Crewlet never takes the gesture, which stays with you; `assist_scope`, that Ask Crewlet makes the change only as one you approve. (`step_up` and `token_refused` are answered under codes of their own, whose messages say what clears them: a fresh proof of who you are, signing in as yourself. `not_shared` is never seen: an artifact nothing relates you to is `404 not_found`.) A refusal with no `reason` gets the code's own sentence, which names every permission there is.

A request the node **cannot decide** (it holds no company yet) is `503 unavailable` with a `Retry-After`, never a `403`: a lead told they lead nobody goes looking for an authority they already hold.

| Needs | What it reaches |
|---|---|
| **everybody** | The [overview](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#everybodys-overview), for every principal the guard resolved whose stage may act: `/agents`, `/agents/activity` and the `agent` and `live_call` questions (an agent's **status**, with its **body** to an administrator and to whoever leads the seat, [below](#a-status-reader-never-receives-a-transcript)), `/org`, `/tools`, `/schedules` and their runs, `/budgets`, `/executors` (status; same body rule), `/tokens/*`, `/viewer`, `/stream/snapshot`, `/ws/stream`, `GET /iam/seats` (masked per reader), `/mcp-servers`, `/mcp-servers/{name}` and `/mcp-catalogue` in [a member's reading](#a-members-reading-of-mcp--tools), the `seat_activity` and `colleague` questions, and the cross-app answers filtered row by row: `/feed`, `decisions`, `answered_decisions` and the `knowledge` question |
| `worklet` | The reads under `/worklet/*`, the [write surface's](#the-human-write-surface) item routes, a project's files (`GET`/`PUT /worklet/files/…`; removing one is the project lead's), every `work_*` question, the inbox's tracker half and the socket's `inbox_changed` push for it, and `/operator/mcp`'s Worklet half. Some verbs also ask a RELATION: re-routing, a project's policy and taking an item out of circulation are its project lead's; a person's inbox, queue and person view are their own and their lead's |
| `doclet` | The reads under `/doclet/pages/*` and `/containers`, the page questions, and writing Doclet's pages. A rename, the trash and a restore are also the container's lead's or the page's creator's; see [the write surface](#the-human-write-surface) |
| `chatlet` | The reads under `/chatlet/*`, every `chat_*` question, the socket's eight `chat_*` pushes, and the chat tools of `/operator/mcp` and `/operator/act`, each made **as a seat**, so a principal acting as itself is refused them `unseated` whatever else it holds; which room it reaches is the chat domain's own rule, not a permission (see [Chatlet](#chatlet)). A room's horizon, an erase and a prune are `admin`'s instead, with a recent proof; see [A chat erase, prune or horizon](#a-chat-erase-prune-or-horizon) |
| `gitlet` | Every door to the company's code ([ADR-0110](../../adr/0110-reaching-a-repository-takes-the-gitlet-permission.md)): git under `/git/`, the reads under `/gitlet/*` and every `code_*` question but who read a repository and the Gitlet nodes' cache report, the inbox's code half, `code_mark_inbox`, `code_mark_viewed` and the socket's `inbox_changed` push for that half, a turn's `code_change` origin, and the code tools of `/operator/mcp` and `/operator/act`. A principal without it is refused `403 unauthorized` naming `gitlet` before any repository is read. Behind it, WHICH repository and what on it is the repository's grant ([Gitlet](#gitlet-git-and-gitlet)): a person maintains every one, a credential bound to no seat reads every one and pushes none. Who read a repository (`GET /gitlet/repos/{name}/readers`, `code_repo_readers`), a verify (`/gitlet/repos/{name}/verify`) and `code_status` are `admin`'s instead |
| `admin` | Running the company and the engine, and **host access**, conferred like it: the configuration it writes runs commands on every engine host (an `mcp_servers` entry, a seat's `mcp_env`, a `providers.llm` model (a harness the host runs) and a `direct` cell, an entry's `run_in` or `providers.sandbox.default_run_in`, which runs agent seats' executors there as fully permissioned harnesses), so a holder can run anything there and read whatever a process there can, the keyring included (see [Identity and Access](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#what-admin-runs)). Every route under `/config*` (the org chart's leads may also read and write what is inside the units they lead: [A lead edits their own team](#a-lead-edits-their-own-team)), `/integrations`, the administrator's reading of `/mcp-servers`, `/mcp-servers/{name}` and `/mcp-catalogue` and a restart (`POST /mcp-servers/{name}/retry`), `/setup`, every `/secrets` route, every `/iam/*` route about anybody but the caller, the deployment's own controls (`/fleet`, `/fleet/broker*`, every `/worklet/retention*` route, `/feeds/dead-letters*`, `/backup`, `/backups`), the company-wide trail (`/events*`, the socket's `event` push and the snapshot's `events` section, the turn, phase, trace and A2A-channel questions, `/iam/audit`, `/artifacts/trail`), a seat's resolved model chain and tool sources on `/org`, the workspace catalogue's writes, a page in the tool-skills container, the artifacts' quota counters (`GET /artifacts/usage`), the three purges (`/worklet/items/{key}/purge`, `/doclet/pages/{id}/purge`, `/artifacts/{id}/purge`) and chat's three destructions (`/chatlet/channels/{channel_id}/erase`, `/prune` and `/retention`). It **includes every app**, and it is the **admin path** of every relation rule: a holder is admitted where a lead or an owner would be |
| `audit.seat.read` | One seat's own trail: `/agents/{id}/memory`, `/agents/{id}/memory/episodes/{episode}`, `memory_overview` (filtered to the seats the caller may read), `turns?seat=` and `phases?seat=`, an executor's tail (`/executors/{turn_id}/tail`), and the seat's executor sessions with each one's transcript (`/agents/{id}/sessions`, `/agents/{id}/sessions/{turn_id}`). Decided per seat: **its lead**, or `admin` |

A question asked on the socket is decided by the same declaration as the REST route (one registry, both transports), so a channel is no way round a permission.

### A status reader never receives a transcript

Everybody sees what the agents are doing; only some read what they *said*. An
agent's and an executor's answers split into a **status** half and a **body**
half — on the `agent` and `live_call` questions, the `agents`, `snapshot` and
`executors` pushes and their mirrors (`/agents`, `/stream/snapshot`), and
`executors` — and the body goes only to an administrator, to whoever leads
that seat (`audit.seat.read`), and, for an executor's parked question, to the
person it is put to. The body is a call's `trigger`, `prompt`,
`prompt_messages`, `response`, `tool_executions` with its `calls_elided` and
`elided_calls`, `round_narration`,
`partial_round` and the `arguments` of each `running_calls` entry, an `llm_history` entry's
`payload`, and an executor's `task_description`, `question`,
`question_context`, `decision`, `held_call`, `held_arguments`, `reply`, `bridge_calls` and `bridge_elided_calls` (`held_call` also
to the person the question is put to, `held_arguments` never). A status reader receives the rest with **`body_withheld:
true`** and the body's version counters at zero, so a client never marks the
call stale and asks for a body it will not be sent. A work item a call or a
turn names (`work_item`, an `llm_history` entry's `work_item` and `task_id`
tags) is Worklet's, and is left out for a reader without `worklet`.

### Some gestures ask how recently you proved who you are

A session lives for days, so the gestures that change what a company *is* ask
for a recent proof of identity: the **step-up**. The same authority-table row
decides it as the permission, so a REST route and a socket question about one
verb cannot disagree. It is asked only **after** the permission or relation
admitted you: a caller who could never make the gesture is told what they lack.

| Window | Setting (default) | What asks for it |
|---|---|---|
| `step_up` | `sign_in.step_up_seconds` (1 hour) | Every write under `/config*` (a [dry run](#dry-runs) excepted), `/setup`'s writes, `PUT`/`DELETE /secrets/{name}`, `POST /secrets/rekey` and revealing a value (`GET /secrets/{name}?reveal=true`, `POST /secrets/reveal`), the deployment's own controls (`POST /backup`, `POST /objects/migrate`, every `POST /worklet/retention*`, both `POST /fleet/broker/remove*` and `POST /feeds/dead-letters/{id}/discard`), the three purges (`POST /worklet/items/{key}/purge`, `POST /doclet/pages/{id}/purge`, `POST /artifacts/{id}/purge`), chat's three destructions (`POST /chatlet/channels/{channel_id}/erase` and `/prune`, `PUT /chatlet/channels/{channel_id}/retention`), and every `/iam` write: `POST /iam/people`, `PATCH /iam/people/{id}`, `DELETE /iam/people/{id}`, `POST /iam/invitations`, `DELETE /iam/invitations/{id}`, `POST /iam/people/{id}/mfa/reset`, `POST /iam/people/{id}/password-reset`, `POST /iam/credentials`, `DELETE /iam/credentials/{id}`, ending somebody else's sessions and `POST /iam/invalidate-all`; and your own `POST /auth/totp` and `POST /auth/totp/recovery` |
| none | | Every read (including `GET /worklet/retention/maintenance`, `GET /worklet/retention/reanchor`, `GET /feeds/dead-letters`); ending your own sessions (`DELETE /iam/people/{id}/sessions` naming yourself; an administrator ending somebody else's asks `step_up`); changing your own password (`POST /auth/password`), whose current password (and code, if you hold a second factor) is the proof; and every work, knowledge, artifact and chat verb but the three purges and chat's three destructions: the tools, `/operator/mcp`, `/operator/act` and the rest of the human write surface |

A proof that is too old is **`403 step_up_required`**, the code the sign-in
surface answers for the same fact, carrying the window so a client can ask the
person to confirm and resend the same request via `POST /auth/step-up` (password
and second factor):

```json
{
  "error": "step_up_required",
  "message": "…",
  "reason": "step_up",
  "window": "step_up",
  "grants": ["admin"]
}
```

The step-up **replaces** the session it was made from, ending it first and
keeping its absolute deadline.

`window` is spelled as the setting that sizes it, and there is ONE window over
every sensitive gesture (GitHub's sudo-mode practice, at its stricter end).
`GET /auth/session` answers the deadline the table judges against (`reauth_at`)
and whether it is already due (`step_up_due`), so a screen can say so before
somebody submits.

**A request is judged at the instant it arrived.** Every check one request
makes (its route's, whatever the handler decides after reading the body, such
as each part of a `/config` write or `?reveal=true` on a secret, and every tool
a route calls for it, as the [human write surface](#the-human-write-surface)'s
routes do) uses that instant, so a proof fresh on arrival never lapses
half-way through.
