**A credential with nobody at a keyboard is fresh by construction**: a Tier A
token (and a session exchanged from one), the development principal, and a
personal access or service token. They can present nothing else, and the
break-glass credential must reach a step-up gesture on the day nobody can sign
in as a person. What keeps a machine token off gestures needing a person is
neither the clock nor a permission it cannot carry (a token may be minted with
`admin`) but two locks.

1. Every row that needs a person says so, and a request presenting a machine
   token is refused there `403 token_refused` with `reason:
   token_refused` and no `grants`, since no permission would change it.
   Its `message` says a token cannot do this and its owner must, signed in (`unauthorized`'s is about a
   missing permission). The rows: revealing a secret; every `/iam/*` write that
   changes who may do anything; ending every session in the company; changing
   how somebody proves who they are (`POST /auth/totp`,
   `POST /auth/totp/recovery`, and revoking a password, a second factor or the
   recovery codes through `DELETE /iam/credentials/{id}`); an artifact's forced
   publish, transfer and purge; and, about anybody but the token's own owner,
   minting or revoking a token and ending sessions. A token may still revoke
   its owner's tokens, itself included, and end its owner's sessions, which ends
   it too: what somebody who finds one leaked reaches for.
2. The identity domain refuses every administrative record (an enrolment, an
   invitation, an edit of somebody's row, a suspension, a removal, ending
   everybody's sessions) written through a machine token, `403 token_refused`,
   whatever the token carries, at the record, so a CLI or a duty is held to it
   as a route is.

`POST /auth/step-up` refuses a token itself: there is nobody to confirm. No tool
a seat may take asks for a proof, since a seat has no keyboard; the one
human-only tool that does, `code_purge_unreachable`, never asks it of a token.

**A node that cannot read identity answers `503`, never `403`.** The principal a
node could not check and the principal that carries nothing are the same empty
value, and reporting the first as the second tells everybody with a good
credential that theirs is invalid for the whole outage. So an unreadable
identity estate is `503 identity_unavailable` with a `Retry-After`; only a
credential this node positively checked and refused is a `401` or `403`.

### A path is taken as it was sent, or refused

A request path with a `.` or `..` segment, or an empty one (`//`), spelled out
or percent-encoded (`%2e%2e`), is refused `400 non_canonical_path` before
anything reads it, not cleaned and redirected: the credential exemption and the
handler are both chosen from the path, and a path reading as `/webhooks/…` to
one and `/config` to the other is what an authority gate must never face. Send
the path it resolves to.

### Security headers on every response

Every response the API writes carries four headers, set before its status line
(a `304` carries them too):

| Header | Value |
|---|---|
| `Content-Security-Policy` | The policy for what the response is (below) |
| `X-Frame-Options` | `DENY` |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `no-referrer` |

| Response | `Content-Security-Policy` |
|---|---|
| The dashboard shell (`/dashboard`), `/favicon.ico` and every `/static/*` asset | `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data: blob:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self' https:; require-trusted-types-for 'script'; trusted-types 'none'` (Trusted Types enforced with no policy, since the dashboard writes no markup or script sink), then `frame-src` naming the artifact origin on a deployment that serves artifacts |
| The landing pages [`/webhooks/github-app`](#get-webhooksgithub-app), [`/webhooks/slack-oauth`](#get-webhooksslack-oauth) and [`/webhooks/mcp-oauth`](#get-webhooksmcp-oauth) | `default-src 'none'; img-src data:` (a page's mark is inlined, since `/static/` is not served on the [public listener](#which-listener-serves-what) these pages move to), then `style-src` and `script-src` naming the `sha256` hash of each page's own inline block (`'none'` where a page has none), then `base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'` |
| Everything else: JSON, plain text, the redirect from `/`, a `404` or a `401` | `default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'` |

A script on this origin acts with the signed-in person's session (the cookie is
`HttpOnly`, but every request carries it), and the landing pages are
unauthenticated pages on that origin rendering query-string values. So each
response carries its own policy: the dashboard runs only its built bundle, a
landing page only the style and script the engine wrote into it, and no response
may be framed by another site.

`form-action` on the dashboard allows `https:` as well as `'self'` for one flow: creating a seat's
GitHub App posts the app manifest as a form to the code host (`github.com` or
the configured GitHub Enterprise Server base). A reverse proxy should pass these
headers through unchanged; one adding its own `Content-Security-Policy` produces
two policies, and a browser enforces both.

**Some answers also carry `Cache-Control: no-store`**: every response under
`/config` (the whole company document); a `/secrets` reveal's value; and
**every response under `/auth`**, refusals and redirects included: the request
guard's own (`401 invalid_token`, `403
second_factor_enrolment_required`, `503 identity_unavailable`), the origin
check's `403`, the router's `404` and `405`, and every route's. Those hold a second-factor seed and its `otpauth://`
URI, recovery codes shown once, who the caller is, an invitation's address, and
every sign-in's `Set-Cookie`. The guard sets it for the whole prefix before
anything beneath writes, so a newly mounted route is covered. Without it a
browser's disk cache, or a shared proxy for everybody behind it, keeps those
past the tab, the session and the step-up. It is `no-store` because `private`
still lets the browser keep it and `no-cache` only revalidates what was kept.

**An answer read by object id is kept under who it is for.** An answer whose
bytes are a function of what its request named (a repository's content read by
whole object ids) is sent with a strong `ETag`,
`Cache-Control: private, max-age=31536000, immutable` and
`Vary: Authorization, X-Crewlet-Reader` only to a request that names who it is
for: a bearer in `Authorization`, or the reader a dashboard tab names on every
request for its person (`X-Crewlet-Reader`), which the request guard holds to
the session it rides beside. The browser keys it on that bearer or reader, **not**
the session cookie, which the engine re-issues every five minutes of use (the
key would stop matching and every kept page would be asked for again). Signing
in, a re-issue, and the session a step-up, a second factor's enrolment or a
password change opens leave the browser's cache alone. So does any answer to a
request presenting a cookie the engine no longer accepts (ended, expired or
never valid): that answer deletes the cookie and nothing else, on every route,
the dashboard's own files and `/health` included.

**A request that names nobody is kept by no cache.** A tab that opened an API
route itself presents its cookie alone, and a browser keys a kept answer on the
headers `Vary` names, so the answer would be kept under one key for the next
person to sign in on that browser. Not every person reads the company's code
(one without the Gitlet permission is answered none of it,
[ADR-0110](../../adr/0110-reaching-a-repository-takes-the-gitlet-permission.md)),
so such a request is answered the same body with `Cache-Control: no-store` and
no `ETag`.

**Signing out empties the browser's cache.** `POST /auth/logout`,
`POST /auth/logout/all`, and `POST /auth/logout/{lineage}` when it ends the
session the browser holds, carry `Clear-Site-Data: "cache"` beside the cookies
they clear, so what a named reader kept is emptied. A browser honours it only in
a secure context (https, or a loopback address) and where it implements the
directive (Firefox again from 138, after dropping it from 94); a reverse proxy
should pass it through unchanged. Chrome holds the sign-out's answer while it
empties the cache, longer for a larger cache. Where it is not honoured, a kept
answer stays until eviction, under its reader's key. The dashboard's own files
are fetched again once after a sign-out.

Read-side handlers live in the `internal/api` package (one module per domain:
`agents`, `events`, `tokens`, `org`, `fleet`, `mcpstatus`, `executors`,
`budgets`, `integrations`, `webhooks`, `dashboard`, `health`); `webhooks` and
`/config/*` keep a stable external contract, while the read/stream surface may
evolve since the dashboard is its only consumer.

### `/iam/*` — the company's people, credentials and sessions (auth-gated)

**Always guarded, reads included**: a map of who can reach a company and how is
worth as much to an attacker as the permissions. Nothing under `/iam` is on the
exemption list and nothing ever will be.

| Route | Who |
|---|---|
| `GET /iam/people` | `admin` |
| `POST /iam/people` | `admin` |
| `GET /iam/people/{id}` | the person themselves, or `admin` |
| `PATCH /iam/people/{id}` | `admin` |
| `DELETE /iam/people/{id}` | `admin` |
| `POST /iam/invitations` | `admin` |
| `GET /iam/invitations[?all=true]` | `admin` |
| `DELETE /iam/invitations/{id}` | `admin` |
| `GET /iam/people/{id}/sessions` | the person themselves, or `admin` |
| `DELETE /iam/people/{id}/sessions` | the person themselves, or `admin` |
| `POST /iam/people/{id}/mfa/reset` | `admin` |
| `POST /iam/people/{id}/password-reset` | `admin`, for somebody holding no permission the caller does not |
| `GET /iam/credentials[?person=]` | the person themselves, or `admin` |
| `POST /iam/credentials[?person=]` | the person themselves, from their own session; `admin` for a **service account** only; never a request presenting a machine token |
| `DELETE /iam/credentials/{id}[?person=]` | the person themselves, or `admin`; revoking a password, a second factor or the recovery codes needs a person present, so a machine token revokes machine tokens only (`403 token_refused`, nothing written, whether or not the node had listed the credential before). Revoking a person's **last** authenticator app revokes their recovery codes in the same record, each announced, because codes alone are a second factor every sign-in would ask for with only those single-use answers |
| `POST /iam/invalidate-all` | `admin`, a person present and a recent proof (the record layer refuses a machine token too). Ends every session **and every machine token** |
| `GET /iam/seats[?unheld=true]` | **everybody**: each holder's name and kind to every reader, their person id, login and stage to an administrator and the holder themselves, and the open invitations and `?unheld=true` to an administrator alone (`403` naming `["admin"]` otherwise) |
| `GET /iam/check` | `admin` |
| `GET /iam/node-tokens` | `admin` |
| `GET /iam/audit` | `admin` |

**Every write here asks for a recent proof**, inside `step_up` (an hour by
default); see
[Some gestures ask how recently you proved who you are](#some-gestures-ask-how-recently-you-proved-who-you-are).
Ending sessions differs by arm: ending your own asks for none, because it is the
first thing to do on finding an intruder (and it ends every machine token you
hold too); an administrator ending somebody else's asks `step_up`.

**The object a route names is a person ID, never a login.** The estate keys on
an id because a person changes their login; a self check against a mutable name
would open somebody else's row the day they swapped.

**Editing your own row is not a self gesture.** `PATCH /iam/people/{id}` has no
self path at all, since changing your own permissions is the escalation this
estate closes (the credential mint and session end are the two gestures a
person legitimately makes about themselves). The record layer refuses it again:
a caller may not confer a permission they do not hold, on anybody, themselves
included, on an edit, a `POST /iam/people` enrolment and a
`POST /iam/invitations` alike, each `403` naming the permission. Judged through
`iam.Expand`, so an administrator may confer every app.

**An administrative record is never written through a machine token.** An
enrolment, an invitation, an edit of somebody's row, a suspension, a removal, a
reset link and `POST /iam/invalidate-all` are refused `403 token_refused` when
the request presented a `pat:` token, whatever it carries, by the authority
table's row and again by the identity record itself, so the CLI and every other
path publishing a record is held to it.

**A listing says what still works.** A session's `live` and a credential's
`revoked` are the request guard's reading: a session or machine token ended by
its person's revocation epoch (a password change, signing out everywhere, an
administrator ending their sessions, a suspension) or by
`POST /iam/invalidate-all` is listed ended, and a named sign-out of a session
listed live finds it live. A session keeps the `ended_reason` and `ended_at` of
whatever ended it: a revocation writes its own on every session it ends and a
later one never rewrites them. `POST /iam/invalidate-all` writes nothing per
session, so it lists its sessions ended "with every session in the company" and
no `ended_at`; neither counter writes a `revoked_at` on a token. A session a
revocation had already ended when its start landed is listed ended "with every
session they held", no `ended_at`, and no later revocation claims it.

#### Every write answers three ways

| Outcome | Status | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `applied` | `200` (`201` on the four routes that hand back what they created: `POST /iam/people`, `POST /iam/invitations`, `POST /iam/credentials`, `POST /iam/people/{id}/password-reset`) | This node has the change; the next read *here* sees it |
| `pending` | `202` with the position | The record is durable and every data node will apply it; this one has not yet, so read at that position to see it |
| `unknown` | `503` with a `Retry-After`, `"outcome": "unknown"` and the op id | The only safe retry is the **same** one: send the op id back as `Idempotency-Key`, since a fresh id would defeat the ledger that makes the retry safe |

Every body carries its `outcome` and `op_id`.

**Nothing is built on, handed out or announced for an `unknown`.** A removal, a
revocation, a second-factor reset or a withdrawn credential announces its event
only once the record is durable; an invitation with an unknown outcome hands out
no link, a person's create no first password link and a mint no token, each
being a value that would answer `410` or `401` on first use. A write this node
refused to decide at all (behind, below the trim floor, or holding a record it
cannot decode) is `503 unavailable` with the op id. It has a `Retry-After` only
where waiting clears it: a node behind or below the floor carries the identity
estate's two seconds; one that is evicted or holds an undecodable record, a log
at its byte ceiling, a record larger than the broker takes and a refusal the
broker named carry **none**, since the same request is refused the same however
often sent, as on `/worklet`. `/auth` follows the same rule on every write. On
both, a write whose snapshot kept moving until the framework gave up is
`409 stale`, as on `/worklet`: nothing was wrong with the request or node, so it
carries no `Retry-After` and the same request sent again decides afresh and
lands. An edit (of a person here, or of your own account on `/auth`: a password
change, a second factor, recovery codes, a sign-out) is told in the words every
surface tells a lost race in, asking you to look at it again first. A gesture on
`/auth` that edits nothing you can look at (a sign-in, a step-up, a token
exchange, an invitation's redemption, a reset link's spend) is told only to try
again.

**A gesture that is several records answers its weakest.** An edit moving a
login and a stage, and a reset followed by its revocation, are sequences: a step
answered `unknown` ends the sequence there (nothing after it is published over a
guess), and a step still `pending` here makes the whole answer `202`. A create
is one record, its seat and a person's first password link included.

A request **without** an `Idempotency-Key` is a new operation every time, with
an op id of its own (two different edits of one person, a second "end every
session" or a second company-wide invalidation are two operations; an op id
derived from the object alone made the broker collapse the second into the
first, acknowledged and never applied). Send a key when you mean a retry, and
only then.

**A create is named by its key.** `POST /iam/people` derives the person it
creates, and `POST /iam/invitations` the invitation it issues, from the
operation's key: the `Idempotency-Key` when sent, otherwise one minted for the
request and answered as `op_id`. So the retry an `unknown` asks for names what
its first attempt may have created: a person that attempt created is answered
from the ledger as applied, and an invitation that landed is answered with its
own link and the deadline it was issued with. The invitation's id and its link's
secret are derived under the company's own key (id from the operation key,
secret from the id), so the retry hands back the very link the first attempt
issued, and an operation key is never a way to compute one. A person's **first
password link** is derived the same way, from the person under the company's
key, so the retry hands back that link with the expiry it stored, or, where it
no longer opens (spent, revoked or aged out), no `url` and a `detail` saying to
issue a [password reset link](#post-iampeopleidpassword-reset-issues-a-one-time-link)
instead. A retry reaching a node that has not applied the create finds the
person or invitation absent there and answers `503
unavailable` with the write's own `outcome` (`pending` or `applied`, never `unknown`), the `op_id`, a person's
`id`, a `Retry-After` and a `detail` saying what landed: send the same request
again under the same key to be handed the link. A new key is a new create,
refused by the address and seat the first now holds. Because the key names what
a create creates, it is a **uuid7**, as every `op_id` is; anything else is
`400 op_id_invalid` naming the header. The same key with a *different* body
(another address, login or grants) is `409 invalid_input` naming
`Idempotency-Key` as its `field` and carrying the `op_id`, as on every surface
taking a key; so is the key of an invitation since redeemed or aged out: a retry
is the same request, and a new person or link is a new key.

An address, login or seat somebody else holds is `409 invalid` **naming who
holds it**: `field` says which value, `held_by` is the holder's id, and `detail`
names them by login. An **open invitation** holds its address and seat as surely
as a person, so a value one holds is the same `409 invalid` naming the
`invitation` instead (the id `DELETE /iam/invitations/{id}` takes), its `detail`
saying to cancel the invitation first or let it lapse. A seat is named in the
`detail` (a handle is no secret); an address never is, since the estate holds it
only as a blind.

**A person holds a human seat for as long as they are here.** A person's create
or an invitation naming no seat, or an edit that would clear a person's seat, is
`400 seat_required` with `field: seat`, its own code because the remedy is
always that field. A seat the company this node runs does not hold, or holds as
an agent's, is `400 invalid_body` (every binding, a service account's too, names
a **human** seat). A seat named on a node that runs no company yet is
`409 no_active_revision` with a `hint`, as `GET /iam/seats` is there: no wait
supplies a company, so it is not the `503` a retry clears.

A refusal on authority is `403`, never lands however often retried, and its code
says what would change it.

- A permission would lift it (a record only `admin` writes, a permission the
  caller cannot confer because they do not hold it): `403 unauthorized` with
  `reason: no_grant` and the `grants` that would lift it.
- The directory's own rule makes it whatever the caller holds (a person's token
  asked for by anybody but that person, a permission the owner does not hold, an
  owner who may not act, a permission this build does not know on the person's
  row): `403 forbidden`, the rule's sentence in `detail`, no `reason` or
  `grants`.
- A request through a machine token: `403 token_refused`.

Other `400`s:

- A login outside its holder's kind: a person's is dotted (`jane.doe`), a
  machine's is coloned (`ci:release`, or `token:<id>` to bind a Tier A token),
  at most 64 characters either way, checked on create and rename. **Every
  principal holds a login** (what a person signs in with, the name a lead finds
  them by, the `by jane.doe` in every trail reason, and the only thing that
  finds a service account), so a service account's create without one is `400`,
  and a person's create without one takes the login proposed from their address,
  as an invitation's form does (`jane.doe@example.com` → `jane.doe`).
- A `kind` other than `person` or `machine`, since a seat belongs to the company
  document and the engine is the node.
- A `reason` longer than 256 bytes (it is rendered into the authentication
  trail beside the op, so it names which cause fired rather than narrating), and
  a permission this build does not know, **added** (by a create, an invitation,
  `add_grants` or a whole-set `grants` naming one the row does not already
  carry), refused naming the six; one already on the row is kept, and
  `remove_grants` may name it.

A write's `reason` is optional; without one the record says what was done and by
whose login, in words (`suspended by
jane.doe`, `every session ended by jane.doe`, `invited by jane.doe`), which is the trail's detail and, for a
suspension or ending somebody's sessions, what each ended session is listed as
ended by. An enrolment is one record, so a refused create leaves nothing behind
and the corrected retry lands.

#### `POST /iam/people` creates a person on their seat, or a service account

```json
{
  "id": "0192f00d-…",
  "kind": "person",
  "login": "sam.lee",
  "seat": "qa-lead",
  "credential": "0192f00e-…",
  "url": "https://crewlet.example.com/dashboard#/reset/<id>.<secret>",
  "expires_at": "2026-06-15T09:12:00Z",
  "detail": "This link is shown only once. Send it to them yourself (Crewlet doesn't send email). It expires at the time above.",
  "outcome": "applied",
  "op_id": "0192f00c-…",
  "position": "CREWLET_IAM_LOG@0:1842"
}
```

The body is `{kind, email, seat, login, name, grants, reason}`, and `kind`
defaults to `person`. `email`, `seat` and `login` are trimmed before judging.
**`grants` is required**, for a person and a service account alike (any of
`admin`, `worklet`, `doclet`, `artifacts`, `chatlet` and `gitlet`, and `[]` for
the [overview](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#everybodys-overview) alone). An
omitted field is `400 invalid_body` naming `grants`, decided before any key is
read or link minted, since a body naming neither every app nor none is one whose
author did not decide. A name this build does not know is the same `400`,
naming the six. The whole create is **one record**, which the directory decides
against every row (address, login and seat together), so a refused create has
created nobody and issued nothing.

**A person is created onto their seat.** `seat` is **required**: a human seat no
person and no open invitation holds, by its handle (`GET /iam/seats?unheld=true`
lists them). Left out, it is `400 seat_required` naming `field: seat`, before
any key is read or anything minted. `email` is required too: it is what they
sign in with. `login` may be left out; the create takes the one proposed from
the address (`jane.doe@example.com` → `jane.doe`, `jane@example.com` →
`jane.example`) and answers it as `login`; an address with nothing to propose
from is `400 invalid_body` naming `field: login`. A created person is `active`
from the moment the create lands: an administrator creating them **is** their
enrolment, and what they lack is a password.

**And handed their first password link.** The same record issues it, and the
`201` carries it once (`credential`, `url` and `expires_at`) with a `detail`
saying so. The `url` is the dashboard's reset screen,
`<api.external_url>/dashboard#/reset/<id>.<secret>` with the `credential` as its
id, and its view (`GET /auth/reset/{id}`) answers `first: true` so it asks the
person to choose their password. Spent through `POST /auth/reset/{id}`, it sets
that password **once** and signs nobody in: they sign in afterwards, and enrol a
second factor there where the company requires one. It is good for **a week**
(an invitation's week, being the same person's position) and is a `reset`
credential like any other: listed among their credentials, replaced by a
[password reset link](#post-iampeopleidpassword-reset-issues-a-one-time-link)
issued later, and ended by whatever ends one (an edit adding a permission to
them, a suspension, their sessions ended, `POST /iam/invalidate-all`). Send it
yourself: this engine sends no mail. Its issue is one
`iam_password_reset_issued` event with `first: true` (for whom, by whom, until
when, never the link), published by the call whose record carried it and by no
retry. So a person's create needs `api.external_url`; a node with none answers
`500 no_external_url` with nothing created. A service account's does not.

**A service account** (`kind: machine`) needs a `login` (coloned, `svc:ci`, or
`token:<id>` to bind a Tier A token) because it has no address to be found or
proposed by; `email` is optional. Its `seat` is optional: one given binds it to
act as that seat and must be a human seat no person and no open invitation
holds, as a person's must. It gets no link (it has no password) and proves
itself with a token minted on it, `POST /iam/credentials?person=<id>`.

**A retry hands back the same link.** The person is derived from the operation's
key and the link from the person under the company's key, so the retry an
`unknown` asks for (the same body under the `op_id` it handed back) answers the
link the first attempt issued, with the expiry that attempt stored. One that no
longer opens is not handed back: no `url`, and a `detail` saying to issue a
password reset link. An `unknown` carries the person's `id` and the `op_id`,
never a link.

| Answer | When |
|---|---|
| `201` | Created, a person and a service account alike: `{id, kind, login, seat?, credential?, url?, expires_at?, detail?}` beside the `outcome`, `op_id` and `position` every write carries; the link's three fields for a person only. `202` is the same answer for a record this node has not applied yet |
| `400 seat_required` | A person's create that names no seat |
| `400 invalid_body` | No `grants` field, or a name in it this build does not know (`field: grants`); a seat the company this node runs does not hold, or holds as an agent's; a person with no address; a service account with no login; a login outside its kind's grammar, or none to propose from the address (`field: login`); a `kind` other than `person` or `machine`; a name or a reason past its cap |
| `400 op_id_invalid` | An `Idempotency-Key` that is not a uuid7 |
| `403 unauthorized` | A permission the caller does not hold |
| `403 token_refused` | The request presented a machine token: an enrolment is an administrative record, refused through a token whatever it carries |
| `409 invalid` | An address, a login or a seat somebody holds (`held_by`), or an open invitation holds (`invitation`) |
| `409 invalid_input` | The key of an earlier create sent with a different body (`field: Idempotency-Key`) |
| `409 no_active_revision` | A node that runs no company yet: it holds no human seat to create anybody on, and the `hint` says to import or create a company that declares one |
| `500 no_external_url` | A person's create on a node with no `api.external_url` |
| `503 unavailable` | A create nothing can confirm (`"outcome": "unknown"`, with `id` and `op_id`), or a node that refused to decide it: send the same request again under that `op_id` |

#### `POST /iam/credentials` mints a machine token

The owner is the person the **route** names (`?person=`, or the caller), never a
body field, because that is the value the authority table decided on. **A
person's token is minted by that person alone**: it acts as them and its value
is shown to whoever minted it, so `admin` mints for service accounts and never
on a person's account. A person mints their own with no `?person=` from their
own session; `crewlet iam token -login` makes exactly that request, signing in
for it and out after. The body is `{"label", "expires_in_days", "grants"}`,
every field optional:

- `grants` omitted: the token carries every permission its owner holds that
  whoever mints it may confer, `admin` included where the minting session holds
  it, and the owner's apps alone on a node whose `api.auth.admin` is `refuse`
  (no session carries admin there).
- `grants: []`: reads the overview alone.
- Lifetime defaults to 90 days.

A token may carry `admin`; what keeps it off gestures needing a person is the
authority table's presence rows and the identity record's refusal of an
administrative record written through a token. The answer is `201` with
`{"id", "person", "token", "grants", "expires_at", "position"}`.

| Answer | When |
|---|---|
| `400 bad_params` | No owner: a Tier A token owns no machine tokens, so it names the service account with `?person=` |
| `400 invalid_body` | An expiry in the past or more than 365 days away, a label past 128 bytes, an owner already holding 64 live credentials (a revoked or expired one gives up its place to the new token, the earliest to lapse first, so revoking an unused token makes room at once) |
| `400 invalid_body` (`field: grants`) | A permission this build does not know, named beside the five |
| `403 token_refused` | The request presented a machine token |
| `403 unauthorized` | A service account's token asked for without `admin`; a permission the caller does not hold (`grants` names it) |
| `403 forbidden` | A **person's** token asked for by anybody but that person; a permission the owner does not hold; an owner who may not act; the row that binds a Tier A token (`token:<id>`) — `detail` says which |
| `404` | Nobody by that id |

**`Idempotency-Key` is ignored here, deliberately.** A retry of a mint that
landed would hand back the first attempt's record (whose secret was shown to
nobody) beside this attempt's value, a token that verifies against nothing. A
mint answered `unknown` is retried as a new mint, and the one that may have
landed is a token nobody holds, which expires. So its `503` carries
`"outcome": "unknown"` and the `op_id` (which finds the attempt in the trail),
and its `detail` says to mint again, not to send the `op_id` back as every other
unknown here does.

Presented as `Authorization: Bearer cwl_pat_…`, the token acts as its owner (a
person's seat, or a service account's where bound to one) carrying the grants it
was minted with that the owner **still** holds, cut to the node's ceiling. It
answers `401` where the node knows it is no good and `503 identity_unavailable`
where the node cannot tell, including a node that has not yet applied the mint.
See [Machine
tokens](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#machine-tokens-a-persons-own-and-a-service-accounts).
#### An edit moves a login and a seat in one record, and that record goes first

A person's login and seat are the **directory's**, decided in one record against every other row; their stage and document (name, grants) are their own subject's. So `PATCH /iam/people/{id}` is up to three records, and the login-and-seat record goes **first**: it is the one a value somebody else holds can refuse, and refused first, nothing has landed. A `login` somebody holds, or a `seat` somebody is bound to or an open invitation holds, is `409` naming which; a `login` its holder's kind's grammar refuses is `400`. The record states the login and seat held from now on, so the old ones are free the moment it lands. `login` and `seat` are trimmed before anything judges them.

**A person's seat is moved, never cleared.** `seat` names the human seat to move somebody to. A person always holds one, so `seat: ""` about a person is `400 seat_required` (the identity record's own refusal, decided on the row's kind in its snapshot; nothing landed). To free a person's seat, move them to another or remove them. A **service account** is unbound with `seat: ""`.

**Grants are the whole set or a change to it, never both.** `grants` replaces what the person holds (what `crewlet iam grant` sends) among `admin`, `worklet`, `doclet`, `artifacts`, `chatlet` and `gitlet`; `admin` includes every app, and the dashboard and CLI store every app beside it, so taking admin away later leaves the apps. `add_grants` and `remove_grants` are applied to what the row holds **when the record is decided**. Sent whole, an editor working from an earlier read would bring back a grant another administrator took away meanwhile and drop one they gave, and nothing would refuse it, since only an addition needs the caller to hold the permission. The dashboard's edit sends the change.

**Everything the surface can judge alone is refused before the first record**:
- a `login` of `""` (a login is only changed, never cleared);
- a `stage` this build cannot name;
- a `reason` past 256 bytes;
- `grants` beside `add_grants` or `remove_grants`;
- a name in both;
- a name this build does not know **added**, in `add_grants` or in a whole `grants` naming one the row does not already carry: `400` naming the six. `remove_grants` may name one; one already on the row is kept and ignored;
- permissions the caller may not confer: `403`.

What only a later record can decide (a grant the caller's own row stopped letting them confer a moment ago) is refused by that record, and the steps before it have landed. So a refusal after the first record carries `landed` (the fields changed: `identity`, `stage`) and a `hint`; an `unknown` met partway carries `landed` too.

A `seat` is named by its **handle**, which is immutable, and the binding records it. Naming the login and seat a person already holds is a no-op (`200`, no record). A seat the running company does not hold, or holds as an agent's, is `400 invalid_body` (a typed value). A node that runs no company yet answers `409 no_active_revision`: it holds no human seat and no wait supplies one. A node holding an identity record it cannot decode refuses a login or seat change `503` with no `Retry-After`: the record may hold the value, so another node decides it.

#### Values that are shown once

`POST /iam/invitations` answers the invitation URL, `POST /iam/people` a person's first password link, `POST /iam/people/{id}/password-reset` a reset link and `POST /iam/credentials` the token. None is stored or readable back: the estate holds the invitation's id and a SHA-256 of the secret its link carries (likewise for a first password link and a reset link), and a SHA-256 of the token. A lost invitation is cancelled and issued again; a lost first password link is handed back only by the retry of its own create under the same key, and is otherwise replaced by a reset link; a reset link is simply issued again.

The invitation URL is the **dashboard's invitation screen**:

```text
<api.external_url>/dashboard#/invite/<id>.<secret>
```

The credential is in the fragment, which a browser never sends, so neither half reaches an access log. The screen reads `GET /auth/invite/{id}` with the secret in the `X-Crewlet-Invite-Secret` header and redeems with `POST /auth/invite/{id}` carrying it in the body.

`POST /iam/invitations` takes `{email, seat, grants, reason}` and answers `201` with `{id, url, expires_at, seat, detail}` beside the `outcome`, `op_id` and `position`.
- **`grants` is required**, as on `POST /iam/people`: what the link confers (any of `admin`, `worklet`, `doclet`, `artifacts`, `chatlet` and `gitlet`; `[]` for the overview alone). An omitted field or unknown name is `400 invalid_body` naming `grants`, decided before any key is read or link minted.
- **`seat` is required**: the human seat the invitee will hold, by handle. One left out is `400 seat_required`, answered before any key is read or anything minted. It must be a **human** seat that no person and no open invitation holds:
  A seat the running company does not hold and an agent's seat are `400 invalid_body`, one a person holds is `409 invalid` naming them, one another open invitation holds is `409 invalid` naming that `invitation`, and a node that runs no company yet answers `409 no_active_revision`.
- The link is good for **a week**.

**An open invitation holds its seat** exactly as it holds its address, from issue until it is redeemed, cancelled or lapses: a create, a move or another invitation naming the seat is refused naming it, `GET /iam/seats` lists it against the seat, and a `/config` write that would take the seat out of the company is [`409 seat_held`](#what-a-write-answers) naming it. Redeeming creates the person bound to that seat in one record. A seat the company has removed, or made an agent's, since the issue (only an offline `crewlet config import` or a write racing the issue can do that, since a `/config` write refuses while the invitation holds it) is the link's `410`; the remedy is a new invitation.

`POST /iam/invitations` on a node with no `api.external_url` is `500 no_external_url`: no address a link could point at, and only the node's own configuration file can supply one.

#### `GET /iam/invitations` lists them, and never a link

```json
{
  "invitations": [
    {"id": "0192f00d-…", "email": "sam@example.com", "seat": "qa-lead",
     "grants": ["worklet", "doclet"], "invited_by": "people-lead",
     "created_at": "2026-06-08T09:12:00Z", "expires_at": "2026-06-15T09:12:00Z",
     "state": "open"}
  ],
  "next": "",
  "position": "CREWLET_IAM_LOG@0:1840"
}
```

Lists the invitations nobody has redeemed and that are still good, paged on their id as `GET /iam/people` pages (`?after=`, `?limit=`). `?all=true` adds the expired and redeemed ones the estate still holds (until the sweep collects them); `state` says which: `open`, `expired` or `redeemed`, the last with `redeemed_at` and the `person` it created. Every row names the `seat` it binds and, while open, holds. `invited_by` names its author as every record does: a person by their seat's handle, a Tier A token or service account by its login. The address is opened on this node's keyring and a row it cannot open reads `sealed`, as a person's does. A redeemed row whose person has since been **removed** carries no `email` and is not `sealed`, because a removal erases every value of theirs other rows hold. **No row carries the link**, its secret or what the estate keeps of it.

#### `DELETE /iam/invitations/{id}` withdraws one nobody redeemed

One directory record, with `?reason=` recorded on it. Its apply deletes the invitation's row, so the link answers `410` as one nobody issued, and the address and seat it held are free at once: the address for a new invitation or a create, the seat for a create, another invitation, a move, or a `/config` write that removes it. It reads an `Idempotency-Key` like every keyed write here.
- An id the estate does not hold (never issued, already cancelled, or collected by the sweep) is `404`.
- A **redeemed** invitation is `409 stale` naming the `person` it created: the redemption overtook the reading the cancel was made from and the link is spent; removing that person undoes it.

Each cancellation is an `iam_invitation_cancelled` event, by the invitation's id and never its address.

#### `POST /iam/people/{id}/password-reset` issues a one-time link

```json
{
  "id": "018f3a9c-…",
  "credential": "0192f00d-…",
  "url": "https://crewlet.example.com/dashboard#/reset/<id>.<secret>",
  "expires_at": "2026-06-09T09:12:00Z",
  "outcome": "applied",
  "position": "CREWLET_IAM_LOG@0:1841"
}
```

`201` with a link that sets the person a new password **once**: the dashboard's reset screen, the credential's id and a secret in the fragment, built as an invitation's link is. A node with no `api.external_url` answers the same `500 no_external_url`.

- The link is a `reset` credential on the person, stored as the SHA-256 of its secret and good for **24 hours**; it travels out of band to somebody locked out.
- It is listed among the person's credentials (`GET /iam/credentials?person=`) and revoked like any of them. Issuing another revokes the one before: a person holds at most one, the [first password link](#post-iampeople-creates-a-person-on-their-seat-or-a-service-account) their create issued included. So a reset link is also how somebody whose first link lapsed or went astray gets a new one; their reset screen then says it sets their first password.
- Once spent it is listed `revoked` and `spent: true`, since setting the password revokes every link the person held, the one used included. It also ends the person's sessions and tokens.
- It is stamped with their revocation epoch and the company's session generation, so it is refused (and listed `revoked`) once any of these moves either: a suspension, a second factor's reset (`POST /iam/people/{id}/mfa/reset`), signing them out everywhere, ending their sessions, or `POST /iam/invalidate-all`. A reactivation does not bring it back. A link needed beside any of those is issued after it, or it is `410 reset_spent` when opened.
- A machine is `409` (no password; mint it a token). So is a person `suspended` or `retired`, naming the `stage`: reactivate them first, since a link would hand back an account somebody stopped.
- A person holding a permission the caller does not is `403 unauthorized` naming it, judged in the record's own snapshot: whoever issues the link could spend it, so it is held to the rule an invitation and an edit are, that nobody hands out what they do not hold. An administrator holds every app, so what reaches that refusal today is a name this build does not know, kept on the row; no permission would make it one, so it is `403 forbidden`, naming the name in `detail`.

**Shown once, and no key is read.** A replay could not hand back a secret its first attempt never showed, so the route ignores `Idempotency-Key`. An issue whose outcome is unknown is `503` naming its `op_id`, with no link; issue again, which revokes the one that may have landed. Each issue is an `iam_password_reset_issued` event (for whom, by whom, until when; never the link). **Spending it** is `POST /auth/reset/{id}`, among the `/auth` routes above: it sets the password, ends every session and machine token the person held, and signs nobody in.

#### `GET /iam/people` pages on a key the applier writes

A person's id is a uuid7, so ordering by it is creation order and `next` is the last id of the page. Nothing sorts on a name or address: both are ciphertext in every row.

`?q=` narrows on the **login and the seat**, the only two identity values held in the clear (a name search would open every person per keystroke).

A removal deletes the person's row, so a removed person is not listed, except on a node that has not applied the removal yet. Ciphertext this node's keyring cannot open (a key dropped before `crewlet secrets rekey` moved the values off it, or a restore under a different keyring) renders as `sealed`: the right keyring ends it, and it is never an outage.

#### `GET /iam/seats` lists the human seats and who holds each

```json
{
  "seats": [
    {"handle": "founder", "name": "Founder",
     "holder": {"person": "018f3a9c-…", "name": "Jane Doe", "kind": "person",
                "login": "jane.doe", "stage": "active"}},
    {"handle": "qa-lead", "name": "QA Lead", "unit": "quality",
     "invitation": {"id": "0192f00d-…", "email": "sam@example.com",
                    "invited_by": "founder",
                    "expires_at": "2026-06-15T09:12:00Z"}},
    {"handle": "designer", "name": "Designer", "unit": "product"}
  ]
}
```

Every human seat of the company this node runs, in the company's declared order, with what holds each. **Everybody reads it** (it is the org chart's people, named; the org chart is [everybody's overview](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#everybodys-overview)), masked per row. The example above is an administrator's.

- **`holder`** is whoever the directory binds to the seat **at any stage short of removal** (a suspended or retired person still holds it), with `name` (opened on this node's keyring, or `sealed: true`) and `kind`, which says which remedy frees it: a `person` is moved to another human seat or removed; a `machine` (a service account, or a Tier A token's `token:<id>` row) is unbound. `name` and `kind` go to every reader; `person`, `login` and `stage` only to an administrator and the holder.
- **`invitation`** is the **open** invitation naming the seat (not redeemed, not past expiry at this node's clock), which holds it until redeemed, cancelled or lapsed: `id` (what `DELETE /iam/invitations/{id}` cancels), the address (opened on this node's keyring, or `sealed`), `invited_by` and `expires_at`. **Never a link**. **Only an administrator** is sent it; to anybody else an invited seat lists as vacant.
- Neither, for a **vacant** seat: the one a person can be invited into or created on (`POST /iam/invitations`, `POST /iam/people`), which is what the seat's **Invite** and **Add person** in **Company › Structure** do.

`?unheld=true` keeps only vacant seats: one with a holder **or** an open invitation is left out, since each holds it against a create, invitation and move alike. It is an administrator's helper; anybody else is refused `403 unauthorized` naming `["admin"]`. A non-boolean `unheld` is `400 invalid_query`. Where two open invitations name one seat (a residue only a build before invitations held seats, or a restore, leaves) the newest is listed; a holder and an invitation on one seat are both listed.

**A listing, not a report**: what is wrong with a binding is `/iam/check`'s. A node that runs no company yet answers `409 no_active_revision` with a `hint`: it holds no human seat to list, so the company declaring one comes first. A node that cannot read the directory answers `503`, never a list of vacancies built from what it could not read. So does one holding two rows bound to one seat (left only by a retained record or a restore): it cannot say which holds it, and another node can.

#### `GET /iam/check` walks the whole directory

```json
{
  "findings": [
    {"kind": "binding_dangling", "person": "018f3a9c-…", "login": "jane.doe",
     "seat": "platform-lead",
     "detail": "seat \"platform-lead\" isn't in the org chart anymore. Move them to another human seat, or remove them"}
  ],
  "position": "CREWLET_IAM_LOG@0:1840",
  "people_with_admin": 2,
  "bindings_unchecked": 0
}
```

`kind` is one of four, and the report is **sorted in this order**, stably (within a kind the directory's order holds, so two nodes over the same rows print the same report):

1. `no_admin_holder`: nobody left who can administer the company except through a Tier A token, i.e. no active **person** holding an **enrolled** credential (a password, second factor or token: a way in they have used) holds `admin`. An unspent first password link does not count, since a company whose only administrator has not chosen a password cannot be administered yet. Neither does a service account holding `admin`: a machine token never writes an administrative identity record, so it can invite, grant and revoke nobody. `people_with_admin` is that count.
2. `person_without_credential`: somebody active with no live way in at all: a person whose first password link lapsed unspent or was revoked, or whose every credential has been; a service account holding no live token. A live link is a way in, so a person created a minute ago is not reported until theirs lapses. An invitation creates nobody until redeemed, so it is never the cause.
3. `binding_dangling`: somebody bound to a seat the company no longer holds as a human seat.
4. `admin_clamped_by_node`: a row holding `admin` on a node whose `api.auth.admin` is `refuse`, which clamps it away here: that person keeps every app on this node and administers nothing through it.

Each finding's `detail` says what to do, and the table in [`crewlet iam check`](cli.md#crewlet-iam-check) says the same per kind.

`binding_dangling` is decided by the **request path's own seat table**, so it names exactly the people a request would refuse or hold off for want of their seat: a seat the company no longer holds, or holds as an agent seat. The `detail` says which, and the remedy for the holder's kind: a person is moved to another human seat or removed, a service account unbound or moved. This report is the one place a dangling binding is said; no [alarm](alarms.md) raises it, since it is a fact about the company's content rather than a node. A Tier A token's row is reported like anybody's, under its `token:<id>` login.

`bindings_unchecked` counts the bound people whose seat this node **could not judge** because it runs no company yet. They are neither reported as dangling nor silently left out, so a report answered before the node's first apply does not read as clean; ask a node that runs the company.

#### `GET /iam/node-tokens` joins this node's Tier A labels to the directory

A Tier A token acts under its own login, `token:<id>`, and a directory row holding that login binds it to a seat: a service account's row, created bound to a human seat in one request (`POST /iam/people` with `kind: machine`, `login: token:<id>` and `seat`). The label (in a node's Tier A file) and the row (through this surface) are written in two places, so a label mistyped on either names a login nobody holds, and the token keeps working as itself, unbound, while its operator believes it acts as a seat. `/iam/check` names a binding whose seat is gone; this names a token whose row was never there. It is a fact about **one node's** configuration, so ask each node whose Tier A you want checked.

```json
{
  "tokens": [
    {"id": "ci", "login": "token:ci", "row": "none", "company_writer": true},
    {"id": "ops", "login": "token:ops", "row": "held", "person": "018f3a9c-…",
     "stage": "active", "seat": "platform-lead"}
  ],
  "company_writers": ["ci"]
}
```

**Labels, never values**: `id` is the token's label in this node's Tier A. `row` is `none` when nobody holds the login (the token acts as itself) and `held` for a row, whose `person`, `stage` and `seat` follow (the seat by handle, absent when the row binds the token to none). **What the row holds, never a verdict on it**: whether that seat is still one the company holds is [`/iam/check`](#get-iamcheck-walks-the-whole-directory)'s `binding_dangling` finding about the same row. A failed directory read answers `503` with a `Retry-After`, never a list missing a row. It backs **Settings › API tokens**.

**`company_writers` is `api.auth.company_writers`**, sorted: the token ids that alone may change the company document when another system [manages it](../concepts/configuration.md#managed-configuration), and `[]` when nothing does (every credential may, as far as that rule goes). `company_writer: true` marks each of this node's tokens the list names; the key is absent on every other token (and on every token when the document is not managed). An operator reading the deployment's `api.auth` thus sees whether the document is managed, and by which credential.

#### `GET /iam/audit` pages by position, never by time

No two nodes' clocks are compared anywhere in this engine, so `since` and `before` are log positions. A caller holding a timestamp passes `at=` and the route resolves it **once**, against the rows' own instants. The answer carries the position this node had applied, so a reader can tell a quiet directory from a lagging node.

Each entry names its `actor` and `actor_kind`, and, where there is one, `operator_id`, the credential the actor acted through: `pat:<id>` for a machine token acting as its owner, `session:<lineage>` for one of their browser sessions, a Tier A token's own login. A token acts as its owner, so `actor` is the owner either way, and `operator_id` tells their token's gesture from their own. A gesture a person makes through the sign-in surface (signing in or out, spending a second factor, redeeming an invitation, setting a password from a reset link, enrolling their own authenticator) is theirs: the node writes it under its own authority, and the entry names the person as `actor` and the session it opened or closed as `operator_id` (their login, where it came through no session yet). An entry the engine decided for itself (a sweep, a re-seal, a password re-hashed at the current cost, a company-wide invalidation) names the node, with `actor_kind` `engine`, and no `operator_id`.

An entry about somebody names them by `person`, their id, and by `login`, the login their row holds when the trail is read; `login` is absent once they are removed, since the removal erases what identified them and the trail keeps the id.

### `/config/*` — live config management (auth-gated)

Every `/config/*` route takes `admin`, reads and writes alike, whatever the credential (a Tier A token, a session, or the development principal). A caller without it is refused `403 unauthorized` naming `admin` (see [Which permission a route needs](#which-permission-a-route-needs)). The routes that can change the org chart (`PUT` and `PATCH /config`, a revert, and the seat and unit entity routes) also admit a unit's **lead** for what is inside the units they lead, read and judged change by change (see [A lead edits their own team](#a-lead-edits-their-own-team)). A write also asks for a proof of identity inside `step_up`, and a session whose proof is older is refused `403 step_up_required` (see [Some gestures ask how recently you proved who you are](#some-gestures-ask-how-recently-you-proved-who-you-are)). See the [Configuration concept doc](../concepts/configuration.md#auth) for the full auth model.

**A managed document refuses every other writer.** When Tier A lists `api.auth.company_writers`, only those token ids may change the document: `PUT`, `PATCH`, every per-entity `PUT`, a revert and the `?dry_run=true` check of each answer any other credential `403 config_managed`, before anything is read or stored, and `/setup`'s connect, disconnect and GitHub App routes answer the same refusal before they touch the secret store or a vendor. Reads and `POST /config/reload` stay open to whoever the authority table admits: `admin`, for a read and a reload alike. The body names who manages the document and what to do:

```json
{
  "error": "config_managed",
  "managed_by": ["gitops"],
  "detail": "The company config is managed by gitops. The credential \"founder\" can read it but not change it.",
  "hint": "Change it in the system that manages it (the token \"gitops\"). Edits here get overwritten. To rotate a leaked credential, write it to /secrets and POST /config/reload. To manage it here, remove `api.auth.company_writers` from every node's config file and restart."
}
```

`403` rather than `401`: the credential was accepted, and a different one is the managing system's to hold, not the caller's to retry with. See [Managed configuration](../concepts/configuration.md#managed-configuration).

**The active revision is the fleet's, on every node.** Every answer here (`GET /config` and its `ETag`, the revision list's `is_active`, a diff against `active`, the references, the charter and the entity reads) and the base every write is built on is the revision the fleet's activation pointer names: the **active revision**. Every node answers it alike, whatever that node runs; one still applying it, or one that refused it and runs the revision before, answers the fleet's revision all the same. So the read after a write answers the write on every node, and a write sent to any node is built on what the fleet runs. What each node runs is separate, reported per node by [`GET /fleet`](#get-fleet) as `config_serving_revision_id`. A node that has not reconciled since the pointer moved answers from the body the pointer carries: no read writes anything, and the node's next reconcile keeps the copy. With no pointer at all (a new fleet, or a lost pointer) the active revision is the company this node knows (see [Concurrent writes](#concurrent-writes)).

**A coordination store that cannot be read is `503 unavailable`.** Every write, and every read but a diff between two revisions this node holds, both named by id, reads the pointer. While it cannot be read the request answers `503
unavailable` with `Retry-After: 2` and a `reason` saying the fleet's activation
could not be read: never an answer from this node's own store (whose `ETag` every write would refuse), and never "nothing is configured" (which would send a create-only write to replace the running company). A store electing a leader is out for a few seconds; send the request again. That holds for a `503` **without** an `outcome` field only: a write that had already stored its revision when the store stopped answering is `503` with `"outcome": "unknown"`, which is not sent again (see [Status codes](#status-codes)).

**Read-only:**

| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/config` | The active revision (the fleet's), redacted (full JSON; `?format=yaml` for YAML). `?section=<key>` answers one top-level section's own value (`assistant`, `integrations`, ...); any other key is `400 bad_params` naming the sections, and one the document leaves unset is `404 no_such_entity` |
| `GET` | `/config/revisions` | Paginated history of the revisions this node holds (newest first), metadata only; the fleet's revision is marked `is_active` |
| `GET` | `/config/revisions/{id}` | Single revision including its payload |
| `GET` | `/config/revisions/{id}/diff?against=<uuid\|active>` | Structural diff |
| `GET` | `/config/references` | Every `${VAR}` the active document names, and every variable it reads without naming it, each with the config path of the field that reads it, plus the `revision` they were read from |
| `GET` | `/config/charter` | The company's mission, vision and policies, with an `ETag` of their content. See [The charter](#the-charter-mission-vision-and-policies) |

The dashboard reads four of those facts over the query channel instead: `config`, `config_audit`, `config_diff` and `config_entities`, each operator-gated like the prefix. The reference index has no query; the Secrets screen reads it over REST beside `/secrets`.

**Why the reference index is a route and not a client-side scan.** It answers "what breaks if I remove this credential". The config keeps `${VAR}` **pointers**, so a removed row leaves every pointer at it resolving to the empty string, and the surfaces holding one start refusing deliveries with nothing naming the row that went away. A client-side scan of `GET /config` would need a second copy of the `${VAR}` grammar (a looser pattern once displayed a literal secret unmasked, and another once minted a live credential into a variable nothing reads), and would miss references the read masks: `GET /config` shows a credential only when it is one whole `${VAR}`, so `"Bearer ${TOKEN}"` arrives as `"__redacted__"`.

The index is built from the unredacted document and answers names and paths only, never a value. The path is the operator's own spelling (`integrations.github.webhook_secret`), the one a validation failure reports; a name with several readers appears once per reader. It also lists every variable the document reads **without naming it**: a `providers.llm` entry whose credential field is empty signs in from a conventional variable instead: its harness's token variable under `subscription` (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, which `crewlet llm login
-capture-token` stores), its key variable under `api-key`
(`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`; never a variable other vendors' keys share, such as Qwen
Code's `OPENAI_API_KEY`, which such an entry names in `auth.api_key`), and `CREWLET_LLM_CLI_<KEY>_CREDENTIALS` for the bundle `crewlet llm export -secret-store` stores.

`providers.embeddings` with no `api_key` reads `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Each is reported at the empty field (`providers.llm.default.auth.token`), where a reference would be written instead; removing that row signs the entry out as surely as removing one it names. The index carries the document's own `ETag`, because it changes exactly when the revision does.

**Full-document write:**

| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `PUT` | `/config` | Replace the active revision. The body is JSON or YAML, read the same way whatever `Content-Type` says. Requires a revision summary: an `X-Summary` header, **or** a top-level `_summary` key in the body. Conditional via `If-Match` / `If-None-Match`, see [below](#conditional-requests). `?dry_run=true` checks it and stores nothing, see [Dry runs](#dry-runs). `?import=true` writes it as an import of a restored file, see [The charter](#the-charter-mission-vision-and-policies) |
| `OPTIONS` | `/config` | `204` with `Allow` and `Accept-Patch: application/merge-patch+json` |
| `PATCH` | `/config` | Merge one or more sections into the active revision, see [below](#patch-config--the-narrower-write). `?dry_run=true` checks it and stores nothing |
| `POST` | `/config/reload` | Re-publish the fleet's document unchanged, so every node re-applies and re-reads the secret store. See [below](#post-configreload-after-a-secret-changes) |
| `POST` | `/config/revisions/{id}/revert` | Create a new active revision whose payload equals revision `{id}` |
| `PUT` | `/config/charter` | Replace the mission, vision and policies, as a new revision of the whole document. Requires `If-Match`. See [The charter](#the-charter-mission-vision-and-policies) |

#### `PATCH /config` — the narrower write

A [JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7396): send only the sections you are changing, in the shape the document already has.

The registered media type is `application/merge-patch+json`; plain `application/json` and an absent `Content-Type` are accepted too. **Any other patch format is `415`** with an `Accept-Patch` header naming what would work, notably not `application/json-patch+json`, an [RFC 6902](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6902) list of operations this surface does not serve. Editing one list member is what the [per-entity routes](#per-entity-read-and-write) are for: a patch addresses by structure, and a seat's position in a unit's list is not its identity, so an index-addressed edit rewrites a different seat the moment anything above it moves.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://engine.example.com/config \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "X-Summary: allow one more self-iteration per turn" \
  -d '{"turn_engine": {"max_iterations": 4}}'
```

- **Deep merge.** `{"providers": {"llm": {"main": {"model": "claude-opus-5"}}}}` changes that model and leaves the provider's type, keys and every other provider alone.
- **`null` deletes.** `{"integrations": {"gitlab": null}}` removes the section.
- **Arrays replace.** RFC 7396 cannot address a list element, so `mcp_servers: [...]` in a patch replaces the whole list; so do `roles:` and `units:`, replacing every seat or unit at that level. Edit one through [`PUT /config/mcp-servers/{name}`](#per-entity-read-and-write), `PUT /config/roles/{handle}` or `PUT /config/units/{id}`. A replacement does not remove a field this build cannot represent: see [Fields a newer build wrote survive every write](#fields-a-newer-build-wrote-survive-every-write).
- **Unknown keys are refused**, not ignored, so a typo cannot silently change nothing while the caller believes otherwise. That holds whatever the key is set to, `null` included: deleting a key this build does not know is refused, because the write [carries it back](#fields-a-newer-build-wrote-survive-every-write) and the caller would be told a deletion landed that did not.
- **Validated as the whole document it produces.** A section fine alone is refused when it leaves the company invalid.
- Same summary rule and same `If-Match` as `PUT /config`, and a **409** when nothing is active: a patch is defined against a document.
- **A patch that changes nothing stores nothing.** One that leaves the document as it stands answers `200` with `changed: false` and the active revision, needs no summary, and activates nothing: see [A write that changes nothing](#a-write-that-changes-nothing).

**A document is held to what its activation carries.** Every write that stores a revision (`PUT`, `PATCH`, a per-entity `PUT`, a reload and a revert) hands the document to every node sealed, as the activation's body: one value of the coordination store, which holds a key to 6,290,346 bytes ([Coordination](../concepts/coordination.md#what-one-key-holds)). A body is held to 4 MiB, but a patch is merged onto the active document and the seal writes it a third larger. A write whose sealed document is past that is refused `413 body_too_large` **before anything is stored**, naming `document_bytes`, `body_bytes` and `max_body_bytes`; a dry run is refused the same way. Make the document smaller: about four and a half mebibytes of company document is the most a body carries. The summary is not counted in it: it rides the activation pointer, which every node reads on every probe, and is held to 4,096 bytes as the pointer encodes it (a `"` or `\` is two bytes there, a control character six), refused `400 summary_too_long` naming `summary_bytes` and `max_summary_bytes`.

**`If-Match` matters more here than on the full write.** A `PUT` carries the caller's whole intended document; a `PATCH` is merged against whatever is active at that instant. See [Concurrent writes](#concurrent-writes) for what the engine does and does not guarantee.
#### What a write answers

Every write that stores a revision (`PUT`, `PATCH`, a per-entity `PUT`, a reload and a revert) answers `201` with the revision, its epoch, and what the engine makes of the stored document:

```json
{
  "revision_id": "3f1c0f0e-8a52-4d3b-9d7e-2b6f3f0c9a41",
  "epoch": 42,
  "warnings": [
    {
      "kind": "dangling_reference", "ref": "manages",
      "path": "roles[0].manages[1]", "segments": ["roles", 0, "manages", 1],
      "seat": "ceo", "unit": "", "from": "ceo", "to": "ghost",
      "message": "seat \"ceo\" manages \"ghost\", which is neither a seat's handle nor a unit's key, so the entry manages nobody. ...",
      "title": "Seats managing someone not in the chart",
      "person": "This seat manages a name that matches no seat or team, so that entry manages nobody. Correct it or remove it.",
      "item": "ghost"
    }
  ],
  "derived": {"seats": [...], "units": [...]}
}
```

- **`warnings`** is what the engine will run but a person should know. Always a list, empty when nothing to say. Each has the locators of a [problem](#refusals-carry-located-problems) (`path`, `segments`, and the `seat` handle or `unit` key it is about, empty when neither), plus `from` and `to` as display text. Three kinds:
  - `dangling_reference`: a reference that resolves to nothing. `ref` says what carries it: `lead` (a unit's lead, a seat handle), `unit` (a root seat's `unit:`, a unit key) or `manages` (one `manages` entry, a seat handle or unit key, at its written index).
  - `admission`: an [admission rule](../concepts/configuration.md#what-a-stored-revision-is-held-to) the stored company breaks, with `ref`, `from` and `to` empty. A write that keeps one is refused, so only a reload or a revert of a company a newer peer admitted under other rules answers with one, one beside each entity the violation names.
  - `advisory`: a valid setting worth knowing before it runs. Either the company's own (a human seat with no account on the Mattermost or Slack workspace the company talks on, which nobody can @-mention there; a token ceiling another ceiling makes unable to refuse a turn; a `${VAR}` nothing supplies; a repository or a seat's `code.access` that will not do what it seems to), or what the company does together with the Tier A of the node that served the write. `path` and `message` locate and say it; `ref`, `from` and `to` are empty. Every node also logs each of the company's own when it applies the revision, as a [`config_advisory`](../concepts/configuration.md#what-an-applied-company-is-worth-knowing) line. The cross-tier ones are [Warnings across the two tiers](../concepts/configuration.md#warnings-across-the-two-tiers): a fleet hosting code on the default `nats` object store (`store.objects.backend`), and a Gitlet node whose explicit `gitlet.cache_max_bytes` is below `code.limits.repo_max_bytes`. **They are judged against the Tier A of the node that answered the write**, so the same `PUT /config` can answer them on a Gitlet node and not on an ingress node without the `gitlet` role. A write answers a budget only where it is set explicitly: a derived one is a share of a volume the write never sees, which each Gitlet node compares itself when it applies the revision (`config_tier_warning`).
  - Every advisory and dangling reference also carries `title` (what it is about in a few words) and `person` (the warning in the words of the person who owns the company: what is wrong and what it costs, then the fix, naming no document key; the dashboard draws it where `message` is the operator's). Both are the same for every warning one rule raises. What it is about is named apart, in `seat` or `unit` and in `item`, the one thing within it as a person reads it in a list (a schedule's name and how often it runs, `poll (24 a day)`; a repository; a server; a variable). An admission warning carries `person` where its rule wrote words for a person (a problem's `said`), and no `title`. An advisory the [setup advisor](../guides/advisor.md) builds a fix for also carries its `class` (`grant.health_unheld`, `learning.auxiliary_model`, `schedule.frequent` or `sandbox.direct_box`).
- **`derived`** is the full hierarchy the engine derives: every seat in the engine's order with its effective unit, primary manager, managers, reports, automatic reports and onboarding chain, and every unit with its effective type, lead and channel (and whether each was inherited). Each seat and unit carries its authored `path`. The fields are those [`GET /org`](#get-org) carries without paths; a client draws the hierarchy from this.

#### A write that changes nothing

A `PATCH /config` or a per-entity `PUT` whose document, once merged or spliced, says exactly what the active revision says (compared as JSON values, whatever the key order or spacing, numbers as written) **stores nothing and activates nothing**. It answers `200`, not `201`, with the revision that already says it:

```json
{"changed": false, "revision_id": "3f1c0f0e-8a52-4d3b-9d7e-2b6f3f0c9a41", "warnings": [], "derived": {"seats": [...], "units": [...]}}
```

- **No summary is needed**; one sent is not stored.
- **An entity's answer carries its `ETag`**, the tag its `GET` answers, so the client's next write is conditional on what it holds.
- **It is decided after everything that refuses the write**: a stale `If-Match`, a document the write would refuse, and a lead's write of a part of the company they do not lead are refused as when the write changes something. Answering a lead's unchanged write would tell somebody who may not read a setting whether it holds a value they guessed.
- **Why.** Storing a no-op would add an empty-diff revision and rebuild every node's seats. Republishing the active document is its own gesture, [`POST /config/reload`](#post-configreload-after-a-secret-changes).
- **A whole document is not answered this way.** `PUT /config` of the document as it stands is stored and published again (`201`), because that is how a caller that renders the document, an operator reconciling it, activates it after writing the values it reads. A revert of the active revision is the same: it is a reload.

A [dry run](#dry-runs) says which a write would be (`changed`).

**Every seat's handle and every unit's key is written into the stored document.** A seat that declares no `handle` is stored with the one its `name` derives, and a unit with no `id` with one minted from its name, so a write built from the stored document (`GET` then `PUT`, `PATCH`, the per-entity routes) never moves the identity when it corrects a name. A body that leaves them out is minted again from the names it carries, so a `PUT` of a file whose names changed and whose handles or keys are absent replaces those seats and units.

**A write that takes a human seat away while something holds it is refused.** Removing a human seat, or making it an agent's, while the identity directory binds somebody to it (at any stage short of their removal) or while an **open invitation** holds it, is `409 seat_held`. `held` maps each such seat's handle to the one thing holding it, never an invitee's address, since the writer may be a unit's lead who holds no grant over the directory:

```json
{
  "error": "seat_held",
  "message": "This change removes a seat someone holds or is invited to. …",
  "detail": "This change removes human seats that somebody still holds: designer (held by sam.lee) and qa-lead (held by an open invitation (0192f00d-…)).",
  "held": {
    "designer": {"person": "018f3a9c-…", "kind": "person", "login": "sam.lee",
                 "stage": "active"},
    "qa-lead": {"invitation": "0192f00d-…",
                "expires_at": "2026-06-15T09:12:00Z"}
  },
  "hint": "Move each person to another human seat (PATCH /iam/people/{person} with seat) or remove them, unbind a service account (PATCH /iam/people/{person} with no seat), cancel an open invitation (DELETE /iam/invitations/{id}), each an admin's gesture, then send the write again."
}
```

The holder's `kind` decides the remedy, which the `hint` spells out: a **person** holds a human seat for as long as they are here, so they are moved to another human seat or removed, never unbound; a **service account** (`kind: machine`) is unbound; an **invitation** is cancelled, or left to be redeemed or to lapse at its `expires_at`. Each is an administrator's gesture. Where a person and an invitation both claim one seat, the person is named.

The check is advisory: a bind or invitation landing between it and the activation is not seen, and an offline `crewlet config import` asks nothing, which leaves the residue [`GET /iam/check`](#get-iamcheck-walks-the-whole-directory) reports. A node that cannot read the directory answers `503
seat_holders_unavailable` naming the `seats` rather than allowing it, and so does
one holding two rows bound to a seat the write removes; its `detail` says what
clears it, and a read no wait clears (an evicted node, a full log) carries no
`Retry-After`. A write that takes no human seat away never asks. A whole
document [replacing an unsealed revision](#a-whole-document-replaces-an-unsealed-revision) always asks, about every seat it does not keep as a human seat, since nothing says which seats the replaced revision had; its `503` names no `seats`.

#### A lead edits their own team

A person whose seat leads a unit may write the seats and units inside it (the unit and every unit beneath it) without `admin`, through the routes that write the org chart: `PUT` and `PATCH /config`, `POST /config/revisions/{id}/revert`, and `PUT /config/roles/{handle}` and `PUT /config/units/{id}`. The route admits anybody bound to a seat before the body is read, and refuses everybody else `403 unauthorized`; an agent is refused `seat_refused` whatever it holds. The write is judged on **what it changes**, on both sides of it:

- Every seat and unit it adds, removes, moves, reorders or edits has to sit inside the caller's subtree where it was and where it lands.
- A unit's own fields are judged on the unit itself before and after (so handing it to another `lead:` is refused).
- A new `lead:` or `manages:` entry has to name something inside the subtree.
- A seat or unit added under a name another object's `lead:` or `manages:` already states has to be named only from inside it.
- Never a lead's: a project, space or channel, a seat's email or contact identity, a credential, a `${VAR}` in any field, a setting, and lifting or loosening an MCP limit any agent seat is held to.

The rule, change by change, is in [Identity and Access](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#a-lead-edits-their-own-team).

A write any part of which is not the caller's is refused whole, by the rule that refused it. On authority (a part outside the caller's subtree, or one that is never a lead's) it is `403 unauthorized` with a `refused` list naming every such part, so a client can show each beside what it is about. The top-level `reason` is the parts' own where they agree and `no_grant` where they do not, and `grants` names the permission that would admit **every** part, today `admin`; each part carries its own `reason` and `grants` too. A bar on the caller (an agent's seat on the org chart's routes) is `403 unauthorized` with that reason, no permission named and no list. A write refused only because the caller's proof of who they are lapsed is `403 step_up_required` naming the window, as the route answers it; every check of one request is judged at the instant it arrived, so a proof the route accepted never lapses half-way through. A [dry run](#dry-runs) answers the same before anything is stored.

```json
{
  "error": "unauthorized", "message": "...",
  "reason": "no_grant", "grants": ["admin"],
  "refused": [
    {"kind": "unit", "id": "platform", "op": "changed", "side": "after",
     "place": "platform", "why": "self", "reason": "not_lead", "grants": ["admin"]},
    {"kind": "unit", "id": "platform", "op": "changed", "side": "after",
     "place": "data", "why": "lead", "value": "data-lead", "reason": "not_lead",
     "grants": ["admin"]},
    {"kind": "seat", "id": "staff-eng", "op": "changed", "place": "",
     "why": "credential", "value": "mcp_env", "reason": "no_grant",
     "grants": ["admin"]},
    {"kind": "setting", "id": "mission", "place": "", "reason": "no_grant",
     "grants": ["admin"]}
  ]
}
```

| Field | What it says |
|---|---|
| `kind`, `id` | A `seat` by handle, a `unit` by key, a `setting` by its top-level key, or the `document` (no `id`) for a write that changes nothing: re-publishing the company unchanged re-activates it on every node, which is `POST /config/reload`'s and `admin`'s; a [dry run](#dry-runs) of a seat or unit sent back unchanged is answered to its lead instead |
| `op` | What the write does to the seat or unit: `added`, `removed`, `moved` or `changed` (its fields, or where it sits among its siblings, since order decides which of a seat's managers is its own) |
| `side` | `before` (the revision replaced) or `after` (the one proposed): the document the place was read in |
| `place` | The key of the unit the change reaches; `""` is the company root, which is nobody's subtree |
