| `why` | What reaches it: `place` (where the object sits), `self` (a unit's own fields), `lead` or `manages` (a new reference, name in `value`), `named` (another object's `lead:` or `manages:` entry that already states the id an added seat or unit takes, id in `value`), `duplicate` (two objects on one id, which only `admin` may write), `credential` (a credential field, compared whole so an `mcp_env` key with nothing under it counts, or a `${VAR}` in any other field, field path in `value`), `key` (a `project`, `space`, `channel`, `email` or `contact` set, cleared or changed, field in `value`), `grant` (a grant the seat's role carries, `health_tools`, set or cleared, field in `value`), `widens` (an [MCP limit](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#narrowing-a-server-for-a-team) the write lifts or loosens for the seat, by editing a block or moving the seat out from under one; `value` is the limit as the seat is held to it: `mcp_limits.<server>.enabled` or `mcp_limits.<server>.tools.<tool>`), or `unchanged` (the `document` itself) |
| `reason` | The authority table's reason: `not_lead` for a place outside the caller's subtree, the company root included, or `no_grant` for a credential, a key, a seat's grant, a widened MCP limit, a setting or an unchanged document |
| `grants` | The permissions any one of which would admit this part: `admin` for every part a lead is refused |

A lead reads what they may write the same way: `GET /config/roles/{handle}` and `GET /config/units/{id}` serve a seat or unit of their subtree, masked like every read here, and refuse one outside it `403 unauthorized`. Both the read and the write of one seat or unit are decided where the id sits **before** it is looked up or the body is read (at the company root for an id the company does not have), so a seat in another team, a seat at the root and an id that does not exist are refused in the same bytes, whatever the body, and only `admin` is told a seat or unit is missing.

A refused write that reaches outside from inside the caller's subtree is more forthcoming by design: each refused part names the place it reaches, which is where something outside the subtree sits (the unit a seat a `manages:` entry names sits in, or the root for a name nothing answers to). The chart's shape (which seats exist and where) is no secret from anybody signed in, who is served the org chart whole; a seat's or unit's fields are. The whole document, its history and its references stay `admin`'s, so a lead edits through the entity routes.

#### Dry runs

`PUT /config?dry_run=true`, `PATCH /config?dry_run=true`, `PUT /config/{kind}/{id}?dry_run=true` and `PUT /config/charter?dry_run=true` are the same request, checked in the same order, that store, activate and publish nothing. The dashboard's organization builder sends one on every edit, and its Budgets screen one before every ceiling it saves. An entity write's caller never sees the rest of the document, so the check is where it learns that a seat fine on its own leaves the company invalid, or that a ceiling it raised now sits above the company's (a warning).

```bash
curl -X PATCH "https://engine.example.com/config?dry_run=true" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "If-Match: \"$REV\"" \
  -d '{"mission": "Ship the thing"}'
```

A valid check answers `200`:

```json
{"valid": true, "base_revision_id": "3f1c0f0e-8a52-4d3b-9d7e-2b6f3f0c9a41", "changed": true, "warnings": [], "derived": {"seats": [...], "units": [...]}}
```

- **`dry_run` is read before anything else**, and takes exactly `true` or `false`, or nothing. Any other value (`1`, `yes`, an empty value, the parameter twice) is `400 invalid_query`: the two readings of a guess differ by whether the fleet's configuration changes.
- **No summary is needed**, because nothing is stored. A `_summary` key in the body is still lifted out, so the document checked is the one the write reads.
- **`base_revision_id`** is the fleet's revision the check was built on, `""` when nothing is active, so a client whose draft was built on a different revision learns the configuration moved.
- **`changed`** says whether the document the write would store differs from the active one; `true` when nothing is active. A patch or entity `PUT` whose check says `false` is [answered unchanged](#a-write-that-changes-nothing) when sent; a whole document's `PUT` is stored and published again all the same.
- **Each warning says whether this write introduces it.** A check's `warnings` are the [write's](#what-a-write-answers), judged on the whole document it would store, so they include every advisory the active revision already carries. Each also has `"introduced": true` when the active revision does not carry it (compared by its kind, seat, unit, reference and message, never by its `path`, which a write moves by adding a seat ahead of it), and `false` when it does. Every warning of a check made with nothing active is introduced. Ask Crewlet shows a change's introduced warnings on its proposal card and leaves the rest off. One warning is the write's alone: a write that moves the company's clock (`timezone`) is warned, at `timezone`, that every budget window and every schedule without a zone of its own moves with it, naming both zones; it is always introduced, and a check of the company as it stands never carries it.
- **Every other refusal is the write's, in the write's order**: `409 no_active_revision` for a patch with nothing to patch, `400 conflicting_preconditions` for `If-Match` beside `If-None-Match`, `412 revision_advanced` for a stale `If-Match`, `412 already_configured` for `If-None-Match: *` on a configured company, and `400` with [problems](#refusals-carry-located-problems) for a document the write would refuse.
- **A dry run is decided as the write, without the step-up** (ADR-0055): the same permission, a [lead's](#a-lead-edits-their-own-team) included, but not the recent proof, because it changes nothing. A person whose sign-in is old checks a change and is asked to confirm it is them only to make it. Ask Crewlet's read access sends a dry run to these routes, and to no other, to check a change before the person is shown it.
- A dry run needs the same token a write does, and a lead's is judged as the write would be: a part that is not theirs is `403` with the `refused` list. One answer differs: a seat or unit sent back **unchanged** to its own address is checked for its lead, though the write would be refused as a re-publish, because the check stores nothing and is how a lead reads what the engine derives of their unit. The whole document sent back unchanged stays refused, since no address decided whose check it is.

#### Refusals carry located problems

A refused document (`400 validation_error`, `400 invalid_patch`, `400 invalid_body`) is the [refusal envelope](#every-refusal-is-one-envelope) with a detail of its own: `detail` (one line per failure) and `hint` beside the `error` code and its `message`, and **`problems`**, the same failures located and classified, so a client puts each beside the field it is about without parsing anything.

```json
{
  "error": "validation_error",
  "detail": "workers.researcher.model: value not in the allowed set: \"nowhere\" is not a configured provider. Use one of providers.llm's: \"zulu\". ...",
  "hint": "The whole company is checked on every change, not only the part that changed, ...",
  "problems": [
    {
      "path": "workers.researcher.model", "segments": ["workers", "researcher", "model"],
      "kind": "unknown_value",
      "message": "workers.researcher.model: value not in the allowed set: ..."
    }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `path` | The authored path in the whole document that was validated. For a per-entity write that is the document the entity was spliced into, and an entity body it cannot read is placed where that entity sits (`mcp_servers[1].comand` for a typo in the second server). `""` only for a failure that belongs to no place, such as a whole document that is not YAML at all |
| `segments` | The path taken apart: strings for keys, numbers for list indexes. A map key can hold a dot, so read these rather than splitting `path`. `null` when `path` is `""` |
| `kind` | `missing`, `unknown_value`, `out_of_range`, `conflict`, `unknown_field`, `shape`, or `invalid` for anything this build does not classify |
| `message` | The failure's whole line, as in `detail`. A duplicate handle or unit key is one line naming every entity and one problem beside each, so there can be more problems than lines |
| `seat` | The engine-derived handle of the seat the problem is about, when it is about one |
| `unit` | The name of the unit the problem is about, when it is about one |
| `line` | The 1-based line in the text sent, for a failure the parser found. A patch's failure found in the merged document names no line, because that text is the engine's merge |
| `range` | For a value outside the range its setting admits, that range: `{min, min_exclusive, max, or_zero}` in the setting's own unit (`min_exclusive`, `max` and `or_zero` omitted when false or unbounded; `or_zero` admits 0 apart from `min` to `max`), the same declaration the `limits` question reports for a cap. Omitted for every other problem |
| `said` | The problem in a person's words, with no key or path, for a rule that writes them: today the rules holding one turn-engine cap to another (a first turn's rounds under their ceiling, a worker's turns under theirs, a task's time limit under its call's), which Settings › Limits can break. Omitted where the rule writes none, and `message` is then the only wording |

A `validation_error` also carries the `derived` hierarchy the engine built from the refused document, as far as it got, so a client can place each problem on the chart.

No message repeats a credential. A document read from `GET /config` carries masks, which a write restores from the stored revision before validating, so the values a refusal judges are ones the caller was never shown: a message says what rule a value breaks and never the value, a fragment of it, or its length.

The [`/setup`](#setting-an-integration-up) submissions that change the document answer their `validation_error` with the same `problems`.

#### Conditional requests

`GET /config` returns an **`ETag`**: the fleet's revision id, quoted, the same on every node while the fleet has an activation. A tag read from one node is good on any other, one that refused the fleet's revision included. An entity's `GET` and its write's `201` carry the entity's own tag instead, a digest of what it serves, so an edit of one entity is conditioned on that entity alone (see the entity routes below).

| Header | On | Meaning |
|--------|-----|---------|
| `If-None-Match: <etag>` | `GET` | `304 Not Modified` when the fleet's revision has not moved |
| `If-Match: <etag>` | writes | Proceed only against that revision; `412 revision_advanced` otherwise, naming the fleet's as `current_revision_id` beside `your_base`, when the request arrives or when another write is activated before this one can be. Never beside `If-None-Match`: `400 conflicting_preconditions` |
| `If-Match: *` | writes | Proceed only if *something* is active; `412 no_active_revision` when nothing is configured |
| `If-None-Match: *` | `/config` writes | Proceed only if **nothing** is configured: the fleet has no activation, and this node knows no company either. `412 already_configured` otherwise, naming the revision it lost to, on a node that joined the fleet and has not reconciled yet too |
| `If-None-Match: *` | entity `PUT` | Proceed only if **that entity** does not exist: the create-only write that adds an MCP server or an LLM provider. `412 entity_exists` when one does; `400 conflicting_preconditions` beside an `If-Match` |

The bare revision id is accepted wherever an `ETag` is, unquoted. `If-None-Match: *` is the only create-only precondition (about the company at `/config`, about the entity at an entity's own address), and every `If-Match` value other than `*` is an entity tag, matched against the fleet's revision and nothing else.

Independently of any header, every write names the revision it derived from as the new revision's parent, and the activation is a compare-and-set on that parent (create-only with no pointer), so a lost update is refused **whether or not** the caller sent a precondition. See [Concurrent writes](#concurrent-writes).

**Nothing under `/config` is cacheable.** Every response the surface writes carries `Cache-Control: no-store`: reads, `304`s, writes, refusals and error bodies, and the `404` and `405` for a path or method it does not serve. A body here is the company's settings (which integrations are wired and where, and the `${VAR}` name behind every credential), and a stored copy would outlive the session and token that read it. Revalidation still works: a client that wants a `304` sends `If-None-Match` with the `ETag` it kept.

#### The charter: mission, vision and policies

The company's **charter** is the part of the document every seat is handed word for word on every turn: `mission`, `vision` and `policies`. It has a resource of its own, which Company › Principles edits in place.

```http
GET /config/charter

200 OK
ETag: "charter-5f0c…"

{"mission": "Help friends split costs fairly.",
 "vision": "Splitting a bill is never the awkward part again.",
 "policies": ["Every amount is exact to the cent.", "Work is tracked on the board."]}
```

Every field is always sent: `""` and `[]` when nothing is written.

```http
PUT /config/charter
If-Match: "charter-5f0c…"
X-Summary: tighten the money policy

{"mission": "…", "vision": "…", "policies": ["…", "…"]}

200 OK
ETag: "charter-91ab…"

{"charter": {"mission": "…", "vision": "…", "policies": ["…", "…"]},
 "changed": true, "revision_id": "0192…", "epoch": 42}
```

- **The body names all three fields and nothing else**, and replaces the charter whole: `policies` is the list in the order every seat reads it. A missing or unknown field is `400 invalid_body`. Each value is trimmed of surrounding space, and an empty mission or vision is removed from the document.
- **`If-Match` is required** (`428 bad_if_match` without it) and its tag is the charter's **content**, not the revision's, so a write elsewhere in the document is not a conflict. A charter that changed since the tag was read is `412 version_moved`, carrying the charter now as `current` and its tag as `etag` (and in `ETag`): show the draft beside it, then send the draft again with that tag to keep it. `If-Match: *` writes whatever the charter says now.
- **It is a revision like any other write.** The same pipeline as `PATCH /config`: the managed-document check, the whole document validated, a sealed revision recording its author and credential, the fleet's compare-and-set and the `config_revision_activated` event. `X-Summary` is optional here: one left out is derived from what changed (`edited the company's mission and policies`). A revision that moved for another reason between the read and the compare-and-set is merged onto, up to three attempts, after which the answer is `409 revision_advanced`.
- **A charter that changes nothing writes nothing**: `200` with `"changed": false` and the active `revision_id`, because a new revision re-activates every node and rebuilds every seat. This is asked before `If-Match`, so a retry whose first answer was lost finds the charter already saying what it asks for and is answered rather than refused.
- `?dry_run=true` judges the write and stores nothing, answering `{"valid": true, "charter": …, "changed": …}`.
- It is `admin`'s, read and written on verbs of its own (`config.principles.read`, `config.principles.write`), decided as `config.read` and `config.write` decide the whole document; the write asks a recent proof as every write here does, and is admitted only while it changes the mission, the vision or the policies and nothing else. The verbs are separate because Ask Crewlet may read the charter as the person and write it only as a change its owner approved, sent with the `If-Match` its preview read (ADR-0052).

**The bounds**, in characters (Unicode code points, the count an editor shows), because every character is in every seat's prompt on every round. A charter past one is `400 validation_error` with the problem located at `mission`, `vision`, `policies` or `policies[i]` (`segments` `["policies", 3]`):

| Field | Bound |
|-------|-------|
| `mission` | at most 1024 characters, on one line |
| `vision` | at most 2048 characters; paragraphs allowed |
| `policies` | at most 25 entries |
| each policy | at most 1024 characters, on one line, not blank, and not a repeat of another |

A line break in the mission or a policy is refused with kind `shape` (each is read inline); a vision's paragraphs are quoted line by line in the prompt.

Each bound is counted on the trimmed value. Every write of the document through the API (`PUT` and `PATCH /config`, a per-entity write, `/setup`) holds them too, judged on [what the write changes](../concepts/configuration.md#mission-vision-and-policies): a write that leaves a faulty part untouched is admitted, with a warning naming it in its answer, so an old fault never locks a company out of its other settings. The charter write judges the parts it changes, not the parts it leaves.

**An import is never refused for the charter.** `PUT /config?import=true` writes the document as an import of a restored or migrated file: every other rule holds as for any write, and the charter is judged warn-only, its faults named in the answer's `warnings`. It is what `crewlet config import` sends to a running node, so a file that ran under an earlier build always imports, as it does into a stopped node and at boot. It is `admin`'s alone (a lead the route admits for their own units is refused `403` before the body is read), asks a recent proof as every write does, and records the revision with `source` `file`, and its activation event with `revision_source: file`, beside the author and the credential (`operator_id`). Decided by `config.write` on the authority table, so a Tier A token may use it (fresh by construction), and so may a machine token whose owner holds `admin`; on a [managed](../concepts/configuration.md#managed-configuration) document only the listed writers may. It relaxes the charter's change rule and nothing else: every other rule, `If-Match` and the managed check hold as for any write. The flag is `true` or `false`, given once, or `400 invalid_query`. The dashboard never sends it (a gate fails if its source does), and the operator's MCP and act surfaces serve no `/config` write at all.
#### Per-entity read and write

Five collections, `GET` and `PUT`, and `DELETE` for a model, a fleet or an MCP server:

| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/config/{kind}/{id}` | One entity, redacted, with its own `ETag` (a digest of what it serves, not the document's revision). **The body is the entity itself**, so it goes straight back into the `PUT` |
| `PUT` | `/config/roles/{handle}` | Replace one seat, root-level or inside a unit at any depth. Every entity `PUT` takes `?dry_run=true`, see [Dry runs](#dry-runs) |
| `PUT` | `/config/units/{id}` | Replace one org unit, by its key |
| `PUT` | `/config/llm-providers/{key}` | Replace one named LLM provider; with `If-None-Match: *`, add one under that key |
| `PUT` | `/config/mcp-servers/{name}` | Replace one MCP server entry; with `If-None-Match: *`, add one after every declared server |
| `PUT` | `/config/llm-fleets/{key}` | Replace one [LLM fleet](../concepts/llm-fleets.md) (`{name, strategy, members, threshold_points}`, `members` in its sequential order); with `If-None-Match: *`, add one under that key. `default-fleet` is served while synthesised, and a write leaving it as synthesised stores nothing |
| `GET` | `/config/llm-providers/{key}/references` | Every written field that names the model (a seat's handle and job, Ask Crewlet's chat, the Advisor's findings) with the field and its whole chain, and the stored values its sign-in reads: what a removal answers, read with no write (`{"revision", "references", "dependants"}`, `dependants` as a removal's dry run answers it; 404 for an undeclared model) |
| `GET` | `/config/llm-fleets/{key}/references` | Every seat job and helper set to `fleet:<key>`, as a fleet's removal answers them (`{"revision", "references"}`; 404 for a fleet the company does not have) |
| `DELETE` | `/config/llm-providers/{key}` | Remove one model and repoint everything naming it, in one revision. See [below](#delete-configllm-providersid-remove-a-model-and-repoint-what-names-it) |
| `DELETE` | `/config/llm-fleets/{key}` | Remove one fleet and repoint every seat job and helper on it, in one revision; `409 not_removable` for `default-fleet`. See [below](#delete-configllm-fleetsid-remove-a-fleet-and-repoint-what-runs-on-it) |
| `DELETE` | `/config/mcp-servers/{name}` | Remove one MCP server and clear everything naming it, in one revision, deleting the stored values only it read where asked. See [below](#delete-configmcp-serversid-remove-an-mcp-server-and-clear-what-names-it) |

Any other method is `405` with an `Allow` header naming the methods the path takes. No other `DELETE` exists: removing a seat or a unit is a full-document edit.

Why: `PUT /config` makes every edit company-wide, so a founder changing one seat's goal sends the whole document and loses to any concurrent edit. An entity write narrows what it *claims* to change, which makes the revision summary meaningful.

It is the same write underneath: an entity `PUT` opens the active revision, splices the entity in, restores the masks the read showed against that revision, **validates the whole document**, and stores a new revision. A change that would leave the company invalid is refused even when the entity is fine (a seat naming a provider that no longer exists). The [seat-holder check](#what-a-write-answers) applies: a unit `PUT` that drops a human seat somebody holds, or an open invitation holds, is `409 seat_held`.

**The precondition is the entity's.** An entity `PUT` takes `If-Match` with the `ETag` its `GET` answered (or `*`), judged against the entity in the revision active when the write lands, never the whole document. A revision that moved for another reason (another seat added, a ceiling patched, a credential sealed) is no conflict: the write is spliced into the then-active revision, up to three times while other writes keep landing, then `409 revision_advanced`. An entity that itself changed since it was read is `412 version_moved`, carrying the entity as it stands (`current`) and its `etag`, so the caller can show its change beside what replaced it and resend with that tag. A `201` carries the `ETag` of the stored entity, the tag its `GET` now answers, so the next edit sends it as `If-Match` with no read between. `If-None-Match: *` is the create-only write, never beside `If-Match`; any other `If-None-Match` is `400 bad_if_match`.

Four rules follow:

- **An unknown field is refused, not dropped.** The body is read by the whole-document parser, JSON or YAML: `gaol` for `goal` is `400 invalid_body` with an `unknown_field` [problem](#refusals-carry-located-problems) placed where the seat sits in the document (`roles[1].gaol`), with its line in the body. Ignoring it would answer `201` with the goal silently gone.
- **A plain `PUT` never creates.** An id nothing carries is `404 no_such_entity` (on `roles` and `units`, to an administrator alone; anybody else gets `403` as for a seat outside their team), its `hint` saying how that collection is added to; a missing id is far more often a typo. Intent to add is SAID with `If-None-Match: *`, the create-only write for the three flat collections (`mcp-servers`, `llm-providers`, `llm-fleets`): a taken id is `412 entity_exists` rather than a replacement, the body's identity must match the path as on any `PUT`, and the whole company is validated with the new entity. An added entity lands LAST in its collection's order: a server after every declared server, a provider at the end of `providers.llm_order` (the order an unpinned seat resolves a provider in). A seat and a unit are `400 not_creatable` (each has a place in the chart the path cannot name); add them by replacing the unit they sit in, or through `PUT /config`. The id is looked up before the body is read, so a mistyped one is a `404` whatever the body holds.
- **The id in the path is the identity, and a `PUT` never renames.** A body whose identity disagrees with the path is `400 identity_mismatch`: nothing pointing at the old identity travels with the splice. A seat's durable id is a UUIDv5 over (company name, handle); a unit's key is referenced by every `manages:` entry and root seat `unit:`; a provider's key is what every seat's `llm:` chain names; an MCP server's name keys every `mcp_env` block and prefixes its tools. A body that leaves `handle` (or a unit's `id`) out keeps the path's, so changing a seat's display name is an ordinary edit. A different handle or unit key is a removal and a creation, made through `PUT /config`, where what must move with it is visible.
- **The same summary and `If-Match` rules apply**, and with nothing configured the write answers `409 no_active_revision`: there is nothing to splice into, and building a company from one seat is not this route's job.

#### `DELETE /config/llm-providers/{id}`: remove a model and repoint what names it

A model is named by every seat field and Ask Crewlet field that runs on it, so removing it alone leaves a document validation refuses. This route takes the removal **and the repoint of every dependant** as one write, addressed by identity (a seat's handle and job, or Ask Crewlet's chat), never by list index, and can delete the stored values its sign-in read. `config.write` (admin, a recent proof), and `secrets.write` as well when the body names a value to delete, asked before anything is read or written; `?dry_run=true` checks and stores nothing; `If-Match` takes the entry's own `ETag` from its `GET` (optional, as on the entity `PUT`); a summary is required unless a dry run: the `X-Summary` header or a `_summary` body key, the header winning when both are sent, as on every config write.

```json
{
  "repoint": [
    {"at": {"seat": "qa", "job": "review"}, "to": "sonnet"},
    {"at": {"seat": "backend-engineer", "job": "executor"}, "to": null},
    {"at": {"assistant": "chat"}, "to": "aux"},
    {"at": {"advisor": "findings"}, "to": null},
    {"at": {"fleet": "claude-opus"}, "to": null}
  ],
  "delete_secrets": ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_SONNET"]
}
```

- `job` is `executor`, `review`, `subagent`, `auxiliary`, `judge` or `triage`. A seat that writes one job twice (`llm_review` and `llm.review`) has both fields answered by its one `repoint`. Each `at` is answered once: a body naming one twice is `400 invalid_body`, naming both rows.
- **`to: <key>`** replaces the entry in that field's chain where it stood, each key once; `to` naming the entry being removed is refused at the field (`kind: "invalid"`). **`to: null`** removes it; a chain left empty clears the field, so the job resolves as an unset one does. `{"assistant": "chat"}` with `null` clears `assistant.model`, turning Ask Crewlet off in the same revision; `{"advisor": "findings"}` with `null` clears `advisor.model`, so the Advisor's checks run with no model. `{"fleet": "<key>"}` answers the model's place in that fleet's `members`: `null` drops it from the fleet, an entry key replaces it there. An `at` names one place: a seat and its job, Ask Crewlet, the Advisor or a fleet.
- The entry leaves `providers.llm` and `providers.llm_order`.
- **`delete_secrets`** names values in the [credential store](#secrets--the-companys-credentials-auth-gated) the model read, to delete once the removal is written, each once. A name the model never read is a problem at `segments: ["delete_secrets", i]` (`kind: "unknown_value"`).
- The **whole document** is validated with the admission rules, so an executor job moved to a harness that cannot run one, or an Ask Crewlet model on a harness no helper can run, is refused at its field.

**Every reference has to be answered.** One left out is `422 validation_error` with one problem per reference (`kind: "conflict"`, its `segments` the written field, its `seat`, and a message such as "qa's reviewing work still names codex-review: repoint it or leave it unset in the same write") and `references`, every written reference as `{at, segments, chain}`. A `repoint` that answers nothing is located at its own row, `segments: ["repoint", i, "at"]` (`kind: "unknown_value"`). A dry run with an empty body is how a page draws the list.

**A move nobody wrote is a warning.** A seat's job naming no model runs on the company's fallback (the entry keyed `default`, else the first in `llm_order`), so removing that entry moves the job although no field named it. Each such move is a warning of kind `resolution_moved` with the seat (`seat`), the job (`ref`), the model it ran on (`from`), the one it will (`to`) and a sentence ("pm's memory and summaries will run on aux"), in the dry run and the write's answer. A job the seat names no model for but whose executor names one runs on the executor's chain and moves with the executor's `repoint`, so it is not warned about. Removing the company's last model leaves `to` empty, and the sentence says the job will have no model to run on.

**The values its sign-in read can go with it.** "Read" is what `/secrets` counts: every `${VAR}` the entry names, and the variable it signs in from where it names none (its harness's API key or token variable, and its credential bundle, `CREWLET_LLM_CLI_<KEY>_CREDENTIALS`, where a device sign-in or `crewlet llm export` stores its login). The dry run's `dependants` lists those the store holds: `secrets`, the ones nothing reads once the model is gone, which `delete_secrets` may name, and `kept_secrets`, each `{name, read_by}` another model, an MCP server or an integration still reads. A kept value is never deleted, even when named. The values go after the revision is written and the answer's `secrets` says what became of each, as an [MCP server's removal](#delete-configmcp-serversid-remove-an-mcp-server-and-clear-what-names-it) does. A device sign-in still running for the model ends at the apply that removes it, and stores no login.

```json
{
  "secrets": ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_SONNET", "CREWLET_LLM_CLI_SONNET_CREDENTIALS"],
  "kept_secrets": [
    {"name": "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", "read_by": ["providers.llm.haiku.auth.api_key"]}
  ]
}
```

Answers: a dry run `200 {valid, base_revision_id, warnings, derived, dependants}`, a write `201 {revision_id, epoch, warnings, derived, secrets}`. Refusals: `404 no_such_entity`, `409 revision_advanced`, `403 config_managed` (a managed document), `403` for a value to delete without `secrets.write`, `412 version_moved` (the entry changed since its `ETag`), `422 validation_error` and `400 summary_required`.

#### `DELETE /config/llm-fleets/{id}`: remove a fleet and repoint what runs on it

Every seat job and helper set to `fleet:<id>` names the fleet, so it is removed **with the repoint of each** as one write, in the model removal's body and rules: `config.write`, `?dry_run=true`, `If-Match` with the fleet's own `ETag`, a summary.

```json
{"repoint": [
  {"at": {"seat": "engineer", "job": "executor"}, "to": "fleet:default-fleet"},
  {"at": {"assistant": "chat"}, "to": "claude-max"}
]}
```

- `to` is `fleet:<key>`, a `providers.llm` key, or `null` (unset). A fleet stands alone, so `to` a fleet in a field that writes a list is refused at the field.
- The fleet leaves `providers.llm_fleets`; its members stay under `providers.llm` and in any other fleet.
- `default-fleet` is never removed: `409 not_removable`, `hint` "The default fleet can't be deleted."

Answers and refusals are the model removal's, `dependants` aside: a fleet reads no stored value.

#### `DELETE /config/mcp-servers/{id}`: remove an MCP server and clear what names it

An MCP server is named from three other places: each seat's and unit's `mcp_env` block keyed on it, each seat's and unit's `mcp_limits` block keyed on it, and each seat's `sandbox.mcp.servers` entry listing it. Removing the entry alone leaves those naming nothing, which validation refuses. This route takes the removal **and the clearing of every field naming the server** as one write, and can delete the stored values only that server read. `config.write` (admin, a recent proof), and `secrets.write` as well when the body names a value to delete, asked before anything is read or written; `?dry_run=true` checks and stores nothing; `If-Match` takes the server's own `ETag` from its `GET` (optional, as on the entity `PUT`); a summary is required unless a dry run: the `X-Summary` header or a `_summary` body key, the header winning when both are sent.

```json
{
  "clear": true,
  "delete_secrets": ["LINEAR_ORG", "PM_LINEAR_TOKEN"]
}
```

- **`clear: true`** clears every field naming the server: each `mcp_env` and `mcp_limits` block keyed on it, a seat's or a unit's, and each `sandbox.mcp.servers` entry listing it. A mapping left empty is dropped, and so is a seat's `sandbox` holding nothing else. An `mcp_env` block the engine reads by its own name (`github`, `gitlab`, `datadog`, `atlassian`, `jira`, `confluence`) is the integration's as well as the server's, so it stays.
- **`delete_secrets`** names values in the [credential store](#secrets--the-companys-credentials-auth-gated) the server or its cleared fields read, to delete once the removal is written, each once, judged as `/secrets` judges what reads a value: every `${VAR}` the document names, and every variable it reads without naming one. One something else still reads is kept.
- An empty body clears and deletes nothing. Any other field is `400 invalid_body`.

**Every field that names the server has to be cleared.** Without `clear`, a server anything names is `422 validation_error`, with one problem per field (`kind: "conflict"`, its `segments` the written field, its `seat` or `unit`, and a message such as `pm's mcp_env block for "linear" still holds
credentials: send clear to clear it in the same write`) and `dependants`. A name in `delete_secrets` the server and its fields never read is a problem at
`segments: ["delete_secrets", i]` (`kind: "unknown_value"`). A dry run with an empty body is how a page draws the list. The **whole document** the removal produces is validated, as on every write.

`dependants`, on the refusal and on a dry run that passes:

```json
{
  "mcp_env": [
    {"kind": "seat", "key": "pm", "name": "PM", "segments": ["roles", 0, "mcp_env", "linear"]},
    {"kind": "unit", "key": "eng", "name": "Eng", "segments": ["units", 0, "mcp_env", "linear"]}
  ],
  "sandbox": [
    {"seat": "pm", "name": "PM", "segments": ["roles", 0, "sandbox", "mcp", "servers", 0]}
  ],
  "mcp_limits": [
    {"kind": "unit", "key": "eng", "name": "Eng", "segments": ["units", 0, "mcp_limits", "linear"]}
  ],
  "secrets": ["LINEAR_ORG", "PM_LINEAR_TOKEN"],
  "kept_secrets": [{"name": "SHARED_TOKEN", "read_by": ["mcp_servers[1].env.SHARED_TOKEN"]}],
  "oauth": true
}
```

In `mcp_env` and `mcp_limits`, `kind` is `seat` (its `key` the handle) or `unit` (its `key` the unit's key), and `name` is the display name. `secrets` lists the stored values nothing reads once the server is gone, which `delete_secrets` may name, and `kept_secrets` those it read that something else still reads, with the paths that read them as the document stands now; a variable a node takes from its environment is never listed. Every list is names, never a value. `oauth` is whether somebody holds an [OAuth grant](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#signing-in-with-oauth) for the server, which the removal gives up.

**The grant goes after the revision is written, before any value:** it is revoked at its vendor where offered and forgotten here, as a [sign-out](#delete-mcp-serversnameoauth) does. The company's OAuth client authenticates that revocation with the secret the server's entry names, which `delete_secrets` may be about to delete. The answer's `oauth` is `{revocation, said}` (`revoked`, `not_offered` or `failed`, and the vendor's words where it refused), or `null` where nobody held a grant.

**The values go after the revision is written,** so a removal that loses its write deletes nothing. Each is asked again of the fleet's revision just before it goes, so one that a write landing meanwhile reads is kept. The answer's `secrets` says what became of each, as `{name, outcome, read_by?}`:

- `deleted`: the store held it and no longer does;
- `absent`: the store held nothing under that name;
- `kept`: the fleet's revision still reads it (something else did all along, or a write landed after the removal), and `read_by` names the paths, so it stays;
- `failed`: the store, or the fleet's revision, did not answer, so the value may still be there, and `DELETE /secrets/{name}` deletes it.

The status stays `201` whatever became of a value, since the server is removed either way. Each value deleted logs `secret_removed` with its name, the server (`provider` for a model) and who removed it, as `DELETE /secrets/{name}` does.

Answers: a dry run `200 {valid, base_revision_id, warnings, derived,
dependants}`, a write `201 {revision_id, epoch, warnings, derived, removed,
cleared, secrets, oauth}`, where `removed` is the server's name and `cleared` is
`{mcp_env, sandbox, mcp_limits}` as above. Refusals: `404 no_such_entity`,
`409 revision_advanced`, `403 config_managed` (a managed document),
`403 unauthorized` for a caller without `secrets.write` (the Dashboard
Assistant never takes it, so it may remove a server and never its values),
`412 version_moved` (the server changed since its `ETag`),
`422 validation_error` and `400 summary_required`.
### `/secrets/*` — the company's credentials (auth-gated)

Every `/secrets/*` and `/setup/*` route takes `admin`, reads included: the listing alone says which credentials a company holds and when each last changed. Every node serving the API serves them, because every node opens the fleet's [coordination store](../concepts/coordination.md) that holds the rows.

| Route | Needs |
|---|---|
| `GET /secrets`, `GET /secrets/{name}` | `admin` |
| `GET /secrets/{name}?reveal=true`, `POST /secrets/reveal` | `admin`, a **person present** (a machine token is refused `403 token_refused`) and a proof inside `step_up`, decided before the store is read, so a refused caller cannot tell a name that exists from one that does not |
| `PUT /secrets/{name}`, `PUT /secrets`, `DELETE /secrets/{name}`, `POST /secrets/rekey` | `admin`, and a proof inside `step_up`. A write of a name the active revision reads also asks `config.write`, before anything is sealed, for the re-activation that follows (below) |
| `GET /setup/integrations`, `GET /setup/integrations/{kind}`, the two `runs` reads | `admin` |
| `POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/inputs`, `POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/verify`, `DELETE /setup/integrations/{kind}`, `POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/check` | `admin` |
| `POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/provision`, `POST /setup/integrations/github/app` | `admin`: a writing pass gets a sink that mints and seals, and an app's private key is sealed on its way back |
| `POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/consent`, `DELETE /setup/integrations/{kind}/consent` | `admin` and `secrets.write`: the sign-in makes a credential the engine seals |
| `GET /setup/integrations/{kind}/access`, `GET /setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}`, `POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/access/plan`, `GET /setup/access/requests/{id}` | `admin` (`setup.read`): the plan writes nothing, so it asks for no proof |
| `POST /setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/scan`, `PUT /setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/{id}`, `PUT /setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/{id}/inventory`, `DELETE /setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/{id}` | `admin` (`setup.connect`) and a proof inside `step_up`: a scan dials an address the caller typed, and a server's fields are a revision of the document |
| `GET /setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/{id}/setup` | `admin` (`setup.read`) |
| `GET /setup/integrations/ssh/audit` | `admin` (`ssh.audit.read`), a person's own read, never Ask Crewlet's: a command's text and a verdict's decision can carry a credential |
| `POST /setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/{id}/test` | `admin` (`setup.connect`) and a proof inside `step_up`, by a person acting as their seat, which the test certificates name |
| `POST /setup/integrations/ssh/rotation` | `admin` (`setup.connect`) and a proof inside `step_up` |
| `PUT /setup/integrations/{kind}/access` | `admin` (`setup.access.write`) and a proof inside `step_up`. A save that raises an agent to an administration role at the vendor, or adds a grant of a permission that is not read-only, also asks `setup.access.raise`, which needs a **person present**: a machine token is refused `403 token_refused` |
| `POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/{action}`, `POST /setup/integrations/slack/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/install`, `POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/credential`, `POST` and `DELETE /setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/identity` | `admin` (`setup.connect`) and a proof inside `step_up`; `rotate`, `credential` and `identity` also ask `secrets.write`, since each seals or clears a credential, and `identity` asks `setup.access.raise`, since it changes who the vendor sees; `keep` writes the document as a save does, so it also asks `setup.access.write`, and `setup.access.raise` where what it keeps is an administration role |

**Connecting is `admin`'s and nothing more.** `/setup` writes nothing itself (a credential goes through the store `/secrets` serves), so connecting asks what writing a credential there asks. Every `/setup` and `/secrets` write and every reveal asks for a proof inside `step_up`; reads ask for none (see [Some gestures ask how recently you proved who you are](#some-gestures-ask-how-recently-you-proved-who-you-are)).

| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/setup/integrations` | What every integration this build can set up still needs, plus the address third-party apps reach this deployment on. `external_url` carries a single `value`, the `config_path` it was read from (`api.public.external_url` when the node has a [public listener](#which-listener-serves-what), `api.external_url` otherwise; never the person's address where they differ, since every webhook, manifest and redirect is built on it), and `loopback`, true when the address names a loopback host (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8` or `::1`), which no third-party app can deliver to. Both are Tier A, required on a node serving this listing and resolved before that file is decoded, so the `present`/`resolved`/`reference` triple of the Tier B pointer cannot occur |
| `GET` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}` | One integration's requirement list and state. SSH's also carries `ssh`: the authority's public line (`ca_public_key`, and `next_ca_public_key` during a rotation), the lines rotations retired (`retired_ca_public_keys`, newest last; each server drops them when its setup runs again), the `setup_version` this engine renders, the closed set of commands run on a server that lets the atlas read it (`inventory_commands`: `{"command", "containers"}`, `containers` marking the one run only where a server's container reads are on), and each server with its key fingerprints, users, whether the atlas reads it (`inventory`), the agents naming it and its latest Test connection with the current authority, as the server is now (a test from before its fields changed is not shown) |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/inputs` | Supply or generate those values: credentials are sealed, the rest is patched into the company |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/verify` | Check one typed credential at its vendor with a read-only call, before anything stores it. Writes nothing: no secret, config, revision or reconcile state. See [Checking a credential before it is stored](#checking-a-credential-before-it-is-stored) |
| `DELETE` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}` | Disconnect: remove what the integration holds at the third-party app, then its block, turning off its agents in the same revision. An integration signed in with a person's consent gives its grant up with the block, as its sign-out does. The block goes within the request only on a forced disconnect (`{"force": true}`), whose `200` answer then carries `oauth`, `{"revocation", "said"}`, where a grant was given up; the `202` of an ordinary disconnect gives the grant up when its teardown drops the block, and answers no `oauth` |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/consent` | Start a person's consent sign-in for an integration that refuses service accounts (a `consent` requirement, [ADR-0178](../../adr/0178-an-integrations-consent-grant-is-a-named-grant-of-the-same-machinery.md)): `201 {"id", "kind", "status", "started_at", "expires_at", "authorize_url"}`; send the browser to `authorize_url`, and the vendor returns it to [`/webhooks/mcp-oauth`](#get-webhooksmcp-oauth). Signed in as the company's own OAuth client for the scopes the product's seats need now; signing in again replaces the grant and revokes nothing. `404 unknown_kind` for a kind no consent product is, `409 no_external_url` on an engine without `api.external_url` (the vendor offers no device sign-in), `409 vendor_refused` with the reason for an integration turned off or naming no client |
| `GET` | `/setup/consent-sign-ins/{id}` | Where a consent sign-in is: `{"id", "kind", "status", "detail", "started_at", "expires_at"}`, `status` `pending`, `completing`, `approved` or `failed` with `detail` saying why. `404 not_found` once it lapsed, ten minutes after it expired |
| `DELETE` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/consent` | Give the integration's consent grant up: Crewlet's sealed copy, its record and any sign-in in progress are deleted, and the access is revoked at the vendor only when no other live consent grant of the company has a client in the same Cloud project. `{"kind", "revocation", "said"}`, `revocation` `revoked`, `not_offered`, `failed` or `shared`, `said` the sentence a person reads (for `shared`, how to end the access at the vendor and which other sign-in that ends). `404 not_connected` when nobody is signed in |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/provision` | Run the third-party app's provisioning pass: mint what it needs, register its webhook |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/check` | Run the same pass read-only, to see whether something fixed at the third-party app took |
| `GET` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/runs` | The passes THIS NODE remembers for one surface, newest first, ten at a time. The node holding the surface's lease runs and remembers a pass in its own process, so the answer carries `scope` saying so: an empty list on a fleet where another node ran the pass is not "no passes" |
| `GET` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/runs/{id}` | One pass, as the node that executed it remembers it |
| `GET` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/access` | Every agent seat on one integration: what the document asks (`desired`), what the vendor showed on the last sync (`observed`), the last sync, the plan the next sync takes, whether the agent's tool is live; what each lane offers now; and the integration's notice. The revision read is `revision` and the `ETag`. See [Each agent's access to an integration](#each-agents-access-to-an-integration) |
| `GET` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}` | One agent's lane as its Agents tab row reads: `{kind, lane, integration, handle, name, status, status_label, grant, holds, app_holds, unused, scope, account, tool, grants, requests, grantable, catalogue_read_at, permissions, lookup, lookup_more, lookup_note, at_vendor, checked_at, applied_at, outcome, refusal, plan}`. `grant` is the agent's grant in Crewlet, `holds` what its credential holds at the vendor now (for GitHub, what its tokens carry); for GitHub, `app_holds` is the permissions the agent's app is registered with and `unused` those the grant leaves out or holds lower, never drift, since every token is narrowed to the grant. On a lane that grants single permissions beside a level: `grants` is each such grant the agent holds, one sentence each (where, until when or for good, who granted it, for which request, whether its credential holds it yet); `requests` each open request, with the two option ids of its question that grant it (`grant-r<id>-t` for its hours, `grant-r<id>-p` for good); `grantable` how many permissions the catalogue (read from the vendor at `catalogue_read_at`) offers beside the level and how many of those the company's own connection lacks; `permissions` each permission the grants and requests name, saying whether the connection can grant it and, where not, what a person adds at the vendor and where. `?permission=` (at most 100 characters, else `400 invalid_query`) looks a permission up by part of its name, ignoring case and punctuation: `lookup` is up to 12 matches, each `{id, name, group, write, level, grantable, missing, action_url}` judged for the agent's level, `lookup_more` that more matched, `lookup_note` why nothing did (no match, a lane that takes no grants, or an unreadable catalogue). `at_vendor`, `{label, add, url}`, is what a person adds to the company's connection at the vendor before a permission can be granted, and where; absent where nothing is missing. `checked_at` is when a pass last read the vendor for the lane (a dry run such as Check now included), `applied_at` when a sync last applied the grant, with `outcome` and, where refused, `refusal`. `404 no_such_seat` names the agents listed; a lane the kind does not grant is `404 no_seat_access` |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/access/plan` | What a draft would do at the vendor, step by step, writing nothing |
| `GET` | `/setup/access/requests/{id}` | One agent's open request for a grant beside its level, as stored when the agent asked with `request_access`: `{id, kind, lane, handle, permission, scope, hours, reason, target, item, ask, asked_at}`. The Inbox builds the grant's draft from it. A request granted, declined or unanswered for thirty days is `404 not_found` |
| `PUT` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/access` | Save a draft as one revision of the company document, held to the revision the tab was read at, then start the sync. A grant the draft adds is sent without `id`, `granted_by` and `granted_at`, which the engine writes; one naming an agent's `request` is built from the stored request. A grant is added or removed, never edited. `?dry_run=true` answers the plan and warnings and writes nothing |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/{action}` | One action on one agent's account: `rotate`, `remove` (only once the agent is off), `keep` (write the vendor's setting into the document), `restore`, `retry`, `done` or `release` (keep the account at the vendor) |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/slack/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/install` | A fresh, single-use link a person follows to approve one agent's Slack app install while the app waits. `{"url": "..."}`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, never stored and never part of a read |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/credential` | A credential a person created at the vendor and pasted for one agent (Expo's robot token, DigitalOcean's personal access token): checked at the vendor, then sealed by the agent's sync. `{"detail", "access"}`, or `400 invalid_input` beside `value` |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/identity` | Check and keep an agent's own identity at the vendor where the lane offers one ([ADR-0179](../../adr/0179-a-seat-may-hold-its-own-identity-at-a-growth-vendor.md)): `{"way": "handed_in" \| "invited" \| "made", "value", "file_name", "id"}`, `value` the handed-in file or token, never echoed. Writes the agent's `identity: own` as a revision where the lane takes that setting and it changes, has its sync check and keep it, and answers `{verdict, access}`. A check the vendor refused is a verdict, not an error: `failed_at` names the step it stopped at (the steps after it did not run) and `steps` what each step that ran found (`said`) and the vendor's answers (`detail`). A lane offering no identity is `404 no_seat_access`, an agent that is off `409`, a refused identity `400` beside `value`, a vendor's definite refusal outside the check `409` in the vendor's words, the vendor not answering `502` |
| `DELETE` | `/setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/identity` | Put the agent back on the company's identity: writes `identity: company`, gives the agent's own up (cleared, and asked to be revoked at the vendor where Crewlet cannot) and answers `{verdict, access}`. A lane whose identity is always the agent's own (App Store Connect, Expo, a Google growth identity) has no company's to go back to: `409`, and turning the agent off gives its identity up |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/scan` | The host keys the server at `{"address", "port"}` presents, read without signing in, one connection per algorithm, 10 seconds each: `{"host_keys": [{"line", "type", "fingerprint_sha256", "problem"}]}`, `problem` naming why a key cannot be pinned. The address is held to the rule a registered server's is. `409 not_connected` while SSH is off, `400 invalid` beside `address`, or beside `port` outside 1 to 65535, `502 server_unreachable` when no key was read, its `detail` saying why in words (name does not resolve, port refuses, server never answers, or answered with no key to pin); the dial's own error goes to the log, never the answer |
| `PUT` | `/setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/{id}` | Add the server `{id}`, or replace it whole: `{"address", "port", "host_keys", "users": {"read", "operate"}, "description", "containers", "inventory", "read_allowlist", "if_match"}`, written as one revision the caller authors and held to the document's rules. `{"key", "revision_id", "epoch"}` |
| `PUT` | `/setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/{id}/inventory` | Switch whether the engine reads the server for the atlas: `{"inventory", "if_match"}`. It changes that one field as one revision the caller authors, so a caller holding none of the server's key lines can switch it; `404 not_found` for a server nobody registered. The server accepts the inventory once its setup is run again ([let the atlas read a server](../integrations/ssh.md#let-the-atlas-read-a-server)). `{"key", "revision_id", "epoch"}` |
| `DELETE` | `/setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/{id}` | Remove the server, refused `409 conflict` while an agent names it, with the agents to change first |
| `GET` | `/setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/{id}/setup` | The server setup trusting the current certificate authority and a staged one: `{"script", "version"}`. Run it as root on the server, then press Test connection |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/ssh/hosts/{id}/test` | Test connection: reach (a failure says how, as a scan does), a pinned host key, a read certificate accepted, the gate's version, an unlisted command refused with 126, on a server that lets the atlas read it an inventory certificate whose command runs instead of the client's (`inventory_binding`), and with an operate user a certificate whose forced command runs instead of the client's. `{"ca": "next"}` tests the staged authority. Every test certificate is recorded on the access log before use. `{"host", "authority", "ok", "steps": [{"id", "ok", "detail"}], "at"}`, kept as the server's latest test with that authority |
| `GET` | `/setup/integrations/ssh/audit` | The access log, newest first: `kind=certificate` (the default), `kind=command`, or `kind=verdict` for verdicts on requests delegated to agent seats. Every kind is narrowed by `seat` (for a verdict, the seat whose request it is; `_engine` for the certificates and commands of the engine's own inventory, purpose `inventory`), `host`, `since` and `until` (RFC 3339), and paged by `cursor` and `limit` (1 to 100, 25 when unset). A verdict page is also narrowed by `delegation_kind` (the request's act: `ssh_operate`), `verdict` (`allow`, `escalate` or `deny`, what took effect), `by_kind` (`agent`, `person` or `engine`), `by` (the giving seat), `request` (one held call or ask), `final` and `sampled` (`true` or `false`); these on another kind are `400 invalid` naming the field. A command row carries its text opened for the administrator, any credential in it replaced by a marker; its output is never kept, only size and digest. A verdict row is `{"seat", "request", "kind", "rule", "turn", "by", "by_kind", "through", "asked", "confidence", "verdict", "final", "overruled", "sampled", "digest", "host", "user", "stdin_bytes", "stdin_sha256", "decision", "item", "at"}` with `subject` (what was decided), `reason` and `findings` opened and redacted as a command's text is, or `subject_unopened` where this node's keyring does not open them. `by` is empty for the engine; `asked` and `confidence` are an agent's answer; `overruled` is the engine's closed words for why it changed or made the verdict; `final` marks the verdict that decided the request (a panel member's that waited is not); `sampled` one chosen for a person's spot-check; `digest` the SHA-256 of the exact request decided. Each page is `{"kind", "rows", "next", "complete"}` |
| `POST` | `/setup/integrations/ssh/rotation` | The certificate authority's rotation, `{"action": "stage" \| "promote" \| "cancel"}`. `stage` seals a new authority as `SSH_CERTIFICATE_AUTHORITY_NEXT`, which the rendered setup trusts beside the current one, and answers its `next_ca_public_key`; refused while one is staged. `promote` is refused until every server's latest Test connection with the staged authority passed on the server as it is now; it then seals it as the current authority, removes the staged copy and reference, and answers `ca_public_key` and the `retired_ca_public_key` (left out on a promote run again over a key already moved), which each server stops trusting once its setup runs again. `cancel` removes the staged authority's key and reference. No sealed key outlives its authority, and the engine never signs with one it has not promoted. Each writes a revision |
| `GET` | `/secrets` | Every stored name with its `key_id`, `updated_at`, `updated_by` (the author), `updated_by_kind`, `operator_id` (the credential it was stored through, empty where none) and `source` (the write path, in its own word: `api` for `PUT /secrets/{name}` whoever calls it, `setup` for an integration's setup, `provision` for a provisioning pass, `cli` or `llm-login` for a `crewlet` command's own write to the fleet's store with its node's engine stopped (`crewlet secrets set`, and `crewlet llm`'s captured token or exported bundle; a provisioner's `-secret-store` run made that way records `provision`), `models` for a credential the Models page wrote, `mcp` for an MCP server's header or variable [stored from its page](#put-mcp-serversnamevalueskey) (the engine's own OAuth grants, `mcp-sign-in` and `integration-sign-in`, are never listed); see [the secret store](../concepts/secret-store.md#the-design)), and `write_only` (no reveal answers the value: true for one stored from Settings › MCP & tools). Also `engine_keys`, a count of the engine's own keys, `{"total": N, "by_key": {"<key id>": n}}`, naming none; and sealed values counted by key id: `identity_values`, `{"people": {"<key id>": n}, "invitations": {"<key id>": n}}` (a person's name, address and second-factor seed, and the address of every invitation still redeemable), `null` on a node with no identity estate; `assistant_values`, Ask Crewlet's, `{"values": {"<key id>": n}}` (a conversation's file counted by the key its content is sealed under in the object store), which no rekey moves (each leaves with its conversation), `null` on a node with no Ask Crewlet estate; `executor_values`, the seats' executor sessions, `{"values": {"<key id>": n}}` (each session a turn's row names, by the key its object is sealed under in the object store), which no rekey moves either (each leaves with its row), `null` on a node with no executor log; `access_values`, the access log's SSH commands and delegated-request verdicts, `{"values": {"<key id>": n}}`, which a rekey moves, `null` on a node with no access log. **Never a value**. A rekey keeps each row's `updated_*` and `source`: it re-seals a value it did not choose, so the row still says who stored it |
| `GET` | `/secrets/{name}` | The same fields for one name. `404 not_found` when it is unset, or the name is past the 255 bytes no row is stored under |
| `GET` | `/secrets/{name}?reveal=true` | **Break-glass.** The decrypted value, `Cache-Control: no-store`, logged by name against the authenticated operator. The longest answer is some 384 KiB (the largest value a write admits, in the characters JSON spells longest) |
| `POST` | `/secrets/reveal` | **Break-glass, for several names at once.** Body `{"names": ["GITLAB_TOKEN_SWE", …]}`, at most 64 names, each an environment-variable name; answer `{"values": {"<name>": "<value>"}, "missing": ["<name>"]}`: every name asked that is held, with its decrypted value (an empty one included), and every name nothing holds. Nothing beside the names asked is opened. `Cache-Control: no-store`, logged by every name asked against the authenticated operator, and decided on the reveal's own row before the body is read. A [CLI run resolving a company document through a running node](cli.md#where-a-command-reads-the-companys-values) uses it: having listed the names with `GET /secrets`, it asks for the variables its command reads that the node lists (and, with a `-secret-store` sink, the planned seats' tokens it reads back) in requests of at most 64, never one reveal per name. `400 invalid_body` for no names, more than 64, a field it does not read or a body that is not JSON; `400 invalid_name` for a name no `${VAR}` reference can hold or one past 255 bytes; `400 invalid_query` for any query parameter; `403 reserved_name` for the engine's own key. The longest answer is about 24 MiB (64 values of the largest size a write admits, each in the characters JSON spells longest) |
| `PUT` | `/secrets/{name}` | Store or rotate one value. **The request body is the value**, raw bytes, up to 64 KiB (the size every store holds a value to, a direct write with the engine stopped included, and what every reveal is sized from); a longer body is `413 body_too_large`. The author is the caller the guard resolved and `source` is this route's own, `api`, never anything the request names; the answer carries `updated_by`, `updated_by_kind`, `operator_id` and `source` as the row records them. `400 invalid_name` when the name is not an environment-variable name or is past 255 bytes, the most a record keeps ([the secret store](../concepts/secret-store.md#the-design)); `400 invalid_query` when the request carries any query parameter but `defer_reload=true|false` (`?source=` included), with a `detail` naming each and a `hint` saying where provenance comes from instead, checked after the name and before the body is read. `?defer_reload=true` seals the value and re-activates nothing, as the batch's `defer_reload` does (`reload` is `{"deferred": true}`; it asks `secrets.write` alone): for a value the JSON batch cannot carry, one that is not UTF-8, sealed first so the batch after it re-activates once for both. The answer also carries `read_by`, the paths of the active revision that read the name (empty when none does), and `reload`, what the [re-activation](#a-secret-write-re-activates-the-revision-that-reads-it) did |
| `PUT` | `/secrets` | Store or rotate **several** values as one write. Body `{"values": {"NAME": "value", …}}`, at most 64 names, each held to the name grammar, at most 255 bytes, and the 64 KiB value bound; any fault refuses the whole body, `400 invalid_body` with `invalid` mapping each bad name to its reason, and nothing is stored. `403 reserved_name` for the engine's own key, `400 invalid_query` for any query parameter. Every value is sealed and the active revision is re-activated **once** when it reads any of them. With `"defer_reload": true` the values are sealed and nothing is re-activated: `reload` is `{"deferred": true}`, saying the values are **not active yet**, and `read_by` says what a later re-activation will reach. A deferred batch asks `secrets.write` alone, never `config.write`, since it changes nothing the company runs: `config.write` is asked of the re-activation that follows (`POST /config/reload`). It is for a writer that seals values one at a time, each durable once it exists, and re-activates once with its last write, as a provisioning run through a node does. Nothing reads a deferred value until a re-activation: a writer that dies before it leaves its values sealed and inactive until the company is next re-activated, by anyone (`POST /config/reload`, or any apply). `200 {"names": [...], "bytes": {"NAME": n}, "read_by": {"NAME": [paths]}, "reload": {...}\|null}`. A seal that fails part way answers `500 internal_error` with `sealed` (the names stored before it) and the `reload` those were given |
| `DELETE` | `/secrets/{name}` | Remove one value. `200` either way, with `{"removed": true\|false, "read_by": [paths], "reload": {...}\|null}`: removing a name the active revision reads re-activates it, so whatever read it falls back or signs out now |
| `POST` | `/secrets/rekey` | Re-seal every record not already under this node's `secrets.active_key_id` (the engine's own keys included) and every person's sealed values in the identity estate, one record per person, answering the names of yours it moved, `engine_keys_moved`, a count of the engine's, and `identity`: `{"people": n, "values": n}`, or `null` with no identity estate. It also moves every SSH command's sealed text and every verdict's sealed words in the access log, one record each, answering `access`, `{"commands": n, "verdicts": n}`, or `null` with no access log. An outstanding invitation's address is not moved (only a re-issue could carry it again) and is counted by the listing instead. A person or command whose record nobody could confirm, or whose value would not open, is `500 rekey_incomplete` carrying what did move; run it again, which moves only what is still under an old key. `?key_id=` is refused with `409` when it names a different key |

#### A secret write re-activates the revision that reads it

A `${VAR}` is resolved when a provider or a transport is built, so a sealed value changes nothing running. `PUT /secrets/{name}`, `PUT /secrets` and `DELETE /secrets/{name}` therefore re-activate the active revision, once per request and synchronously, when it reads a name they wrote ([ADR-0070](../../adr/0070-a-secret-write-re-activates-the-revision-that-reads-it.md); what reads a name is what [`GET /config/references`](#config--live-config-management-auth-gated) answers). The answer's `reload` is one of:

| `reload` | Means |
|---|---|
| `null` | Nothing the active revision reads names it; nothing was re-activated |
| `{"deferred": true}` | A batch sent with `defer_reload`: sealed and **not active yet**, until the caller's own re-activation or any later one |
| `{"revision_id": "…", "epoch": 42}` | The revision that re-published the company, and the epoch every node converges on |
| `{"error": "revision_advanced", "detail": "…", "stored_revision_id": "…", "node": "…"}` | Another configuration write activated first. The value is sealed; `POST /config/reload` re-activates the company that runs now |
| `{"error": "validation_error", "detail": "…"}` | The active company does not pass this build's validation, so it was not re-published |
| `{"error": "body_too_large", "detail": "…"}` | The active company, sealed, exceeds what one key of the coordination store holds ([Coordination](../concepts/coordination.md#what-one-key-holds)), so it was not re-published: shrink the document, then `POST /config/reload` |
| `{"error": "summary_too_long", "detail": "…"}` | The re-activation's summary is past the 4,096 bytes the activation pointer carries, so it was not re-published: `POST /config/reload` with a shorter `X-Summary` |
| `{"error": "origin_too_long", "detail": "…"}` | The name the write was made under leaves the activation pointer past its 8 KiB, so it was not re-published: `POST /config/reload` through a credential with a shorter name |
| `{"error": "unavailable", "detail": "…", "stored_revision_id": "…", "node": "…"}` | The re-activation was stored and the coordination store did not answer: whether the fleet runs it is unknown |
| `{"error": "no_active_revision" \| "internal_error", "detail": "…"}` | Nothing to re-activate, or a failure this node's log names |

**The status is `200` whatever `reload` says**, because the value is sealed before the re-activation is asked for: a client that reads only the status, as crewlet-operator does, is told the truth about the write.

**The engine's own keys are not addressable here.** The identity directory's blind-index key shares the bucket under a path-shaped name (`iam/blind-index-key`). Every route that takes a name answers `403 reserved_name` first (reveal, overwrite and delete alike, whatever the caller holds), because a delete or overwrite would orphan every address in the directory. See [the secret store](../concepts/secret-store.md#the-engines-own-keys-share-the-bucket-and-never-the-namespace).

**The name is an environment-variable name, and a write that is not one is refused**: letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter or underscore. The store is keyed by the name a `${VAR}` resolves through, so `gitlab-token` or `my token` would be sealed and read by nothing, a failure found only when a provider fails to authenticate hours later. The refusal comes before the body is read. A name outside the grammar names no secret, so reading one answers `404` and removing one answers `{"removed": false}`.

**The body is the value, not a JSON wrapper.** A credential is arbitrary bytes (a PEM key has newlines), and an encoding step between the operator and what the vendor compares is a `401` nobody can explain.

**Provenance is the node's, and a write that names its own is refused.** Who stored a value is the credential the request authenticated with (`updated_by`, `updated_by_kind`, `operator_id`), and `source` is the route's own, `api`, so a write cannot make a row claim another path. The route takes no query parameter at all: one sent anyway, `?source=` included, is `400 invalid_query` naming it, not ignored.

**Reveal is opt-in on the wire.** Without `?reveal=true` the route answers what a listing answers for one name, so a browser, a crawl or a link preview cannot pull a credential out by accident.

**A value stored write-only is never revealed.** The headers and variables [Settings › MCP & tools stores](#put-mcp-serversnamevalueskey) are sealed on a row marked write-only: the engine resolves it for the `${VAR}` references that name it, and both reveals refuse it `403 write_only`, naming it under `names`, before anything is opened (the batched read refuses its whole request). The listing and one row's metadata carry `write_only`. The mark is the row's: a later `PUT /secrets/{name}` keeps it, a rekey re-seals the row with it, and only `DELETE /secrets/{name}` clears it.

**Every value is sealed under the node's keyring.** There is no plaintext mode: `crewlet validate` refuses a Tier A file with no `secrets.keys`, and the engine refuses to start without one.

**Every refusal here is the engine's envelope**: `error`, the sentence `message` a screen shows, and the route's own detail:
- `reserved_name`
- `write_only` (a reveal naming a write-only value, with its `names`)
- `invalid_name`
- `invalid_query` (a write or multi-name reveal carrying any query parameter, with a `detail` naming each and a `hint`)
- `invalid_body` (a reveal or multi-name write that names none, too many, or a field it does not read; a multi-name write whose names or values the store refuses, with `invalid`)
- `not_found`
- on a rekey, `key_id_mismatch` (with `key_id` and `your_key_id`) and `rekey_incomplete` (with the `moved` names and the `engine_keys_moved` count)

`crewlet secrets` is the client for all of this while its node's engine runs, or with `-api` naming a node that does; see [the secret store](../concepts/secret-store.md#which-store-the-cli-writes) for why the CLI goes through a running node rather than reaching the KV beside it. With that node's engine stopped it reaches the fleet's store itself, through no route here: no node logs a `secret_revealed` line for what it reads, and a write records the shell's user as its author, with no credential, under the command's own `source`.

### `/llm/*`: models (Settings › Models & Fleets)

What each model is doing is a question, answered on the query channel and by the named routes below; what changes something is a route of its own, one verb each. Every answer that depends on the node names it (`node`).

| Method | Path | Needs | Description |
|--------|------|-------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/llm/entries` | anybody | Every model's condition across the fleet (query `llm_entries`): an administrator's reading, or a member's with nothing that names a credential |
| `GET` | `/llm/fleets` | anybody | Every LLM fleet's members as its balancer reads them, and what each helper and seat runs on now (query `llm_fleets`) |
| `GET` | `/llm/runners` | `admin` | Whether each executor cell (`direct`, `container`) can start a box on each node (query `llm_runners`) |
| `GET` | `/llm/models?harness=<built-in harness>[&provider=…]` | `admin` | The models a model step suggests (query `llm_models`) |
| `GET` | `/llm/device-sign-ins/{id}` | `admin` | One device sign-in while its record lingers (query `llm_device_sign_in`) |
| `GET` | `/llm/providers/{key}/check` | `admin` | One model's latest check, running or ended, from any node, while its record answers (query `llm_check`) |
| `PUT` | `/llm/providers/{key}/credential` | `secrets.write`, and `config.write` with a draft `entity` or when it re-activates | Test candidate credential values with the model's own harness, and store them only if they sign it in; `?dry_run=true` tests and stores nothing |
| `POST` | `/llm/providers/{key}/check` | `models.check`; with a draft `entity`, also `config.write` and `secrets.write` | The doctor over the API, run on this node's own time and read back at `GET` on the same path |
| `POST` | `/llm/providers/{key}/retry` | `models.retry` | Probe a sitting-out model once, or clear its sit-out on every node |
| `POST` | `/llm/providers/{key}/host-login/check` | `models.check` | Read a harness login's status on this node now |
| `POST` | `/llm/providers/{key}/device-sign-in` | `secrets.write` | Start a Codex device-code sign-in |
| `DELETE` | `/llm/device-sign-ins/{id}` | `secrets.write` | Cancel one |

`models.check` and `models.retry` are an administrator's at any recency, and Ask Crewlet's only on the person's approval: they change runtime state, never config or a credential. `secrets.write` asks a recent proof and is never Ask Crewlet's, since a credential's value travels in the body.

**A draft is decided as the writes it stands for.** A draft entry chooses its harness, overrides and env, and resolves its `${VAR}`s through the secret store as an apply would, so a check or credential test of one also asks `config.write` and `secrets.write`: an administrator's, with a recent proof, never Ask Crewlet's. A credential test's `dry_run=true` is asked at the write's own proof, not a check's: it runs the harness and spends tokens.

**Every call is audited**, refused ones included (by the route, or by the guard before it: a member's `403 unauthorized`, a stale proof's `step_up_required`), as one `model_acted` in the runtime audit (`actor`, `actor_kind`, `operator_id`, `action`, `provider_key`, the secret `names` a credential call touched and never a value, `dry_run`, `outcome` and `refusal`, and the `revision_id` a credential's re-activation activated). The node is the envelope's. `action` is `check`, `retry`, `clear`, `credential`, `host_login_check`, `device_sign_in` (a start) or `device_sign_in_cancel`. How a device sign-in **ended** is a row of its own, `device_sign_in_ended`, with `status` (`approved`, `failed`, `expired` or `cancelled`), published by the node that ran the session, or by the sweep that fails one whose node is gone, and attributed to whoever started it; an approved session whose login could not be stored or carried to the fleet is `outcome: "failed"`.
#### `GET /llm/entries`

Built from every live node's
[status record](../concepts/coordination.md#its-status-record), counted at its
presence's epoch: each model's sign-in route, sit-out, last answer and failure,
parked seats and host login, plus what this node resolved per entry. An
unreadable lease table or record store is `503 unavailable`, so a blip is never
drawn as "no node knows".

```json
{
  "reading": "admin",
  "node": "node-1",
  "nodes": [{"id": "node-1", "reported": true}, {"id": "node-2", "reported": false}],
  "entries": [{
    "key": "default", "harness": "claude-code", "model": "claude-opus-5-5",
    "health": "expiring", "plan": "3f9a1c0e22b1",
    "sign_in": {"route": "token", "mode": "subscription", "variable": "CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN",
      "source": "store", "resolves": true, "hint": "sk-ant-oat01-…Qm4x",
      "stored_at": "2025-11-04T18:37:00Z", "stored_by": "miles",
      "expires_at": "2026-11-04T18:37:00Z", "expiry_basis": "stored_at+365d", "host_logins": []},
    "sitting_out": null, "last_success": "2026-10-28T21:56:00Z", "last_failure": null,
    "waiting": null,
    "usage": {"days": 7, "calls": 412, "total_tokens": 38400000},
    "used_by": [{"seat": "pm", "job": "executor", "position": 0, "written": false, "source": "default-entry"}],
    "device_sign_in": null,
    "limits": [
      {"window": "session", "hours": 5, "state": "ok", "used": 0.05, "resets_at": "2026-10-29T00:00:00Z",
       "until": null, "seen": "2026-10-28T21:56:00Z", "stale": false},
      {"window": "weekly", "hours": 168, "state": "warning", "used": 0.83, "resets_at": "2026-11-02T09:00:00Z",
       "until": null, "seen": "2026-10-28T21:56:00Z", "stale": false}
    ]
  }],
  "alarms": [{"kind": "llm_credential_expiring", "title": "A model sign-in expires soon", "person": "…",
              "detail": "…", "remedy": "…", "entries": [...]}]
}
```

- `health` is the first that applies: `sitting_out` (a live node sits it out and
  the window has not ended), `no_sign_in` (no route on the answering node, or a
  credential that does not resolve), `rejected` (an auth failure newer than its
  last answer, or an expiry past), `expiring` (within seven days), `untested`
  (no answer, failure or call in the window), `ready`.
- `sign_in.route` is `token`, `credentials`, `api-key`, `env`, `inherit-env`,
  `environment`, `device` or `none`, as the answering node resolves it;
  `source` is `store`, `environment` or `none`. A stored token's `expires_at` is
  its row's `stored_at` plus the lifetime its vendor documents (the token is
  opaque); `expiry_basis` says so. The row, `stored_at` and `stored_by` are
  those of the value the answering node resolves, as its snapshot holds it,
  which the node's expiry alarms judge too: a value written with its reload
  deferred moves them at the next apply.
- `sitting_out` is the latest window across live nodes (`until`, `resets_at`,
