  `window`, `said`, `since`) and the `nodes` sitting it out; `last_success` and
  `last_failure` (`kind`, `at`, `said`, `node`) are the latest across live nodes;
  `waiting` is the seats parked on a chain naming it, by handle, and since when.
- `usage` is the trailing seven days of the [spend rollup](#get-tokensbreakdown)'s
  per-entry row, in calls and tokens, never money (the dashboard shows no price;
  the rollup carries `cost_usd`).
- `used_by` is the engine's resolution of every agent seat's jobs (`position` 0
  runs the job, more is a fallback; `written` is whether the seat wrote the
  field; `source` the level that decided it: `seat`, `executor`, `fleet`
  (default-fleet, for a seat naming nothing), `default-entry`, `first-entry`;
  `fleet` the LLM fleet the use goes through, `position` then the entry's place
  in its list), `{"assistant": "chat", "position": 0}` for Ask Crewlet and
  `{"advisor": "findings", "position": 0}` for the Advisor.
- `limits` is the sign-in's vendor limit windows, the newest report of each
  across live nodes: `window` (`session`, `weekly`, `model`, `unknown`),
  `hours` (0 where unsaid), `model` (a model window's family), `state` (`ok`,
  `warning` from 80% used or the vendor's word, `reached`), `used` (the
  fraction, null where unsaid or the window has turned over), `resets_at`,
  `until` (where the model sits this window out), `seen` and `stale` (older than
  30 minutes). Empty where the harness reports no window.
- `alarms` is this node's latest evaluation of the five model alarms, each with
  its `title` and `person` (the kind's words for a company owner) beside its
  `detail` and `remedy`.

**A member's reading** (`"reading": "member"`) keeps each entry's `key`,
`harness`, `model`, `health`, `sign_in.route` and `sign_in.resolves`,
`sitting_out` without `said` and `nodes`, `last_success`, `waiting`,
`used_by` and `limits`, and answers `alarms: null`: nothing in it names a credential, an
account, a vendor's sentence or a cost.

#### `GET /llm/fleets`

Every LLM fleet (`providers.llm_fleets`, `default-fleet` listed first whether or
not the document holds it), read from the same status records as
[`GET /llm/entries`](#get-llmentries), and what every helper and agent seat runs
on now, by the rule the engine's balancer picks with. Both readings carry the
same words; `reading` says which was asked.

```json
{
  "reading": "admin",
  "fleets": [{
    "key": "claude-opus", "name": "Claude Opus", "is_default": false,
    "class": "Claude Opus", "harness": "claude-code", "strategy": "balanced",
    "threshold_points": 5, "spread": 8,
    "members": [
      {"entry": "claude-max", "kind": "plan", "state": "available", "until": null, "why": "",
       "share": 30, "overflow": false, "last_served_at": "2026-11-24T08:50:00Z", "serving": ["engineer"]},
      {"entry": "claude-api", "kind": "api", "state": "limit", "until": "2026-11-24T09:40:00Z",
       "why": "Throttled by the key's rate limit", "share": 0, "overflow": true,
       "last_served_at": null, "serving": []}
    ]
  }],
  "assignments": [{
    "subject": "engineer", "kind": "seat", "name": "Engineer",
    "target": {"fleet": "claude-opus"}, "now": "claude-max", "now_kind": "running", "waiting_until": null,
    "jobs": [{"job": "executor", "target": {"fleet": "claude-opus"}, "now": "claude-max", "now_kind": "running",
              "waiting_until": null},
             {"job": "review", "target": {"pinned": "claude-sonnet"}, "now": "claude-sonnet", "now_kind": "next",
              "waiting_until": null}]
  }, {
    "subject": "assistant", "kind": "helper", "name": "Ask Crewlet",
    "target": {"fleet": "claude-opus"}, "now": "claude-max", "now_kind": "next", "waiting_until": null
  }]
}
```

- A member's `state` is `available`, `near` (a session or weekly window from
  80% used), `limit` (a live node sits it out, or a window reads reached;
  `until` is when it has room, null where unknown) or `signedout` (an auth
  failure newer than its last answer, or a sign-in the Models page reads as
  refused or not signed in on a node that reports it). A window heard more than 30 minutes ago
  says nothing. `share` is a plan's higher window use in whole points, `0` for
  a key, cloud account or gateway, null where unknown; `overflow` is a non-plan
  member of a Balanced fleet. `kind` is `plan`, `api`, `cloud` or `gateway`.
- `spread` is the points between the most and least used members taking new
  work, null for a Sequential fleet or one with fewer than two known shares.
- `serving` is the subjects with work in flight on the member now: the calls
  the nodes' status records carry as running and the executor runs launching
  or running on it. It is never a prediction, so it is empty while nothing runs.
- `now` is the member the job's work in flight runs on (`now_kind`
  `running`), else the one its next piece of work would go to (`next`), from
  the home the node holding the seat publishes; the next picks of every
  subject take their member in turn, as the engine's picks do, so equal or
  unknown shares spread them. `now` is null while no member can take it, with
  `waiting_until` the earliest instant one has room (null for a fleet with no
  members), and `now_kind` is then absent.
- `target` is `{"fleet": key}` or `{"pinned": entry}`, `""` where nothing is
  set and the company's fallback runs it. A seat always carries `jobs`, by the
  engine's job names (`executor`, `review`, `subagent`, `auxiliary`, `judge`,
  `triage`); its own fields are its executor's. Helpers are `assistant` and
  `advisor`.

#### `GET /llm/runners`

```json
{
  "default_run_in": "container",
  "declared": true,
  "cells": {"direct": {"ready_on": ["node-1"], "not_ready_on": []}, …},
  "nodes": [{"id": "node-1", "reported": true,
    "direct": {"state": "ready", "detail": "box root /home/crewlet/.crewlet/sandboxes writable", "fix": null, "checked_at": "…"}, …}]
}
```

`declared` says whether the company configures `providers.sandbox` at all;
without it every cell reads `unconfigured`. A refusal carries its `fix`.

#### `GET /llm/models`

```json
{"source": "models.dev", "fetched_at": "…", "provider": "anthropic",
 "aliases": [{"id": "sonnet", "name": "Sonnet", "detail": "The harness's latest Sonnet",
   "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "version": "5.5"}],
 "models": [{"id": "claude-opus-5-5", "name": "Claude Opus 5.5", "family": "claude-opus",
   "released": "2026-…", "tool_call": true}],
 "docs_url": "https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config"}
```

Read from the public [models.dev](https://models.dev) catalogue, which needs no
key: no credential leaves the engine to name models, and whether a plan reaches
one is what the test call says. Claude Code reads provider `anthropic`, Codex
`openai`, Gemini CLI `google` and Grok `xai`; OpenCode and Pi name their
`provider` and are offered `<provider>/<id>`. Every other built-in harness names
its own models and is answered its aliases and page with `"source": "none"`. An
alias's `model` and `version` are what it resolves to on the vendor's service,
from the harness profile, and are absent where the profile does not know. A copy
is kept for a day and revalidated; a catalogue that cannot be read keeps the
last copy and says how old it is in `reason`; with no copy the answer is
`"source": "none"` with `models: []` and the `reason`. `400 bad_params` for an
unknown `harness`, `custom`, or OpenCode or Pi without `provider`; `422
unknown_provider` for a provider the catalogue does not list.

#### `PUT /llm/providers/{key}/credential`

```json
{"values": {"ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_SONNET": "sk-ant-api03-…"},
 "entity": {"harness": "claude-code", "model": "sonnet",
   "auth": {"mode": "api-key", "api_key": "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_SONNET}"}}}
```

**Tested before it is stored.** In this order:

1. The target is the active entry, or the draft `entity` (a create, or an edit
   that changes how it signs in), validated by splicing it into a copy of the
   active document as the entity route's dry run does (`422 validation_error`
   with problems under `providers.llm.<key>`). `404 not_found` for an absent key
   with no `entity`; `403 config_managed` for a draft on a managed document.
2. Every name must be a variable the entry reads (`422 validation_error` at
   `["values", NAME]`), and a value of the wrong kind by its vendor's prefix (an
   API key in a token's slot, or the reverse) is refused there too, before any
   call. Whitespace around each value is trimmed; a value holding a space, line
   break, tab or invisible formatting character inside is refused at the value
   with how many and where ("This token contains 2 spaces (characters 66 and
   67)."): a terminal that wraps a long token turns the break into spaces when
   copied, and Claude Code ignores such a token outright.
3. `If-None-Match: *` refuses a name already stored: `412 already_exists` with
   `names`, so a create never overwrites a secret another model reads. It is
   decided again at the seal, in one step of the store's: a name another write
   stored while this one was tested is the same `412`, with `sealed` naming
   what this write stored before it, and nothing is re-activated.
   **A create is keyed** by its operation key: the `Idempotency-Key` header,
   or one minted for it, scoped by the caller as on every keyed route. Each
   row it seals carries the key. A create that stopped part way (a `500` with
   `sealed`, or a `412` on a later name) answers `op_id`. The same request sent
   again under that key re-seals the names its key sealed, within a day of
   their seal by the engine's own clock (never the time the key carries, which
   its caller writes), with the values it sends now, and creates the rest. Any
   other create naming them is `412`, whatever value it sends: the store is
   never read for a value, so no answer says whether a guess equals what is
   stored. The key is in no other answer, listing, log or audit row.
4. When the write will re-activate the company, `config.write` is asked before
   anything is tested or sealed.
5. The candidate values are handed to the model's own harness, in an isolated
   home, for one one-turn call, within the entry's `timeout_seconds` capped at
   120 s. That call is the whole test: the check's `shell` and `web` lines say
   their probes were skipped (they read what the entry lets its harness reach,
   which a credential does not change); the entry's own
   [check](#post-llmproviderskeycheck) probes them.
   A refusal is `422 credential_rejected` at the value, and nothing is stored.
   Its `detail` says what the failure meant rather than quoting the harness: the
   vendor refused the credential (wrong, expired or revoked, with the command
   that makes a new token where the harness has one), or the harness never used
   it, so the vendor never saw it (the profile's `auth_markers`
   `meaning: unread`). The harness's own words stay on the check's lines, and a failing
   line carries `meaning` (`refused` or `unread`) beside its `kind`. A vendor
   that did not answer is `502 credential_untested`; a harness that cannot run
   (no binary) is `422 validation_error` at `providers.llm.<key>.harness` with
   the doctor's remedy. A `429` passes: it proves the credential authenticated,
   and the answer's `limited` says so, 
   `{"until", "resets_at", "window", "said"}`, with `until` null (a test sits nothing out) and `resets_at` the
   vendor's reset when it named one.
6. With `dry_run=true` the answer is `200 {"ok": true, "verified", "hints",
   "check", "limited"}` and nothing is stored.
7. Each value is sealed (source `models`), and the revision that reads any of
   them is [re-activated](#a-secret-write-re-activates-the-revision-that-reads-it)
   once, held to `If-Match` when the caller sent one. From here the write
   finishes even when the caller disconnects. A seal that fails part way is
   `500 internal_error` with `sealed`, the names stored before it, and
   re-activates nothing; send the values again.

```json
{"verified": "Answered a one-turn Claude Code run in 3.4 s with only this value.",
 "check": {"at": "…", "node": "node-1", "ok": true, "lines": [{"check": "binary", "ok": true, "detail": "…"}]},
 "names": ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_SONNET"], "hints": {"ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_SONNET": "sk-ant-api03-…7d2K"},
 "entries": ["sonnet"], "reload": {"revision_id": "…", "epoch": 42},
 "cleared": ["sonnet"], "running_runs": 1, "limited": null}
```

`entries` is every model that reads one of the names, which all sign in with it
now; `cleared` the ones this node had sitting out on the replaced sign-in, which
start clean; `running_runs` the executor runs still running on them, which keep
the old credential until their segment ends (`null` when it could not be
counted). A re-activation that raced another write answers `200` with
`reload.error: "revision_advanced"`: the values are sealed and stay.

#### `POST /llm/providers/{key}/check`

`{"smoke": true}` checks the active entry, `{"smoke": true, "entity": {...}}`
a draft, which resolves its `${VAR}`s through the store as an apply would. The
body carries **no credential value**: a typed credential is tested by the
credential route's dry run. A check of an existing entry is a real call on its
sign-in, so its outcome is remembered as any call's is.

**The check runs on the answering node's own time.** With its smoke calls it
makes up to four harness runs within 180 s, longer than the two minutes of
silence a proxy in front of the API is asked to allow
([Deployment](../guides/deployment.md)), so the node starts it, waits up to two
seconds, and answers `202 Accepted` with the check running and `Location:
/llm/providers/{key}/check` — or `200` where it ended within those two seconds,
as a check without `smoke` does. Either answer, and `GET` on the same path from
any node, is the check:

```json
{"id": "…", "entry": "sonnet", "node": "node-1", "state": "running",
 "draft": false, "smoke": true, "started_at": "…", "deadline": "…",
 "ended_at": null, "by": "jane.doe",
 "check": {"at", "node", "ok", "failure", "lines": [{"check", "ok", "detail", "kind", "remedy"}]},
 "failure": "…"}
```

`state` is `running`, `ended` or `lost`. An ended check carries `check`, one
line per check (`binary`, `version`, `sign-in`, `usage`, `smoke`, `shell`, `web`,
`executor`), each line's `detail` and `remedy` cut, longest first, where the
answer would pass 64 KiB; or `failure`, why it found nothing (the node running
it stopped, or the model was removed while it ran). A check still running past
its `deadline` is `lost`, its `failure` naming the node, which stopped before it
could record the end. `GET /llm/providers/{key}/check` answers the latest check
for ten minutes after it ended, or after its deadline, then `404`; the apply that
removes the model removes it at once.

**One check of a model at a time, across the fleet.** Asked while one runs, with
the same `smoke` and no draft, the route answers the running check (`202`)
rather than starting another. Any other ask while one runs (a draft, or the
other `smoke`) is `409 check_in_progress` with the `running` check. A check
asked of a node that has begun to stop is `503 unavailable` with the drain's
`Retry-After`. `404`, `422 validation_error` for a draft.

#### `POST /llm/providers/{key}/retry`

`{"mode": "probe"}` makes one call within 60 s on the answering node and, if
it answers, clears the sit-out on every node. A limit met again is
`{"cleared": false, "still": {"until", "resets_at", "window", "said"}}` and
clears nothing. A probe that failed for any other reason (a refused sign-in, a
vendor that did not answer) clears nothing and says why in `failed`, present
only then, so the person tests the model rather than retrying again.
`{"mode": "clear"}` clears it at once, and every chain parked on the model
probes again. `200 {"cleared", "mode", "node", "still", "failed"}`;
`404`; `409 not_sitting_out` for a probe of a model no live node sits out.

#### `POST /llm/providers/{key}/host-login/check`

Runs the harness's own status command on the answering node:
`{"node", "state": "signed_in" | "signed_out" | "unknown", "method", "account",
"checked_at", "command": "crewlet llm login <key>", "shares_login_with": [...]}`.
`shares_login_with` is every model on the same harness and login directory, which
one login signs in. It never signs anything in: `command` is what to run on that
node. `404`; `422 no_host_login` for a model that signs in with a token, a key
or its env.

#### Device sign-in

`POST /llm/providers/{key}/device-sign-in` (body `{}`) starts the harness's
device-code sign-in on this node and answers `201` as soon as the harness printed
its code: `{"id", "entry", "node", "url", "code", "status": "pending",
"started_at", "expires_at"}`. The person approves at the vendor's page; nothing
is pasted back. On approval the node seals the login as the model's credential
bundle and re-activates, so every node restores it, and the record's `reload`
names the revision. `GET /llm/device-sign-ins/{id}` reads it (`status`
`starting`, `pending`, `approved`, `failed`, `expired` or `cancelled`, a
`detail` on failure) until ten minutes after its code expires, then `404`.
`DELETE /llm/device-sign-ins/{id}` cancels it: `200 {"id", "status":
"cancelled"}`, forwarded to the node running it.

Refusals: `404`; `409 sign_in_in_progress` with the `running` session;
`422 no_device_sign_in` for a harness with none or a model whose sign-in reads no
login (an API key or its env); `502 device_sign_in_unavailable` with the harness's
first line when it printed no code in time.

### Concurrent writes

**There is no leader**: any node's API can write the config, and the activation pointer in the coordination KV is the shared truth. Writes take no lock, but a concurrent one is *detected*: the activation is a compare-and-set.

- Every write reads the fleet's revision from the pointer, derives from it, and names it as the new revision's parent. The activation lands only while the pointer still names that parent; a write that lost is refused **`revision_advanced`**, **whether or not the caller sent `If-Match`**. A pointer removed since the read (deleted, or lost with a rebuilt coordination store) refuses it the same way: read `/config` again and rebuild the edit. The status follows RFC 9110 §13.1.1: **`412`** where `If-Match` named a revision, **`409`** where it named none or sent `If-Match: *` (that a company exists is still true of the winner). A write whose `If-Match` is another resource's tag (a charter write's, a per-entity write's), and a reload or a revert, lose as `409`.
- `If-Match: <revision_id>` is still worth sending: it is checked before any work, so a caller editing a moved revision is told without a document being built, validated and stored first.
- A losing write's revision **is kept**: the `409` (or `412`) names it as `stored_revision_id`, beside the **`node`** that served the write. It is valid, inert history on that node alone: `GET /config/revisions/{id}/diff` and `POST /config/revisions/{id}/revert` reach it there, by that node's own address where a load balancer or shared Service fronts several; any other node answers `404`. No node boots on a revision until its own engine has applied it, so the loser is never offered to the fleet at a restart.
- **What `/config` answers and what a node runs are two facts.** `/config` answers the fleet's revision on every node. A node runs the revision its engine last applied, which trails the pointer by an apply and stays behind it on a node that refused the fleet's revision (a missing environment variable, an MCP binary its image lacks). Such a node keeps running what it served and restarts onto the revision its boot row names. Its row in [`GET /fleet`](#get-fleet) names the revision it refused, `config_applied_epoch` (the epoch it last applied), `config_serving_revision_id` (the revision it runs) and `config_boot_revision_id` (the one it would boot on: the same as the one it runs, except while a write to its boot row is retried; absent on a node whose database is discarded at every start, `store.scratch`, so every node without the `data` role, which boots on nothing and applies the fleet's revision from scratch). Writes through such a node are built on the fleet's revision and land, so the write that corrects a refused revision can go to any node, that one included.
- **With no pointer, every write is a create.** When the coordination store holds no activation (a new fleet, or a lost pointer, such as a rebuilt external NATS cluster or a removed bucket), `/config` answers the company this node knows: a change an offline command made on the fleet's revision as this node last saw it, else that revision (refused here or not), else the revision it boots on (see [Control Plane](../concepts/control-plane.md#a-nodes-own-store-keeps-three-facts-apart)); `404 no_active_revision` when it knows none. Every write is then a **create-only compare-and-set**: it lands only while the fleet still has no activation, and the first to land is the fleet's pointer again. A node that joined a running fleet and has not reconciled yet reads the same pointer as every node, so `If-None-Match: *` there is `412 already_configured`. Replacing a running company would rename it, change every seat id derived from the name and orphan their memory.
- **The boot publish is a compare-and-set too.** A starting node publishes at most one revision. A change an offline command made on it (`crewlet config import`, `activate` or `rekey` while its engine was stopped) is published only while the fleet still runs the revision that change was built on, expecting the very activation the start read (or the earlier offline change it replaced, where a start published that one and could not confirm it); with no pointer, when that is the revision this node last saw the fleet run. Otherwise, over a lost pointer or a pointer another node **restored** naming a revision this node holds that was activated before the one it last saw, it publishes the fleet's revision it last saw (having seen none, the one it boots on). A pointer somebody chose is the company however old its instant, and no boot replaces it. A publish that loses re-reads the pointer and decides again, so a write landing while a node starts is never replaced. An offline change the fleet has moved on from is withheld, never published over the fleet, and the node logs `offline_revision_not_published` at warn: at every start while the change is what it boots on, and once more when it applies the fleet's revision, which replaces the change as what it boots on and keeps it as history. The hint names the change: `GET /config/revisions/{id}/diff?against=<built_on>` on that node shows what the offline change did, to make again on the fleet's document; `POST /config/revisions/{id}/revert` there puts it up as it stands, undoing what the fleet changed since. See [What a booting node publishes](../concepts/control-plane.md#what-a-booting-node-publishes). The one unconditional activation is `crewlet run -import-company`, which replaces whatever the fleet runs with its file.

On either, re-read `/config` and send the edit again.

### Status codes

- `200 OK`: a successful read, a [dry run](#dry-runs) that found the write valid (`{"valid", "base_revision_id", "warnings", "derived"}`), or a [charter](#the-charter-mission-vision-and-policies) write (`{"charter", "changed", "revision_id", "epoch"}`), which replaces a resource rather than creating one
- `201 Created`: a write produced a new revision: `{"revision_id", "epoch", "warnings", "derived"}` (see [What a write answers](#what-a-write-answers)). A per-entity write, a reload and a revert return it too.
- `400 Bad Request`: `invalid_body`, `invalid_patch` or `validation_error`, each with `detail` (the field path and what to change) and [`problems`](#refusals-carry-located-problems); `summary_required` when a write has neither an `X-Summary` header nor a `_summary` body key (asked last, once the write is admitted and its document checked, so a caller who may not make the change gets the `403` first); `summary_too_long` with `summary_bytes` and `max_summary_bytes` when the summary is past the 4,096 bytes the activation pointer carries, measured as the pointer encodes it (refused, never cut); `origin_too_long` with `pointer_bytes` and `max_pointer_bytes` when the name the write was made under leaves the pointer past its 8 KiB; `invalid_query` when `dry_run` is not `true` or `false`; `identity_mismatch` when a per-entity body renames what the path addresses; `conflicting_preconditions` when a write sends `If-Match` beside `If-None-Match`
- `401 Unauthorized`: `invalid_token` for a missing or invalid bearer token, in the same [refusal envelope](#every-refusal-is-one-envelope) every route answers with, written by the guard before any route runs
- `403 Forbidden`: `unauthorized` when the credential holds neither the grant nor, on the org chart, the lead relation (`reason` is the rule that refused; `refused` lists [a lead's write](#a-lead-edits-their-own-team)'s); `step_up_required` for a write whose proof of identity is older than `step_up`, whether the route or the write's parts found it; `config_managed` when `api.auth.company_writers` names the document's writers and this credential is not one of them (a person's session, a machine token and a lead's write among them), with `managed_by`, `detail` and `hint`, for a write and its dry run alike, never a read or a reload, asked before the body is read (see [Managed configuration](../concepts/configuration.md#managed-configuration))
- `404 Not Found`: a revision that is not there; `no_active_revision` on a read when nothing is configured (no activation and this node knows no company); `no_such_entity` on a per-entity read or write naming an id the active revision does not carry (of a seat or a unit, told only to `admin`; anybody else gets `403` as for one outside their team); `no_route` for a `/config` path this surface does not serve
- `405 Method Not Allowed`: `method_not_allowed` for a `/config` path under a method it does not take, with `Allow`
- `409 Conflict`: `revision_advanced` (a race with a concurrent writer or the pointer's removal, for a write that named no revision in `If-Match`); `no_active_revision` (a `PATCH`, a charter write, a per-entity write or a reload when nothing is configured); `seat_held` when a write takes away a human seat somebody holds or is invited to (see [What a write answers](#what-a-write-answers)); `unreadable_revision`, `unsealed_revision`, `unreadable_fleet_revision`, `unsealed_fleet_revision` or `unknown_seal_revision` when the revision a read or write needs does not open on this node (see [A revision this node cannot open is refused, whichever route reads it](#a-revision-this-node-cannot-open-is-refused-whichever-route-reads-it)). A `revision_advanced` from a write that lost at its activation names the kept revision as `stored_revision_id` and its node as `node` (see [Concurrent writes](#concurrent-writes))
- `412 Precondition Failed`: `revision_advanced` when `If-Match` names a revision that is not the fleet's or stops being so before activation (naming the kept revision and its `node` as the `409` does where it lost at activation); `already_configured` when `If-None-Match: *` meets an active revision (a create-only write that lost at activation names the kept revision and `node` likewise); `no_active_revision` when `If-Match` names a revision and none is active; `version_moved` when a charter write's or per-entity write's `If-Match` names a charter or entity that has changed, carrying it as `current` and its `etag`
- `428 Precondition Required`: `bad_if_match` for a charter write with no `If-Match`
- `415 Unsupported Media Type`: `unsupported_patch_media_type` when a `PATCH` body is a patch format other than a JSON Merge Patch, with `Accept-Patch`
- `503 Service Unavailable`:
  - `unavailable` when the coordination store cannot be read, so the fleet's revision cannot be either (every write and every read that needs it), with `Retry-After: 2` and a `reason`.
  - `unavailable` for any other node condition (a store too busy to take a write's revision, one closed while the node adopts a snapshot or shuts down, a state-log refusal behind a read, a request out of time), with a one-sentence `detail` and a `Retry-After` exactly where waiting clears it.
  - `unavailable` with **`"outcome": "unknown"`** when a write stored its revision and the coordination store did not answer the activation, which may have landed. The body names `stored_revision_id`, `your_base` (the revision the write was built on) and `node` (that stored it), with no `op_id`: the pointer says whether it landed, and `GET /config` names the stored revision or not once the store answers. Sending the write again makes another revision, over this one if it landed. If it did not, the stored revision is in that node's history alone: `GET /config/revisions/{id}/diff` shows it and `POST /config/revisions/{id}/revert` makes it the company **on that node**, reached by its own address behind a load balancer or shared Service; any other node answers `404`. Every write here can answer it (`PUT`, `PATCH`, a per-entity or charter write, a reload, a revert), and so can a [`/setup`](#supplying-them) submission.
  - `seat_holders_unavailable` when a write that takes a human seat away cannot read the identity directory to see who holds it: nothing was written, `seats` names the seats (none for a whole document [replacing an unsealed revision](#a-whole-document-replaces-an-unsealed-revision), which asks about every seat it does not keep), and a `Retry-After` comes where waiting clears it.
  - `draining` when the node has been told to stop, with a `Retry-After` (see [During a drain](#during-a-drain)).

### The `config_audit` query

Revision metadata for the dashboard's Configuration and Audit screens. **A query, not a REST route** (there is no `GET /config/audit`): it answers the revision records `GET /config/revisions` serves, as a bare array (the one question in the set that is not an object).

```
query config_audit { "limit": <N> }
```

| Parameter | Default | Range | Description |
|-----------------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `limit` | `50` | `1..500` | Revisions to return, newest first. An out-of-range number is CLAMPED to the range; a non-number reads as the default. |

Response (`200 OK`):

```json
[
  {
    "revision_id": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
    "parent_revision_id": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000",
    "created_at": "2026-05-17T10:31:02.118431Z",
    "created_by": "jane.doe",
    "created_by_kind": "operator",
    "operator_id": "pat:0192f00d-0000-7000-8000-00000000000a",
    "source": "api",
    "summary": "add Designer role",
    "is_active": true,
    "activated_at": "2026-05-17T10:31:02.118431Z"
  }
]
```

Payloads are NOT included; fetch a revision via `GET /config/revisions/{id}` for the full JSON.

The records are the revisions **this node** holds, and two fields are about the
fleet rather than the revision:

- **`is_active`** marks the fleet's revision, the one the activation pointer
  names: the same row on every node that holds it, whatever the answering node
  runs. A node that refused the fleet's revision marks the fleet's, not the one
  it still runs; what each node runs is [`GET /fleet`](#get-fleet)'s.
- **`activated_at`** is the latest activation of the revision this node has
  met, on every row alike, the revision it boots on included: raised by each
  activation this node's reconciler sees on the pointer and each it publishes,
  never lowered. The [retention
  sweep](../guides/retention.md#the-configuration-archive-and-the-one-thing-a-purge-cannot-reach)
  dates an old revision activated again by it. It is **not** the activation a node
  applied: a node that refused a re-activation of the revision it runs (the
  [rotation](../concepts/control-plane.md#rotation) gesture, on a node that lost
  the credential) reports the fleet's newer instant all the same. What each
  node runs is [`GET /fleet`](#get-fleet)'s; the instant its engine applied
  is the store's `served_at`, not carried here (see [A node's
  own store keeps three facts
  apart](../concepts/control-plane.md#a-nodes-own-store-keeps-three-facts-apart)).
  Absent on a revision nothing has activated, such as one that lost a race or
  an offline import not yet published.

`created_by` is the revision's author, `created_by_kind` its kind and
`operator_id` the credential it was written through (see [who a write is
attributed to](#who-a-write-is-attributed-to)), on this answer, on
`GET /config/revisions` and on `GET /config/revisions/{id}` alike. The kind is
one vocabulary across every trail the engine keeps (`agent`, `human`,
`operator`, `system`):

| `created_by_kind` | Who wrote the revision | `created_by` |
|---|---|---|
| `human` | A person (every person holds a seat), or a Tier A token or service account the identity directory binds to one, on `/config` or `/setup` | The seat's handle |
| `operator` | A credential nobody is bound through (a Tier A token or a service account bound to no seat) on `/config` or `/setup`; or whoever ran `crewlet config import` / `crewlet config rekey` on the host | The credential's login (`token:<id>` for a Tier A token), or the host login (`$CREWLET_OPERATOR`, else `$USER`) |
| `system` | The engine itself: a node seeding the store from its `-company` file at boot, or the reconcile loop's own writes (removing a disconnected integration, recording a discovered site, reloading after sealing a credential) | The node's id for a seed; `reconcile loop` for the loop |

`operator_id` is empty for every `system` revision and host-side CLI write.
Read the kind, not the label: the name spaces overlap. A revision reads the same
on every node, since the activation pointer carries its author, kind and
credential (see [Control Plane](../concepts/control-plane.md#the-design)). A kind
a newer engine adds arrives as itself.

### `GET /config/revisions/{id}/diff`

A **structural** diff of two revisions: one entry per path that moved, with
the value on each side. `?against=` names the other side and defaults to the
fleet's revision (`active`); the direction reads as "what `against` became", so a bare
call answers "what would reverting to this change". The dashboard gets the same
answer as the `config_diff` query.

```json
{
  "from": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000",
  "to": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
  "changes": [
    { "path": "providers.llm.main.model", "kind": "changed",
      "from": "claude-sonnet-5", "to": "claude-opus-5" },
    { "path": "mcp_servers[1].url", "kind": "added", "to": "https://mcp.example.com/sse" }
  ],
  "changes_total": 2
}
```

`kind` is `added`, `removed` or `changed`, and `from`/`to` are absent on the
side where the path does not exist. **Both sides are redacted**, always: a
rotated credential shows as a changed mask and never as either value.

**`changes_total` is how many differences there are; `changes` is how many
this answer carries**: the listing is cut at 500 entries, so render the total
and say what was left out. `crewlet config diff` prints every change.

`changes` is always a list: two identical revisions answer `[]` with a
`changes_total` of `0`, never `null`.

---


#### `POST /config/reload`: after a secret changes

Takes no body and changes nothing. It stores a **new revision carrying the
fleet's document** and activates it over the fleet's revision, which advances
the epoch and makes every node apply again. Whichever node it is sent to, it
re-publishes the fleet's revision, on a node that refused that revision too,
never the one the node still runs.

That is the gesture a rotated credential needs: a `${VAR}` secret pointer is
resolved from a snapshot taken at apply time, so only a new apply refreshes it.
A write through `/secrets` of a name the active revision reads does this same
reload itself ([above](#a-secret-write-re-activates-the-revision-that-reads-it));
the route is for a value written any other way (engine stopped, a store an
external broker holds) and for a write whose own re-activation answered an
error. A new revision, never a re-pointed old one, keeps history append-only.
`X-Summary` names it; unset, it records `reload configuration`.

Answers `201` with the revision, its epoch and its warnings (see
[What a write answers](#what-a-write-answers)),
`409 no_active_revision` when nothing is configured, `409 revision_advanced`
when another write moved the pointer between the reload's read and its
activation, and `400 validation_error` when the active document breaks a
runnable rule of this build (a reload is an apply, so it re-publishes only a
company every node can run; correct it with `PUT` or `PATCH`). A document that
breaks only an [admission rule](../concepts/configuration.md#what-a-stored-revision-is-held-to),
such as two sandbox setup steps of one name a newer peer admitted, reloads, so a
credential rotation still reaches a company carrying one; its
answer lists each violation as an `admission` warning.

On a **stopped** node the same gesture is
[`crewlet config activate <UUID>`](cli.md#crewlet-config-activate) naming the
company's own revision, the one [`crewlet config revisions`](cli.md#crewlet-config-revisions)
marks `fleet's`. It opens the node's own store, so it cannot run beside that
node's engine, and makes an offer: the node publishes it at its next start as a
new activation of the same revision, but only while the fleet still runs the
revision the offer was built on (or, with no pointer, while that is the
revision this node last saw the fleet run). If the fleet has moved on
meanwhile, the offer is withheld and the node says so at warn, as
`offline_revision_not_published`; once it applies the fleet's revision it runs
that one, and boots on it once its boot row has moved, and the offer stays in
its history. A running fleet takes this route.

**Open on a managed document.** A reload changes no byte of the company, so
[`api.auth.company_writers`](../concepts/configuration.md#managed-configuration)
does not refuse it: it is how a credential somebody rotated in an emergency
reaches the running seats when the system that manages the document cannot
know it has to.
#### Stored revisions are read as they are

A read never validates. `GET /config`, a revision read, a diff, the reference index, the entity reads and the prior a write restores its masks from all open a stored revision as it is, even one this build's validator would refuse (a later build can leave one in the store). Validation happens only where a document would RUN, to the rules that question needs:

- **A write** (`PUT`, `PATCH`, a per-entity `PUT`, a `/setup` submission that changes the document) validates the whole document it produces against every rule, admission rules included. A revision this build refuses stays readable, a corrected `PUT` or `PATCH` replaces it, and a write that leaves it uncorrected is refused `400 validation_error`, even when the write touched nothing near the problem.
- **A reload or a revert** (including a `/setup` submission that only rotates a sealed credential, which reloads) validates what it re-activates against the runnable rules only. A revert to a revision that breaks one answers `400 validation_error` naming the field; a revert to one that breaks only an admission rule is accepted, and each node logs `org_admission_warning` when it applies it.

#### A revision this node cannot open is refused, whichever route reads it

A read does not skip the **seal**. Every reader, and a revert and a write whose prior it is (except the one write [below](#a-whole-document-replaces-an-unsealed-revision)), opens the revision under the node's keyring first. One that does not open is answered `409` naming it (`revision_id`) under one of five codes, each with its own remedy; the first two are met in this node's own copy or only through the fleet's pointer:

- **`unreadable_revision`**: sealed under a key the keyring no longer holds. `hint` says to put that key back in the node's `secrets.keys`.
- **`unsealed_revision`**: stored **without a seal**. A node reads only sealed revisions, because the seal says a node of this fleet wrote it; a plaintext one could come from anything that reached the store, so it can't be shown, compared, edited or reverted to. `hint` says an admin sends the whole document again from their own copy with `PUT /config`, or imports it with `crewlet config import`; either stores it sealed (see [below](#a-whole-document-replaces-an-unsealed-revision)).
- **`unreadable_fleet_revision`**: the fleet's revision, met only through the pointer with no row held, is sealed under a key this node was never given. `hint` says to add it to this node's `secrets.keys` and restart.
- **`unsealed_fleet_revision`**: the fleet's revision arrived on the pointer **without a seal**, so it came from outside the fleet (every node seals what it activates). `hint`: an admin sends the whole document with `PUT /config`, or imports it with `crewlet config import`; either stores it sealed and activates it.
- **`unknown_seal_revision`**: **sealed in a form this build does not read**, in this node's own copy or the fleet's, most likely by a newer build. It is somebody's document, not an unsealed one, so no write replaces it, `PUT /config` included. `hint` names the build that sealed it: upgrade this node to the build the rest of the fleet runs, or run that build here again where this node's own copy came from it.

`detail` says what happened; the keyring's own error goes to the node's log. The dashboard's config questions answer the same five codes, on the socket and on [`/query`](#live-stream), with `detail` and `hint` as one sentence on the frame's `detail`. A [`/setup`](#supplying-them) write that meets one answers them too, naming what it sealed before as `wrote_secrets`. None is a `500 internal_error`.

#### A whole document replaces an unsealed revision

`PUT /config`, with or without `?import=true` and as a `?dry_run=true` check, is accepted over an active revision stored without a seal, and reads **nothing** from it, as an offline `crewlet config import` does. It is still the revision the write is built on: `If-Match` and `If-None-Match` are judged against it, and the activation is conditioned on it. Reading nothing means:

- **No mask is restored.** A credential still holding the redaction marker has no value behind it and is refused `400 validation_error`, the problem naming the field and saying to write the real value or a `${VAR}` reference. Every other problem is reported beside it.
- **Nothing a newer build wrote is carried back**: [that rule](#fields-a-newer-build-wrote-survive-every-write) holds only for a revision that opens.
- **It is judged as a document replacing nothing.** Against nothing a write changes every setting, so only `admin` replaces one; a lead is refused `403 unauthorized`, `refused` listing every part outside their team, the company's settings among them. The charter's rules are judged as for a first write, which warns, and `?import=true` keeps its own rules.
- **Every held seat is kept.** With no revision to say which seats the write takes away, it asks the identity directory about every seat the document does not keep as a human seat. One somebody holds (a person at any stage short of removal, a service account, an open invitation) is refused `409
seat_held` as a [removal](#what-a-write-answers) is. Its `detail` names the seats the document doesn't keep, a seat no revision names any more included; `hint` offers keeping each as a human seat first, since freeing one by moving a person to another human seat needs a company running on the node, which a node with an unsealed active revision may lack. A node that cannot read the directory refuses `503
seat_holders_unavailable`, naming no `seats`.
- **A body the fleet's pointer carried is not kept.** Where the unsealed revision is this node's own copy, the new revision names it as its parent, as the offline import does. One met only through the pointer never enters this node's history, so the new revision names no parent, and its activation is still conditioned on it.

Every other write (`PATCH /config`, a per-entity `PUT`, a revert, `PUT
/config/charter`, a `/setup` submission, `POST /config/reload`) is built from the active document and is refused over an unsealed one with the same `409`. Over a revision that is sealed but does not open here (a key the keyring lacks, or a form this build does not read), every write is refused, `PUT /config` included: giving the node that key or build recovers the document whole, while a replacement would discard every credential and field in it.

#### Fields a newer build wrote survive every write

During a rolling upgrade an older node holds, byte for byte, documents a newer node wrote, including settings the older build has no field for. `GET /config` there cannot show them, so a document read there and sent back never names them. Every write keeps them anyway: `PUT`, `PATCH`, a per-entity `PUT`, a reload and a revert store a document built from the stored bytes and carry back each key the writing build cannot represent that the write does not name.

- **Only keys the writing build cannot decode are carried.** A key it knows and the write left out was removed on purpose and stays removed. A caller of the older build cannot name an unknown key (the strict reader refuses it), so no write through it can mean to remove one.
- **A list member is matched by identity, not position**: a seat by its handle and a unit by its key anywhere in the document, so a seat moved to another unit keeps its settings; an MCP server or a sandbox setup step by its name within its own list. An identity held twice in the stored document, or empty, matches nothing. A member of a list with no identity keeps nothing the write replaced.
- **A `PATCH` replaces only what it names.** Everything else is stored as it was, so a list the patch leaves alone keeps every member's settings, and a member with no identity loses a newer build's settings only when the patch replaces its list.
- **A reload and a revert store the document exactly as stored**, since neither changes it.
- **A renamed MCP server or setup step is a new identity**, so it keeps none of the old one's unknown settings.

### `/artifacts/{id}/data/*`: an artifact's datastore (auth-gated)

An artifact page published with the `db` capability keeps its rows in the artifact's **datastore**: named collections of JSON documents, each declaring its columns (checkbox, chip, select, person, status, text, long text, number, date) and its rules (who reads its rows, who writes them, which fields only a person may set, which are written once). Every route is decided **per artifact**: the caller's role on it, through the owner's standing or a share, is read from the artifact's head on every request and stamped into the write, and the applier decides from that stamp and the store's rows alone, so every data node reaches the same verdict. An artifact the caller has no relation to is `404` `not_found`, as one that does not exist.

| Method | Path | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/{collection}` | One page of a collection's documents (`limit`, 100 by default, at most 500; the `cursor` a page answered as `after`), each with its fields, who created and last changed it, and its `version`. `since=` a version answers only what changed after it, deletions included: the catch-up after a reconnect. Each page answers `through`, the `since` of the next catch-up, which a client adopts only once the read's last page (no `after`) is in: a whole read's pages answer the version its first page was read at, so a document changed under an already-read page is caught up, not skipped. A catch-up from before a read rule changed, a collection was dropped with its deletions, or a row changed hands in an `own_rows` or `private` collection answers `resync` (read whole). The query `artifact_data` |
| `GET` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/{collection}/{doc}` | One document. The query `artifact_data_doc` |
| `GET` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/{collection}/query` | `q=` a query as JSON: up to 16 filters (`eq`, `ne`, `lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge`, `in`, `contains`, `prefix`) on declared columns, ANDed, an `order_by` and a `limit`, compiled to the field index. Every top-level field is indexed, and a nested path (`a.b`) once the collection lists it in `indexed`; a filter or order on any other path is `400` `bad_params`, naming it. The query `artifact_data_query` |
| `GET` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/history` | The store's last seven days of writes, newest first, narrowed by `collection`, `doc`, `field` (one cell's history) or `actor`: who wrote, through which surface, the verdict, each changed field's value before and after (over 4 KiB as its hash) and whether it can still be undone. In an `own_rows` or `private` collection each change is shown by the row's creator when it was made, never its creator now. The query `artifact_data_history` |
| `GET` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/schema` | The store's collections, its footprint against its quota, its state digest and the caller's role. A collection only editors may read is left out below editor. The query `artifact_data_schema` |
| `GET` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/state` | The caller's own per-viewer state keys on this artifact, nobody else's. The query `artifact_data_state` |
| `GET` | `/artifacts/data/usage` | The company's datastore footprint against `artifacts.limits.data_bytes` *(needs `admin`)*. The query `artifact_data_usage` |
| `POST` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/writes` | **One atomic batch**: `{"ops": [...]}`, 1 to 100 ops of `set`, `merge`, `delete`, `increment`, `append`, `add` and `remove`, at most 1 MiB, applied all or none. An op with `if_version` is a conflict when its document moved since; one without is a blind write, and where two blind writes meet, each field keeps the value the log ordered last |
| `POST` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/undo` | `{"seq": N}`: reverts one write of the last seven days, as a write of the caller's own under the same rules, conditioned on every document it changed being where it left them, else `409` `stale_version` naming it. `409` `not_undoable` (the detail says which) for a write older than the history, one that was refused, a schema change, one holding a value the history kept only as its hash, and one whose undo would restore more than one write carries (a bulk delete of large rows, inverse over 1 MiB). The history's `undoable` is false for each, so a client never offers an undo that cannot land |
| `POST` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/state` | `{"key", "value"}` or `{"key", "delete": true}`: sets or removes one of the caller's own per-viewer state keys, the backing of the page runtime's state API |
| `PUT` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/schema` | `{"collections": [...]}`, every collection the store keeps after the change *(editor and above)*. Decided against every write before it; a change that would rewrite more documents than one record carries is `422` `migration_too_large` |
| `GET` | `/artifacts/{id}/data/export.csv` | `collection=` one collection as CSV, streamed a page at a time *(editor and above)*, under the collection's read rule, written for a person: each column headed by its label (its key if none), choices as labels, a person as the seat's name, attribution under `ID`, `Created by`, `Created at`, `Updated by`, `Updated at` and `Version`, and any cell a spreadsheet would run as a formula written as text. A trashed artifact is `409` `artifact_trashed`, a purged one's store `410` `data_gone` |

Every read is a read of the artifact's content: a trashed artifact answers none (`409` `artifact_trashed` on routes and questions alike, to a reader it is disclosed to), and an administrator only the admin path admits is recorded as reading it before a row is sent, or answered `503` with nothing when that record cannot be written. Every write route takes an `Idempotency-Key`, refuses a field it does not declare, and refuses a write to a trashed artifact (`409` `artifact_trashed`; `410` `data_gone` is a purge's) until it is restored. A write from a browser session states its surface as `via`: `dashboard`, or `bridge` with the `version` of the page whose script made it, which must declare `db` (or `state`, for a state key) or the write is `403`. A bearer credential's write is stamped as the API's whatever it says.

**A write answers its verdict**, read back from the node's own rows once it has applied the record. `verdict` is the one field that says how the write ended, beside `op_id`, `position` and, once decided, the `seq` an undo names; a refusal carries it next to its `error`:

| Status | `error` | When |
|---|---|---|
| `200` | | `verdict: "applied"`, with the write's `seq`, which an undo names |
| `202` | | `verdict: "pending"`: the record landed and this node has not applied it yet, so its verdict is on the `position` answered |
| `409` | `stale_version` | An `if_version` that no longer matches; `conflict` names the documents |
| `422` | `invalid` | A value outside its column's type, a field the collection does not declare, a long text written whole without its guard |
| `403` | `forbidden` | The caller's role, or the column's rule, does not let them write it |
| `409` | `quota_exceeded` | The write would take what is kept past a limit: the store's or the company's footprint (a Tier A setting an operator raises), a collection's rows or one participant's rows (caps its schema sets), or the collections and documents one store holds. `detail` is the applier's reason, naming the limit. A write that shrinks the store is never refused for it |
| `410` | `data_gone` | The store was purged |
| `429` | `write_budget` | This node's write budget for the caller on this store, or for the store, is spent. Weighed by the rows a batch's apply writes (each named document's whole field index, not just the fields named), in units of sixteen rows: 20 units a second with a burst of 100 per caller and store; 40 a second with a burst of 100 per store. `Retry-After`, `scope` and `retry_after_ms` say when it holds the cost again. Per node, never a lockout |

Every refused write is still on the log and in the store's history with its reason, applied identically on every data node, so `GET .../history` answers what was refused as well as what landed.

## Setting an integration up

Connecting an integration puts a credential into the fleet's sealed secret store and everything else into the company document. `/setup` does both in the one safe order, so the dashboard never sequences it and never holds a credential across two requests.

**Every route takes a grant, reads included**, on the same terms as `/config` and `/secrets`: it answers with the *names* of the credentials a company holds, which are unset, and the pages at each third-party app an administrator would visit, a map of what to attack. Reading and connecting both take `admin` — see [what each route takes](#secrets--the-companys-credentials-auth-gated).

**On a managed document** (Tier A `api.auth.company_writers`), a submission that would write a pointer into the document, a disconnect, and the begin of an agent's GitHub App answer a credential the list does not name `403 config_managed` — the [same refusal `/config` answers](#config--live-config-management-auth-gated) — before a value is sealed, a teardown is queued or GitHub is asked for anything. A submission that only rotates a value the document already points at is not a change to it and is served, ending in a reload; so are the provisioning pass and its read-only check. A provisioning pass any operator starts may still record what it discovered into the document (where `integrations.jira` or `integrations.confluence` has no `cloud_id`, the Atlassian pass records the site's `cloud_id` and `site_url`), and that revision is written as the node (`reconcile loop`), not the credential that started the pass. A GitHub App creation carries the operator who began it in its signed state, so the callback records the app (its revision and sealed key) as that credential, and asks again before it exchanges GitHub's one-time code.

### The requirement list

`GET /setup/integrations/{kind}` answers what that third-party app needs, whether or not the company has configured it:

```json
{
  "key": "datadog",
  "configured": false,
  "enabled": false,
  "satisfied": false,
  "inbound_path": "/webhooks/datadog",
  "public_url": "https://engine.example.com/webhooks/datadog",
  "summary": "Crewlet registers a webhook so alerts reach your agents, and gives each agent its own Datadog account.",
  "prepare": [
    {"text": [{"text": "Sign in to Datadog as someone who can manage users and roles."}]},
    {"text": [
      {"text": "Create a key on your "},
      {"text": "API keys page", "url": "https://app.datadoghq.com/organization-settings/api-keys"},
      {"text": " and one on your "},
      {"text": "application keys page", "url": "https://app.datadoghq.com/organization-settings/application-keys"},
      {"text": "."}
    ], "yields": "app_key"},
    {"text": [{"text": "Paste both here and test them."}]}
  ],
  "requirements": [
    {
      "field": "api_key",
      "label": "API key",
      "kind": "secret",
      "config_path": "integrations.datadog.provisioning.api_key",
      "secret_name": "DATADOG_API_KEY",
      "required": true,
      "connect": true,
      "hint": [
        {"text": "Create one on your "},
        {"text": "API keys page", "url": "https://app.datadoghq.com/organization-settings/api-keys"},
        {"text": "."}
      ],
      "check_note": "It is tested together with the application key.",
      "present": false,
      "resolved": null
    }
  ]
}
```

**The words a form draws each have their own job**, so a form lays them out rather than running them together under one input:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `summary` | One sentence on what connecting the tool does, which the form opens with |
| `prepare` | The steps to take at the third-party app, in order: `text` (imperative, one sentence, as [vendor text](#vendor-text)), `grants` (the permissions, roles or scopes to grant, in the app's own words) and `yields` (the field the step produces a value for) |
| `caution` | `{"title", "body"}`: the one risk the tool's credential carries, absent where none is worth a warning |
| `hint` | A requirement's one line, under fifteen words, as [vendor text](#vendor-text): what the value is and where it is found |
| `more` | What a person may want once about the field, behind a disclosure, as vendor text: where else it is shown, what a check covers |

`summary`, `prepare` and `caution` are a tool's, carried by one surface of it: Atlassian's organization speaks for Jira and Confluence, whose own answers carry none. A `{field}` in `hint` or `more`, in its words or a part's `url`, reads what that field of the form holds, falling back to its `default`; a link is no link until each has a value.

#### Vendor text

Words a person follows at a vendor (a step, a field's `hint` and `more`, a set's `hint`, an identity's `where`, and an identity sheet's steps, note and hand-in ([ADR-0179](../../adr/0179-a-seat-may-hold-its-own-identity-at-a-growth-vendor.md))) are a list of parts, never a string with markup. Each part is `{"text"}` (plain words; a value to type is in backticks), or `{"ui": [...]}` (a name on the vendor's screen as it prints it, a button, field, role or page; several are a menu path, outermost first), either with `url`: the vendor page it links. A page is linked on the first words that name it, so no separate button repeats it.

`kind` is one of `secret`, `url`, `id`, `choice`, `text`, `handle`, `toggle`. Each third-party app's own package declares its list, so the surface serves an app it has no screen for and the dashboard renders one it has no code for. A `toggle` is a JSON boolean in the document; a `handle` must name a seat this company has.

A `secret`'s **credential** is never echoed. Its `value` carries the field's `${VAR}` reference when the document holds one: that is a *name* (which sealed-store entry the field reads), already visible through `GET /config` to anybody this surface answers, and without it a client could not tell "this reads `SHARED_TOKEN`" from "type here to replace what is behind this field". A document holding a **literal** there sends no `value`, and a composite such as `https://${HOST}/hook` counts as a literal: it names a variable beside an address, so it references nothing.

`present` and `resolved` are `secret_present` and `secret_usable` asked per field: written down, and usable in this process. `resolved` is `null` for a field the document leaves empty. `blocks` names the [reconcile finding](../concepts/integration-reconcile.md) that this input being absent produces, so a row reporting `credential_missing` can offer exactly the fields that clear it.

`mintable` means the engine can generate the value, so nobody is asked to invent it. **No route here ever returns a credential.** Most minted values are a random token; a field that signs takes an ES256 key, an ECDSA P-256 private key in PKCS#8 PEM, sealed whole and never shown. Where a person must hand the vendor something made from a minted value, the field carries `public`: `{"text": ..., "language": "sh"}`, text rendered from the public half alone (a key set, or a command block holding it), drawn as code to copy. A requirement whose public view would hold the value itself or any private key is never sent. A field that depends on a minted value is `required` only once that value is held, so the Save that mints it can leave the dependent field empty.

`multiline` marks a value that spans lines, a PEM private key, which a form draws in a box that keeps line breaks; `accept` names the file types it comes in (`.pem,.key`), for a file picker. A PEM key whose line breaks a one-line box dropped, or turned into spaces, is taken: its line breaks are written back before it is judged and sealed, and anything that is not one key of the field's kind is still refused.

`checkable` means the credential can be [checked at its vendor](#checking-a-credential-before-it-is-stored) before it is stored, so a form offers a Test button. A `secret` that cannot be checked ahead carries `check_note` instead: when the vendor proves it, which a form says after `more`. A webhook signing secret is the usual case: the vendor never presents it, only signs deliveries with it.

`check_with`, on a `checkable` field only, names the other fields of the same list that one check is made with, for a vendor that accepts or refuses several values together. A form offers one Test control after that field, enabled once it and every named field holds a value, and sends them in one request. A credential named there is not `checkable` on its own, and its `check_note` says where it is tested. Datadog alone uses it: `app_key` carries `"check_with": ["site", "api_key"]`. Absent, a field is checked on its own.

### Supplying them

```bash
curl -X POST https://engine.example.com/setup/integrations/datadog/inputs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
        "if_match": "<revision_id>",
        "values": {"enabled": "true", "route_to": "sre-lead"},
        "generate": ["webhook_token"]
      }'
```

`generate` is separate from `values` on purpose, so a client can't send a weak token by accident; a field is one or the other, never both.

**Any field the engine reads through the resolver may hold a `${VAR}`**, not only credentials: the Atlassian organization id, a site address, a cloud id and an account email all are, so a company can keep them in the sealed store and name them here. `present` and `resolved` then report separately, and a reference naming a missing entry reports `resolved: false`.

A field holding a reference also carries `resolved_value`: what that `${VAR}` currently reads as. Links this surface describes are built from values (the Atlassian API keys page is per-organization, so an organization id kept in the store would otherwise put the literal `${ATLASSIAN_ORG_ID}` in the path). **Never present on a `secret`**, on a literal, or on a reference naming nothing.

**A `secret` field's value may be a `${VAR}` instead of a credential.** The route writes that reference into the config path and seals nothing, so one stored credential can serve several fields and rotating it is one write. It needs no secret store in the answering process, because naming an entry is not writing one. Anything else in that position, a composite included, is a credential and is sealed under the field's own name.

What the route does, in this order:

1. **Refuses a stale base.** `if_match` names the revision the requirement list was read against: the fleet's, which `GET /setup/integrations` answers as `revision_id` on every node. An older one is refused *before anything is sealed*, so a stale page leaves no credential in the store that nothing points at. Without `if_match`, the submission is built on the revision this request read the fields from, in the same read: what each field holds (empty, a `${VAR}`, a literal) decides the write, so it lands on that revision or is refused `409 revision_advanced`.
2. **Seals every credential**, under the name the third-party app declared or one derived as `VENDOR_FIELD[_HANDLE]`. The row records `source: "setup"`.
3. **Patches the document** with the non-secret values and, for a credential whose slot was empty, a whole `${VAR}` pointing at the name from step 2. A slot already holding a `${VAR}` is written *through*, so rotating a credential changes the store, not the company. A slot holding a literal is `409 literal_in_config`, naming the path: overwriting it would edit the company from a setup form and destroy a credential somebody put there on purpose.
4. **Activates**, through the same merge, validation and compare-and-set `PATCH /config` performs. When the pointer needed no change (a rotation) it [reloads](#post-configreload-after-a-secret-changes) instead, because a value written to the store after the last apply is invisible to every running seat until something activates; the answer says `"reloaded": true`. The reload is held to the base of step 1 up to its own compare-and-set: a write landing between the read and the reload (one that put a literal in the slot, or the company from before the integration was connected) is `409 revision_advanced`.

Answers `201 {"revision_id", "epoch", "wrote_secrets", "reloaded", "state"}`. Refusals: `400 invalid_input`, `400 validation_error`, `404 unknown_kind`, `409 revision_advanced` (the body's `if_match` is stale), `409 literal_in_config`, `409 no_active_revision`; `409` under one of the five codes for a revision this node [cannot open](#a-revision-this-node-cannot-open-is-refused-whichever-route-reads-it), naming what the submission sealed before it as `wrote_secrets`; `503 unavailable` with a `Retry-After` when the coordination store cannot be read, or did not answer a credential's own write in step 2 (the body then names that credential as **`unanswered_secret`**, since its write may have landed), with a `detail` in a person's words for any other node condition (a store too busy to take the revision, one closed for a snapshot, a request out of time) and a `Retry-After` exactly where waiting clears it, and with `"outcome": "unknown"`, `stored_revision_id` and `node` when the document was stored and its activation went unanswered, as on [the config surface](#status-codes). A `409 revision_advanced` from a write that lost at its activation names the revision it kept, inert, as `stored_revision_id`, beside the `node` whose history alone holds it.

**A refusal after the first credential is sealed names what it sealed** as `wrote_secrets` (a lost race, an unanswered activation, an unreadable pointer, a later credential's failed write, a rotation's reload): the credentials are in the store whatever became of the document, nothing may point at them yet, and a resend overwrites them by name. So a `503` **without** `outcome` is sent again as it stands, whatever `wrote_secrets` and `unanswered_secret` it names: the document was not changed, and the resend writes every credential again, the unanswered one included. Only the `503` with `"outcome": "unknown"` is not, because its document may already be the company.

### Checking a credential before it is stored

`POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/verify` asks the vendor whether a typed credential works, with one read-only identity call, and **stores nothing**: not the value, not a `${VAR}` pointer, not a revision, not a reconcile finding. It is what a connect form's Test button calls, so a key is checked while the vendor's page is still open rather than by the next reconcile pass. It is `setup.connect`, the verb connecting is, because it spends a credential at a vendor on a person's hand.

```bash
curl -X POST https://engine.example.com/setup/integrations/datadog/verify \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"field": "app_key", "value": "<the typed key>",
       "values": {"site": "datadoghq.eu", "api_key": "${DATADOG_API_KEY}"}}'
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `field` | The requirement to check, by its `field`. It must be a `secret` |
| `value` | What was typed, or a whole `${NAME}` naming a stored secret |
| `seat` | The seat a per-seat credential belongs to, such as a Slack agent's bot token |
| `values` | The other fields typed in the same form, by `field`. Each may be a whole `${NAME}` too |

**Every field the person did not type is read as a submission would read it**: what the company document holds for it (a whole `${VAR}` resolved through this node's chain), else the field's `default`. So a key changed on a working integration is checked against the region, instance and other key already in force. Jira and Confluence are checked under the company's declared `integrations.atlassian.deployment`, and at the site the Atlassian organization names when neither the form nor the document gives one.

Answers `200 {"outcome", "summary", "facts", "warnings"}`, the shape every credential check answers in. None of it repeats the checked value.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `summary` | The answer in one sentence: that it works, or what failed |
| `facts` | What the check read, each a `label` and a `value`: who the credential is, what it reaches, when it expires, what the vendor said. Absent where none |
| `warnings` | What to act on, each a `title` (the risk) and an `action` (what to do). A failed check may omit `title` when `summary` already says what is wrong; `action` is always there. Absent where none |

| `outcome` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `works` | The vendor accepted it, and `facts` say who or what it authenticates as where the vendor says: "Works. Both keys are valid.", with the facts `Organization` Acme, `Site` datadoghq.eu and `They can read` Users, roles and webhooks. `warnings` carries any risk the credential holds, such as an expiry inside the warning window |
| `refused` | The vendor answered and refused it: a 401 or 403, Slack's `invalid_auth`, or a credential that authenticates without what the integration needs (a Mattermost account that is not a system administrator, a GitLab token without its scope, an Atlassian key created with scopes, a Slack user token where a bot token belongs). The vendor's own reason is a fact, labelled `<vendor> said`, where short, and `warnings` says what to do where the engine knows |
| `unreachable` | The vendor gave no answer about the credential: no connection, ten seconds without an answer, a `429` or `5xx`, or an answer that is not the vendor's API (often a wrong address). The last fact is `Stored` Nothing |
| `unchecked` | The field cannot be checked ahead without acting on it, and `summary` is its `check_note` |

What each surface checks, and with what:

| Surface | Checkable | Read-only call | Proved later, by the vendor's first delivery |
|---|---|---|---|
| `atlassian` | `api_key`, against `org_id` | one page of the organization's service accounts, which a scoped key is refused | |
| `confluence` | `token`, with `email` on Cloud | `GET /rest/api/user/current` | `webhook_token` (Cloud), `webhook_secret` (Data Center) |
| `datadog` | `app_key`, checked with `api_key` in `site` (`check_with`); `api_key` alone answers its `check_note` | in stages, stopping at the first refusal so the summary names the key or permission that failed: `GET /api/v1/validate` (the API key alone), `GET /api/v1/org` (both keys), then one row of `/api/v2/users` and `/api/v2/roles` and a read of the configured webhook (absent is fine). See [Testing the keys](../integrations/datadog.md#testing-the-keys-before-you-save-them) | `webhook_token` |
| `github` | `token`, at `url` for Enterprise Server | `GET /user` | `webhook_secret` |
| `gitlab` | `admin_token` (needs `api`) and `token` (needs `read_api`), at `url` | `GET /user`, then the token's own scopes and expiry where the instance describes them | `signing_secret` |
| `jira` | `token`, with `email` on Cloud | `GET /myself` | `webhook_secret` |
| `mattermost` | `admin_token`, at `url` | `GET /users/me`, and the `system_admin` role | |
| `slack` | a seat's `bot_token` | `auth.test` | a seat's `signing_secret` |

Refusals: `400 invalid_body` for an unknown key; `400 invalid_input` when `field` is not a requirement of that surface (or seat) or is not a `secret`, when `value` is empty, when a key in `values` is not a field of the surface, when a `${NAME}` names no stored secret ("There is no secret NAME."), when a typed value is one its field refuses as a save would (whitespace or an invisible character inside a credential, a space inside an address or identifier, a character outside the vendor's alphabet where the field declares one), with `field` and `path` and before any vendor is asked, and when the check cannot be made from what was given (Datadog's other key, a site address, an organization id), each with a sentence saying what is missing; `404 unknown_kind`; `404 invalid_input` for a seat that takes no per-seat setup; `409 no_active_revision`; `409` under one of the five codes for a revision this node [cannot open](#a-revision-this-node-cannot-open-is-refused-whichever-route-reads-it).

### Running the provisioning pass

Some third-party apps need something done *at* them, not just written down: a webhook registered, a signing secret minted and pushed. That is the app's provisioning pass, and `POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/provision` runs it.

**The reconcile loop does this on its own.** It runs the same provisioning function every few minutes with the sink and public base supplied, because connecting an integration is the permission: a person named that app and handed over an administrator credential for exactly this. This route is the same work on demand, for an operator who wants a pass now rather than at the next tick; it holds a fleet lease under its own name so the two never overlap. Nothing in the dashboard calls it.

`can_provision` on a tool's state says whether this build has a pass for it. `needs_operator` is present only for an app whose pass still asks for a credential per run; none in this build does. GitLab's group Owner token and Mattermost's system-admin token are ordinary **stored** requirements, sealed in the fleet secret store with a `${VAR}` in the document like every other credential. They are held because the **disconnect** needs the authority that created a service account, and without it every account the engine created would outlive its integration; a disconnect names them in `orphaned_secrets`, so an operator knows exactly what to revoke.
### Disconnecting

`DELETE /setup/integrations/{kind}` **asks**; it does not remove. It answers
`202` and records the intent on the fleet row; the reconcile loop removes what
the integration holds at the third-party app (the webhooks it registered, and
the accounts it created when asked) before the block leaves the company
document. The block carries the credential the teardown authenticates with, so
dropping it first would strand every webhook and account. Until the teardown
succeeds the surface reports phase `disconnecting`, labelled **Disconnecting**;
a failure holds it there and retries.

**The block and the agents on through it leave in one revision.** The company
document refuses an agent turned on at an integration the company has not
connected (Mattermost, Jira, Confluence, SSH), so the revision that removes the
block also turns off every seat that was on there: `enabled` becomes `false`
and the rest of the seat's block (roles, channels, projects, servers) is kept,
so connecting again and turning the agent on restores it. A seat already off,
or with no block, is left as it is. A forced disconnect answers the handles it
turned off as `seats_off`.

A failed teardown pass is recorded on the surface's reconcile row with
`teardown_held_by`: `vendor` where the third-party app's half failed, and
`settings` where that half finished and the company's settings refused the
revision that removes the block (some other rule the removal breaks, which
`last_error` names by path). Forcing writes the same revision, so a disconnect
the settings hold is moved by changing the setting, then disconnecting again.

```json
{ "remove_seats": false, "force": false }
```

`remove_seats` is the console's *"also remove the accounts Crewlet created"*.
It defaults to **false** and is never inferred: the engine's own webhooks come
out either way, but an account is a colleague at that third-party app with
history attached. Mattermost bots are **disabled** rather than deleted,
because deleting a Mattermost user takes its posts with it.

`force` drops the block immediately without waiting for the third-party app,
answers `200`, and is the way out of a teardown that can never succeed (a
revoked credential, an instance that is gone). The operator is saying they
will remove what the third-party app holds themselves. A forced disconnect may
carry `If-Match` naming the revision it was decided on; one the configuration
has moved past is `412 revision_advanced`, with nothing dropped. That is the
status `/config` answers the same header with; a connect, whose base is the
body's `if_match`, loses as `409`.

**Either way the removal is recorded as yours.** The intent carries who asked
(the author, their kind and the credential they asked through) and the loop
carries the teardown out for them: the revision that drops the block, each
Slack seat's cleared app credentials and the sealed values the teardown
deletes are recorded under that party, exactly as on the `force` path, not under the loop's own `reconcile loop` of kind `system`.

Either way the sealed credentials are **named, not deleted**, in
`orphaned_secrets`: one an operator may share with another deployment is not
for a disconnect to decide. `crewlet secrets unset` is the deliberate path.
The list is computed once, before the request splits, because every name is
derived from a `${VAR}` in the company document, which both paths end by
removing. It covers each seat's own credential too (the token a pass minted
under the name the seat's `mcp_env` points at, Atlassian's address slot beside
it, Slack's per-seat bot token and signing secret). The dashboard shows the
list rather than closing.

> **A credential a sibling surface still reads is not on the list.** Jira and
> Confluence normally share one seat credential (one Atlassian API token per
