> account, usually in the shared `mcp_env.atlassian` block), so disconnecting
> one product alone does not name a token the other still resolves. A sibling
> counts as a user unless it is itself disconnecting: the dashboard takes a
> card's surfaces in order, each request records its intent before the next,
> and the union the dialog shows names the shared credential exactly once.

> **GitHub's per-seat App credentials are on the list too.** Nobody typed
> them in: the engine converts a manifest and writes what GitHub returns, so
> an agent's `private_key` and its App's webhook secret exist without an
> operator choosing either name. They survive a disconnect by design: GitHub
> has no API for deleting an App registration, so the engine uninstalls the
> App and hands over a link to the page a person deletes it from. This list is
> the only place either value is mentioned.

Refusals: `503 surface_busy` when a reconcile tick or an operator's own pass is
writing at this surface right now. It is the one refusal here that clears on
its own, so it carries its own code: a caller that cannot tell a race from a
fault treats both as terminal (never `internal_error`). The request first waits a busy surface out for
a few seconds, then names it; repeating the request is correct, because every
step of a disconnect is idempotent. A busy surface is waited out rather than
skipped because the order matters: the organization's credential is what
removes the accounts. The `Retry-After` it carries (three seconds) is the
whole of how long the dashboard waits between attempts, for at most 45 seconds
in all; a `surface_busy` with no `Retry-After` is not waited out.

Refusals worth knowing: `409 requirements_outstanding` names the fields still
missing (a pass writes at the third-party app and must not run against a
half-configured integration), `409 no_external_url` when nothing has told
the engine what address third-party apps reach it on, and `409 pass_in_flight`
when another pass for the same third-party app is already running. That last
one is a refusal rather than a queue on purpose: a retry should not paper over
minting twice.

`POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/check` runs the **same pass with no sink**,
which makes it read-only: every vendor gates its registration and minting on
having somewhere to seal a credential, so a run without one reads and reports
and writes nothing at the third-party app. It answers "did what I just fixed
at the third-party app take".

A check **does** get the webhook address — `api.public.external_url` behind a
[public listener](#which-listener-serves-what), `api.external_url` otherwise, and the `409
no_external_url` refusal above is the writing route's alone; its `config_path`
names whichever of the two keys this node reads. Withholding the
address would make the check report `ingress_blocked` owed by an admin and, as
a check records findings through the same fold as everything else, flip the
card to **Action required** over a value that was already set. Supplying the
base is not the permission to register; having a sink is.

Both record their outcome on the same fleet integration status the reconcile
loop writes, through the same fold, so a pass run by hand and a later tick
cannot disagree, and Company › Integrations updates with no extra plumbing. A
pass that **failed** is recorded too, as the loop records one: phase
`activating`, actor `engine`, findings dropped, because a failed pass observed
nothing.

`recreate_webhooks` re-registers with a fresh secret and is **destructive
across deployments**: the previous secret stops working everywhere else this
company runs. On GitLab it also rotates every seat's token, which revokes the
credential each agent is currently authenticating with. A fresh secret is
minted into the whole `${VAR}` the secret's field names, so on GitHub, Jira
and Confluence a field holding a literal, or a reference inside other text,
has nowhere to put one; the pass is refused naming the field, its shape (never
its value) and `recreate_webhooks` itself. Point the field at a whole `${VAR}`
and send it again, or leave `recreate_webhooks` out to register the value the
field holds as it is. GitLab leaves a literal signing secret alone and
rotates the seats' tokens all the same.

**No pass on this surface deletes anything.** Decommissioning a service
account whose seat left the configuration stays a command-line gesture,
because a company mid-edit looks exactly like one that removed a seat.

### Per-seat setup

Two third-party apps put an agent's identity on the **seat** rather than the
company, because on both one app is one bot: Slack, whose credentials an
operator pastes in, and GitHub, whose app the engine creates. Both carry a
`seats` array in their tool state, one entry per agent seat. Every agent seat
is listed, configured or not, because a screen renders its form from the list;
human seats are excluded, as the engine holds no token for a person's Slack
account.

Slack's entries are a form: each agent has its own Slack app, so each has its
own bot token and signing secret, and every entry carries its own requirement
list, its own `inbound_path` and its own `satisfied`. A submission names the
seat:

```json
{"seat": "sre-lead", "values": {"bot_token": "...", "signing_secret": "..."}}
```

These write through the **entity route**, not a merge patch, because a merge
patch replaces an array wholesale and would delete every other seat. The
engine addresses the seat by its handle (its identity, not its position) and
everything the submission did not send stays as stored. The revision is
written as the caller, [attributed](#who-a-write-is-attributed-to) like every
other write here: a person connecting their seat through their own machine
token is its author, of their own kind, with `pat:<id>` beside them.

**Without an app configuration token it does not create the apps.** Creation
goes through Slack's app-manifest API, which authenticates with a
configuration token Slack issues only by hand and an organisation may decline
to allow. With one (the `app_config_token` field), the reconcile loop creates
and keeps every agent's app. Without one, this surface makes a hand-created
app usable: it takes the two values Slack shows on the app's own page and
seals them.

#### GitHub: the app the engine writes

A GitHub seat's entry carries **no requirement list**, deliberately: nothing
here is typed in. The app is created from a manifest, and GitHub returns its
id, slug and private key once, to the engine, which seals the key and records
the rest on the seat. The entry answers what is still outstanding for that
agent:

```json
{
  "handle": "builder",
  "name": "Builder",
  "requirements": [],
  "step": "install_app",
  "action_url": "https://github.com/apps/acme-builder/installations/new",
  "present": true,
  "satisfied": false,
  "detail": "the app exists and nothing has installed it, so it sees no repository and mints no usable token"
}
```

`step` and `action_url` are the two clicks, described under
[One agent's own GitHub App](#one-agents-own-github-app). What the seat may do
at GitHub is its own permissions, read and changed through
`GET /setup/integrations/{kind}/access` (with `github` as the kind) and `PUT`
on the same path, not part of this roster.

**`present`** is whether the seat has an app at all; **`satisfied`** needs that
app installed *and* its sealed key readable by this node. A `${VAR}` naming a
secret the store does not hold reads as configured everywhere else while the
agent mints no token, so `detail` names the variable to set (the reference,
never a key).

An unfinished roster does **not** hold the card open: the company block decides
whether deliveries arrive, and a company running apps for three of its ten
agents chose that.

**A seat is never `satisfied` on an integration the company does not
declare.** Its `detail` says the seat is waiting for the integration to be
connected.

**Nor is it `satisfied` when the reconcile loop has a finding about it.** The
document and sealed store only establish that a credential exists where the app
looks for one; a key deleted at the third-party app leaves the pointer
resolving while every call is refused. The loop is the only thing that has
asked the vendor, so a seat named by a finding on that surface's status row
comes back unsatisfied, with the loop's own sentence as its `detail`. Advisory
findings are skipped (a permission wider than the role asked for is a note on a
working agent).

One window stays open: between a credential being destroyed at the vendor and
the loop next looking, nothing knows. That window is
`integrations.check_interval_seconds` (600 by default, floor 60), and
`POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/check` asks immediately.

### One agent's own GitHub App

GitHub is the other per-seat case, and not a form. A
[GitHub App](../integrations/github.md#one-github-app-per-agent) is created by
POSTing a manifest from a page carrying the operator's own GitHub session, so
this surface hands the dashboard what to submit, and the two clicks that
follow are a person's. There is no server-to-server equivalent, so a reconcile
pass cannot do this alone.

**`POST /setup/integrations/github/app`** begins it, naming the seat:

```bash
curl -X POST https://engine.example.com/setup/integrations/github/app \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"seat": "senior-engineer"}'
```

```json
{
  "seat": "senior-engineer",
  "permissions": {"contents": "read", "issues": "write", "pull_requests": "write"},
  "action_url": "https://github.com/organizations/acme/settings/apps/new",
  "manifest": {"name": "Acme Senior Engineer", "public": false, "...": "..."},
  "state": "<sealed token naming the seat and who began the creation>",
  "webhook_active": true
}
```

The browser POSTs the `manifest` as a form field to `action_url`, carrying
`state` on that URL so the redirect ties back to the seat and to whoever
started it, because the callback's writes are theirs. The state is **sealed**
under the fleet keyring, not signed: it travels through GitHub, browser history
and ingress logs, where who began a creation is nobody's business. It is
URL-safe as it stands, and any node opens it, including one that has already
made the next keyring key active. `action_url` is the organization's own app
registration page whenever `integrations.github.provisioning.org` names one,
because an app registered under a person's account cannot be installed on the
organization that owns the repositories.

`webhook_active` says whether the app will deliver events here. It is `false`
when the webhook address is one GitHub cannot reach (a local engine's
`http://localhost:8200`): the manifest then carries no `hook_attributes` and no
`default_events`, the only form GitHub accepts from such an address. The app
still works for everything the agent does on GitHub, which is outbound; see
[Running locally, with no public
address](../integrations/github.md#running-locally-with-no-public-address).

Refusals: `400 invalid_body`, `400 seat_required`, `409 no_active_revision`,
`404 no_such_seat`, and `409 no_external_url` when the webhook address is
unset (`api.public.external_url` behind a [public listener](#which-listener-serves-what), `api.external_url`
otherwise, named in `config_path`). The last matters because an app is
created with its redirect and setup addresses baked in, and only a person at
GitHub can change them afterwards. An address that is set but unreachable for
GitHub is not refused: the operator's browser is all the redirect and setup
page need.

**`GET /webhooks/github-app`** is where GitHub returns the browser, twice. It
is unauthenticated because a redirect carries no engine credential; the `state`
stands in its place and is validated first.

- With a `code`, the engine converts the manifest, **seals the app's private
  key and webhook secret first**, then records `app_id`, `app_slug` and a
  `${VAR}` pointing at the sealed key on the seat, through the entity route as
  [per-seat setup](#per-seat-setup) does. All three writes are **the
  beginner's**: the sealed rows and the revision name whoever began the
  creation, with the credential they began it through, never `setup`. `installation_id` is
  written as `0`: the install is a second act. The page then links to the
  install. The seal comes first because GitHub returns those two values exactly
  once, so a failure after it costs a retry and a failure before it costs the
  app.
- With `?installed=<handle>`, it confirms the install and **writes nothing**.
  Installing is GitHub's own act and returns no code, and an agent's app is
  private, so it is installed from the organization's own installations page,
  which sends back no `state`; an unsigned query must never reach the company
  document. The [reconcile loop](../concepts/integration-reconcile.md) adopts
  the installation on its next pass, having *listed the app's own
  installations*, the reading that tells a real id from a typed one.
- With `?error=`, it says in its own words that the creation was cancelled
  (`access_denied`) or that GitHub didn't create the app, and logs GitHub's
  `error` and `error_description` as `github_app_create_refused`. The
  description is never printed: the route is unauthenticated, so it is
  whatever the address that brought the browser here says, on the dashboard's
  own origin.

The page names a seat only where the value can be a seat's handle: an install
arrival's `installed` is whatever the caller typed.

A link is spent the first time it's presented, so asking for the same address
again (a refresh, or Back from GitHub's install page) runs nothing. The page
then says what the agent the link names has: its app, in which case there's
nothing left to do and the install button is still offered, or no app yet, in
which case it says to give the app a minute to show before starting again.

The status is whose the stop was:

| Status | When |
|---|---|
| `200` | A completion, an install, or a link presented again whose agent has its app |
| `400` | GitHub refused or the person cancelled, GitHub sent no code, or the link or GitHub's code is expired, forged or already used |
| `403` | The company's settings are managed outside Crewlet |
| `404` | The agent the link names is no longer one of the company's |
| `409` | No company is set up |
| `502` | GitHub didn't finish converting the code |
| `500` | Crewlet couldn't finish: it couldn't check the link, read the company's settings, save the app's key or webhook secret, add the app to the agent, or confirm that it did |

None is a `503`, because the same request can't succeed later: the link is
spent before anything that can fail for a while, so sent again it runs nothing
and is answered as already used, by whether the agent it names has its app.
That settles an app whose record on the agent the coordination store took
without answering (the `500` that says to refresh: the change may have landed,
so the page reads the agent back once first and answers `200` when the app is
there); a new creation clears any other passing condition. Once GitHub has
handed the app over, the heading says the app was created but not finished, or,
on that unanswered record, that Crewlet is confirming it was added. The page
always uses the engine's own wording, chosen by the step that stopped, never a
quote of an error or of GitHub's response body, which carries the app's
private key. Every answer carries `Cache-Control: no-store`.

**The roster says what is outstanding.** A seat entry in a tool's `seats` array
carries two more fields where a per-seat app has clicks: `step` is what is
left, a closed set of `create_app` and `install_app` (two acts minutes or days
apart, so an operator who has done the first is told the second is left), and
`action_url` is where a person goes to do it. `action_url` is **empty for
`create_app`**, not by omission: an app is created by POSTing a manifest, not
following a link, so the dashboard asks the begin route above for one and
submits a form.
### Each agent's access to an integration

Every integration that has an account or credential per agent (Slack, Mattermost, Atlassian for Jira and Confluence, GitHub, GitLab, Datadog, Cloudflare, Expo, DigitalOcean, Scaleway, AWS, Google Cloud and SSH) has an Agents tab; these routes are what it reads and writes. Each agent seat's setting lives in the company document under `roles[].integrations.<lane>`, in the vendor's own terms: whether the agent is on, its role or level as the identifier the vendor's API takes, GitHub's permissions, and the scope it is narrowed to.

- Level identifiers: a Datadog role id, a GitLab access level, a Jira project role id.
- Cloudflare: `read`, `operate`, `configure` or `secure`, each a fixed set of permission groups.
- Expo: `viewer`, `runner`, `developer` or `release_manager`, each a fixed set of Expo permissions.
- DigitalOcean: `read`, `operate` or `administer`, each a fixed set of token scopes.
- Scaleway: `read`, `operate` or `administer`, each a fixed set of permission sets.
- AWS: `read`, `operate` or `administer`, each a set of Crewlet's customer managed policies.
- Google Cloud: `viewer`, `operator` or `administer`, each a fixed set of Google's roles.
- SSH: `read` or `operate`; operate needs a step-up.
- Scope: Scaleway's and Google Cloud's are the project IDs the level is granted on, SSH's the host ids the agent may reach; each names at least one while the agent is on.

A lane is the block's key: `atlassian` has two, `jira` and `confluence`, over one account per agent; every other integration has one named after itself. Jira and Confluence asked for by their own names answer `404 no_seat_access`.

The agent's credential is never in the document or a request. The engine seals it under a name it derives for the seat (`DATADOG_APP_KEY_SRE`, `GITLAB_TOKEN_SRE`), binds it to the integration's tool server itself, and answers the name and when it was minted, never the value.

**`GET /setup/integrations/{kind}/access`** answers the tab:

```json
{
  "kind": "datadog",
  "revision": "01J9...",
  "syncing": false,
  "last_sync_at": "2026-10-29T17:02:11Z",
  "options": [{"lane": "datadog", "live": true, "levels": [
    {"id": "4f0e2b3c-...", "name": "Datadog Read Only Role"},
    {"id": "7d1a9e44-...", "name": "Datadog Admin Role", "administers": true}]}],
  "seats": [{"handle": "sre", "name": "SRE", "lanes": {"datadog": {
    "desired": {"enabled": true, "level": "7d1a9e44-..."},
    "observed": {"exists": true, "enabled": true, "level": "7d1a9e44-...",
      "account": "crewlet-sre@agents.crewlet.invalid",
      "credential": {"variable": "DATADOG_APP_KEY_SRE", "minted_at": "2026-10-29T17:02:10Z"}},
    "observed_at": "2026-10-29T17:12:40Z",
    "sync": {"at": "2026-10-29T17:02:11Z", "outcome": "ok", "steps": []},
    "status": "in_sync", "plan": [], "tool": "live", "administers": true}}}]
}
```

Each seat lane's `status` is the lane as one word, computed by the engine so the tab and Ask Crewlet read a lane alike. It is the first of these that holds:

- `departed`: the seat left the document.
- `syncing`: steps to take while a sync of the integration runs.
- `refused`: the last sync failed.
- `changed_at_vendor`: somebody changed the account at the vendor; the next sync restores it.
- `needs_you`: a step only a person takes, or a sync that ended waiting on one.
- `next_sync`: steps the next sync takes.
- `in_sync`, `off_account_kept` and `off`.

`status_label` is it in the tab's words ("Changed at Datadog"), which a reader that does not know the status draws instead.

A lane carries two clocks. `observed_at` is when a pass last read the vendor for it, every pass including the check's dry run (`POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/check`). `sync.at` is when a writing sync last ended, which a dry run leaves alone: a refusal a dry run finds (a sealing step the sync would refuse) is reported on the integration and leaves the lane's last sync as it was. The tab draws them as one value ("Checked 1 minute ago, last applied 10 minutes ago"); its header's "Last check" is the integration's own pass. On GitHub, `observed.ceiling` is the permissions the agent's app is registered with, which every token is narrowed from: a permission there that `desired` leaves out or holds lower is one the agent does not use, never drift, and the tab says so under the row.

A level the company's connection cannot grant yet carries `unavailable`, the sentence saying what it waits on ("The Configure level is unavailable until the provisioner token holds Zone Settings: Edit and Response Compression: Edit"); the tab offers it disabled with that reason.

Each seat lane's `tool` says whether the agent can use its credential through a tool right now:

- `live`.
- `waiting`: a server reads it and it is not sealed yet.
- `builtin`: Jira and Confluence, whose credential the engine's own tools read, and SSH, whose tools are the engine's own `ssh_read` and `ssh_operate`.
- `no_server`: no server the company declares reads it.
- `server_off`: every server that reads it is turned off (`enabled: false`).
- `off`: the seat or its account is off.

A `waiting` tool also carries `tool_reason`, a sentence in the engine's words, where it waits on the vendor applying a grant the last sync wrote (a new account not yet grantable, a grant not yet in effect): that sync ended `ok`, since nobody owes a step, and the tool reads as it otherwise would once the vendor's stated wait ends.

A seat lane whose integration puts anything in the agent's own box while it is on (Expo's EAS CLI, DigitalOcean's doctl, Scaleway's scw, GitHub's and GitLab's token for git, AWS's CLI, Google Cloud's gcloud) also carries `box`, what Crewlet puts there, by reference as configured and never by value; it is absent for a seat that is off.

- `env` lists first the credentials the lane's tool (a CLI in the box) reads, each set to the seat's own sealed name and marked `"tool": true`, then every other variable by name: a credential a CLI beside the tool reads (GitHub's `GITHUB_TOKEN`) and the non-secret settings: `{"env": [{"name": "EXPO_TOKEN", "value": "${EXPO_TOKEN_QA}", "tool": true}]}`. Scaleway's lists `SCW_ACCESS_KEY` and `SCW_SECRET_KEY` as its tool's, then `SCW_DEFAULT_ORGANIZATION_ID`, `SCW_DEFAULT_PROJECT_ID` and `SCW_DISABLE_CHECK_VERSION`, which a line of the seat's own under the same name overrides; a line of the seat's own under a credential's name is ignored ([An agent's own integration credentials](../concepts/code-sandbox.md#an-agents-own-integration-credentials)).
- `files` lists the files the engine writes into the box itself, by path under the box's home, each with its reference as configured and never its value, and `rewritten` where the completion poll keeps it current: `{"path": ".config/crewlet/token", "value": "${VENDOR_TOKEN_QA}",
"rewritten": true}`. It is absent where the engine writes none, and `env` is a list, empty or not, wherever `box` is sent.
- A file a vendor's CLI finds through a variable adds that variable to `env`, its value the file's path from the box's home: `{"name": "CLI_TOKEN_FILE", "value": "~/.config/crewlet/token"}`. The launch sets it to the file's absolute path in the agent's box, joined onto that box's own home, so it is right in every cell.
- With no server, a lane whose tool is a CLI in the box reads `live` or `waiting` while the seat is on, since Crewlet sets its credentials there itself.

Where a person makes the agent's credential at the vendor and pastes it (Expo, DigitalOcean), the answer says exactly what to make there. Each seat lane carries `hand_in`, the name to give the credential at the vendor at the seat's desired level, computed by the engine and never read back (`{"name": "crewlet-sre-operate"}`). The lane's `options` entry carries `vendor_account`, the account, organization or team the company connected as the vendor shows it. Where the person grants the level's permissions by hand (DigitalOcean's token scopes), each level carries `grants`, every permission it holds in the vendor's own names, and the entry carries `refused`, the permissions no level grants that a pasted credential must not hold, and `unneeded`, the ones no level grants that it may still hold: each permission the vendor offers is in exactly one.

`revision` is the company revision the answer was read at, and the `ETag` is the same value quoted.

Fields of an `options` entry:

- An entry whose vendor did not answer just now carries no levels: which of its levels administers is unknown, so a turn-on or a change of level on that lane asks the step-up a raise does, and the next read asks the vendor again.
- `read_at`: when the entry was read from the vendor, kept for the minute that read is reused; absent on an entry drawn without one.
- `scoped`: the lane is scoped, whatever its list holds. `scope` is the entries the company's connection reaches, or `scope_open` where the company does not narrow it: any entry the vendor accepts is within reach, and `scope` then holds what the vendor listed to choose from (the apps of App Store Connect's connected teams, which an agent's own key lists), possibly nothing. `scope_names` names an entry where the vendor names one apart from its id, and `scope_details` gives the vendor's second identifier for one (an app's bundle ID); `scope_live` says the list is known: written in the company document (GitLab's projects, GitHub's repositories, Mattermost's channels, the Jira projects and Confluence spaces the org model names, and each growth product's accounts), or read from the vendor just now. An entry without it could not be read, so its empty `scope` says nothing about the reach. The sync judges a seat's scope by this same reach.
- `scope_required`: the agent, once on, must name at least one scope entry.
- `tool_server`: the `mcp_servers` entry a per-seat tool server for the lane is started from: the company's own where it declares one reading the lane's credential (an enabled one first), else the name the catalogue's server is conventionally declared under. Absent where no server reads the lane's credential (Expo, whose tool is the CLI in the agent's box).
- `rotatable`: a person can ask for a credential on the lane to be rotated.
- `releasable`: they may keep at the vendor an account a step waits for them to delete.
- `action_url`: where they take the lane's own steps at the vendor; each of their steps in a `plan` carries it.
- `"managed": "external"`: the engine does not provision the integration for the company, wherever it lacks the authority that creates an agent's account: Datadog, GitLab or Mattermost without a `provisioning` block, Jira and Confluence on Data Center or without the Atlassian organization key, GitHub without `provisioning` or on a document only the operator writes (the engine records each agent's app in the document), and Slack without `integrations.slack.app_config_token`, the token the engine creates agents' apps with. On such a lane a seat's switch still binds its tool to the credential handed in from outside Crewlet, its access is managed where that credential was issued, and its `observed.credential` names the variable the seat holds with `"source": "external"`.

`observed.credential`'s `source`:

- `"source": "minted"`: Crewlet sealed it; only such a credential carries `minted_at`.
- `"source": "issued"`: the engine issues it at use and never seals it; it names the seat's variable while the seat is on and its account exists, with no `minted_at` (each node issues its own).
- `"source": "external"`: see above.

`observed.retired` lists the credentials an account still holds besides the sealed one (`label`, what the vendor shows of each, and `since`, when it was created as near as Crewlet knows), where the vendor can tell: while it is non-empty on a lane that is on, every pass plans the `retire` op, a person's step to delete them at the vendor.

Where the operator writes the company document (`api.auth.company_writers`), the answer carries `"managed_by": "operator"` and the tab is read-only: a save and `keep` are refused `403 config_managed`, naming the Seat object as the place to change the agent's access. A seat the document no longer has whose account the engine still records is listed with `"departed": true`, and only `remove` applies to it. `notice` carries a company-level warning, such as the one the migration raises when an agent's credential was kept in a variable something else also names (a company setting, a unit's shared credentials or another agent): the integration's own [`credential_shared`](../concepts/integration-reconcile.md#what-a-pass-reports) finding, drawn on the tab until the variable is written again.

A lane has a `plan` only where the sync takes steps on it: an integration the engine provisions, once its migration onto per-seat access has finished. On a lane managed outside Crewlet, and on an integration still waiting on its migration, `plan` is empty and a draft's plan lists no steps.

**`POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/access/plan`** takes a draft and answers what saving it would do at the vendor, writing nothing. It is the plan the sync takes its steps from:

```bash
curl -X POST https://engine.example.com/setup/integrations/datadog/access/plan \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"seats": {"qa": {"datadog": {"enabled": true, "level": "4f0e2b3c-..."}}}}'
```

```json
{"kind": "datadog", "revision": "01J9...", "step_up": false,
 "plans": [{"handle": "qa", "lane": "datadog", "steps": [
   {"op": "create", "verb": "create", "text": "Create crewlet-qa@agents.crewlet.invalid with Datadog Read Only Role", "by": "crewlet"},
   {"op": "create", "verb": "mint", "text": "Mint an application key, sealed as DATADOG_APP_KEY_QA", "by": "crewlet"}]}]}
```

`reviews` names each agent whose access the draft changes, by the closed list a turn is told, and that has open work raised under its access now: `{handle,
open, at_least?, changes}`, `open` counting its distinct open items (the questions it asked that are still
open, what its executor waits on a person for and its work items in progress or blocked, each work item once), `at_least` set where the tracker stopped counting at its ceiling so `open` is a floor, and `changes` the change worded about the agent. The draft is measured by the same seat edits the save writes. Each reviews that work once the draft is saved ([ADR-0111](../../adr/0111-an-agent-whose-access-changed-reviews-its-open-work-once.md)). It is absent where the open work could not be counted.

A draft names each seat by handle and each lane by its key; a seat or lane it leaves out keeps its setting. Its fields are `enabled`, `level`, `permissions` (GitHub only, each `read` or `write`) and `scope`; any other field is refused `400 invalid_body`, so a body cannot name a variable. Refusals:

- A person's seat or a seat the company does not hold: `404 no_such_seat`.
- A lane the integration does not grant: `400 no_seat_access`.
- A level, permission or scope entry the vendor does not offer now: `400 access_not_offered`, naming the first such `seat`, its `lane`, the `field` it is about (`level`, `permissions` or `scope`) and the `detail`, with what is `offered` instead where a list says it, or the level a set is `required` to hold.
- A live-listed level (a Datadog role, a Jira project role) is judged only when the vendor answered just now; otherwise the sync reports an id it does not hold as a finding. A scope entry is judged the same way, only when `scope_live` says the list was read.
- On a lane with `scope_required`, a seat turned on with an empty `scope` is `400 access_not_offered` whatever was read; the sync reports a stored one as a finding, and `crewlet validate` refuses it in the document at the lane's scope key.
- A GitLab project is within reach only inside the group the company's connection joins agents to, so where the connection lists no projects, a project outside that group is `400 access_not_offered` too.

**`PUT /setup/integrations/{kind}/access`** saves the same body as one revision of the company document and starts the sync for that integration. Every access sync ends in the same read-only pass `POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/check` runs, recorded on the integration's status through the loop's fold; the tab reads `syncing` until that pass is recorded, so the integration's issues and notes say what the change left as soon as the sync is over.

- Send the tab's `revision` back as `If-Match` (or as `revision` in the body); a save on a revision the fleet has left is `409 revision_advanced` and writes nothing.
- The revision records the caller as its author and a history line naming what changed (`agents' access on datadog: turn on QA Engineer on datadog`), with an optional `summary` after it.
- The answer is the tab, as `GET` answers it, with `syncing` while the sync runs. Where the tab cannot be read again just after a save landed, the answer is the tab as read before the save, at the revision the save wrote, with the saved settings in place, not an error.
- A seat removed from the document between the tab's read and the save is `404 no_such_seat`, and nothing is written.
- A save made while a sync runs is not refused: it lands, and a sync follows.
- `?dry_run=true` answers the plan, `step_up` and the `warnings` the revision would introduce, and stores nothing (see [Dry runs](#dry-runs)).

A save that raises an agent to an administration role at the vendor (Datadog Admin Role, GitLab Maintainer or Owner, Jira Administrators, Confluence Admin, Mattermost System Admin, or GitHub Read and write on Contents or Workflows) asks for a person present and a fresh proof inside `step_up`: a machine token is refused `403 token_refused`, and a stale proof `403 step_up_required`. The plan's `step_up` says so before the save. Keeping a role an agent already holds and lowering one never ask. Where the vendor's levels could not be read, a turn-on or a change of level asks as a raise does. So does an integration still waiting on its migration: the saved setting is the one the sync applies once the migration finishes.

The same rule holds on every other write of the company document by a person or a token: `PUT` and `PATCH /config`, a seat's `PUT /config/roles/{id}` and a revert. Each compares the revision it replaces with the one it proposes, and one that raises an agent's access is refused for a machine token (`403 token_refused`) or a stale proof (`403 step_up_required`), naming each raise in `raises` (`kind`, `handle`, `lane`) and storing nothing. A dry run of it is answered, since it writes nothing. A document the operator writes is judged by the operator's own authority instead.

Turning an agent off disables its account at the vendor and keeps it, so its history keeps its author and turning it back on needs no person (except Slack's install). Nothing a document edit does removes an account.

**`POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/{action}`** acts on one agent's account, and answers the tab:

| Action | Does |
|---|---|
| `rotate` | Mints a new credential, seals it under the agent's name, and revokes the old one. Asks `secrets.write` too. A credential handed in from outside Crewlet is refused `409 credential_external`: it is rotated where it was issued |
| `remove` | Removes the account at the vendor, where the vendor allows it, and stops the engine tracking it. Only once the agent is off on this lane: `409 seat_still_on` otherwise. On a lane managed outside Crewlet it is `409 access_external`: the account is removed at the vendor |
| `keep` | Writes what the vendor shows into the document as a new revision, in the vendor's own terms: after a role or scope was changed at the vendor ("Keep the vendor's setting"), or after the account was turned off there ("Keep off", which keeps the role the document names for when it is turned back on). Nothing is restored. Asks `setup.access.write`, and `setup.access.raise` where the role kept is an administration role. A Datadog account holding several roles is refused `409 invalid_input`, since an agent holds one |
| `restore` | Turns back on an account somebody turned off at the vendor, which no sync does unasked, or restores a changed role now rather than on the next pass. On a lane managed outside Crewlet it is `409 access_external` |
| `retry` | Runs the sync again after a vendor refusal was settled |
| `done` | Reads the vendor again after a person took a step there (a GitHub App's creation or permission request, a Slack install) |
| `release` | Keeps at the vendor an account a step waits for a person to delete ("Keep the robot at Expo"): the step closes, the engine stops tracking the account, and the audit records the person's choice. Only on a lane whose options say `releasable` (never DigitalOcean's, where a kept token would be live access nobody watches), and only while the lane waits on its `remove` step: `409 invalid_input` otherwise |

Every action but `keep` is carried by a sync, and one asked while a sync of the same integration runs is `409 pass_in_flight`. `keep` writes its revision and then starts a sync, as a save does, which finds the vendor already matching. Each of these syncs ends in the check's own pass, as a save's does.

**`POST /setup/integrations/slack/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/install`** answers `{"url": "https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?..."}`: a link signed for the agent's own app, recorded as issued and spent by the install it completes, so it works once and only for a short while. It is minted only while the agent is on in Slack and its app waits for a person to approve the install (`409 invalid_input` otherwise), never stored, never logged and never part of `GET`. It writes nothing to the company document, so it is offered where the operator writes the document too.

**`POST /setup/integrations/{kind}/access/seats/{handle}/{lane}/credential`** takes `{"value": "<token>"}`: a credential a person created at the vendor for one agent, for an integration whose accounts only a person can create (Expo's robots, DigitalOcean's personal access tokens). It asks `secrets.write` beside the route's own verb, since it seals a credential, before it reads the body; both ask a proof inside `step_up`.
- **Route checks:** before anything reaches the vendor, an empty value, a `${VAR}` reference, and stray whitespace or invisible characters are each refused as `400 invalid_input` with `"field": "value"`.
- **Vendor check:** the engine then checks the value at the vendor with reads only. For Expo it checks that the token works, that it is a robot's, that the robot holds a role on the company's account, that the role is the agent's level and not Admin or Owner, and that no other agent has the robot. For DigitalOcean it checks that the value is a personal access token and no other agent's, that it works in the company's team, and, with requests that cannot change anything, that it holds no refused scope and exactly its level's scopes as far as they can be proven. A refusal is `400 invalid_input` with the vendor's sentence in `detail`, what to do in `hint`, and `"field": "value"`.
- **Sealing:** a value that passes is sealed by the agent's own sync under the name the engine derives for it, the agent is read back with it, and the answer is `{"verdict": <the shape a check answers in>, "access": <the Agents
  tab>}`, see [Checking a credential before it is stored](#checking-a-credential-before-it-is-stored). The value is never echoed, logged or recorded: the audit line names the seat, the lane, the account and its id, and what the vendor shows of the credential (Expo's token prefix, DigitalOcean's expected token name).
- **Other refusals:** an agent that is not on at the integration is `409 invalid_input`, a kind that takes no pasted credential is `404 no_seat_access`, and a sync in flight is `409 pass_in_flight`.

#### Moving a company onto per-seat access

A document written before per-seat access named a `${VAR}` to say an agent was on at a vendor, and set one role for the whole company (`provisioning.role`, `access_level`, a GitHub `tier`). On first start the engine migrates it, one integration at a time, in one revision attributed to `seat access migration`: each agent seat states `enabled` per integration, judged on the credentials it named itself and the ones its unit's `mcp_env` shares with it, as the earlier engine read them.

- An agent whose account exists keeps the role or level the vendor shows for it; only an agent with no account yet takes the company's role, in the vendor's own terms (a Datadog role is looked up at Datadog by name).
- A Datadog account holding several roles is not guessed at: Datadog waits, naming the agent, until the account holds one role or a person saves the one it keeps.
- A Jira or Confluence agent with no role of its own keeps product access only (no project or space role).
- A Mattermost bot's channels are written out, each credential the engine minted is re-sealed under the agent's own name, every account the engine made for an agent it had on is recorded, and the retired fields are removed.
- A credential is never sealed over one the agent already holds under its own name, and GitHub's installation tokens, which the engine issues at use, are never moved.
- A credential that named a variable something else also names (a company setting, a unit's shared credentials or another agent) is never moved: the agent gets a new one from its next sync, and the Agents tab warns that the shared credential must be replaced until it is.
- A unit's shared key for a tool server the engine now binds itself is removed from the unit.

The document lists the integrations it has moved in `seat_access_migrated`, and the access sync for an integration acts on no agent until it is listed. An integration whose vendor does not answer stays unlisted, with its seats exactly as they were, and the engine tries again every minute. Its access pass reports an `identity_missing` finding that names the integration, says its access migration has not finished, and gives the reason the last attempt gave (for example, that the lookup of Datadog's role failed); the log's `seat_access_migration_pending` line carries the same reason. An integration the company does not connect is not waiting on the migration and reports nothing. Reverting to a revision written before the migration closes the gate again, and the next attempt migrates that document.

### One tool, several surfaces

Atlassian is reached over three keys: `jira`, `confluence` and the Forge relay. Each is its own block in the company document and its own entry here, written on its own, so a submission is atomic on what it changes; a screen presenting them as one tool asks for one section per key and submits one request per section. The Forge app id is the exception and rides with `jira`: one app relays both surfaces, so it is one value, not two forms writing one field.


## Live Stream

`/ws/stream` is where the dashboard READS. State comes down it and questions go up it: the handshake snapshot carries every section a screen needs on first paint, subsequent pushes carry what changed, and anything fetched on demand (an agent's LLM history, one event's payload, a trace, a different spend window) is a query sent on the same socket and answered on it. The socket carries no write.

REST carries the rest, which is two things:

- **Writes.** A change to the company's work is `POST /operator/act/{tool}`, made as the principal the dashboard's session resolves to (see [`/operator/act`](#operatoract--the-dashboards-write-surface)); a person's directory row is `/iam`; the company document, its org chart included, is `/config`; a credential is `/secrets`; an integration's setup is `/setup`; a backup is `POST /backup`. A write answers with the position it landed at, and the reads it moved are asked again on the socket at that position.
- **Guarded reads the query registry does not answer**: the secret names (`/secrets`), where each `${VAR}` resolves from (`/config/references`), an integration's setup (`/setup/integrations`) and the identity directory (`/iam`). They are credential-scoped surfaces with their own refusals, read through the dashboard's one REST loader rather than mirrored onto the socket.

The REST read routes below are also a public read API, and `GET /stream/snapshot` is the fallback for a browser that cannot upgrade to a WebSocket (corporate proxies).

Every named read route is an **adapter**, never a second implementation: it resolves its path values and hands them to the same answer the socket's query channel reaches. The generic form `GET /query/{what}?a=b` reaches the same answers by name and is what the socket's own frames map onto, so the two can never drift. A question whose source this node lacks (an event log, a schedule ledger, or Worklet where the company does not run it) is *unknown* rather than answered empty, so its route replies `404` with `unknown_query`, which tells it apart from the `no_route` a path nothing serves answers. A question refused on authority answers `403` in the [refusal envelope](#every-refusal-is-one-envelope) every route answers the same decision with (`unauthorized`, its `reason` and its `grants`), and never `step_up_required` or `token_refused`, because no question is decided by a verb that asks either. Worklet and Doclet are asked of the engine per request, because a node that booted with no company builds them at its first revision on them: see [Worklet and Doclet](#worklet-and-doclet).

### An event on the wire

One shape, whether it came from the live projection or from the event store, with the same field names either way:

```json
{
  "id": "…", "type": "external_notification", "source": "notify.mattermost",
  "timestamp": "2026-08-25T12:00:00Z", "category": "notification",
  "summary": "…", "actor": "…",
  "trace_id": "…", "span_id": "…", "parent_span_id": "…",
  "failed": false,
  "payload": { }
}
```

`payload` is present only where the event was fetched by id or by trace: a listing never selects it.

A stored event also carries `node`, the node that **published** it (where the work it describes ran), on every read, listings included. It is not the node that answered with it: a node without the `data` role keeps no event log, and the data node keeping its events in [custody](../guides/deployment.md#custody-the-rows-of-a-node-without-data) holds rows it never published. It is absent only on an event no node published (a test harness's).

Every stored type reaches the activity feed (the snapshot's `events` and each `event` frame) except `auxiliary_spend`, which is accounting rather than activity: what the auxiliary model cost, coalesced per key per flush. It is a row like any other in `GET /events`, a turn's `turn` answer and a trace, and it reaches every spend figure through the rollups; it is never pushed as an `event` frame and never takes a row of the feed (see [Event System](../concepts/event-system.md)). A read merged with the feed or drawn beside it asks `feed_only=true` on `events` and `event_series` and gets the feed's rows alone, as the dashboard's event log, its Live strip and a seat's latest events do.

### A seat's LLM history

`llm_history` is the seat's **finished** phases, read from the event store of **every live data node** (placement moves a seat, and the phases it ran are kept by the data node it ran on, or, where it ran on a node without `data`, by the data node keeping that node's events in custody): one row per `agent_phase_completed` and per `executor_collected`, newest first, capped at 50, with the answer's `coverage` saying which nodes it heard from (see [Reading the fleet's history](#reading-the-fleets-history-coverage)). The calls *in flight* are `live.live_calls`, from the projection. Each history row carries the same fields a live one does (`turn_id`, `phase`, `iteration`, `model`, `response`, `tool_executions`, `round_narration`, `partial_round`, `total_tokens`) plus the envelope's `timestamp` and `failed`.

It is the stored record, its payloads held to their shares of one message, so a long phase's row may list some of its calls and say the rest (`calls_elided`, `elided_calls`, `rounds_elided`; see [what an agent record keeps](../concepts/event-system.md#what-an-agent-record-keeps)). It also carries the phase's price where its own harness reported one (`cost_usd`), which the dashboard never reads ([rule 19](dashboard-design.md#rules-a-change-has-to-keep)).

Each launch of an executor's run is a row of its own, an `executor_collected`, published when it is collected: **no phase** (it names none, and is the work of the `execute` round that launched it, `iteration`), with its tokens, its harness's own turns (`harness_turns`), its `launch_id` (a round can launch twice, so the launch is part of that row's identity), its report as `response` and its `activity_transcript`; see [each launch is published as its own record](../concepts/code-sandbox.md#what-ends-a-run-each-launch-is-published-as-its-own-record).

A finished row also carries `duration_ms`, which a live one cannot: the engine's own measurement of the phase, published on the record. Zero means *not measured* (an executor's rounds ran inside its coding harness's own loop, in another process), never *took no time*. A phase that failed before it reached a provider also truncates to zero at this resolution; `failed` separates the two. It measures the phase's **own segments**: the executor launches its run and parks, and when the run is collected the same turn re-enters the phase (after a restart, possibly on another node), so the one record the phase publishes carries the launch segment's time, carried across on the park, plus the collection's, and never the run between them. The run's own time and tokens are on each launch's `executor_collected` row.

A finished row carries the phase's **timeline** too, and so does every other reader of the record (`phases`, `turn`, `trace` and `event` answer the stored payload verbatim):

- `started_at`: when this segment began (not published minus `duration_ms`, which on a resumed phase also counts the launch segment, as `agent_phase_started` pairing would).
- `rounds[]`: one `{round, started_at, duration_ms, model, input_tokens, output_tokens,
cache_read_tokens, cache_write_tokens, tool_calls, stop_reason}` per model request the harness's record showed, the model's half of the round only;
`stop_reason` is `end`, `tool_use` or `cap`.
- `invocations[]`: one `{started_at, duration_ms, provider_key, model, outcome, first_round,
last_round, requests_observed, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens,
cache_write_tokens, tool_calls}` per harness run, `outcome` one of `end`, `cap`, `stopped` and `failed`.
- Each `tool_executions[]` row's `call_id`, `started_at`, `duration_ms`, `origin` (`builtin` or `mcp:<server>`) and `server` (who answered), `source` (whose tool the call named, a call refused before any tool ran included) and `refusal` (the class of a failure the engine classified).
- The phase's `cache_read_tokens` / `cache_write_tokens` (a breakdown of `input_tokens`, never an addition to it), `max_rounds` / `round_ceiling`, a worker's or a judge's `host_round`, a resumed executor's `launch_id` and the turn's `work_item`.
- `steers[]`: `{round, note_id, boundary}` for each person's note the phase read; a read by the phase's executor in its box is at round 1, with the kind of step that read it.

The live frame carries the same so far plus `round_started_at`, the `run_started_at` of the harness run in flight and the `running_calls` in flight. Each is **absent** where nothing measured it (a tool call nobody timed has no `duration_ms`, never a zero), so a reader treats absent as *not recorded*. The whole field list, and why each is measured where it is, is in [what a turn records about its time](../concepts/turn-engine.md#what-a-turn-records-about-its-time).

An unreadable or absent event log costs the history and nothing else: the answer still carries the seat and its live state.

### What the handshake snapshot carries

One frame, `kind: "snapshot"`, with every section a screen needs on first paint. Three are derived from **configuration** rather than from anything that has happened, and are present from the moment the socket opens, before a single turn has run:

| Section | What it is |
|---|---|
| `agents` | The company's agent seats, each merged with its live overlay. Every seat in the company, not only the ones this node runs, because the dashboard is a view of the company. Human seats are excluded (no turn, phase or spend); they appear in `org` with `"kind": "human"` |
| `org` | The same projection [`GET /org`](#get-org) answers, built for the socket's audience: the charter, the company's resolved `timezone`, its `token_budget` and the `services` it runs, root-level `roles` and `units` nesting to any depth, with only the fields that projection declares for each, a seat's resolved `llm` chain and `tool_sources` only to an audience holding `admin` |
| `tools` | The catalogue this node serves, each entry tagged with the `source` that registered it: `builtin` or the MCP server's name. Empty on a node that runs no company yet, which has no catalogue |
| `events`, `executors`, `tokens`, `budget`, `health` | The live projection: what has happened |

Every seat carries **one seat-state vocabulary**, computed by the engine and never by a client: `activity` is `working`, `needs`, `stopped` or `idle`, and `stopped_reason` is `paused`, `unplaced`, `budget` or `provider` on a stopped seat and `null` otherwise. Both keys are on every row, a seat no event has mentioned included. What each word means, which inputs it is read from and in what order they win is [Agent States](../concepts/agent-runtime.md#agent-states). Placement is the **fleet's** lease table, read on every snapshot and on the five-second tick, so a seat a peer runs reads `idle` or `working` here, and a seat no node holds reads `stopped`/`unplaced`. A token meter report names every capped seat whether or not anything runs it, and moves a seat's state only when one of its windows is refusing.

The three company-derived sections are **re-sent on every published company**, as `seats`, `org` and `tools` pushes (with `schedules`), since a seat change produces no event a projection could learn from.

**A company is published by a node's boot and by every config apply**, and these four pushes follow every one of them, as the last step of [the convergence](../concepts/configuration.md#what-follows-a-published-company). Each is a WHOLE payload that replaces its predecessor: the hub drops the oldest queued envelope without telling the client.

**The `tools` push is also re-sent alone** when the catalogue moves between publishes: the one part of a published company that does is its shared MCP servers' tools, refiled when a server [comes back](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#a-server-that-dies-or-will-not-start) from a crash listing different tools, or comes up on a retry of a start that failed. The other three have not moved, so they are not sent.
### Live-state projection (`api/stream` + `LiveState`)

Every node that serves the API keeps an **in-memory projection** of every agent's current state (`internal/api/livestate.LiveState`, owned by `internal/api/stream.Service`). It is fed by the same event stream as the WebSocket fan-out and read in O(1), so `/agents`, `/stream/snapshot` and the WebSocket handshake never re-derive state from an event scan.

It holds what has **happened**: a phase, an in-flight call, a spend. Who the seats are, their organisation, tools and schedules come from the company document ([the handshake snapshot](#what-the-handshake-snapshot-carries)).

**Live state is keyed by AGENT ID**, the id derived from the seat's handle ([organization model](../concepts/organization-model.md)), which every event a seat publishes carries as `agent_id`. Never by name: names are prose and two seats may share one, which gave both every overlay either moved. An event naming no agent id moves no seat's state. The roster row carries the same `agent_id`, every overlay in the `agents` push is matched to its row by it, and the durable seat-scoped reads (history, turns, phases, spend) are narrowed by it.

What the projection computes, it also **pushes**; a dashboard mirrors it rather than re-deriving it. Applying an event yields a change set, and the changed agents' overlays, the sandbox list and the spend rollup go out as their own envelopes.

The projection holds each agent's **in-flight LLM calls**, one per turn it runs, each the latest `agent_turn_progress` of its turn (phase, round, model, accumulated response, tool calls so far), and surfaces them as `live_calls` on the agent in every snapshot, so a tab that refreshes or reconnects mid-call re-renders the live row at once. `agent_turn_progress` is *stream-only*, never written to the event store. Its `response` is built by the function that builds the finished phase record's, so the live row and the expanded turn are the same text ([Turn Engine § What streams during a turn](../concepts/turn-engine.md#what-streams-during-a-turn)).

- Each phase publishes an opening `agent_turn_progress` (`round_num = -1`) before its first provider call, carrying the prompt.
- `round_num` is ZERO-BASED, so the round a reader counts is `round_num + 1`. `-1` is neither round zero nor missing: it is the phase's FIRST round, in flight and unanswered. The frame carries `max_rounds`, so a row can say "round 1 of 24" at once.
- A surface drawing it resolves every case through `lib/seats.ts`'s `roundOf` (at least 1 while there is a call) and `roundLabel`, whose hint says when the first round has not come back.

State transitions are gated on the event timestamp, so out-of-order delivery (JetStream returns a NAK'd message *behind* never-delivered ones, and several fleet nodes publish at once) can't clobber newer state with an older event, including a final progress round that overtakes its own phase completion and would re-open a finished phase's row.

Every comparison first normalizes to one ordering key. The same instant arrives in several encodings (`Z`, `+00:00`, naive, a non-UTC offset) that order differently as raw strings (`…05Z` sorts after `…05+00:00`; `13:00+01:00` sorts after `12:30+00:00` though half an hour earlier), so a straggler round would resurrect a finished phase.

A **failed** phase is first-class: the projection stamps its in-flight call `failed`, keeps it on screen, and records the classified cause on the agent as `last_error`.

The agent detail page paints from an `agent` query, then stays current from pushes. `agent_phase_completed` / `agent_turn_completed` envelopes append to the phase transcript live, and each of the agent's `live_calls`, pushed every round, is the in-flight row inside its turn's card until the completed record replaces it. Progress envelopes carry `turn_id` / `phase` / `iteration` for this correlation.

The **spend rollup** HOLDS the spend records of its own 24-hour window: each phase's and each `auxiliary_spend` record (what the auxiliary model cost), the newest 24 000 of them. It is the WHOLE COMPANY's, since every projection is fed fleet-wide (about 2 600 turns a day; a company past that sees a rollup covering slightly less than a day, not a wrong total). It folds them with `internal/tokens`, which folds the named windows' company days into the same breakdown, so changing the window cannot change what a phase counts as. The window ROLLS, aged on the serving node's clock and never a record's stamp; every read leaves out what the window has aged past, and an arriving record and the shared tick both drop it:

- a record stamped before the window is not counted, however late it arrives;
- one stamped ahead (a node whose clock runs fast) is aged from when it arrived (from the startup seed, for one read from history), so it leaves a day after it came, or the cap takes it, rather than moving the window or outliving it. It still shows its published stamp, which is how the wrong-clock node is found;
- one whose stamp does not parse is kept (nothing can age it) and is the first the 24 000 cap drops.

The rollup's `since` and `until` are the instants the window was cut at. It ships in the snapshot and is re-pushed on the shared 5-second tick after any phase completed or any record aged out, so a client stays live without a fetch, and a quiet company sees its spend leave the window. (The bundled dashboard's Settings › Token spend reads [named windows](#token-spend-breakdown) instead.) A seat's spend is that rollup's per-agent row; the projection keeps no second total.

**The projection is seeded from the fleet's event stores at process start**, after the broadcast subscription is attached and before the node hands its listener the API surface. Three bounded reads run side by side, so a slow one does not use up the others' budget:

- the newest 400 persisted events, for the feed;
- the newest 24 000 spend records (phases and auxiliary) inside the 24-hour window, read in pages of 4 096 records a node, because a busy node's day exceeds one scatter reply (8 MiB) and a cut reply would cut every node's records;
- the newest three turns of every agent seat, for its `last_turn` and any turn it left parked. Each node reads them from its newest rows, an hour and then a doubled span until it holds them, so the cost is those turns' rows, not the seat's week.

Each read goes to **every live data node** through the scatter the history queries use ([Reading the fleet's history](#reading-the-fleets-history-coverage)). A data node's store holds only what that node published (plus what a data-less node handed it, [Deployment → The event store](../guides/deployment.md#the-event-store)), so a one-store seed would show a restarted node only its own share, and without any seed a restart, deploy or join shows a company that apparently did nothing. The projection records which nodes answered as a `coverage`; a failed read makes it incomplete. An event arriving both ways (the stream before the read, or the read finding a row the publisher wrote inline) is recognised by id and listed and counted once. History is ordered behind the live rows it predates, and a seat's turn the stream already moved is left as the stream left it.

**Paused seats are seeded from the coordination record**, beside the reads above and before the node serves: a pause taken before this process started is in no event it will hear, and a paused seat drawn as working is the one state a person pausing it must not see. The pause is in force whether or not the seed has landed.

**Executors in flight are reconciled against their durable record**, read once before the node serves and then every 30 seconds. The stream is lossy and in memory, so only the record can say which executors are out; [the panel of executors in flight](../concepts/code-sandbox.md) says which wins on disagreement. A reconcile that changed the set pushes it as `executors`; one that changed nothing pushes nothing.

**Each of the three seeds is read until it lands.** The node waits at most five seconds for them before it serves (until then every webhook is answered `503 starting`, so a seed must not hold the node back). A seed not landed by then (`boot_seeds_pending` names it) lands when it completes. A seed that failed, or whose history a node did not answer, is logged as `live_projection_not_seeded`, `seat_pauses_not_seeded` or `sandbox_panel_not_seeded` (first attempt and every tenth) and retried 2 seconds after the first attempt, doubling to every 30 seconds, until it completes. `live_projection_seeded`, `seat_pauses_seeded` or `sandbox_panel_seeded` says when it lands after the node began to serve. A seed landing while a dashboard is connected is sent to it: the history as a fresh `snapshot` (applied like the first), the paused seats as an `agents` push.

### `GET /stream/snapshot`

Single-shot bundle equal to the WebSocket handshake's first envelope: every section a dashboard screen needs on first paint, assembled from the in-memory projection with no database round-trip. Fallback when the browser cannot upgrade to a WebSocket (corporate proxies).

**Each section is the caller's**, decided by what its push kind needs on the socket: the bundle is for every principal the guard resolved whose stage may act. The `events` section is present only for an administrator, absent rather than empty (an empty feed reads as a company that did nothing). `agents` and `executors` carry each call's and run's **body** only where the caller may read it ([A status reader never receives a transcript](#a-status-reader-never-receives-a-transcript)). `GET /agents`, `GET /org` and `GET /tools` are the same sections served alone, shaped the same way.

**Response**

```json
{
  "health":    { /* the whole health envelope described below */ },
  "agents":    [ { /* /agents row: activity (working | needs | stopped |
                      idle) + stopped_reason (paused | unplaced | budget |
                      provider, or null) + budget meter + live_calls (the
                      in-flight LLM calls, one per turn, [] between turns) +
                      last_error (the phase failure that stopped this
                      seat, or null) + turns (the turns the seat is on,
                      or []) + last_turn (the newest turn it ended,
                      or null) + paused ({by, at, reason, stop_running}
                      while a person has the seat paused, or null) */ }, ... ],
  "events":    [ { /* recent event row, newest first — payload-free, plus
                      a `failed` boolean */ }, ... ],
  "executors": [ { /* an executor run in flight: turn_id, role,
                      agent_handle, agent_id, harness, provider_key
                      (the executor-chain member it was launched on, to an
                      admin alone) and model, sandbox_id, task, status (the
                      run record's own word), started_at, question,
                      audience, work_item, owner, paused_at */ }, ... ],
  "tools":     [ { /* one catalogue entry — see The Tool Catalogue below */ } ],
  "org":       { /* /org payload */ },
  "tokens":    { /* the spend rollup — same shape as /tokens/breakdown */ },
  "budget":    { /* the live org-wide token meter, or null before any node has reported — see below */ },
  "schedules": [ { /* configured schedule + computed next_run */ }, ... ]
}
```

Each `events` row is the payload-free feed shape: `id`, `type`, `timestamp`, `source`, `actor`, `summary`, `category`, `trace_id`, `span_id`, `parent_span_id`, `topic`, plus:

- **`agent_id`**: the seat the event concerns (the store's own `agent_id`; absent for an event about no seat). It lets a client narrow LIVE rows to one seat exactly as `/events?seat=` narrows stored ones.
- **`refs`**: what `summary` names that a person can open, each `{kind, id, text}` with `text` the words the summary spells it with (absent where it names nothing; see [What a line names](#what-a-line-names)).
- **`failed`**: `true` when the work the event reports did not succeed: an event carrying its own `failed` field (a phase or turn that died) or an event type that *is* a failure (`executor_failed`, `llm_unavailable`, `budget_exhausted`, `turn.guard_breach`). Deciding it once here spares a dashboard its own type list.

The flag survives a restart: the event-store writer stamps a `failed` tag on those events and the projection reads it back when seeding its feed. The store's listing (`EventLog.List`) never selects the payload column, so without the tag every historical failure would read as a success.

### The health envelope

One builder (`App.health`, `internal/api/health.go`) answers `GET /health`, the snapshot's `health` section and the 5-second `health` push. All three carry the **whole** envelope, so they cannot disagree about whether the engine is healthy. There is no query for it (no `stream` query): a screen reads the push.

The envelope is **public** (`GET /health` is an unguarded probe and the push reaches an anonymous tab), so the fleet and the alarm table appear only as counts (`nodes`, `alarms`), never rows. Which node holds what is the `admin` [`fleet`](#get-fleet) answer; what each alarm measured is `work_retention`'s.

```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "node": "core-1",
  "configured": true,
  "version": "v0.4.0",
  "started_at": "2026-04-01T11:58:03Z",
  "queue": "jetstream-embedded",
  "clients": 3,
  "event_history_seconds": 2592000,
  "spend_history_seconds": 15638400,
  "in_flight": 2,
  "shutting_down": false,
  "posture": "serve",
  "applied_epoch": 41,
  "config_attempt": {"epoch": 41, "revision_id": "01JA8Q2W5H5S1Q9P0N1C7K3M2D", "status": "ok"},
  "seats": ["ceo", "cto"],
  "identity_duty_seconds": {"iam_sweep": 3600},
  "unproven_seconds": {"eng": 312.5},
  "nodes": 3,
  "alarms": {"count": 1, "worst": "trim_blocked", "worst_title": "Log cleanup is stuck"},
  "seeded_from": {
    "nodes": [
      {"id": "core-1", "answered": true, "error": ""},
      {"id": "core-2", "answered": true, "error": ""}
    ],
    "complete": true
  },
  "identity": "ready",
  "objects": {"direct_upload": "available"}
}
```

Before anybody is in the company, the body says so. The remedy is the first person, put onto a human seat the company declares under a Tier A token (invited into it, or created on it), so a company declaring no human seat declares one first ([How the first person exists](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#how-the-first-person-exists)):

```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "node": "core-1",
  "identity": "unclaimed"
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `status` | In order of precedence: `shutting_down`, `unconfigured`, a diverged posture (`shed`, `stuck` or `isolated`), or `ok`. `starting` is the shorter body a node answers before it serves ([While a node is starting](#while-a-node-is-starting)) and never appears in this envelope. The ordinary postures `serve` and `wait` read as `ok`. A node applying its first company reads `unconfigured` until that apply completes; a later apply reads `ok` throughout. |
| `node` | The name this node's engine runs under: `node.id`, else `CREWLET_NODE_ID`, else `node-0`. It is what its presence lease carries and how a caller tells which node a load balancer sent it to. |
| `configured` | Whether this node's engine runs a company revision, read off the live epoch on every call. When `false` the node **refuses** every inbound webhook with `503`. |
| `version` | The `crewlet` version this process runs. |
| `started_at` | When this node's **engine** started (the API is served inside its process). The fleet view reports the same instant. |
| `queue` | The event queue's backend: `jetstream-embedded` (a NATS server inside this process), `jetstream` (an external NATS cluster this node dialled) or `memory`. Read off the `EventQueue` contract's `Backend()`. Display only; nothing may branch on it. |
| `clients` | Dashboards connected to this node. |
| `event_history_seconds` | How far back the event log can be read: the hard bottom of [paging](#paging-the-event-history). Once a cursor crosses it every page is empty forever, so a client that cannot name the floor draws it as "the org went quiet". The store's own constant, so a retention change reaches every screen without an edit; in seconds because the retention is a duration. |
| `spend_history_seconds` | How far back a **named** spend window can reach: the replicated `usage` domain's history (181 days, [ADR-0020](../../adr/0020-a-nodes-own-day-is-a-compacted-domain.md)), not the event log's. A spend chart states this floor, never `event_history_seconds`: one answers "can I still chart that month", the other "can I still open that turn". |
| `in_flight` | Turns running on this node. Always present; `0` is a real zero, since every API-serving process runs the engine beside it. |
| `shutting_down` | `true` from the first moment of a drain; the listener keeps serving until the drain completes. See [During a drain](#during-a-drain). |
| `posture` | The node's [config posture](../concepts/control-plane.md#posture-what-a-lagging-node-does): `serve`, `wait`, `shed`, `isolated` or `stuck`. The only place to see *why* a node left rotation, since `/ready` answers a bare `503` either way. A node applying a revision reads `wait` until the apply ends and `serve` once it succeeds, so a client polling across a `PUT /config` sees no diverged posture from a write that applies (a corrected revision after a failed one included). `shed`, `isolated` and `stuck` follow only an attempt at that epoch that concluded in failure, or (`shed`) a lag on that epoch past 45 s while a peer has it. |
| `identity_duty_seconds` | Each [identity duty](../guides/retention.md#the-identity-duties) **this node** armed, mapped to its interval in seconds, whenever it holds that duty's lease. `{}` on a node that armed none: one running no `workers` role (every duty is a worker singleton), or in a maintenance mode, which publishes nothing. A node with no company arms them like any other (the identity estate runs from boot on every data node). A never-armed duty looks like one quietly finding nothing to do, so this is where you read that the retention sweep runs at all. Which node holds each lease is the coordination store's answer. |
| `applied_epoch` | The activation epoch this node last applied; `0` until its first apply since it started (a node that booted on one revision and then refused the fleet's answers `0`). Which revision a node runs is [`GET /fleet`](#get-fleet)'s `config_serving_revision_id`. |
| `config_attempt` | `{epoch, revision_id, status}`: this node's last concluded apply attempt, with `status` `ok`, `error` (refused, still on the previous epoch) or `degraded` (refused after part of the company was already rebuilt). **Absent** until this process concluded one. It tells a refusal from an apply still running, which `applied_epoch` cannot. Never the reason, which can quote the config value given: why a node refused is [`GET /fleet`](#get-fleet)'s `config_error`, an admin's. The revision rides beside the epoch because a rebuilt coordination store restarts the count, so one epoch number can name two revisions. |
| `seats` | Handles of the seats this node holds; `[]` if none. |
| `stall_lag_seconds` | Present only when the node's watched duty is behind: its last beat is older than the beat interval it keeps (a second at the shipped lease TTL). Value is the seconds since that beat, climbing toward the seat lease TTL, at which the watchdog ends the process. Absent on a node on its beat, so its presence is what to alert on. |
| `identity` | Whether the company has its **first person**: `ready` once a person is enrolled; `unclaimed` while nobody is (a service account alone signs nobody in with a password, so it does not count), a fresh install waiting for [its first person](../concepts/identity-and-access.md#how-the-first-person-exists) to be invited into or created on a declared human seat under a Tier A token. A person an administrator creates makes it `ready` the moment the create lands, before they spend their first password link. `unknown` where this node cannot read its identity estate **or has not applied all of it** (a node just joined holds empty rows until its applier catches up, so "nobody" is proved against the identity log's end); never reported as `unclaimed`, which would tell an operator to put a first person into a company that may have started. Every node answers it, one with no company included, since the identity estate runs from boot. `/health` is the one surface an unclaimed company can reach (never guarded; no credential exists before the first person), hence its place here. It does **not** move `status`. |
| `nodes` | How many nodes hold a presence lease: the fleet this node's fan-outs (search, fleet history) divide their work by. **Absent** when the presence read failed or did not finish inside the probe's coordination budget (an eighth of the 15-second reconcile interval, under two seconds; it runs beside the posture read, so a wedged broker slows `/health` by that budget instead of hanging it). Never `0`, since the answering node is one. A screen says "node count unavailable" for an absence. |
| `alarms` | `{count, worst, worst_title}`: how many of this node's [alarms](alarms.md) are firing (one per kind however many logs it stands on); `worst`, the one firing **longest** (the table asserts no severity; the longest-unanswered condition is the one the dashboard's engine panel names first); and `worst_title`, its title in words for a company owner (both absent when `count` is 0). `worst` is a KIND, naming no log: an alarm that stands on logs (`log_headroom`, `log_ceiling_short`, `backup_age`, `trim_blocked`, `deferred_old`, `floor_unknown` and `census_drift`) lists them in its `domains`, each a measurement with its logs, on the operator-only [`/worklet/retention`](#get-workletretention-what-the-log-is-holding) answer. From the **same** evaluation come the `crewlet.alarm.active` gauge (one series per kind) and the `alarm_raised` / `alarm_cleared` log lines (a per-log condition writes them per log, so a second log joining an up alarm, and the first leaving it, are each said); it runs every ten seconds on every node running a state log. **Absent** before the first evaluation and on a node running none (no `data` role): `{count: 0}` would read as healthy. |
| `seeded_from` | Which nodes this node's live projection was seeded from at boot (the activity feed, each seat's last turn, and the live spend window behind the [`tokens` push](#pushes)), in the fleet [`coverage`](#reading-the-fleets-history-coverage) shape. Absent until a seed has landed. A failed or incomplete seed is retried ([Live-state projection](#live-state-projection-apistream--livestate)); this is the latest attempt's coverage, and `complete` turns `true` once one attempt was answered by every node. Until then those surfaces are short, and this keeps that visible after the log line scrolled away. |
| `objects` | `{direct_upload}`: whether an upload may go straight to the object store's S3 bucket on a presigned put. `available`, or `unavailable (<reason>)`: always so on the default `nats` backend (only the fleet reaches its bucket), and on an `s3` bucket whose provider the boot probe could not prove refuses a body not matching its `x-amz-checksum-sha256` and a second put under `If-None-Match: *` (see [The boot probe](../concepts/object-store.md#the-boot-probe-and-direct-uploads)). Unavailable is no fault: uploads then stream through the engine. Absent on a node running no object store. |
| `unproven_seconds` | Each seat whose teardown this node could not prove, mapped to seconds stranded; present only when one is. Such a seat is still leased by this node, so no peer can claim it, and this node will not run it (hence absent from `seats`). Alert on the duration, not the field's presence: a release that fails once and succeeds on the next heartbeat is a working system. See [Seat ownership](../concepts/seat-ownership.md#what-ownership-looks-like-from-outside). |

Per-socket facts (envelopes *this* connection dropped, its queue depth) are deliberately **not** here: the tick encodes one JSON string for every client, and a per-client field would force one encode per client per tick. A connection that lost envelopes to backpressure is logged as `stream_client_left_behind`, with the count, when it disconnects.
