A bound caller, every person, and a token bound to a seat, carries a `handle`; an unbound one, a Tier A token or a service account bound to none, carries a login and no seat, which is an ordinary state rather than a refusal (a person is never unbound: every person holds a seat). `owner` is the name the caller's OWN record is kept under, the seat when bound, the login when not, and it is what a screen asks the personal questions by, never `handle`. `config_writer` is whether the caller's credential may change the company document, false for an anonymous caller and for every credential a managed document's `api.auth.company_writers` does not list, and `config_managed_by` is that list, `[]` when the document is not managed and for an anonymous caller, so a screen draws every editing control disabled with who manages it rather than offering a save the engine refuses. `chat_vendors` is the vendor chat surfaces (`mattermost`, `slack`) a company whose chat is a vendor's declares, the one further fact a screen naming where the company talks needs beside the org answer's [`services`](#get-org), answered to a principal holding `chatlet` and `[]` to anybody else, on a company on its own chat or on none, and on a node with no company yet |
| `home_board` | `{}` | `GET /home/board`. `{seat, board, revision}`: `seat` is the human seat the board is kept under, `""` for a credential bound to no seat or a seat that is no person's, which has no stored Home (no error); `board` is the document exactly as last saved, a JSON object whose `widgets` is a list the engine never reads inside, or `null` when none is stored; `revision` is the stored board's revision, `0` when none, which the next [`save_home_board`](#saving-your-home-board) names as `if_match`. Registered only where the node reaches the coordination store. |
| `work_person` | `{handle}` | `GET /worklet/people/{handle}`. Scoped like `work_my_work`: absent is the caller's own record, and somebody else's takes their lead or `admin`, with `worklet` either way. `due` is the snoozes whose time has come, REPORTED rather than promoted: putting one back in the unread list is a write, and a read that performed one would change fleet state from a path with no operation id and no record. `priorities_set_by` is who last set the queue when it was not this person (the name their writes are recorded under, a person's seat), which is how a lead's authority is made visible beside the `prioritised` wake the write sends them: a wake that names the task now at the top of the list, because a notification here is task-shaped and "your list changed" names nothing to act on. `max_snooze_ahead` is how far ahead a snooze may be set, in SECONDS: the engine's bound, so a screen offers only the presets `mark_inbox` will accept |
| `work_views` | `{container, counts}` | `GET /worklet/views`. `container` is the strip's own (`workspace`, `project:ENG`, `unit:engineering`, `person:ana`), and it is REQUIRED, because a strip belongs to exactly one. Whose personal views appear and whose pins come first is the CALLER's, never a parameter: their [own record](#whose-record-a-personal-question-answers-for), which is the login of a Tier A token or service account bound to no seat; a caller the engine can name nothing for gets the shared strip: no pins and no personal views but the shared ones. Every row carries `builtin`, which is what tells the six nobody saved from the ones somebody did: a builtin row has no `id`, so there is nothing to rename, protect, rank or pin. `params` is the saved query in `work_items`' own parameter names (this channel's, not the `list_work_items` TOOL's, which renames four of them for a model), so a caller either hands them straight back or, simpler, passes the view's `id` as `view=` and lets the engine expand it. `counts=true` adds `count` to every row PINNED for the caller (the `total_hint` `work_items{view, container}` answers for it, run as the caller on the company's clock, with `count_capped` when it stopped at 10,000), or `count_refused` naming why a view that no longer compiles could not be counted. At most 32 counts, in the strip's one read; only a record has pins, so it is refused `bad_params` to a credential that names no record of its own |
| `work_saved_views` | `{counts}` | `GET /worklet/views/saved`. Every SAVED view (never a builtin) that the caller can see across every container: the shared ones, and the caller's own personal ones, pinned-for-them first and then by container (the workspace, projects, units, people) and the strip's own rank. Each row is `work_views`' row shape, so `container` says where it lives and `params` is its saved query. A sibling of `work_views` rather than a `container=` it takes, because a strip is ONE container's tabs and this is one PERSON's views (the inventory of what somebody saved and the pins a sidebar draws), which the workspace strip could not answer: a view saved on a project board appeared in neither. Whose is the caller's [own record](#whose-record-a-personal-question-answers-for), never a parameter, and `counts=true` takes the same rule as `work_views`: every pinned row's `count` is its view run IN ITS OWN CONTAINER, which is what opening it runs |
| `work_files` | `{project, folder, removed, limit, after}` | `GET /worklet/files`. Answers `{project, files, next}` plus the coverage half. Each file carries its `path`, `content_type`, `size`, `hash` (the SHA-256 of its whole content), `version`, who created and last wrote it and when, and (only with `removed`) who removed it and when. `next` is absent on the last page. The listing is rows only: the bytes are read through the byte route, never through the socket |

Each page carries `children`: how many pages sit directly under it that the SAME listing would show (its `status` and `skills` narrowing applied to them), absent when none: what a tree draws its expander off. With `skills=true` on a node that reads the replicated `usage` domain the answer also carries `skill_loaded_by`: page id → the `page` answer's `skill_loaded_by` list for that page, answered for the whole window in ONE read rather than one per row. On a tool-skill page, `skill_loaded_by` is every seat it reached as a skill over the last 30 company days, most recent first: `{handle, last_at, count, loaded, offered}`, where `loaded` counts the seat asking for the body (`load_tool_skill`) and `offered` a phase's catalogue putting its summary in front of the seat; absent on a node that does not read the `usage` domain, and `[]` when nobody was. `linked_from` is who LINKS here, from the index of a data node whose copies of both Doclet and Worklet serve (this node's, where its own do): `pages` (`{id, container, title}`, published pages whose body carries this page's address) and `tasks` (`{id, key, key_collision?, title, status, via}`, where `via` is `linked_page` for a page relation and `description` for an address in the description, and `key_collision` marks a task whose key another task claimed first, so a link to it goes by its `id`: the key opens the claimant), each capped at 50 with `pages_total` / `tasks_total` beside it. A link is a page id in either address the engine reads (`/doclet/pages/<id>` or the dashboard's `#/doclet/pages/<id>`), outside code; a title is not an address, since a rename moves it. Absent on a node with no index. A node that HAS an index and cannot answer sends `linked_from_status` instead of an empty list: `building` while its index is on its first lap over pages and tasks (a fresh or joined node's first minutes: an empty list then would claim nothing links here before every body was read), `unavailable` when the read failed or no data node's copies of both serve; the page itself is served either way. `folder` is the listing's |
| `page_reads` | `{page, days}` | Who READ a page: one row per (seat, way of reading) over `days` company days (1–30, default 30, anything else `bad_params`) from the replicated `usage` domain, so every data node's reads are counted (a departed node's included), and every node answers alike. `via` is `get_page`, `search`, `prefetch` or `skill_loaded`; a skill's catalogue OFFER is deliberately not a read (it would make every skill "read by every agent today") and is what `page`'s `skill_loaded_by` counts. Each row carries `count`, `last_at`, and the newest read's `last_turn_id`, `last_work_key`, `last_query` and, where the run was charged to a task in Worklet, `last_work_item{id, key, title, ordinal}`, as in "turn 2 on ENG-412". At most 100 rows, newest first, with `readers_total`; `distinct_seats_today` is the seats that read it since the company's midnight, and `elided` how many (page, way) entries the per-seat-day cap dropped across the window, COMPANY-WIDE rather than for this page: some may have been this page's and none may have been, so a non-zero value says the list MAY be short (0: it is certainly complete). `since`, `until` and `days` name the window. | `containers` | `{}` | `GET /containers`. A separate question from `pages` rather than a facet of it: a browser draws the container list once and the page list on every navigation |
| `page_activity` | `{page, container, kinds, actor_kinds, since, cursor, limit}` | What happened to a page, or to everything in a container: Doclet's own change log, mirroring `work_activity`. `kinds` is a CSV of the ten change kinds and `actor_kinds` of the three author kinds (`agent`, `human`, `operator`), the latter refused when it names one this build does not have and read one kind at a time, merged into one page; `work_activity`'s note says why. `since` bounds the window and `cursor` pages it: the same unit, two parameters, because the cursor moves with every page and the bound does not. | `artifact_data_state` | `{id}` | `GET /artifacts/{id}/data/state`. The caller's own per-viewer state keys |

| `code_counts` | `{repo, parts, read_level, …}` | `GET /gitlet/counts`. A scope's changes counted by state, the company's or one repository's, the company's repositories by kind and status, and the live entries of merge queues: see [Counting changes](../concepts/gitlet.md#counting-changes) |
| `code_search` | `{q, mode, ignore_case, repo, path, ref, limit, context, per_file, read_level}` | [`GET /gitlet/search`](#get-gitletsearch). The cursor is the room's own message number, sent back as it was answered, so it steps over the replies between two posts; a cursor the room refuses is `400 bad_params` in the domain's own words. | `chat_links` | `{channel_id, cursor, limit, read_level, …}` | `GET /chatlet/channels/{channel_id}/links`. `{channel_id, links, next_cursor}`: every link the room's messages carried, newest first, each `{url, message_id, thread_root, author, author_kind, at, channel_seq}` |
| `chat_message` | `{channel_id, message_id, read_level, …}` | `GET /chatlet/channels/{channel_id}/messages/{message_id}`. `{channel_name, channel_kind, view, root, before}`: one message, with its thread's root and the two replies before it when it is a reply |

A github.com pull request under an owner the GitHub configuration names is previewed with its repository and number (`code`), title, state and size (`meta`), read through the company's GitHub wiring ([pull request previews](../integrations/github.md#pull-request-previews-in-chat)). Every other link is absent and drawn by the link rules |
| `chat_search` | `{q, channel_id, author, limit, read_level, …}` | `GET /chatlet/search`. `{hits, searched, building, note, read_level, position}`: each hit its `message_id`, `channel_id`, the room's `channel_name` (none for a direct conversation) and `channel_kind`, as a mention carries them, `thread_root` (empty for a room post), `author` and `author_kind` (`system` for the engine's own line, which no seat said whatever name it is stored under), `snippet` — the message around the words that matched, cut by the index and marked where it was — `at` and `score`. `searched` is how many rooms the search ran over, which tells "nothing matched" from "nothing was looked at"; `building` (with a `note` saying it in words) says the answering node's index had not caught up with its transcript — a message, an edit or an erasure past what it has indexed, a rebuild under way, or an index built from a copy of the estate that has since been replaced, measured on both sides of the search and `true` too when the node could not tell — so the hits may be drawn from part of it. The visible set is resolved by the data node that answers, from the caller's seat: every public and unit room, joined or not, and the private rooms and conversations the caller is in; a `channel_id` the caller may not read narrows to nothing rather than being refused. `q` takes at most 400 bytes and is refused past that, never cut. `limit` is 20 when absent and 40 at most — a larger one is answered with 40, the most one answer holds — and there is no next page, so a full page may have more matches behind it. Unregistered on a node with no chat index |
| `chat_room_names` | `{read_level, …}` | `GET /chatlet/room-names`. `{rooms, truncated}` plus the read's `read_level`, `complete` and `position`: every named room the caller may read, each its `id`, `name`, `kind` and `archived`: every public and unit room, joined or not, and the private rooms the caller is in. The live rooms come in name order, then the archived ones, the most recently archived first, at most 1000 (`chatlet.MaxRoomNames`, the most live rooms a company holds), and `truncated` says rooms were left out. What a reader draws a room named in prose by: a room's name may be spelled as a colour (`#e2e`) or an issue's number (`#2026`) |
| `chat_rooms` | `{read_level, …}` | `GET /chatlet/rooms`. `{rooms, truncated, unreadable}` plus the read's `read_level`, `complete` and `position`: every named room the caller may read, joined or not, the archived ones included, in `chat_room_names`' set and order and at its bound. Each is the whole `channel`, its `members` (how many seats are in it), `member` (the caller is one) and `last_at` (when somebody last said something there, absent for a room nobody has spoken in; a room event is not activity). What a person browses to find a room to join |
| `config` | `{}` | `GET /config` *(needs `admin`)* |
| `config_audit` | `{limit}` | The revision history — no REST twin; `GET /config/revisions` serves the same records *(needs `admin`)* |
| `config_diff` | `{revision_id}` | [`GET /config/revisions/{id}/diff`](#get-configrevisionsiddiff) — the listing is cut at 500 and `changes_total` is how many there are *(needs `admin`)* |
| `config_entities` | `{kind, id}` | One addressable collection of the active revision: its ids, or one entity out of it. The read half of Settings › Configuration, whose write half is `PUT /config/{kind}/{id}` *(needs `admin`)* |

**Every Worklet answer carries how far this node had got, and both halves
matter.** `read_level` is the level the read was ACTUALLY served at, never the
one asked for — a level never silently downgrades, so the two can differ only
by a refusal you can see. `log_seq` is this node's committed position and
`applied_through` the prefix whose consequences it actually holds; they are two
numbers because a node applying nothing while its position advances looks
identical to a caught-up one from either alone. `log_lag` is **absent** rather
than zero when the broker could not be reached, because a read asks how far
behind an answer may be and an unreachable broker answering "not at all" is the
confident wrong answer. A caller that will not accept an answer of any age says
so with `max_lag_seconds` and/or `max_lag_seq` beside `read_level=stale`, and
the read refuses `too_stale` past whichever is reached first — the two are
readings of ONE distance rather than two, the record count being what the
broker actually answers and the duration being derived from it through this
node's own drain rate. Both are refused at every other level, because they are
a staleness bound and nothing else is. **`min_position` is the read-your-writes
half**: a log position — `<stream>@<generation>:<sequence>`, the form every
write's answer carries as `position` and every wake carries — and the answer
is served from no earlier than it, at whatever level. At `stale` it turns
"whatever this node holds" into "whatever this node holds, from here on", still
labelled with its lag; a node that has not reached it within the read budget
refuses `behind` rather than serving rows from before the write, and a position
on a log the answer is not read from is refused `400 bad_params` rather than
waited for — the caller's mistake, which every node answers the same, so it is
never an `unavailable` telling a client to ask another node. **It repeats, once
per log**: `min_position=<tracker position>&min_position=<pages position>`, or
an array of the tokens in a socket frame's params, at most one per log and
four in all (two on one log, or a fifth, are `400 bad_params`). A question read
from one log waits on its log's floor and refuses one on any other; a question
read from several — `company_feed` reads the tracker's log and the knowledge
base's — holds each half to its own log's floor, reads a half whose log a
`session` ask named no floor on at `stale`, and reports the weakest level any
half was read at ([One floor per log](../guides/consistency.md#one-floor-per-log)). It is
also what makes `read_level=session` an honest ask here: a session read waits
for the caller's own last write, so it is accepted **only beside a
`min_position`** and refused without one, the refusal naming the key and the
two other asks a caller who typed `session` might have meant — `linearizable`,
or `stale` with `max_lag_seq`. Absent, the level resolves to **this surface's**
default, which is `stale`; a seat's own tools resolve theirs to `linearizable`
and cannot be asked for anything else. See [Read consistency](../guides/consistency.md).

**`read_level`, `max_lag_seconds`, `max_lag_seq` and `min_position` work on
every question that carries a read level**, not only on `/worklet/items`:
`/worklet/items/{id}`, `/worklet/views`, `/worklet/catalogue`,
`/worklet/people/{handle}`, `/worklet/projects`, `/worklet/projects/{key}`,
`/worklet/activity`, `/worklet/my-work`, `/doclet/pages`, `/doclet/pages/{id}`,
`/containers` and every `/chatlet/` read all resolve them the same way. They did not until recently:
each of those wrote a hardcoded `stale` into its read and never looked at the
keys, so a caller asking for a stronger answer was served this node's rows and
told, in the answer's own `read_level`, that it came back at the level asked
for, and the two single-object reads, `/worklet/{id}` and `/doclet/pages/{id}`,
then took the level and dropped the bounds beside it, on the claim that a bound
is enforced against a set's coverage and one row has no set. It is not: a bound
is about **this node's lag**, checked before any row is read, and one row is
exactly as far behind as a board on the same node. And `complete: false` — with `incomplete` naming the
count, the lowest position among the records (`from`, as `{stream, generation,
seq}` — the object form every position in an answer takes, `seen_through` and a
listing's `position` included; a position in a *parameter* is the token
`<stream>@<generation>:<sequence>`) and the record version — says rows may be missing,
rows that should have gone may still be present, and the totals were computed
over the incomplete set. That is a different fact from staleness, and a client
that renders `read_level` and swallows `complete` looks confidently right.

**A read no data node could answer is `unavailable`, never a list.** Worklet,
Doclet, Chatlet and the usage history behind the spend, activity and readers
screens are answered by a data node whose copy of that domain serves (this
node's own where it holds one, another data node's otherwise), and a
read nobody answered is refused `unavailable` (REST: `503` with a
`Retry-After`) rather than answered as an empty list, which would say the
company has nothing in it. `knowledge` is the one exception, because a search is
best effort: a search no data node ran answers no hits with `served_mode`
empty and `coverage.complete` false, which a screen renders as "could not be
searched" rather than "nothing matched".

### Whose record a personal question answers for

Five questions answer about **one person or seat** rather than the company: `work_my_work`, `work_inbox`, `work_person`, `executor_sessions` and `executor_session`. Each takes a `handle`, and the rule for whose is:

1. **No handle** answers for the caller's **own record** (for the two sessions questions, the caller's own seat).
2. **Your own handle** says the same explicitly; on the three person questions either of your names is your own, since a person's login names the same record their seat does.
3. **Somebody else's login** names **their** record, looked up in the identity directory: the seat it binds them to (every person holds one), or the login itself for a service account bound to none. `ana.diaz`, bound to the seat `ana`, reads `ana`'s inbox, where everything addressed to her is kept. A login is never matched against the chart's seats. A **`token:<id>` login** is held by the Tier A entry of that id in the answering node's `api.auth.tokens`, not by a directory row: it names that token's record (the seat an active directory row binds it to, or the login itself), and a `token:` login no entry declares is held by nobody, whatever the directory says, so a mistyped `token:opps` names no record. **The directory is asked only after the question has decided what it can without it**: `admin` is admitted whatever the login is, and a caller who leads somebody may be, so for those two the login is looked up and the question decided again on the record it names. Everybody else (somebody who leads nobody) is refused as on any seat they do not lead, before anything is looked up, so the refusal never says whether the login exists or whose seat it holds. A login nobody holds, or one whose holder is bound to a seat the chart no longer has, names no record (`404`) for `admin` and is refused as below for a lead. A node that cannot read the directory answers `503`, to those two only, without the directory's own words (they name the seat a login is bound to).
4. **Anybody else's handle** is decided by the authority table on the record it resolved to, each question asking its own verb. The first three are somebody's QUEUE and take the owner-or-lead rule: whoever leads that person (so a lead may name their report by seat or by login) or a caller holding `admin`, each with `worklet`. A node that cannot read the chart to tell answers `503`, never a refusal, so a lead is not told they lead nobody. `executor_sessions` and `executor_session` are a seat's TRAIL (what its harness wrote on each turn, and how each ended) and take `audit.seat.read`, the rule `/agents/{id}/memory` and an executor's tail take: the seat's lead, or `admin`, with no app.

A refusal on authority is `403 unauthorized` naming the deciding rule in `reason` and, in `grants`, the permissions any one of which would have admitted the caller: `admin` for a colleague's queue or a seat's sessions, `worklet` for a lead who does not use it. An empty `grants` means no permission would.

**A caller's own record is kept under ONE name**, the name every write they make is [attributed to](#who-a-write-is-attributed-to): the seat's handle for a person (every person holds a seat) and for a token or service account the directory binds to one; the login (`svc:ci`, `token:ops`) for one it binds to none. The tools write a caller's inbox marks, pins, priorities and personal views under that name, and every question here reads them back under it. Binding changes where the record is kept, not whether there is one.

A seat's trail belongs to the seat: a caller bound to no seat who names none on a sessions question is refused `bad_params`, not `unauthorized`. Nobody was denied anything; the remedy is a binding in the directory, not a different credential.

No parameter names a viewer anywhere on this surface. Whose board, queue and view strip is the CALLER's; a question about somebody else takes the `handle` above and its rule.

### One frame per posture, and how a frame is routed

Both facts are properties of the *client*, not the push.

**Its posture decides the bytes.** A socket is served `live` or `degraded`, and two sockets in the same posture receive the byte-identical frame from a single encode: the engine marshals one push **once per posture present**, never once per connection.

**Its route decides the audience.** Every kind in the table above is one of three:

| Route | Kinds | Reaches |
|---|---|---|
| broadcast | `event`, `agents`, `seats`, `executors`, `tokens`, `budget`, `schedules`, `org`, `tools`, `health` | Every connected client whose posture takes the kind. |
| room | `inbox_changed`, `artifact_changed`, `artifact_data`, `artifact_presence` | Only the clients in the frame's room: a seat's room (clients whose `watch` for that seat was allowed; the frame names the seat in its `seat` field) or an artifact's room (clients whose `artifact_join` was allowed; the payload names the artifact). |
| direct | `snapshot`, `result`, `error`, `pong` | The one client it answers. |

One keyed index holds both kinds of room. A room-routed frame that lost its room is **dropped**, never fanned out: a result carries one client's correlation id and a targeted frame one room's audience, so "everybody" is the unsafe default.

### Presence in an artifact's room

Presence is **told, never stored**: who is in a room and what they look at lives in the memory of the node holding each socket and crosses between nodes on an ephemeral broadcast, with no row, log record or coordination key. Every inter-node frame is sealed under the fleet keyring (`secrets.keys`) with a 60-second validity inside the seal; a frame the fleet did not seal shows nobody. Each node rebroadcasts its members every 15 seconds, a member not heard for 45 seconds is dropped, and a node gaining a room's first socket asks its peers once. Everybody who can open the artifact and has it open is in the roster; there is no invisible mode. An agent reading or writing the artifact appears as an `agent` for 45 seconds after its last call.

### A degraded node keeps the socket open

When a node's own posture leaves rotation because its copy of the company is **wrong rather than behind** (`shed` or `stuck`, the set [`/ready`](#routes) refuses on), its sockets move to the `degraded` posture instead of closing. A closed socket reconnects on a backoff, learns nothing, and shows "retrying"; one that stays open is told.

In that posture:

- **Keepalives continue.** `ping` is answered with `pong`, and the 5-second `health` frame still arrives; its `status` names the posture.
- **Pushes stop.** Every other broadcast kind is withheld, being derived from the copy the fleet abandoned.
- **Queries are refused** with `unavailable`, and the query surface is never reached. `unavailable` must never be flattened into an empty result. The frame carries `retry_after` (one health tick, the soonest the posture can change) and names no `refusal`, since none of the state log's is behind it; the `health` frame says why.
- **`snapshot` still arrives** on connect: a direct frame carrying the node's own health, so it says why the rest stopped.

`wait` and `isolated` stay **live**, as `/ready` stays ready on them: `wait` is ordinary propagation during a rollout, and `isolated` means no node applied the revision, so blinding every operator would turn one bad revision into an outage.

### Close codes

A refused handshake **cannot** carry a close code (the connection never opened); it is answered `401` before the upgrade ([`GET /ws/stream`](#ws-wsstream) above). These codes are for an open socket.

**An open socket is authenticated at its handshake and ended by what ends its credential.** There is no periodic re-check; each of these events is handled:

- **an identity record names it**: its session was signed out, ended by an administrator or replaced by a step-up; the person it acts for was suspended, removed, signed out everywhere, given other grants, bound to another seat or had a machine token revoked; or the directory row a Tier A token is bound through (`token:<id>`) moved. Every node serving the API holds the estate and applies the identity log, so each hears this from its own applier; the sockets the record names, and only those, are decided again by the guard over the request they were opened with. A revocation reaches an open tab within the time it takes to apply.
- **an identity move names nobody**: the company's session generation moved (every session ended at once), this node **retained** a record instead of applying it (one a newer build wrote during a rolling upgrade, or one signed under a keyring key it was not restarted with), a join replaced its identity estate, or its identity applier **stopped keeping up** (halted on a record it cannot read, or frozen behind a broker) and its lag has just passed the stall grace, the instant every identity read on the node starts answering `503`. **Every** open socket closes `1013` at once and nothing is read on its behalf; each tab reconnects on its backoff and its handshake decides: `401` sends it to sign in, `503` says this node cannot tell yet, and an untouched credential is back on a fresh snapshot.
- **a company was published**: every configuration apply, a hire or any other edit of the org chart. Each socket is decided against the new company, in memory, with no identity read: one whose person's seat the company no longer holds as a human seat closes `4403`, one whose seat now answers to another handle closes `1013` so its handshake resolves the binding afresh, and every `watch` is decided again.
- **its credential ends on its own**: a session's absolute deadline, a machine token's expiry. No record is written then, so each socket keeps a timer for it, and the guard decides it.
- and **once as it starts listening**, so a record landing between handshake and that moment is not missed.

A session's **idle** deadline does not end an open socket: an open live view is activity, and a socket can never be re-issued a cookie. The browser's cookie is moved only by a REST response, so a client that talks to the node over the socket alone makes an ordinary REST request now and then to keep its session past the idle deadline.

Each answer does one thing:

| Answer | Code | What a client does |
|---|---|---|
| The session ended, expired or was revoked; the token is no longer accepted | `4401` | Re-dial with the credential the browser holds now; if the handshake answers `401`, sign in. |
| The person resolves but their seat is gone from the chart | `4403` | Stop reconnecting and show why: the credential is fine, what it may do is not. |
| This node will not vouch for the credential now: it could not read what decides it, an identity move named nobody, or the seat answers to another handle | `1013` | The standard's *try again later*: reconnect on a backoff. The handshake decides, answering `503 identity_unavailable` with a `Retry-After` for as long as the node cannot say, before any snapshot is built. |
| Resolved as somebody else: renamed, bound to another seat or to none, given or refused a grant | `1013` | Reconnect, and ask who you are again (`viewer`): the handshake builds the snapshot for the new grants, and a screen naming the old login or seat is redrawn as the new one. |
| Resolved as the same login, seat and grants | *(no close)* | Nothing; later questions are asked as the principal just resolved. |

**A node behind its identity log** hears no record it has not applied, so inside the stall grace its open sockets are served on their last decision, as its REST routes are served on the rows it has. Past the grace it can vouch for nobody and every open socket closes `1013` at that instant, including on a node whose applier **halted** on the very record meant to end them.

`4401` and `4403` sit in the 4000–4999 range the standard reserves for applications and echo the HTTP status they mean; `1013` is the standard's own. Nothing else closes this socket for a fault.

### Wiring

Every node that serves the API feeds its projection through one entry point, `stream.Service.Ingest`, from an **ephemeral broadcast subscription** to the event stream (`observe.Projector`). It receives every event from every node, because a dashboard served by one node must show turns that ran on another; a publish listener would see only its own node's. The event store takes the other route, a publish listener inline on the publishing node (or, for a node without `data`, the one data node that keeps the event in [custody](../guides/deployment.md#custody-the-rows-of-a-node-without-data)), so no two nodes keep one row. Each event updates the live-state projection *and* fans out to connected dashboards. Backpressure is per-WebSocket: a stalled tab drops the oldest queued envelope so it cannot stall the publish path or other tabs.

The dashboard is a React + TypeScript application, built by Vite from `crewlet/dashboard/` into `crewlet/static/dashboard/`, which the binary embeds. Its wire half is `src/protocol/`: a store that mirrors the projection and derives nothing (`protocol/store.ts`), a reconnecting WebSocket client with heartbeat, query channel and REST-snapshot fallback (`protocol/socket.ts`), the one REST transport (`protocol/rest.ts`) and the one write client (`protocol/act.ts`). Every list the engine owns and the dashboard must repeat (event categories, push kinds, act refusals, tools a button may call) is declared once in `src/contract/`, and a Go gate holds each against the engine's own value. A hash router keeps every screen, section and filter in the URL, with one file per screen. `/dashboard` serves the shell; `/static/{path}` serves its assets. The build output is COMMITTED, so `go build ./...` needs no Node.

Two caching classes, decided by where the build put the file:

| Files | `Cache-Control` | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Everything under `/static/dashboard/assets/` — the entry module, every chunk, the stylesheet | `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` | Each name carries a content hash, so different bytes are a different URL; a browser that has the file never asks again, reload included |
| Everything else — the shell (`/dashboard`), `/favicon.ico`, `/static/dashboard/crewlet-icon.svg`, the fonts and the notices | `no-cache` | The name does not change with the bytes, so the browser revalidates on every load and a redeploy is picked up on the next; the shell names the new hashed files |

Every file answers with a strong `ETag`, and `If-None-Match` is read as a list under weak comparison, so `"a", "b"`, `W/"a"` and `*` each earn a `304`. `HEAD` and `Range` are answered too.

**Text is gzipped for a client that asks for it**: HTML, JavaScript, CSS, SVG, JSON, plain text and the `.ico` favicon are compressed once per file per process, at gzip's best level, and served with `Content-Encoding: gzip` when the request's `Accept-Encoding` admits `gzip` (or `x-gzip`, or `*`) with a weight above zero and the result is smaller than the file. A member that names gzip outranks the wildcard, so `*, gzip;q=0` gets the file as it is, as does a request with no `Accept-Encoding` (scripts and probes, which would print the compressed bytes). Fonts and images are never recompressed (woff2 and PNG already are). The gzip representation has its own `ETag` (the identity tag with `-gz` before the closing quote), and every response for a file that has one carries `Vary: Accept-Encoding`, its `304` included. On the committed build the four files a first load fetches go from 1.47 MB to 401 KB. A reverse proxy needs no compression or caching rule for the dashboard; one that compresses leaves an already-encoded response as it is.

`/static/dashboard/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt` (served as `text/plain`) holds the license text of every npm package the bundle contains (the design system's four among them), written by Vite's `build.license`, then the NOTICE file any of them ships (the design system's Apache-2.0 packages do), the SIL Open Font License of the embedded Geist and Geist Mono faces, and the ISC License of the Lucide drawings every glyph is one of (with Feather's MIT text for the glyphs Lucide derives from it). The release archives and container image carry the same file, beside the notices for the Go modules the binary links.

The product's mark is `/static/dashboard/crewlet-icon.svg`, emitted by the build from `@crewlethq/icons` beside the raster `favicon.ico`; the tab icon, the dashboard's lockup and the GitHub App landing page all draw that one file.

A second build target, `static/protocol/protocol.js`, is the wire protocol alone as plain ESM (`src/protocol/`, the store included, nothing of React): `internal/e2e` replays a real company's captured frames through it under `node`, checking the client's understanding of this contract against a real server. It is committed beside the dashboard's tree and never embedded or served.

Its visual system (token layer, measured palette, rules a change has to keep) is in [Dashboard Design System](dashboard-design.md).

---

## Organization

### `GET /org`

The company's charter and organization tree, as a reader holding no permission at all may see it. The same object is the `org` section of the [handshake snapshot](#what-the-handshake-snapshot-carries) and the body of every `org` push.

Every reference in it is an **identity, not a display name**: a seat's `manages` entry carries another seat's `handle` or a unit's `id`, and a unit's `lead` carries a seat's `handle`. A unit carries its `id` (its `id` field, or its name where it declares none), so a client can resolve a reference against something else in the same response.

```json
{
  "name": "Nimbus",
  "mission": "...",
  "vision": "...",
  "policies": ["..."],
  "timezone": "Europe/Berlin",
  "token_budget": {"month": 40000000},
  "services": {"tracker": "worklet", "knowledge": "confluence", "code": "native"},
  "roles": [
    {"name": "Founder", "kind": "human", "manages": ["cto"], "availability": "CET business hours"}
  ],
  "units": [
    {
      "id": "engineering",
      "name": "Engineering",
      "type": "department",
      "purpose": "...",
      "lead": "cto",
      "goals": ["..."],
      "channel": "engineering",
      "knowledge": ["..."],
      "roles": [
        {
          "name": "CTO",
          "handle": "cto",
          "goal": "...",
          "backstory": "...",
          "responsibilities": ["..."],
          "behavioral_guidelines": ["..."],
          "manages": ["platform"],
          "token_budget": {"day": 2000000},
          "avatar": {"character": "hexlet", "color": "cyan"},
          "llm": {
            "execute": ["fast", "backup"], "review": ["big", "fast"],
            "subagent": ["fast", "backup"], "auxiliary": ["cheap"], "judge": ["cheap"],
            "onboarding": ["fast", "backup"]
          },
          "tool_sources": ["builtin", "mcp:search", "mcp:github"]
        }
      ],
      "children": [
        {
          "id": "platform",
          "name": "Platform",
          "purpose": "...",
          "roles": [
            {
              "name": "Platform Engineer",
              "goal": "...",
              "avatar": {"character": "crewlet", "color": "purple"}
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "derived": {
    "seats": [
      {
        "handle": "cto", "name": "CTO", "kind": "agent",
        "manager": "founder", "managers": ["founder"],
        "reports": ["platform-engineer"], "auto_reports": ["platform-engineer"],
        "onboarding_chain": ["Engineering"]
      }
    ],
    "units": [
      {
        "name": "Platform", "type": "team", "lead": "cto", "lead_inherited": true,
        "channel": "engineering", "channel_inherited": true,
        "seats": ["platform-engineer"]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

In that document `manages: ["cto"]` is a seat **handle** and `manages: ["platform"]` is a unit **key**; a seat is always named by its handle and a unit by its key, never by a display name.

**`derived` is the hierarchy the engine derives from the company it is RUNNING**, so a client draws a chart rather than deriving one. Its rules: a handle is a slug with Go's own case mapping; a lead and a channel cascade to child units that set none; a `manages` entry keying a unit stands for the seats in its subtree; a unit's lead manages the members nobody else manages; the primary manager is the first seat in the engine's own order that manages a seat. It is on every answer for a company, derived in the same call as the tree, and absent only from `{}`.

**From the company this node runs.** The whole answer (`roles:` and `units:` as well as `derived`) is cut from the organization of the epoch this node applied, so it changes exactly when a revision is applied.

The fields outside `derived` stay as WRITTEN, so a reader can tell a declared lead from an inherited one. Every list may arrive as `null`; treat it as empty. The authored `path`, `unit_path` and `placed_by_ref` of each entry are omitted (they say where a seat was WRITTEN). Membership is each unit's `seats`.

**What it carries, and nothing else.** The company's `name`, `mission`, `vision`, `policies`, `timezone`, `token_budget`, `services` and `derived`; for each seat its `name`, `kind`, `handle`, `goal`, `backstory`, `responsibilities`, `behavioral_guidelines`, `manages`, `availability`, `token_budget`, `avatar`, `llm` and `tool_sources`; for each unit its `name`, `type`, `purpose`, `lead`, `goals`, `channel`, `knowledge`, `roles` and `children`. Every value is the one the company document holds, as written: a seat with no declared `handle` has none here (the engine derives it from the name), and a unit that inherits its lead has no `lead` of its own. An empty field is omitted, and a node with no active company answers `{}`.

**`timezone` is the one value the engine resolves**: the company's [one clock](../getting-started/configuration.md#the-companys-clock). An unwritten clock IS UTC, so a running company always carries a zone name here (`UTC` where the document writes none), never an empty string a client would default to its browser's zone. Every day the engine cuts ("today", a due band, an overdue mark, a person's own day) is cut on it, so a screen deciding which day something falls on cuts on this.

**`services` is which tracker, knowledge base and chat the company runs, and whether the engine hosts its code**, as the engine resolves them, on every answer for a company and to every reader. All four are closed sets:

- `tracker`: `worklet`, `jira` or `none`.
- `knowledge`: `doclet`, `confluence` or `none`.
- `chat`: `chatlet` (Crewlet's own chat), `vendor` or `none`. It names a posture, not a product; which vendors a `vendor` company talks on is told to a holder of `chatlet` as the [`viewer`](#queries) answer's `chat_vendors`.
- `code`: `native` where the document sets [`code.backend: gitlet`](../getting-started/configuration.md#code), else `none`, whatever vendor the company connects beside it (a GitHub or GitLab repository is an integration its seats call, not a host the dashboard draws).

A `backend` the document leaves empty resolves as the engine resolves it: the vendor whose `integrations` block is connected, else `worklet`, `doclet` and `chatlet` respectively. `services` decides which dashboard surfaces exist: a company not running Worklet has no Worklet section and no My work, one not running Chatlet has no Chatlet, and every question about such a service is refused there; one hosting no code has no Gitlet workspace. It names the backend and nothing else of the `tracker:`, `knowledge:`, `chat:` and `code:` blocks, which stay guarded: no project or space key, site, URL, room policy, credential, repository or limit. Absent only from `{}`, so "no company yet" is never mistaken for `none`.

**`services.restart` is which of the four THE ANSWERING NODE serves only once it restarts**, each by its key (`tracker`, `knowledge`, `chat`, `code`): one of Crewlet's own services the company turned on while this node's runtime was already running without it ([A native backend changes at a restart](../concepts/control-plane.md#a-native-backend-changes-at-a-restart)). Until the restart, every question about it is refused there `unavailable` under `native_backend_needs_restart` with no `Retry-After`, so a client treats it as a service it cannot reach on this node, not one the company does not run. Absent where the node serves everything the company runs.

**`token_budget` is the ceilings as written**, on the company and on each seat that names its own: one number per calendar window it caps (`day`, `week`, `month`, on the company clock), nothing for a window left open, so an absent key is "no ceiling", never zero. How much is spent, and when each window resets, is [`GET /budgets`](#get-budgets).

**A seat's `avatar`, `llm` and `tool_sources` are RESOLVED**, since a client would get the rule wrong. All three are absent on a human seat, which runs neither. `avatar` is published to everybody; `llm` and `tool_sources` **only to a reader holding `admin`**, being computed from seat configuration no other reader is shown.

- **`avatar`** is how the agent seat is drawn: its `character` and `color`, each as the seat's `avatar` block writes it, else the default (`crewlet` and `purple`), so every agent seat carries both. A value a newer engine admitted that this dashboard does not draw arrives as written; the dashboard draws that part as the default.
- **`llm`** is every phase's provider chain exactly as a turn resolves it, keyed by phase (`execute`, `review`, `subagent`, `auxiliary`, `judge`, `onboarding`): the first key is the model that phase runs on, every later one a fallback in the order tried. A flat `llm_<phase>` field wins over the same phase inside the `llm` mapping, a phase naming nothing takes the seat's `llm`, and a seat naming nothing lands on the company's `default` provider or, without one, the first provider declared. Values are provider KEYS, the labels `providers.llm` gives its entries; the model, endpoint and credentials stay guarded. Absent when the company configures no provider.
- **`tool_sources`** is where the seat's tools come from, in the tool registry's origin grammar: `builtin` first, then `mcp:<server>` for each granted server in the order `mcp_servers` declares them. A server is granted by its entry's `access` (every agent seat where it has none), or, for one reading each agent's own vendor credential, by the integration lane the seat is on ([Tools and MCP › Choosing which agents get a server](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#choosing-which-agents-get-a-server)); never by a seat's `mcp_env` block, which holds values. It is the GRANT, not what is running: a server that failed to start is still listed; the node status record's MCP report says it failed.

**What it never carries.** A seat's `contact` identities, `email`, `unit` reference, `workers`, `learning_enabled`, `mcp_env`, `sandbox`, `placement`, `integrations` and `schedules`, and its authored `llm` / `llm_*` fields (their effect is the resolved `llm`); a unit's `mcp_env`, `integrations` and `schedules`; and every company block outside the charter and its budget (providers, MCP servers, integrations, the knowledge and tracker blocks beyond the resolved `services`, notification and learning settings, worker templates). Those are read through the `admin`-gated `config` query or [`GET /config`](#config--live-config-management-auth-gated), which masks credentials. Schedules have their own read surface under the same posture as `/org`: [`GET /schedules`](#routes) answers every configured schedule with its task and next run.

**Why an explicit shape.** `/org` is readable by every caller. Serialising the config's own seat and unit types would make every field added to a seat public the day it landed, whatever it held. The shape is declared field by field in `internal/api`, and a test fails when the config gains a company, seat or unit field nobody has classified as public, resolved or guarded.

Founder prose is served as written. Nothing in the public fields is resolved as a `${VAR}`, so a reference typed into a goal is shown as text; keep credentials in the fields built for them.

---

## `/operator/mcp` — your own assistant

The premise of running Crewlet is that an AI manages your company, and the person doing that management often works through an AI of their own (a coding agent, an assistant). This endpoint lets it read the board, file what you just decided, and read what the company has written down, instead of having the dashboard described to it.

Point any MCP client at it:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "crewlet": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://crewlet.example.com/operator/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${CREWLET_API_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}
```

### What it serves

The **same tools a seat holds**, not a parallel implementation: `list_work_items`,
`get_work_item`, `create_work_item`, `update_work_item`, `comment_on_work_item`,
`merge_work_item`, `move_work_item`, `search_work_items`, `get_work_catalogue`, `list_projects`, `describe_project`, `write_project`,
`list_project_files`, `read_project_file`, `write_project_file`, `remove_project_file`,
`task_activity`, `my_work`,
`list_pages`, `get_page`, `write_page`, `save_page`, `comment_on_page`,
`search_knowledge`; wherever the node takes artifact uploads,
`list_artifacts`, `get_artifact`, `list_dashboard_sources`,
`get_artifact_format`, `get_company_brand`, `list_artifact_comments`,
`create_artifact`, `publish_artifact`, `update_artifact`,
`share_artifact`, `unshare_artifact`, `upload_artifact_asset`,
`create_artifact_folder`, `move_artifact`, `comment_on_artifact`,
`resolve_artifact_comment`, `edit_artifact_comment`,
`remove_artifact_comment`, `read_artifact_data`, `query_artifact_data`,
`write_artifact_data` and `set_artifact_schema` (see
[Artifacts](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#artifacts)), each artifact and datastore
write answering its `op_id` here, and taking it back, by Worklet's own rule
(below); and, where the company runs
Chatlet, `list_channels`, `read_channel`, `search_messages`,
`post_message`, `reply_in_thread`, `send_dm`, `react_to_message`,
`join_channel` and `leave_channel` — where `list_channels` also counts each
room's unread messages against the caller's own read state, which no seat's
turn has: each row carries `unread` (and `unread_capped` past the cap), a room
the caller muted carries `muted: true`, and a caller in do-not-disturb gets a
top-level `dnd_until`, as the rail shows them. When that read state cannot be
read it says so in a top-level `read_state: "unknown: …"` and puts no count on
any row, rather than counting from zero.
Wherever the company hosts its repositories in the engine
(`code.backend: gitlet`), it serves the code reads too — `code_list_repos`,
`code_get_repo`, `code_resolve`, `code_read`, `code_diff`, `code_compare`,
`code_landed_in`, `code_log`, `code_blame`, and a repository's changes,
`code_list_changes` and `code_get_change`, a commit's checks, `code_get_check_failures`,
and a search across every repository, `code_search`, the
[`code_search` question](#get-gitletsearch) as a tool (see [The company's code](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#the-companys-code)) —
read as you, so every repository while you hold `gitlet` and none without it,
and none recorded as `operator_acted` — and,
where Gitlet's writes are served, the code writes: `code_commit_files`,
`code_revert`, `code_cherry_pick`, `code_create_branch`, `code_delete_branch`,
`code_create_tag`, `code_delete_tag`, `code_create_repo`, `code_update_repo`, `code_delete_repo`,
`code_restore_repo`, `code_protect_branch`, a change's `code_open_change`,
`code_update_change` and `code_close_change`, and its conversation's
`code_request_review`, `code_review_change`, `code_comment_on_change`,
`code_delete_comment` and `code_resolve_finding`, `code_apply_suggestions`,
`code_rebase_change`,
`code_merge_change`, `code_dequeue_change` and `code_revert_change`, and a commit's checks'
`code_rerun_checks` and `code_report_check` — the last your own CI's report of a check, which no seat
is given ([External CI](../guides/gitlet.md#external-ci)) — and a repository's `code_purge_unreachable`,
a purge of its unreachable objects that no seat is given either and that asks a fresh proof of who
you are, and `code_import_repo`, a repository created from one at another host, which no seat is given
either — each made as the human seat you
hold through the credential you came with (a token bound to nobody writes
nothing), each answering its `op_id` here and taking it back by Worklet's
own rule, and each one `operator_acted`. Every code tool, read or write, takes
the Gitlet permission, refused `unauthorized` naming `gitlet` to a caller or a
token without it
([ADR-0110](../../adr/0110-reaching-a-repository-takes-the-gitlet-permission.md)). And
it serves the deployment's health — `fleet_health`, and `code_status` where the
code reads are — an administrator's reads, refused to anybody else, which an
agent seat holds only by its role's grant (see
[The health tools](../guides/fleet.md#the-health-tools)). And it serves the
company's [atlas](../concepts/atlas.md) to a holder of `atlas`, with the three
tools every agent seat holds: `atlas_search`, a `query` (part of a name or key,
or an id), a `kind` and a `limit` (default 50, at most 500), answered with
`entries` and the `total` that matched; `atlas_get`, one entry in full by its
`id` or its exact `name` or key, with `used_by`, what relies on it; and
`atlas_trace`, from one entry `up` to what depends on it (the default) or
`down` to what it depends on, at most six hops (`depth`) and fifty entries,
every relation with `all`. Each answers each source's `coverage` and how many
values were `withheld` for being shaped like a credential, and lists
repositories only for a caller who holds `gitlet` too
([ADR-0127](../../adr/0127-reading-the-atlas-takes-the-atlas-permission.md)).
A schema, a default, a trimmed field
and the wording of a refusal are each written once — two copies of "file an
item" drift on exactly the parts nobody looks at, and only one of the two is
ever tested.

**An argument a tool does not take is refused, naming it** and the arguments
the tool does read, rather than dropped. A tool reads what its schema declares
and nothing else, so an assistant still sending an argument a tool has retired
— `save_work_view`'s old `owner` is the one that saved a personal view as a
shared tab on the project, under an answer saying it had worked — or one it
misspelt was answered as though it had asked for less, and never told which.

Every write's answer carries its three-valued `outcome`, the object's new
`version`, and **`position`** — where the record landed, as
`<stream>@<generation>:<sequence>`, or `null` on an `unknown` outcome, where
the broker never said. That is the value a client hands back as `min_position`
on any read above, so an assistant that files an item here and redraws the
board over `GET /worklet` is served an answer that includes it rather than
whatever this node happened to hold. The tools' own reads need none of it —
they read `linearizable` — but the answer travels to a client that does not.

A write's answer here also carries **`op_id`**: the operation that call *was*.
A seat's writes derive their operation ids from its turn, so a seat repeating a
call is the same operation; a call here has no turn, so each one is minted an
operation of its own and told it. To finish a write that came back `unknown`,
or a gesture that stopped part of the way through, send the call again with
exactly the same arguments and that `op_id` — every write it makes is then the
same operation again, a created item or a new comment or saved view included,
answered from the ledger where it landed and finished where it did not. A call
without one is a new operation: repeated, a create files a second item. The
argument is offered by the tracker's writes — `create_work_item`,
`update_work_item`, `comment_on_work_item`, `merge_work_item`,
`move_work_item`, `place_work_item`, `remove_work_item`, `restore_work_item`,
`set_priorities`, `set_pins`, `mark_inbox`, `save_work_view`,
`delete_work_view`, `write_project_file` and `remove_project_file` — and by the artifacts' and the
datastore's — `create_artifact`, `publish_artifact`, `update_artifact`,
`share_artifact`, `unshare_artifact`, `upload_artifact_asset`,
`create_artifact_folder`, `move_artifact`, `write_artifact_data` and
`set_artifact_schema` — under one rule and in one set of words, and held to the
rule every route that takes an `Idempotency-Key` holds that key
to: an id this engine minted, at most 128 bytes of visible ASCII — anything
else is refused naming `op_id`. An `op_id` belongs to **the one call it was
answered for**: the id names that call's tool and carries a digest of its
arguments, so brought back with the same tool and exactly the same arguments it
is that operation again, and with any other argument — another item, another
project, another title, another blocker — or with another tool, it is refused
naming `op_id` before anything is written. Nothing is ever made twice under
one, and nothing is half-made: a looser rule would answer the steps the two
calls share from the first call and write the ones they do not. To make a
different write, leave `op_id` out. One case is refused later, by the ledger,
and says so: an operation whose step now meets another object — a move whose
item somebody else moved in between, so the key it aliases is another — is
refused `op_reused`, and the answer says to leave `op_id` out.

The one field that differs is **who the call acts as**. There is no turn and no
seat here, so this surface supplies its own identity, and every tool resolves
the caller through that rather than through the turn — a read that asked the
turn first refused every call on this endpoint while the writes beside it
worked. A comment's `@handle` is resolved here too, against the company chart
current when the comment is written, so mentioning somebody from your own
assistant wakes them exactly as it does from a seat.

That identity is the **request's principal**, and nothing the caller sends
can change it — there is deliberately no way to ask this surface to act as a
seat. A person — every person holds a human seat — acts **as their seat**,
and so does a token the identity directory binds to one: their writes are recorded under its handle with author kind `human`, and every
tool that asks who the caller **is** rather than who wrote it keys on it —
`mark_inbox`, `set_pins` and `set_priorities` write the seat's record;
`my_work`, `get_person` and `work_inbox` answer for it, and so does the viewer
`list_work_items` expands `preset=my_queue` and `preset=priorities` against; a
`watch: true`, a comment and a create record it as the watcher; a create with
no `project` files into its team's; and the lead relation `routing_unit` and
`write_project` are gated on is resolved for it. A credential nobody is bound
through — a Tier A token or a service account bound to no seat — writes under
its own login with author kind `operator`, and keeps its own record under that login,
which is ordinary. Being the seat is also what keeps a wake from coming back to
you: the change you just made is not announced to whoever made it, so filing
work through your own assistant does not wake you about it. See
[who a write is attributed to](#who-a-write-is-attributed-to) and
[Humans in the org](../concepts/humans-in-the-org.md).

The three person writes take **moves, not lists**, and each is resolved against
the person's record as the write finds it — so two screens writing at once both
land, and nothing a call does not name changes:

| Tool | Arguments |
|---|---|
| `mark_inbox` | `read`, `unread`, `unsnooze` — lists of the `record_id`s `work_inbox` returns; `snooze` — `[{record_id, until}]`, `until` RFC3339, in the future and at most a year away; `read_through` — a log position, `<stream>@<generation>:<sequence>`, that only ever moves forward; `primary_reasons` — omitted leaves the choice, `[]` takes the default back; `seen` (optional) — how far you read the tracker's log, `CREWLET_TRACKER_LOG@<generation>:<sequence>`, the `position` of the newest work notice you were shown, or the tracker source's `newest`: a mark is decided by whichever data node it is asked of, which may not yet have applied a notice the page was read with elsewhere, so the decide waits for `seen` first, and a node that cannot reach it within the write budget answers `unavailable` (behind) and appends nothing — the same call lands once it has — rather than refusing a notice you were shown as no change the company recorded. Without it the mark waits for nothing, and a notice the deciding node has not reached is refused `invalid`; a `seen` on another log is refused `invalid`. The dashboard sends each notice's own position, the furthest of the notices an answered question marks, and "Mark all read" the position it reads through; `PUT /worklet/people/{handle}/inbox` takes it in its body likewise. A notice named twice in one call is refused `invalid`; a list the call would leave past 256 entries is refused `inbox_full`. |
| `code_mark_inbox` | The same arguments as `mark_inbox`, over your own CODE notices — the `record_id`s `inbox` answers under `source: "code"`, and a `read_through` on the code log (`CREWLET_CODE_LOG@<generation>:<sequence>`); `primary_reasons` names Gitlet's reasons (`mention`, `review_requested`, `changes_requested`, `checks_failed`, `target_broken`, `conflicted`, `dequeued`, `finding_replied`, `ready_to_merge`, `merged`, `review_submitted`, `re_review`, `thread`, `watcher`, `lead_fallback`). Each domain keeps the marks over its own notices on its own log, so a position on one says nothing of the other's. `seen` (optional) is how far you read the code log, `CREWLET_CODE_LOG@<generation>:<sequence>` — the `position` of the newest code notice you were shown, or the code source's `newest`: a mark is decided by whichever data node it is asked of, which may not yet have applied a notice the page was read with elsewhere, so the decide waits for `seen` first, and a node that cannot reach it within the write budget hands the mark to the next one rather than refusing a notice you were shown as none of yours. Without it the mark waits for nothing, and a notice the deciding node has not reached is refused `invalid`; a `seen` on another log is refused. The dashboard sends each notice's own position, and "Mark all read" the position it reads through. Your own record alone, as the human seat you hold: a mark of anybody else's — whatever authority the caller holds — and a record that reached somebody else are refused. It takes `gitlet`, as Worklet's marks take `worklet`: without it no code notice is yours to list, count or mark. Offered where the company hosts code. |
| `code_mark_viewed` | `repo` and `change`, the change; `viewed`, the files to mark, each `{path, blob_oid, mode}`: the path as `code_get_change` part=files names it and that file's `new_oid` and `new_mode` from the same answer, neither for a file the change deletes; `unviewed`, the paths whose mark to take back; `seen` (optional), the `position` the change was read at. At most 32 files a call. A mark stays while later revisions give the file the same object id and mode, and reads unviewed once either changes; only a draft or open change keeps marks (a closed or merged one is refused `conflict`), and a person holds at most 2 000, the oldest going first. The caller's own record alone; a seat is never offered it. |
| `artifact_mark_inbox` | The same arguments as `mark_inbox`, over your own COMMENT notices: the `record_id`s `inbox` answers under `source: "artifacts"`, a `read_through` and a `seen` on the artifacts log (`CREWLET_ARTIFACTS_LOG@<generation>:<sequence>`), and `primary_reasons` naming the comment reasons (`owner`, `assignee`, `mention`, `participant`; the default primary half is `owner`, `mention` and `assignee`). Your own record alone, as the human seat you hold, and no app: a comment is a relation to an artifact, never an app. Served beside the artifacts tools, and no seat is given it. |
| `set_pins` | `views` and `favorites`, each `{add, remove}` or `{set}` — never both, and a bare list is refused naming the shape. The caps are held against the list the change would leave. |
| `set_priorities` | `handle`, `items` — the whole order, most important first — and `if_match`, the `version` `get_person` answered: given, a reorder against an older record is refused `stale_version`. |

Plus **thirty-one no seat is given**: `list_work_views`, `save_work_view`,
`delete_work_view`, `write_work_catalogue`, `get_person`, `work_inbox`,
`mark_inbox`, `set_pins`, `set_priorities`,
`remove_work_item`, `restore_work_item`,
[`place_work_item`](#moving-a-card-on-a-board),
[`answer_executor`](#answering-a-parked-executor),
[`pause_seat` and `resume_seat`](#pausing-and-resuming-a-seat),
[`run_schedule`](#running-a-schedule-now),
[`steer_turn`](#steering-a-running-turn),
[`answer_knowledge`](#answering-a-question-from-the-companys-knowledge),
[`atlas_refresh`](#asking-for-a-read-of-an-atlas-source),
[`save_home_board`](#saving-your-home-board), and
[the eight chat gestures only a person makes](#the-chat-gestures-only-a-person-makes),
and, beside the code reads and on their terms,
[`code_repo_readers`](#get-gitletreposnamereaders), who read a `visibility: unit`
repository, and beside the code writes `code_mark_inbox`, a person's marks
over their own code notices: a seat is woken, never shown an inbox, so it has
none to mark; and `code_mark_viewed`, the files of a change a person marked
viewed: a seat reviews a change whole and keeps none. A view is furniture (a name, a shape
and a filter, arranged so a person finds the same question tomorrow), and a
seat's job is the work rather than the furniture around it. And the
catalogue is the company's own vocabulary: a seat adding a type so its own
create succeeds is a seat editing the rules it is judged by, and the refusal it
was working around is the signal a person needs to see — which is why reading
the catalogue *is* a seat's and writing it is not. And a person's record is a
HUMAN's: a seat has a mailbox — the durable subscription the engine attaches
when it acquires the seat — and nothing on a person's record describes one.
The trash is another: a removal takes an item off every board in the
company, and a seat that could hide work it did not want to do would be marking
its own homework in the one way that leaves no trace. Neither destroys
anything: a removal is reversible at any age, and a purge (`crewlet worklet purge`, or `POST /worklet/items/{key}/purge`) is the
one that is not. A board's manual order is furniture too — where a card sits
says what a person wants looked at first — so dragging one is a person's; a
seat moves work between lanes with `update_work_item`. And an executor's question is a person's to answer: a seat
that could answer its own executor would be guessing on its own behalf. Whether a
seat works at all is a person's decision about it too: a seat that could pause
a colleague, or resume itself, would be overruling the people who run the
company. And when a seat's scheduled work runs is a person's decision too: a
seat that could run a schedule would be starting its colleagues' turns, or its
own, outside the times the people who run the company set. And a note to a
running turn is a person redirecting the work: a seat that could steer a
colleague's turn would be directing it past the person who asked for the work. And who read a unit's code is an audit of the people who
read it — an admin's, which no other person is answered either: a seat that
could ask would be a model watching the people it works for.

### Asking for a read of an atlas source

`atlas_refresh` asks that one integration be read for the atlas now, not on its next scheduled read ([Sources](../guides/atlas.md#sources-and-refresh-now)). It takes `atlas` and is a person's: an agent is refused it whatever it holds.

| Tool | Arguments |
|---|---|
| `atlas_refresh` | `integration`, one the company connects that the atlas reads, as [`atlas_sources`](#the-atlas) lists them |

It answers `source`, `requested_at`, `requested_by` and `changed` (`false` where an ask already waited on the source: that ask is returned). The ask is a record in the coordination store, which the node holding the collect duty honours within a minute. A source read less than five minutes ago is refused `conflict`, naming the instant it can be asked from; a name that is no connected source is refused `not_found`, naming the ones that are. It writes no state log, so its answer carries no `position`.

### Saving your Home board

`save_home_board` saves your own Home board on the dashboard, the widgets you placed and how you arranged them, under the human seat you hold, so the same board follows you to every browser and passes with the seat to its next holder. It takes no app (Home is everybody's) and is a seated person's: an agent is refused it, and so is a credential bound to no seat (`unseated`), whose board the dashboard keeps in that browser alone.

| Tool | Arguments |
|---|---|
| `save_home_board` | `board`, the whole board: a JSON object whose `widgets` is a list, stored as given (the dashboard validates it on every read; the engine reads nothing inside it); and `if_match`, the `revision` [`home_board`](#queries) answered, `0` when none is stored |

It answers `seat` and the new `revision`, the `if_match` of the next save, beside the `outcome` (`applied`) and `position` (`null`) every write carries. A board saved since you read it is refused `stale_version` and nothing changes: read `home_board` again. A board that is no object, has no `widgets` list or encodes to more than 512 KiB is refused `invalid`. The board is a record in the coordination store, on no log, landed when it answers; one whose answer was lost is `unknown`, and `home_board`'s `revision` says whether it landed. A seat removed from the company keeps its board for the mailbox's grace and loses it after, as its chat read state.

### Changing the atlas

And the atlas's **eleven writes**, each a claim in the person's own name on the atlas's log ([Changing the atlas](../concepts/atlas.md#changing-the-atlas)): every one takes `atlas` but the purge, which is `admin`'s with a proof inside `step_up`. Every one is a person's, made as the seat they hold: refused to an agent whatever it holds, and to a credential bound to no seat (`unseated`).
An entry is named by `atlas_entry` (and `to` or `other` where a write names a second one): its `id`, or `kind:key` (`host:ssh/web-1`). Every write takes an optional `if_match`, the entry's `version` it was decided from, and is refused `stale_version` when the entry moved since. It answers `entry` (the id), the new `version`, what it recorded (`change`, and the fact, relation, value or owner) and the `outcome` and `position` every write carries, or `unchanged` where what it asked for already held. Over MCP each also takes back the `op_id` its answer carried, as the tracker's writes do.

A write is refused `unavailable` (`503`, with a `Retry-After`) only while a source that could state a fact of an entry it touches did not answer in full; the `detail` names that source. A source that describes none of its entries, or only reports health and use, never holds it ([how a write is decided](../concepts/atlas.md)).

| Tool | Arguments |
|---|---|
| `atlas_add_entry` | `kind`, `key` in its kind's grammar, and optionally `name`, a one-line `purpose`, the vendor account it belongs to (`belongs_to`, an entry), its owner (`seat` or `unit`) and the Doclet page documenting it (`doclet_page`, the page's id). Each is a record after the entry's; the same call again finishes one that stopped part way. An existing entry is refused `exists` (a retired one comes back with `atlas_restore`); a tool server, a model, a server keyed `ssh/` and a Gitlet repository, which the settings or Gitlet name, are refused `conflict` |
| `atlas_correct` | `atlas_entry`, `fact` (one its kind carries), and `value` in the fact's grammar, which a fact holding many values gains as one more; or `wrong: true`, saying the `value` shown (the one value of a fact of one) is wrong. A fact the settings, Gitlet or the engine's own records declare is refused `conflict` |
| `atlas_confirm` | `atlas_entry`, and either `fact` (with `value` for a fact holding many, or to confirm another value a source reports) or `relation` and `to`; neither confirms the entry itself |
| `atlas_relate` | `atlas_entry`, `relation` (any but `owned_by`), and `to`; with `documented_in`, `doclet_page` (a Doclet page's id) in place of `to`. The page is not read: Doclet decides on every read whether it exists and who may read it |
| `atlas_unrelate` | `atlas_entry`, `relation`, and `to` or, with `documented_in`, `doclet_page`: a relation the settings declare is refused `conflict` |
| `atlas_set_owner` | `atlas_entry`, and one of `seat` (a handle of the chart), `unit` (a unit's key) or `clear: true`. The owner a person named before is withdrawn; an owner Gitlet declares is refused `conflict` |
| `atlas_retire`, `atlas_restore` | `atlas_entry`. An entry the settings declare is refused `conflict` |
| `atlas_merge`, `atlas_split` | `atlas_entry` and `other`, of one kind. A merge first withdraws a "not the same" between them |
| `atlas_purge` | `atlas_entry`, or `value` exactly as the atlas holds it, never both. Nothing undoes it; the answer never repeats the value, and only its digest leaves the node it was asked of |

### The chat gestures only a person makes

Where the company runs Chatlet, the dashboard's chat screen makes every change it makes through this catalogue (a person's own assistant reaches the same tools), and eight of them are given to no seat:

| Tool | Arguments | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `create_channel` | `channel` — the new room's name — and optionally `kind` (`public` or `private`; omitted takes `chat.chatlet.default_channel_private`), `topic`, `purpose`, `members` | Makes a named room, with the caller in it. The name is its address: of two people asking for one, one is refused `exists`. A unit's own room is the org chart's (the engine opens one for each unit that declares a `channel`); a create of kind `unit` is refused `forbidden`. A horizon of its own for a room is an administrator's to set. |
| `open_dm` | `to` — the other handles | Opens the conversation between the caller and them, or reaches the one already open, saying nothing; `created` says which. Its id is its participants, so opening it twice is one room. |
| `update_channel` | `channel`, and any of `topic`, `purpose`, `archived`, `auto_join`, and `template` beside a `topic` or `purpose` | Changes only what it names: an empty `topic` clears it, an absent one leaves it. A topic and a purpose are any member's, each at most 250 characters, each change a line in the room's transcript; `template` names the template they were set from (at most 64 characters), and the transcript records that one line instead. `auto_join` puts every seat the company takes on from then in the room; administrator's, public room only (`chat.channel.autojoin`). `archived` closes the room to new messages (`false` reopens it) and is **not** any member's: it is decided on the stored room (`chat.channel.archive`), for its creator, the lead of the unit a unit's room belongs to or of a unit above it, or an administrator. An archived room is still read and searched. |
| `set_channel_members` | `channel`, `members`, optionally `expected_members` | States the room's WHOLE membership: whoever is left out is taken out, and an empty list empties it. Each member is a handle or `{handle, follow_all}`; `follow_all` makes every message in the room reach them. `expected_members` is the membership the change was built from: if the room holds anybody else, or anybody follows it differently, when the write lands, it is refused as a conflict and the caller reads the room again. Refused for a unit's room (membership is the org chart's) and a direct conversation (id is its participants). |
| `add_channel_members` | `channel`, `members` (handles) | Puts those named in the room and takes nobody out, decided against the room as it stands when the write lands, so two people adding at once both land. `added` answers who it put there; anybody already in the room is left as they are. Refused as `set_channel_members` is for a unit's room and a direct conversation, and for a handle that is no seat of the company. |
| `edit_message` | `channel`, `message_id`, `body`, and optionally `links` | Rewrites a message; only its author may. Whoever the new words name for the first time is told; nobody else is woken again. `links` changes only when sent: omitted, the message keeps its links; a list replaces them, an empty list removes them. Each link is an absolute `http`, `https` or `mailto` address, stored as sent; any other is refused `invalid`, naming every entry that is not one (`links[1]`). |
| `delete_message` | `channel`, `message_id` | Takes a message back: its words go and its row stays, so a thread hung off it keeps its root. Its author may, and so may an administrator — moderation, decided before the message is read, so it reaches a message in any room (a private room or direct conversation the administrator is not in included) without showing it to them. |
| `mark_chat_read` | any of `cursors` (room id → the position read through), `thread_cursors` (thread root id → the position read through in it), `rewind` (room id → the position to set its place back to), `notify` (room id → `all`, `mentions` or `muted`), `mute`, `unmute`, `star` and `unstar` (room ids), `save` and `unsave` (`{channel_id, message_id}`), `follow` and `unfollow` (`{channel_id, root_id}`), `dnd_until` (RFC 3339; empty ends it) | Records how far the caller has read, which rooms they mute or unmute and whether they are in do-not-disturb, under their seat, and the marks of [what a reader keeps](../concepts/chatlet.md#what-a-reader-keeps). Every id it names is the one the engine gave the room, message or thread root (a UUID); any other is refused `invalid` naming the argument, and nothing is recorded. A cursor only moves forward, and past 256 rooms the one read least recently is forgotten. A mute is a ROOM AT A TIME, not a list: each named room is muted or unmuted and every other keeps its state, so two screens toggling two rooms at once both land. A mute that would take the set past 256 rooms is refused `invalid` rather than cut, and so is one room both muted and unmuted in one call. The answer's `read` is the caller's whole read state as the write left it, named by its `handle`; `read.revision` orders it against any other state of the same record. Not a record on the log: it is written to the coordination store and answers `applied` at no position. A flush whose write went out and whose answer was lost answers `unknown` (on `/operator/act`, the 503 with `outcome: unknown`): sending the same call again is safe, because a cursor only moves forward and a mute, an unmute or a do-not-disturb sent twice is stated twice. |

`members` is a list of handles, or of `{handle, follow_all}` where the member should hear everything said in the room.
