The company's [atlas](../concepts/atlas.md), the map and catalogue of everything it runs on, is read through twelve questions, each on the socket and as a REST route. **Every one needs the `atlas` permission** ([ADR-0127](../../adr/0127-reading-the-atlas-takes-the-atlas-permission.md)); a person without it is refused, as an agent's turn is when the person who woke it does not hold it.

| Question | Route | Parameters | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `atlas_entries` | `GET /atlas` | the filters below; `sort` (`key`, the map's order, by default; `name`; `last_seen`; `health`, the most urgent first and the map's order inside each); `cursor`; `limit` (50 by default, at most 500) | `rows`, one summary per entry; `next_cursor`, absent on the last page; `total` |
| `atlas_map` | `GET /atlas/map` | the filters below; `closed`, the group keys the reader closed, comma separated; `relations` (`structural`, the relations drawn at rest, by default, or `all`) | `lanes` (every lane, an empty one included), `groups`, `nodes`, `edges` (each relation between two drawn entries, with its `family`), `collapsed` |
| `atlas_entry` | `GET /atlas/{id}` | `id` | `entry`, in full; its `health`, what the signals its reader may read add up to; its `vendor`; `used_by`, every entry with a relation to it |
| `atlas_trace` | `GET /atlas/{id}/trace` | `id`; `direction` (`up`, what depends on it, by default; `down`, what it depends on); `depth` (1 to 6, 6 by default); `relations` (`structural`, by default, or `all`) | `from`, `direction`, `hops` by distance, `edges`, `truncated` |
| `atlas_facets` | `GET /atlas/facets` | the filters below | how many entries each `kinds`, `lanes`, `vendors`, `words` and `health` value leaves, each counted over every other filter, and `total` |
| `atlas_log` | `GET /atlas/log`, `GET /atlas/{id}/log` | `id`, for one entry's lines rather than the company's; `cursor`; `limit` (50 by default, at most 200); `unconfirmed` | `lines`, newest first; `next_cursor`, absent on the last page |
| `atlas_review` | `GET /atlas/review` | `kind` (`disagreement`, `unconfirmed` or `likely`; every kind by default); `mine` (`true` for only what contradicts the asker's own word: a fact or relation they set or confirmed that a newer report differs from, which is what their Inbox is told of; a credential acting as no seat is answered none, and `total` and `counts` are then of the asker's alone); `cursor`; `limit` (50 by default, at most 500) | `items`, what waits for a person, computed on the read and stored nowhere: first the facts and relations the sources disagree on (each with its `fact` or `relation`, every other value beside the one shown, and the `target` a relation points at), then the entries only an agent reported, those with nothing the engine could check before those backed by a call or a file, each with its `reports`: every agent's newest word on it, newest first, at most five, as its `source` (the seat in `name`, the `turn`, the `evidence` class and the cited call's `tool` by name, absent on a record made before the name was kept) and `observed_at`; each item's `entry` summary and `since`, its newest claim; `next_cursor`, absent on the last page; `total` of the asked kind and `counts` of each kind |
| `atlas_sources` | `GET /atlas/sources` | none | `sources`, one per integration the atlas reads that the company connects, in the order of their names: its `kind`; its `state` (`never`, `read`, `partial` where the read finished and was refused some part, or `failed`); `last_attempt_at` and `last_complete_at`; the last whole read's `entries`, `calls` and `withheld` (values left out for their shape, counted and never sent); what the last attempt wrote (`recorded`, `retired`, `purged`); `missing`, the entries complete reads have stopped seeing and not retired yet; `unread`, each part it was refused with its `detail` and, for a server's part, its `scope`, and `unread_overflow`, how many more there were; `scopes`, for the servers each server's `id`, its `last_read_at` (its last whole read) and `unread`; `next_read_at`, absent where it is due now; `refresh_requested_at` and `refresh_requested_by` while an ask waits on it; `refreshable_at`, the first instant an ask is honoured, absent where that is now; and `last_error`, the fault of a failed read, sent to an administrator alone. Beside them `refresh_interval_seconds` and `refresh_floor_seconds`. It carries none of the read members below: it reads the coordination store, never the atlas |
| `atlas_activity` | `GET /atlas/activity` | `unconfirmed` | `from`, the first instant of the window; `days`, the company's lines on each of its 14 UTC days, oldest first and today last; `entries`, one per entry the log holds a line of: its `id`, its own `days` (absent where it took none in the window) and `last`, its newest line however old |
| `atlas_work` | `GET /atlas/work` | none | `open`, how many open tasks name each entry, by the entry's id; `capped`, where more than 2,000 entries have open work; `unread`, why no work was read, and then `open` is empty |
| `atlas_entry_work` | `GET /atlas/{id}/work` | `id` | `open`, the open tasks that name the entry, most recently changed first, and `recent`, the ones finished in the last 30 days, each at most 50 rows of the shape `work_items` answers; `open_total` and `recent_total`, each `{total, capped?}`; `unread`, why no work was read |
| `atlas_named` | `GET /atlas/named` | `ids`, 1 to 128 entry ids separated by commas | `named`, one `{id, entry}` per asked id that names an entry, in the order asked: the id as asked and the summary of the entry it merged into, so two ids of one entry carry the same summary; `missing`, the asked ids that name no entry the reader's atlas holds |

The filters are `q` (part of a name or a key, or an entry's id), `kind`, `lane`, `vendor`, `confidence` (`confirmed`, `likely` or `unconfirmed`), `health` (`alerting`, `needs_look` or `quiet`), `show` (`current`, every entry but the retired, by default; `retired`; `all`) and `unconfirmed` (`true` to take in the entries only an agent reported with nothing the engine could check; they are left out by default until a person confirms them, and `confidence=unconfirmed` takes them in too). The `words` facet counts the unconfirmed entries either way. A value outside its set is refused with `bad_params`, naming the parameter and the values it takes; an `id` no entry answers to is `not_found`. An entry merged into another by an exact key is found by its own id too.

Every answer also carries `revision`, the settings revision it was read from (empty where the serving node cannot tell), `coverage`, each source the read reads and whether it was read in full, with the reason where it was not, and `withheld`, how many values were left out for being shaped like a credential, counted and never shown. A source that fails leaves the rest answering.

**A summary** (a row of `rows`, a node of `nodes`, an entry of a trace or of `used_by`) is what a list row or a map card shows: the entry's `id`, `kind`, `lane`, `name`, `key` and `vendor`; its `state`, its `word` and its `health`; `signals`, how many open signals its reader may read; `review`, `not_used_recently` and `last_seen`; and four members a row needs without opening the entry:

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `owner` | `{kind, name}`: the `seat` (by handle) or the `unit` (by key) a person or the engine's records name. Absent where nobody has, and never an owner an integration or an agent only suggested |
| `purpose` | the one line a person gave the entry. Somebody's words: draw it as plain text |
| `relations` | `{depends_on, used_by}`: how many entries it relies on and how many rely on it, through the relations the map draws at rest, counted between current entries the read shows (never a retired entry or an unconfirmed one the read leaves out) |
| `reason` | why the entry is not `quiet`, in one sentence: its most urgent open signal and how many more are open, or that its sources disagree. Absent for a quiet entry. It counts only the signals its reader may read |

**Every sentence the engine writes is its own.** A `reason`, and a log line's `text`, is built from the closed words of the vocabulary and a count, never from a name, a label, a value or an alarm's text. What a vendor, an agent or a person wrote reaches a reader only in the typed members beside the sentence (`name`, `purpose`, `value`, `target`), each to be drawn as plain text.

**Relations and their families.** Each edge of a map or a trace carries the `family` its relation is drawn in: `calls`, a relation a request travels along (`depends_on`, `exposes`, `served_by`, `fronted_by`); `runs_on`, a relation to what an entry stands on (`runs_on`, `resolves_to`); and `around`, every other one (`in_zone`, `built_from`, `deployed_by`, `monitored_by`, `secured_by`, `belongs_to`). A map asked for `relations=all` draws every relation between two entries it draws; a relation to a seat, a unit or a page is on the entry's own answer, since it joins no two entries.

**The log.** A line is one claim recorded on the atlas's own log ([The atlas's own log](../concepts/atlas.md#the-atlass-own-log)): by a person, by an integration's read, or by an agent. What the engine computes at every read is not recorded, so it leaves no line.

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | the line's own id, stable across reads |
| `at` | when the record that wrote it was stored |
| `entry`, `name`, `kind` | the entry the line is about, as the reader's atlas names it |
| `change` | `recorded` (an entry a source said is there), `retired`, `fact_set`, `fact_denied` (a value a person said is wrong), `related`, `unrelated`, `joined` and `kept_apart` (two entries a person said are, or are not, the same thing), and `withdrawn` (a claim its source stopped making: what an integration's read no longer holds, or a "the same" a person took back) |
| `text` | the change in one sentence of the engine's own words |
| `fact`, `value` | the fact a line is about and the value recorded, where it is about one |
| `relation`, `target` | the relation a line is about and what it names: another entry by `id` and `name`, or a seat, a unit or a page by `external` and `name` |
| `source` | whose voice the claim is in |

A line is shown only to a reader who is shown its entry and the entry it names: a line on, or naming, a repository or a check of Gitlet's is read only by a reader Gitlet lists that repository to, and a line on an entry only an agent reported is left out unless the read asks for `unconfirmed`, or asks for that entry's own log by its `id`. `atlas_activity` counts exactly the lines `atlas_log` would show its reader, and an entry whose newest record the reader is not shown carries no `last`. A page may hold fewer lines than its `limit` where many of the log's lines are not the reader's to see; `next_cursor` says whether there is more. Lines are kept as long as the atlas keeps its history.

**The atlas is never a way round another permission.** A reader without the `gitlet` permission is read no repository, and Gitlet is not asked; one with it is read the repositories Gitlet lists to them. The work on an entry is Worklet's: `atlas_work` and `atlas_entry_work` read the tracker only for a reader who also holds `worklet`, and answer anybody else `unread` with the reason and no task ([ADR-0140](../../adr/0140-a-task-names-the-atlas-entries-it-touches-by-id-on-its-own-record.md)). An integration's standing and a server's connection test are signals only an administrator reads, as the screens they come from are. A standing alarm on a tool server or a model entry is every holder's.

**The work that touches an entry.** A Worklet task names the entries it touches (`update_work_item`'s `linked_entries`), each by its id, on the task's own record; the atlas is never written. A link is read through whichever entry its id merged into, so `open` is keyed by the entry the map draws and an entry's work is the tasks naming any id it answers to. A task that names an entry the reader's atlas does not hold marks nothing. A company whose work is kept outside Worklet has none to read, and both questions say so in `unread`.

**The bounds.** A page is 50 entries and at most 500. The map draws at most 2,000 entries open: past that it closes groups, the largest first, and names them in `collapsed`, so an answer never draws a partial map as if it were whole. A trace walks at most 6 hops and stops at 200 entries, saying so in `truncated`. A page of the log is 50 lines and at most 200. The activity window is 14 days, today included (two weeks show a weekly rhythm twice); a day is a UTC day.

**What the widest answers cost.** At the map's bound (2,000 entries with owner and purpose; `internal/atlas.BenchmarkMapAtItsBound`) the map takes 15 ms to draw and encode: at rest 1,218 KiB of JSON (136 KiB compressed) for 3,100 edges, with every relation 1,771 KiB (191 KiB compressed) for 7,300. On a 20,860-line log (`internal/atlasdomain`'s benchmarks) a page of 200 lines takes 7 ms and the activity read 147 ms, beside 220 ms for every live claim.
## Worklet and Doclet

`GET /worklet`, `GET /doclet/pages` and their neighbours read Worklet and
Doclet **through this node's estate router**: from this node's copy while it
serves, else a data node's. A seat's tools read through the same facade, so an
operator and an agent see one item.

**They are answered only where the company runs that backend.** A company on
`tracker.backend: jira` has no `work_items` question to answer: asking gets
`unknown_query` / `404`, because an empty board would claim a Worklet record
exists that no node holds.
Whether the backend runs is asked **at every request**: a node that booted with
no company builds Worklet and Doclet at the first revision it applies, so a
company bootstrapped live is served from then on with no restart. After that,
the halves a node serves are those its runtime was built with until it
restarts: a revision that moves the company onto Jira or Confluence (or turns
on a half the node was built without) activates, logs
`native_backend_needs_restart`, and changes these answers only at the next
restart (see
[A native backend changes at a restart](../concepts/control-plane.md#a-native-backend-changes-at-a-restart)).
Until then a question about a half the revision turned ON is refused
`unavailable` (`503`) under `native_backend_needs_restart`, with no
`Retry-After` and a detail naming the half ("this node was already running when
the company turned Chatlet on, and it starts Chatlet when it restarts: restart
this node, or ask another one"), never `unknown_query`; the org answer names it
in [`services.restart`](#get-org).

**A copy that has not caught up refuses.** Where the answering copy is behind
what the read needs, the answer is `unavailable` (`503`, with a `Retry-After`),
never an empty list: "this company has no work" is an answer people act on. A
copy that has not applied this node's own writes is passed over for another
data node's; a read no data node's copy could take is refused the same way.

**Every** state-log refusal is `unavailable` (`503` over REST, the
`unavailable` frame on the socket), carrying the refusal's code as `refusal`
and a sentence for the reader as `detail` (what happened and what to do; the
refusal's own detail goes to the node's log): the node understood the question
and cannot answer it *here*. A `Retry-After` is sent only where waiting clears
the refusal, and it is that refusal's own hint:

- `behind`: derived, from how far behind the copy is over how fast it drains.
- `no_quorum` and `broker_unreachable`: the broker's election timeout.
- `broker_stalled`: one barrier budget (a log one member stores, whose own
  write did not complete, holds no election).
- `below_floor` and `floor_unknown`: one position heartbeat.

A refusal waiting cannot clear carries **none**: a record this node cannot
decode (`deferred`), a log at its byte ceiling (`log_full`), a barrier its
broker refused (`broker_refused`), an evicted node. The client asks another
node or waits for an operator; see
[the fifteen refusals](../guides/consistency.md#the-fifteen-refusals). A
`min_position` on a log the answer is not read from is the request's mistake:
`400 bad_params`.

**The reads are here and the writes are tools.** Every write is attributed to
somebody, never to "the dashboard": a seat through its own tools, a person at
the dashboard through
[`/operator/act`](#operatoract--the-dashboards-write-surface), a script through
[the write surface](#the-human-write-surface), an assistant through the
[MCP surface](#operatormcp--your-own-assistant), all with the same tools. The
routes under `/worklet/retention/` are not about items: they are operator
gestures against the log's own history, attributed to the credential that made
them.

### Paging and filters

Both listings take `limit` (default 50, max 500) and page by an opaque CURSOR,
never an `offset`, since seats write while they are read and an offset skips or
repeats rows. The work listing takes `cursor` and answers `next_cursor`; the
pages listing takes `after` and answers `after`, beside its `total`.

Multi-valued filters are **comma-separated** (`?status=todo,in_progress`),
because the socket's query channel carries a JSON object, which cannot repeat a
key.

Openness is **not** a boolean (`open=false`) on the work listing. Rules in Worklet are
written at the four status *groups*, so open work is
`?status_group=not_started,active`. `show_closed` is the separate three-stated
question of whether finished work is in the answer: absent or `false` leaves it
out, `true` puts it in, and `recent:<dur>` puts in only what finished inside
that window.

The pages listing's `skills` is **three-stated**:

| Filter | Absent | `true` | `false` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `skills` (pages) | every page | only tool-skill pages | everything but them |

An unknown enum value is refused naming the closed set (`?status=finished`
answers `400` saying which statuses exist), never matched to nothing.

### Project files

A project holds **files** beside its work: a row in Worklet (a path, a type, a
size and SHA-256, a version and who wrote it), whose content is one object in
the [object store](../concepts/object-store.md), shared by the whole fleet. See
[A project's files](../guides/worklet.md#a-projects-files) for what a seat does
with them.

The listing is an ordinary read (`GET /worklet/files`, the `work_files` query).
The three byte routes add streaming: a download streams the content back and an
upload streams it in, neither holding the file in memory.

```bash
# upload, replacing version 3 and nothing newer
curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $CREWLET_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: text/csv" -H 'If-Match: "3"' \
  --data-binary @q3.csv "http://localhost:8000/worklet/files/ENG/reports/q3.csv"

# download
curl -OJ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CREWLET_API_TOKEN" \
  "http://localhost:8000/worklet/files/ENG/reports/q3.csv"
```

```json
{
  "project": "ENG", "path": "reports/q3.csv", "size": 48213,
  "hash": "9f2c…", "content_type": "text/csv",
  "outcome": "applied", "op_id": "…", "position": "…", "version": 4
}
```

**The content goes first.** An upload streams the whole body into one new
object before it records the file, so a listed file is one whose content the
fleet holds. A write cut off halfway, or refused once its object is stored,
leaves an unnamed object the collector removes a day later, never a row
pointing at missing content. A body whose `Content-Length` is over 1 GiB, and
an upload into a project that does not exist (`404 no_project`) or is archived
(`409 conflict`), are refused before any of it is read.

**A write names the version it replaces.** `If-Match` carries the `ETag` the
download answered. Absent, the write creates the path or overwrites what is
there; present, a file that moved since is `412 version_moved` and nothing is
written. A file has no per-field merge (unlike a work item), since two people
editing one spreadsheet would lose one.

**A write is decided and attributed like every other write on this surface.**
Reading a file or the listing and uploading one take `worklet`; removing one is
its project's lead's, or `admin`'s, with `worklet`. The write is recorded under
whoever the request resolved to (a person as their seat, a credential nobody is
bound through under its own login), with the credential it came through beside
it ([Who a write is attributed to](#who-a-write-is-attributed-to)), so a file's
history names the person, never the relaying process. Every write leaves an
`operator_acted` record as a [write-surface](#the-human-write-surface) verb
does.

**The answer is three-valued.** `outcome` is `applied`, `pending` or
`unknown`, as every Worklet write's is (see
[Read Consistency](../guides/consistency.md)); `position` and `version` are
present only where the write is known to have landed. Retry an `unknown` by
sending the same request with the `op_id` it answered as its `Idempotency-Key`
(the key sent, or the one minted), as on the
[write surface](#a-retry-is-the-same-operation): a fresh key makes a second
write.

**Each mebibyte has 30 seconds to cross**, in either direction: an upload's
mebibyte has 30 seconds of the time the server waits for the client to send it
(not the time spent storing what arrived), and a download's has 30 seconds of
the time the server waits for the client to take it (not the time spent
fetching from the store). That is a floor of about 35 KB/s, far under any real
link and the same floor the object store holds its own transfers to. A
whole-body deadline would cap real uploads of up to a gibibyte, and none would
let a client trickle bytes or never read a download. An upload that stops
arriving (a closed connection included) answers `400 unreadable_body` and
records nothing; a download the client stops taking, or whose content stops
being readable part way, is cut, which the client sees as a body shorter than
its `Content-Length`.

**A download is served as an attachment**, with the file's own type and the
`default-src 'none'` policy every non-dashboard response carries, so an
uploaded HTML file downloads rather than running on the dashboard's origin.

| Status | `error` | When |
|---|---|---|
| `400` | `bad_path` | The path is empty, longer than 1024 bytes, not UTF-8, ends in `/`, has an empty folder or a `.` or `..` in it, or carries a control character or a backslash. A leading `/` is dropped rather than refused |
| `400` | `bad_if_match` | `If-Match` is not a version |
| `409` | `conflict` | The project is archived (its state, met until somebody unarchives it); the [one refusal rule](#which-class-a-refusal-is) |
| `422` | `invalid` | The write can never land as sent: the content type is over 255 bytes or spans lines |
| `400` | `unreadable_body` | The body stopped arriving: connection closed, or a mebibyte took over 30 seconds |
| `403` | `unauthorized` | The authority table refused: `reason` and `grants` say why and what would admit |
| `404` | `no_project` / `no_file` | No such project, or no file at that path |
| `412` | `version_moved` | `If-Match` names a version the file has moved past |
| `409` | `upload_expired` | The upload outlasted the twelve hours a write may name its object after (from its key's minting); send it again |
| `413` | `body_too_large` | The content is over 1 GiB: refused before reading where `Content-Length` says so, else once the body passes it |
| `500` | `content_corrupt` | The store's content is not what the file records; retrying reads the same bytes, so restore from a backup or upload again |
| `507` | `store_full` | The object store has no room for the upload (the fleet's NATS bucket holds as many bytes as it [reserves](../concepts/object-store.md#its-byte-reservation), or an S3-compatible bucket's provider [refuses the write for room](../concepts/object-store.md#an-s3-bucket--s3)); nothing was stored or recorded. **No** `Retry-After`: the upload is refused until an operator makes room, which the `hint` names; the node logs `api_file_store_full` with the store's own answer |
| `500` | `internal_error` | An upload failed in this node, classed by the store as neither of the two below (it stopped reading the content before its end); retrying doesn't clear it; the reason is in the node's log |
| `503` | `unavailable` / `content_unavailable` | Worklet or the object store could not be reached, or the file's content could not be read right now. An upload the store did not take is `unavailable` under an election's `Retry-After`; one it refused because it is full is `unavailable` with no `Retry-After`, and an administrator makes room (see [its byte reservation](../concepts/object-store.md#its-byte-reservation)). An artifact's upload, an image attached to an Ask Crewlet question, `write_project_file` and the artifact tools answer both the same way, including the bucket failing every attempt of a request for forty seconds to a minute (which ends an upload or download then, not at its deadline) and the store taking no more of an upload and not answering it for a minute (which ends the upload then); an upload in parts is answered up to thirty seconds later, once its unfinished upload has been abandoned |

A download is served wherever the company runs Worklet **and** the node runs
the object store. The upload and the removal also need the node to hand out
Worklet's writer, which a node in a
[maintenance mode](../guides/retention.md#the-three-modes) does not: there they
answer `404 no_route`, like any path the node does not serve, while a download
is a read and is served as usual. A company on Jira has no project files to
serve. Whether the node serves them is asked at every request, so a node that
booted with no company serves them from its first revision on Worklet, with no
restart.

### `GET /worklet/retention`: what the log is holding

**Takes `admin`, reads included**, as `/config` and `/secrets` do: the answer
names every node, its position, disk and snapshot repository, a map of which
machine to take out to lose the company's history, so it needs its own grant on
top of authentication.

The node you ask assembles the document: half its fields are facts only that
node can state (its own applier's lag, snapshot, disk), half are fleet-wide,
read from coordination. `node_id` is on the document, so a pasted report is not
three per-node facts attributed to a fleet.

```json
{
  "node_id": "node-1",
  "at": "2031-04-02T03:14:00Z",
  "backup_owner": "platform-oncall",
  "register_readable": true,
  "domains": [
    {
      "domain": "tracker",
      "stream": "CREWLET_TRACKER_LOG",
      "generation": 0,
      "first_seq": 918100000,
      "last_seq": 918280001,
      "bytes": 67108864,
      "max_bytes": 4294967296,
      "reserve_bytes": 268435456,
      "headroom_fraction": 0.983,
      "bytes_per_day": 23068672,
      "trim_floor": 918100000,
      "trim_to": 0,
      "blocked_by": "backup_floor",
      "blocked_since": "2031-03-30T02:00:00Z",
      "backup_at": "2031-03-29T02:00:00Z",
      "prose": "Nothing is being trimmed on tracker: ...",
      "terms": [{"name": "applied", "state": "ok", "seq": 918279004, "detail": "..."}]
    }
  ],
  "nodes": [...],
  "snapshots": [...],
  "replica": {"store_bytes": 10415140864, "projected_join_seconds": 308,
              "rejoin_window_seconds": 1800},
  "alarms": [{"kind": "backup_age", "title": "No recent backup", "person": "...",
              "detail": "...", "remedy": "...",
              "domains": [{"domains": ["tracker"],
                           "detail": "the newest verified backup is 97h 14m old, and the policy asks for 24h; the trim has not advanced for 73h 14m, and the log is keeping up to 1840 record(s) older than its 24h replay window",
                           "term": "backup_floor", "since": "2031-03-30T02:00:00Z"}]}]
}
```

`domains`, `nodes`, `snapshots`, `alarms` and each domain's `terms` are always
lists: `[]` when empty, never `null` (`"alarms": []`).

**`alarms`** holds each standing [alarm](alarms.md) once: `kind`, `title` and
`person` (what is wrong, what it affects and what to do, in the kind's own
words for a company owner), `detail` (the measurement, in the thing's units)
and `remedy` (the operator's steps). A condition that is a property of a log
names every log it stands on in **`domains`**: each entry is one measurement,
its `detail`, and its own **`domains`** list of the logs it was taken on. That
is one log for a held trim, with the `term` holding it and `since`, when it
stopped advancing; otherwise every log measured in the same words, so a fleet
with no backup yet is one entry naming every log. The alarm's own `detail` is
then the most pressing log's.

A log that would raise `trim_blocked` (held longer than its replay window plus
a trim tick, while keeping records older than the window) is listed under
`backup_age` instead while the backup term holds it and that log's own
`backup_age` fires, because the backup is its remedy: its entry carries the
`term` and `since`, and its `detail` is its backup's measurement followed by
what the hold is keeping. A younger backup hold raises no `trim_blocked` to
fold, and a backup hold on a log whose own backup is inside the policy stays
under `trim_blocked`. So `alarms` has one entry per kind, and its length is the
health envelope's `alarms.count`. The `alarm_raised` and `alarm_cleared` log
lines are the one place a log stands alone: a per-log condition writes a pair
per log, carrying it as `domain`, so a log joining an alarm already up, and a
log leaving one that stays up, are each said with their own start.

`trim_floor` and `trim_to` differ, and a blocked domain is where they part.
`trim_floor` is the floor the fleet has published: everything below it may
already be deleted, it is written before the delete it licenses and never moves
down within a generation, so a blocked domain keeps the floor its last advance
reached. `trim_to` is what the last tick concluded: zero while blocked, and
below the floor whenever the lowest counted node is. The first is what a node
must hold to replay; the second says whether the trim is moving. Both, with
`terms`, `blocked_by` and `blocked_since`, come from the row the trim published
at the domain's OWN `generation` only (just after a reanchor, the row is about
the stream the domain left). **`trim_floor_state`** says which it is:

- `published`: the floor, the conclusion, the terms and the blocking term are
  that tick's.
- `none_at_generation`: the trim has concluded nothing about this generation
  yet (a fresh fleet before its first tick, or any fleet after a reanchor until
  the first tick on the adopted stream).
- `unreadable`: the floor register could not be read.

Only `published` makes `trim_floor` and `trim_to` worth reading; `terms` is
then an **empty** list where nothing is concluded. See
[Retention](../guides/retention.md#the-trim-floor).

**`not_ready`** is present when the answering node refuses every read of the
domain right now (the refusal its readiness probe reads), with `code`
(`wrong_stream`, `stalled`, `below_floor`, `behind`, `floor_unknown`,
`evicted`, or `broker_unreachable` where its health could not be read),
`causes` naming each identity finding behind a `wrong_stream` (`recreated`,
`ahead_of_log`, `log_diverged`, `generation_passed`) and `detail`, the
refusal's sentence. **`writes_refused`** is present while the node serves the
domain's reads and refuses its writes: `code` `log_truncated`, with `detail`
naming the peer whose rows hold records the log lost. Both are the answering
node's own facts, like the replica block.

Each node's per-domain row carries **`generation_state`**: `current`, `left`
(a generation the log has since left), `ahead` (one above the answering node's)
or `unknown` (a domain the answering node does not run). `lag` is present only
where it is `current`, since a sequence from another generation is in another
space. The row also carries the node's own **`log_diverged`**, and
**`stream_created_at`** and **`checkpoint_stored_at`** (the stream its rows are
keyed to and the record its checkpoint stands on) where the node published
them.

A term's `state` is one of four, and `seq` is an answer in exactly one: `ok`
carries the sequence the term permits, `unknown` is a term that could not be
evaluated (which blocks), `n/a` is one this domain does not have, and
`unbounded` is one that was read and binds nothing (no hold pins the log, or a
solo fleet takes no snapshots). `seq` is `0` in the other three rather than
absent, so a term permitting nothing *yet* (what holds a young fleet's trim) is
distinguishable from one with no sequence to give.

`register_readable` keeps an empty `nodes` block honest: "this fleet has no
nodes" cannot happen, while "coordination could not be listed" happens during
exactly the outage somebody is running this in.

`maintenance_unread` lists every log whose capacity window the answering node
couldn't read, and is **absent** when it read every one. `maintenance` lists
only the windows found open, so a log missing from both has no window, and a
log named in `maintenance_unread` may have one. The `maintenance_open` alarm
judges such a log on the window the node last read there, as old as that read,
and its `detail` says so
([the retention guide](../guides/retention.md#where-it-stands-and-what-is-holding-it)).
Each open window's `participants_missing` and `admissions_blocking` are read
beside it, and one the node couldn't read is `acks_unread: true` or
`admissions_unread: true` with its list absent, never empty.

A node row's **`evicted`** is its tombstone once every log holds one, dated
from the latest and naming in `by` whoever made the eviction that reached the
last of them.

**`evictions_unreadable`** is `true` on an identity-claiming log's row when the
answering node could not read that log's evictions while assembling the report
(a failed store read, or its replicated estate closed for a snapshot adoption's
rename or a shutdown), and absent otherwise. An unread log contributes no
tombstone, so every node reads as **not** evicted there and stays counted (the
trim's conservative side), and "not evicted" is then not an answer. Read it
before concluding a node was readmitted; both `crewlet retention status` and
**Settings › Backups & retention** say so above the node block, and that screen
keeps an eviction it just made on the row until a report whose evictions were
read.

**`backup_at`** is when the backup this log's trim counts was taken: the newest
verified point the `backup_floor` policy takes the word of that covers this
log's stream (a node's copy under `engine`, the operator's acknowledgement of
this log under `operator`). It is **absent** where no counted backup covers the
log, the state the `backup_floor` term blocks on. The `backup_age` alarm is
evaluated per log from it and lists each log in its `domains` with its own age
(under `operator` every log is acknowledged on its own); logs whose
measurement reads the same, such as none backed up yet, share one entry.

`headroom_fraction` is a **pointer**, absent when the broker could not be
asked: a fraction of an unknown ceiling is not zero headroom, and zero is what
the one alarm an operator cannot ignore fires on. It is a fraction of the
ceiling **ordinary writes** are held to: `max_bytes` less `reserve_bytes`. On
every identity-claiming log `reserve_bytes` is the top of the ceiling kept for
the records that install or lift a gate (the larger of a sixteenth of it and
seven of the log's largest records with a mebibyte beside them), so an eviction
still lands on a log full for everything else
([the gate reserve](../guides/retention.md#the-gate-reserve)). It is absent on
a log that keeps none (the vector changelog and the usage log), where the
headroom is of the whole ceiling.

`bytes_per_day` is what the log took in over the trailing day, as this node's
last trim tick measured it from the log's own records: the rate the
`log_ceiling_short` alarm holds `max_bytes` against `min_age` of. It is a
pointer too, because `0` means the log took in nothing, the most benign
reading, and the field is **absent** where nothing was measured: a compacted
log (whose size follows its subjects, not its age), a log in its first two days
(whose trailing day would contain its import day), and every log on a node
whose trim has not ticked yet. See
[Retention](../guides/retention.md#the-one-number-to-watch).

`crewlet retention status` renders exactly these bytes.
### The three retention gestures that write

All three are **POSTs** and, like every `/worklet/retention*` route, take `admin`: moving the floor the trim deletes against, and stopping and re-allowing a machine's writes, are the deployment's own controls. A caller without it gets `403` naming it.

| Route | What it does |
|---|---|
| `POST /worklet/retention/ack?stream=NAME&position=N&taken_at=TIME` | Publishes an operator backup floor. `400 position_required` naming both when either is missing; `404` when the stream is not one this node runs (on a node running no state log, every stream). The point is stamped with **that stream's own generation**, read from the running log (a bare sequence at another generation names a number space the copy does not cover), and **filed under that stream**: acknowledging another log leaves this one standing, and each log's trim reads its own (under `backup_floor: operator`, one acknowledgement per log). `taken_at` is the RFC 3339 instant the copy was taken; `backup_age` and the backup check age the copy from it. `400 taken_at_required` when missing, zero or not RFC 3339 (send an offset's `+` as `%2B`; unescaped it arrives as a space); `400 taken_at_in_future` when later than this node's clock, the detail saying what the clock reads. The answer echoes `stream`, `position`, `generation` and `taken_at`. |
| `POST /worklet/retention/evict/{node}?confirm={node}` | Installs the eviction gate on every identity-claiming log: Worklet's, Doclet's, the identity estate's, the artifacts log's, the artifact datastore's, Ask Crewlet's, Chatlet's, the executor log's and the code log's; the vector and usage logs count no node and get none. **`409 eviction_refused`**, nothing written, while the node still holds a live presence lease (it still reaches the fleet, and eviction would drop everything it writes); the body carries `detail`, `hint`, `op_id` and `actions` `["wait", "force"]`: stop the node and let its lease lapse, or force it. `force=true` overrides that for a node wedged so that it still renews its lease. A node that cannot read the presence leases answers **`503 eviction_unjudged`** (with `hint` and `actions` `["retry_same_op", "force"]`); `force=true` overrides that too, since the leases are the judgement's only input, and the node logs `retention_eviction_forced_unjudged`. A node in a [capacity window](../guides/retention.md#changing-a-logs-ceiling) answers **`409 not_publishing`** before anything is judged, with `detail`, `hint` and `actions` `["wait"]`: a gate record is an append, and the window's mode appends nothing. Readmission answers the same. |
| `POST /worklet/retention/readmit/{node}?confirm={node}` | The inverse commit, on every one of those logs. **`409 readmission_refused`**, nothing written, when on any log the node has not applied every record up to the one just before the higher of that log's published floor (at its current generation) and its first surviving sequence (its last published position is more than one below that bound), or its last published position is from a generation the log has since left. The body carries `detail`, `hint`, `actions` `["wait"]` and the numbers `domain`, `position`, `generation`, `floor`, `first_seq`, `floor_generation` and `published` (false for a node that never published a position, judged as holding nothing). A judgement that could not be made refuses too, nothing written, as **`503 readmission_unjudged`**: the register or a floor unreadable, a log's first surviving sequence unreadable, or this node behind a reanchor the fleet has made. The body carries `detail`, `hint`, `actions` `["retry_same_op", "other_node"]` and, where one log could not be judged, that `log`. `force` has no effect and nothing overrides this refusal: the floor is a fact about what the node holds, not a lease. |

`confirm` echoes the node id; a mismatch is `400`. A node id no node could run under (the [`node.id`](../concepts/configuration.md#nodeid) rule; the id becomes a subject token on every log) is `400 invalid_gate`, nothing judged or written.

**A refusal's `detail` is its own sentence**, the one the operator acts on: no package name before it and no broker or store words after it (those go to this node's log). A judgement that stopped on a fault nothing told is `500 gate_failed`, saying nothing was written and carrying `node` and `op_id`, so the same request can be sent again under it.

The gate is written **as the caller**: the eviction's `by` (`crewlet retention status` prints it as "evicted by") is their name as [a write is attributed](#who-a-write-is-attributed-to), and the record carries the credential they used beside it. A capacity operation names its opener the same way, `by` beside `operator_id`, on the operation and on its entry in the report's `maintenance` list, which names every open window, oldest first.

**The gesture is judged once, before any log is written**; its record then goes to every identity-claiming log at once, each written by the node the request reached through its own write authority (every data node holds the whole estate, [the retention guide](../guides/retention.md#eviction)). The trim counts nodes per log, so a record on one log lifts that log's pin and no other. A `200` answers **per log**:

```json
{
  "node": "node-4",
  "evicted": true,
  "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4",
  "complete": false,
  "domains": [
    {"domain": "tracker", "stream": "CREWLET_TRACKER_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.tracker:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_TRACKER_LOG", "generation": 1, "seq": 918280002}},
    {"domain": "pages", "stream": "CREWLET_PAGES_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.pages:node-4",
     "outcome": "unknown",
     "actions": ["retry_same_op"],
     "hint": "its outcome is unknown: the same gesture under the same operation id answers from this log's own ledger if the record landed, and writes it if it did not"},
    {"domain": "iam", "stream": "CREWLET_IAM_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.iam:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_IAM_LOG", "generation": 0, "seq": 58311}},
    {"domain": "artifacts", "stream": "CREWLET_ARTIFACTS_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.artifacts:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_ARTIFACTS_LOG", "generation": 0, "seq": 30552}},
    {"domain": "artifactdata", "stream": "CREWLET_ARTIFACT_DATA_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.artifactdata:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_ARTIFACT_DATA_LOG", "generation": 0, "seq": 112940}},
    {"domain": "assistant", "stream": "CREWLET_ASSISTANT_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.assistant:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_ASSISTANT_LOG", "generation": 0, "seq": 15734}},
    {"domain": "chat", "stream": "CREWLET_CHAT_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.chat:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_CHAT_LOG", "generation": 0, "seq": 207714}},
    {"domain": "executor", "stream": "CREWLET_EXECUTOR_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.executor:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_EXECUTOR_LOG", "generation": 0, "seq": 30870}},
    {"domain": "code", "stream": "CREWLET_CODE_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.code:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_CODE_LOG", "generation": 1, "seq": 2207}},
    {"domain": "access", "stream": "CREWLET_ACCESS_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.access:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_ACCESS_LOG", "generation": 0, "seq": 4120}},
    {"domain": "atlas", "stream": "CREWLET_ATLAS_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.atlas:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_ATLAS_LOG", "generation": 0, "seq": 310}},
    {"domain": "advisor", "stream": "CREWLET_ADVISOR_LOG",
     "op_id": "01a0cd85-735a-7294-9d3e-38998abd698c.evict-node-4.evict.advisor:node-4",
     "outcome": "applied",
     "position": {"stream": "CREWLET_ADVISOR_LOG", "generation": 0, "seq": 5140}}
  ]
}
```

Each entry is one log's own answer. `outcome` is the write's [three-valued outcome](../guides/replication.md#a-write-has-three-outcomes), `applied`, `pending` or `unknown`, with the `position` the record holds (absent for `unknown`). A `pending` gate is a node about to stop writing, not one that has. An entry with `error` in place of `outcome` was **not written**; `reason` names why in the vocabulary every write refusal uses (`log_full`, `evicted`, ...). A log that answered holds its record whatever the others did.

An `unknown` entry may carry **`"unvouched": true`**: this node's operation ledger may have lost the row the operation needs (minted before the ledger's sweep reached it), so the node published nothing, cannot tell whether the record landed, and the same request here answers the same every time. It offers `other_node` rather than `retry_same_op`: send the same request with the same `op_id` through a node whose ledger reaches back that far.

A log the gesture did not finish also carries **`actions`** (what to do, in order) and **`hint`** (why); both are absent on a log that holds its record. The actions are a closed set a client switches on, and `hint` names no client's controls: `crewlet retention evict` renders an action as its own flags and the dashboard's evict dialog as its own buttons (never `-force` beside a screen with no such flag). Every refusal answer above carries `actions` beside its `hint` and the `op_id` the request was sent under, so `retry_same_op` on `503 eviction_unjudged` is the same request with that `op_id`. Nothing was written under it, so a fresh one is equally safe.

| Action | What the operator does | Where the gate answers it |
|---|---|---|
| `retry_same_op` | Send the same request again with the answer's `op_id` | An `unknown` outcome (unless `unvouched`), a lost race, a failure before the write answered, and a refusal that clears on its own (`behind`, `deferred`, `floor_unknown`, `below_floor`, `eviction_unknown`); a gate refusal (`evicted`, `overtaken`, `abandoned`) of **another node's copy** of the operation, which this node's append was collapsed onto (`hint` names that node): the reason is that node's standing, so this node finishes it once the log's duplicate window (two minutes from when the copy landed) has passed; `503 eviction_unjudged`; and `503 readmission_unjudged` (beside `other_node`) |
| `new_gesture` | Start a new gesture, without `op_id` | `superseded` (the operation's record landed and a later gate record on the same node undid it, e.g. an eviction retried after a readmission) and `op_reused` (an operation id that already names a record on another object) |
| `force` | Send the eviction again with `force=true` | `409 eviction_refused`, `503 eviction_unjudged` |
| `other_node` | Send it, with the same `op_id`, through another node the fleet still counts | This node's own standing or record: `evicted` (this node is evicted), `overtaken` and `abandoned` (this node wrote the record from rows a reanchor left behind; use a node on the log's current generation), an `unvouched` unknown, and beside `retry_same_op` on `deferred`, `below_floor` and `503 readmission_unjudged`. An `overtaken` or `abandoned` refusal, and an `evicted` one whose `hint` says the gesture's own record on that log applies nowhere, is a record that landed and applies nowhere: it holds the `op_id` on that log for the duplicate window (two minutes) from when it landed, and the same `op_id` sent sooner, through any node, is answered the same way, so `hint` says to wait that out first. An `evicted` refusal held at another operation's record (the newest on the log's subject when the gesture's answer was lost, possibly a healthy peer's) is this node's own eviction: send it through another node at once; if this node's own record did land, that node's answer says so and when |
| `reanchor` | [Re-anchor the log](../guides/retention.md#re-anchoring-a-recreated-or-restored-log) first, then send the same request with the same `op_id` | `wrong_stream` |
| `set_capacity` | [Raise the log's ceiling](../guides/retention.md#changing-a-logs-ceiling), then send the same request with the same `op_id` | `log_full`: a gate record is admitted into the log's [gate reserve](../guides/retention.md#the-gate-reserve), so this is a log full to its broker ceiling past even that |
| `wait` | Wait for what `hint` names to clear, then run it again; a client reads the answer's `error` beside the action | `409 eviction_refused` (the lease to lapse), `409 readmission_refused` (the node to catch up), `409 not_publishing` (the fleet to leave its capacity window) |
| `restore` | Restore the store and the stream from one backup | `skew` |

A log with a `hint` and **no** `actions` is one no gesture clears: a record larger than its log's declared largest or the broker's `max_payload`, a refusal the broker named, or a refusal reason this build has no word for. The hint carries the refusal's own detail, which says what does clear it (the limit and what moves it, or the broker's words). Only `retry_same_op` makes the same request, sent again **now**, the remedy. Four actions (`retry_same_op`, `other_node`, `reanchor`, `set_capacity`) keep the gesture's own `op_id` as how it is finished after the operator has acted: a gesture sent afresh after raising a ceiling is a second one, which rewrites every log that already holds the first one's record, re-dates the eviction, restarts its fence window and turns the first `op_id` into `superseded`. Only `new_gesture` ends the operation for good.

`complete` is true only when every log answered `applied` or `pending`. When it is false and a log offers `retry_same_op`, send **the same request again with `op_id`** set to the operation id the answer carried. Each log's record is published under an id derived from it (the entry's own `op_id`, carrying the gesture's sign, the log and the node), and each log's snapshot reads that id's ledger row first: a log whose record is already the gate in force answers at its position and is not written twice, and only a missing log is written, however long after the first request, since the broker's two-minute duplicate window plays no part. Without `op_id` the route mints a fresh one, which is a second gesture; an id carried from an eviction to the readmission after it is a different operation on every log, and one carried to another node is that node's own operation.

Anything but a valid `op_id` is `400 op_id_invalid`, nothing judged or written. Valid is **in the engine's grammar** (a UUIDv7 whose leading 48 bits are the Unix millisecond it was minted at, optionally followed by `.` and a name) and **at most 128 bytes** of **visible ASCII with no space**. A client may mint its own before the first request, as both engine clients do (`crewlet retention evict` on the workstation's clock, the dashboard's evict dialog on the browser's). The state log reads the mint instant to decide whether its ledger can vouch for a retry, so a client clock far ahead of the fleet's is the one case this trusts a caller with. An id with no instant gives nothing to read. The rest is the broker's: only the leading uuid is minted, and the whole id travels as the broker's message-id header, which trims its ends and turns a line break into a space, so such an id would be deduplicated as a different id from the one every ledger answers for. It is refused rather than cleaned because a retry must send back the id it holds byte for byte; every id an answer carries already fits.

**The gesture does not stop when its caller does.** The judgement runs under the request within twenty seconds, so a request abandoned before it wrote nothing; once the first record is about to be written the node finishes under its own budget, thirty seconds for the logs, all written at once, so a dropped connection or client timeout never leaves a node evicted on one log and counted on another. A node answers within **fifty seconds** at most, so a client waiting a minute (as both engine clients do) or a reverse proxy at its usual sixty-second read timeout always reads the node's own answer. A caller that sent its own `op_id` can ask again with it and read every log's answer; one that let the route mint it lost the id with the answer that never arrived.

Every node running the state log serves both routes, whichever backends the company uses (a company on an external tracker still runs every log). A node with no log to write a gate to answers `503`, not `404`: the routes exist on this build. The node is asked at every request: one that booted with no company serves both routes, with no restart, from the first revision that runs a log.

### The capacity window

A log's Tier A ceiling is only the value its stream is created with; these routes are the window in which a running log's ceiling changes. The [procedure is documented once](../guides/retention.md#changing-a-logs-ceiling); this is the wire surface. Every route here, the status read included, takes `admin`.

| Route | What it does |
|---|---|
| `POST /worklet/retention/capacity?stream=NAME&bytes=N&confirm=N` | Opens or resumes the operation and drives it as far as this node's mode allows. `confirm` repeats `bytes`; a mismatch is `400` (the target is chosen once for the life of an operation). `assert_excluded=true` is required only on an external broker. A window names at most 16 participants: on a fleet that counts more (every live member and data node, and every node with a position row that isn't retired), no window opens and the answer is `409 capacity_refused` naming each node counted only for its row and how to retire it. An admission from a still-running process (it holds its node's presence) closes the window again as it opens: `409 capacity_refused` naming the node, with no `operation`. An admission from a process that isn't running answers `409 capacity_refused` naming the node and the commands past it, with the window open at `opened` in `operation`: nothing is sent until that node restarts into a maintenance mode or is excluded, and the window refuses every node that starts in service until then. An admission whose node another process now holds is withdrawn by the window. A `200` also answers `open_windows` (every window open on any log, this one included, each with `stream`, `operation_id`, `phase` and `target_max_bytes`) and `unread_windows` (every log whose window this node couldn't read); a node won't start in service while either is non-empty. |
| `GET /worklet/retention/maintenance?stream=NAME` | The operation, every acknowledgement of this log's window (each naming its `stream`; one a node made as it booted with no window open names no operation: empty `operation_id`, `attempt` 0, which a baseline reads and a seal never takes), every admission, and what the window's next step waits on, computed here. At `opened` that is the baseline: `restarts_missing` (participants with no restart into a maintenance mode recorded) and `admissions_blocking` (every admission but an excluded node's). From baseline to seal it is the seal: `sealed` and `blocking`, which no longer reads an admission. Once `sealed` and `confirmed` it is `sealed: true` and no `blocking`. The operation's `retired` names each participant whose retirement stands as this node judged it. |
| `POST /worklet/retention/maintenance/abandon?stream=NAME&confirm=OPERATION-ID` | From `opened` clears the operation outright and answers no `operation`; from anywhere else enters the seal, and the operation records who abandoned it as `abandoned_by`. Either answers `open_windows` and `unread_windows` as `capacity` does. `confirm` repeats the open operation's id and is checked first: missing is `400 confirm_required`; another operation's id is `400 confirm_required` naming the open one in `detail`, with it in `operation`. |
| `POST /worklet/retention/maintenance/exclude?stream=NAME&node=ID&confirm=ID` | Waives one node's acknowledgement and withdraws its admission; the operation records who asserted it under `excluded_by`, keyed by the node, and the node leaves `participants` for `excluded`. An excluded node's admission no longer stops the window, whether or not it could be withdrawn. A running node (one holding a live presence lease, one whose broker the fleet's metadata group hears, or this node), a window's last participant once it has sent a request, an exclusion past the 16 a window keeps, a window that moved while the node was being judged, and an id no node could run under are `409 capacity_refused` in the engine's words; presence or membership that couldn't be read is too, and nothing is written. An exclusion lapses if the node is running, judged the same way, when the window's next request leaves, which records it again. Answers `open_windows` and `unread_windows` as `capacity` does. |
| `POST /worklet/retention/maintenance/retire?node=ID&confirm=ID` | Records that no process will run under the node id again, for the whole fleet and every capacity window to come ([Who has to acknowledge](../guides/retention.md#who-has-to-acknowledge)), and answers `retired` (`node_id`, `by`, `by_kind`, `operator_id`, `at`). No window counts the id while it runs nothing (no presence, no broker the metadata group hears) and writes no position row; an open window's `operation` names each participant so waived, judged as it was read, under `retired`. `confirm` repeats `node`; missing or different is `400 confirm_required`. A running node (as `exclude` judges it), this node, or an id no node could run under is `409 capacity_refused` in the engine's words; presence or membership that couldn't be read is too, and nothing is written. |

**A blocked operation says why twice**: `blocked` is a code for scripts (`abandoned_by_operator`, `capacity_operation_unsealed`, `capacity_fleet_too_large`, with `outgrown` the count of nodes the next request would have counted, `capacity_window_records_too_many`, with `outgrown` the count it would have recorded, recounted after each exclusion or retirement since, or `capacity_journal_full`) and `blocked_detail` is the sentence a person reads: what blocked the window and what clears it, with every command as the CLI takes it. An abandoned window's sentence is decided by its seal, so an answer carrying one reads the window's acknowledgements. Every answer carrying an `operation` carries both, as does each entry in the retention report's `maintenance` list. A code this build doesn't know still gets a sentence, saying so.

**Every gesture on the window names who made it**: `by` and `operator_id` for its opener, and the same pair under `abandoned_by` and, per node, `excluded_by`: the author and the credential they acted through. An abandonment from `opened` clears the record it would have been written on, so only that log names who made it.

**A node in `normal` mode refuses the write routes**, naming the restart: the usage a resize is decided against must be a quantity nothing can move.

**Every refusal is `409 capacity_refused` in its own words**: what was refused, what to do, the numbers it turns on, never the error underneath (that goes to this node's log). A gesture that stopped on a fault nothing told is `500 capacity_failed`, pointing at the status read. A status read that couldn't read the window is `503 maintenance_unreadable` with a `Retry-After` (ask again once coordination answers); one that read the window but not its acknowledgements or the admissions answers `200` with the window and `acks_unread: true` or `admissions_unread: true`, leaving out that register and every list formed from it (`restarts_missing`, `admissions_blocking`, `sealed`, `blocking`). One that couldn't judge which participants are retired answers `retired_unread: true`, no `retired`, and none of those lists, each of which waives the retired. An `operation` in any answer that couldn't judge them carries `retired_unread: true` too, and its `blocked_detail` says so rather than naming a node to restart. A stream this node doesn't keep is `404 unknown_stream`, naming the ones it does. Each answer to a write carries `operation` where there is one. The three-mode boot is `crewlet run -mode`; see [the CLI reference](cli.md#crewlet-run).

`restarts_missing` / `admissions_blocking` and `sealed` / `blocking` are **computed server-side** from the predicates the coordinator itself runs; a client re-deriving them would be a second opinion that drifts.

### Re-anchoring

| Route | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /worklet/retention/reanchor?stream=NAME` | The LIVE stream's own `created_at`, read from the broker on the call (the instant a `wrong_stream` refusal names), the generation that stream's domain stands at, and what a reanchor run now would do: `case`: `recreated` (another stream than the rows are keyed to, followed from its first surviving record), `restored` (the same stream brought back from an older copy, ending below the checkpoint or holding another record at it since, followed from its end, one below the node's own generation record where an earlier attempt already appended it) or `abandoned` (the same stream, continuing in a generation only an evicted peer held, followed from this node's own checkpoint with that generation's records void), with `cursor`, the sequence the new checkpoint would sit at. With nothing to re-anchor there is no `case`, and `nothing_to_reanchor` says why. A restored log holding records this node's rows do not hold, written after the restore, also answers `discards` (the newest of them: `seq`, `kind`, `subject`, `writer`, `op_id`, `stored_at`, and `ledger_lost_before` when its operation is older than the instant this node's operation ledger may have lost rows from: the rows may hold it after all) and `discarding` (why a reanchor refuses without `discard=true`). `404 unknown_stream` for a stream this node does not run; `503 stream_unreadable` when the broker did not answer the read (worth retrying). |
| `POST /worklet/retention/reanchor?stream=NAME&confirm=<created_at>[&force=true][&discard=true]` | Runs that ONE domain's generation transition, answering with the new `generation`, the `case` it answered, the `cursor` its checkpoint went to (for a restored log, one below the generation record the transition appended; once that record is appended the transition finishes on its own, so a disconnecting client does not stop it halfway) and, when it discarded records written after a restore, the newest as `discarded`. No other domain's checkpoint moves, and the domain's applier resumes with no restart. |

`confirm` is the `GET`'s value, supplied by the caller: it means *I looked at the thing I am re-anchoring*, so the two are separate round trips. It is compared as an instant at microsecond precision, so the RFC 3339 value the `GET` answers is accepted as it came. `force=true` overrides the rule that only the most caught-up node may re-anchor, for a fleet whose register cannot say; it never overrides a peer that has already re-anchored the stream, whose rows are the fleet's history in the new generation and which the refusal names. `discard=true` accepts that a restored log's records this node's rows do not hold (written after the restore, named by the `GET` as `discards`) are applied on no node; without it that reanchor is `409 reanchor_refused`, and with it the answer carries the newest as `discarded`. The flags are separate because neither answers the other's question. A node in a [capacity window](../guides/retention.md#changing-a-logs-ceiling) refuses every reanchor `409 reanchor_refused`, naming its mode: the reanchor appends a generation record, and the window's mode appends nothing.

Every refusal, and every transition that stopped where it can say what was committed and what to do, is `409 reanchor_refused` in those words, as `nothing_to_reanchor` and `discarding` are (no package name, no broker words; those go to this node's log). A transition that stopped on a fault nothing told is `500 reanchor_failed`, pointing at the status read; a status read the broker didn't answer is `503 stream_unreadable`; a stream this node doesn't keep is `404 unknown_stream`, naming the ones it does.

## Artifacts

An **artifact** is a page, a doc or a native sheet a person or a seat publishes for others to open: immutable numbered versions of its files, shared with seats, units or the whole company at a role (`viewer`, `commenter`, `contributor`, `editor`; the owner holds every role). Its records are the `artifacts` state log's, every data node holds them, and its bytes are objects in the [object store](../concepts/object-store.md). These routes are served on `api.port`; the pages themselves are served only on the separate artifact origin (`api.artifacts`), inside a sandboxed frame, never here.

### Who may do what

Every route decides one verb of the authority table on the artifact's own owner and shares, **before** a version, file or byte is read:

- **A caller with no relation to an artifact is answered `404 not_found`**, byte for byte as an id nothing holds, on every route, so nothing says a private artifact exists.
- **A relation below the verb's role** is `403 unauthorized` with `reason:
  role` and `role` naming what it needs, which the owner can share.
- **Authoring asks the artifacts app** beside the role: creating, publishing, renaming, labelling, adding an asset. Reading and sharing ask the relation alone, so a person invited with no app reads what was shared with them.
- **An agent is kept to `contributor`** on an artifact it does not own unless the company sets `artifacts.agents_manage_others`. **The lead of an agent** holds owner on that agent's artifacts, and nothing on a person's.
- **Trash, restore and transfer are a person's**; a transfer and a forced publish need a person present, which a machine token never is (`403 token_refused`). **A purge is an administrator's**, with a proof of identity inside the step-up window (`403 step_up_required` otherwise) and a person present.
- **An administrator may open any artifact.** Every read only the admin path admits writes an elevated-read record first (one per day, administrator, artifact and version), which the artifact's history shows its owner and editors and the company trail (`GET /artifacts/trail`) shows every administrator; a read whose record cannot be written is `503` and not served. That covers every read of content: a version's files, source and frame, every datastore question and the CSV export, a room's join, and the live entry a `412 version_moved` hands back. An administrator who holds a share is admitted as that share, at its role; the admin path (owner, recorded) opens only for a verb their relations do not reach. A listing never shows an artifact on the admin path.
- **The trash stops serving content at once.** A trashed artifact's head, its
  versions and its history stay readable to its audience for the trash view;
  its files, source, frames, export and datastore questions are `409
  artifact_trashed` (`artifact_trashed` on the socket), and a room's join is
  refused `artifact_trashed`, before anything is read or recorded — to a reader
  it is disclosed to: one with no relation is told `not_found`, as for an id
  nothing holds. The trash is a state its owner's restore ends, which
  `not_found` would deny; a purge is for good, which `not_found` — and a
  purged store's `410 data_gone` — say truly.
- **A purge is committed before anything it removes is gone.** Its first step stamps the artifact on its own record (`purge_begun_at` on the head, and into the trash if it was live), and only then does the datastore go, which no restore can bring back. From then on a restore is `409 artifact_purging` and the artifact is never served or written again; a purge that stopped part way finishes on its retry under the same key, an administrator's purge, or the trash reaper's next pass, which takes every begun purge whatever its trash term.

What the decision concluded is stamped into the record every write forms: the caller's role on the artifact, whether only the admin path admitted them, the Tier A quotas in force, the surface the request came through (`dashboard` for a browser session, `api` for a bearer token) and the work item it was made for. The domain's applier decides from the record alone.
### Writes

| Method and path | Verb | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /artifacts/uploads` | `create_artifact` | Upload intent for a new artifact |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/uploads` | `publish_artifact`, or `upload_artifact_asset` with `asset: true` | Upload intent for the next version, or into the asset store |
| `PUT /artifacts/uploads/{upload}/files/{path}` | the intent's own verb, decided again | One file's bytes, streamed through the engine |
| `POST /artifacts` | `create_artifact` | A new artifact and its first version, owned by the caller. `"starter": true` begins from its kind's starter content, which the engine holds and publishes inline, naming no upload, files or entry; a kind with no starter is `422 invalid`. A `slides` starter takes an optional `"deck": {"theme": "<id>", "slides": [{"layout": "<id>", "title": "..."}]}` (at most 60 slides, each title at most 200 bytes); absent, it opens with a cover, an agenda, two columns and a closing slide in the `ink` theme. An unknown theme or layout is `422 invalid`. A doc's starter may carry `"doc": {"body": "<markdown>"}`: the title becomes the tab's heading, the body goes under it, held to the doc format, at most 1 MiB in all. A design's starter is the `layout` sent with it: its `boards` (each a `title`, `x`, `y`, `w`, `h` and optional `brief`, the first the cover) and `notes` (as `canvas.json` holds them), published as `canvas.json` and one placeholder page per board under `boards/`, every typed word escaped as text; a design starter with no layout, or a layout outside the canvas format's bounds, is `422 invalid`, each problem named at its place (`boards[2].w`). `deck`, `doc` or `layout` without `starter`, or on any other kind, is `422 invalid`. `"folder": "<id>"` creates it in that folder, which asks `artifacts.folder.file` on it beside the create: a folder the caller cannot see, or a removed one, is `404 folder_not_found` |
| `POST /artifacts/checks` | `create_artifact` | A page's text files judged as a publish of its kind would judge them, writing nothing: `{"kind": "html", "entry": "index.html", "files": [{"path": "index.html", "text": "..."}]}`, answered `200` with every `refusals` and `warnings` finding (path, line, code, message). Framed kinds only, 1 to 64 text files, at most 2 MiB of text. An allowlisted CDN file is named where its copy would be served and never fetched, so a CDN that refuses it is found only at publish. Budget per node: two checks a second per person, burst of ten; past it `429 check_budget` with a `Retry-After` |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/versions` | `publish_artifact`; `artifacts.publish.force` beside it when forced | The next version, based on `If-Match: "<n>"` |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/versions/{n}/restore` | `publish_artifact` | Version `n` again as a new version, every file carried, based on `If-Match` |
| `PATCH /artifacts/{id}` | `update_artifact` | The title, the description or the icon |
| `PATCH /artifacts/{id}/versions/{n}` | `update_artifact` | Version `n`'s label (`{"label": ""}` clears it); a labelled version is kept past the hundred unlabelled ones |
| `PUT /artifacts/{id}/shares` | `share_artifact` | `{"audience": {"kind": "seat", "id": "bob"}, "role": "editor"}`; never above the sharer's own role, never the company from an agent. A NEW audience is held to the grant rule: a seat audience is a seat handle, never a login (`token:maya` or `jane.doe` is refused 422, `invalid`), and a seat or unit the company's roster does not hold is refused the same way, with the sentence that says which; a create's `shares` follow the same rule. An audience the artifact already shares with may change its role whatever it names |
| `DELETE /artifacts/{id}/shares/{audience}` | `unshare_artifact` | The audience as `seat:<handle>`, `unit:<key>` or `company`. Any audience a share can be stored under is withdrawn, never held to the grant rule or roster, so an owner can remove a share to a login or to a seat the chart has since removed |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/transfer` | `artifacts.transfer` | `{"to": "<seat>"}` |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/work-items` | `get_artifact` on the artifact and `update_work_item` on the item | `{"work_item": "ENG-12", "after"?: "CREWLET_TRACKER_LOG@1:9"}`: links the artifact to a work item Worklet holds, so the item's Artifacts panel lists it. `after` is the `position` the item's create answered with; the item is read from no earlier than it. See [Linking to a work item](#linking-to-a-work-item) |
| `DELETE /artifacts/{id}` | `artifacts.trash` | Into the trash: every frame stops loading at once; purged after thirty days |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/restore` | `artifacts.restore` | Out of the trash; `409 artifact_purging` once a purge has begun |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/purge` | `artifacts.purge` | Gone for good, in three steps: the artifact is committed to its purge (into the trash, never restored), its datastore goes, then its own rows |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/assets` | `upload_artifact_asset` | `{"upload": "<upload>", "name": "<name>"}`: finalize an asset |
| `DELETE /artifacts/{id}/assets/{asset}` | `upload_artifact_asset` | Remove one |
| `PUT`, `DELETE /artifacts/{id}/pin` | `artifacts.pin` | The caller's own pin |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/comments` | `comment_on_artifact` | Open a thread with its first remark: `{"body": "<markdown>", "version"?, "anchor"?, "quote"?, "crop"?, "crop_type"?}`. `version` is the version it is about (absent, the head), `anchor` where on it, as [Artifacts](../concepts/artifacts.md#comments) says each kind takes (absent, the whole version), `quote` the page's words (at most 1 KiB), `crop` a picture of the part as standard base64, `crop_type` `image/png`, `image/jpeg` or `image/webp` (at most 64 KiB, 800 pixels on the longer side). Answers the `thread` and `remark` ids. A remark is at most 16 KiB; one carrying a credential is `422 credential_refused`; a trashed artifact is `409 artifact_trashed`; one at 2000 threads is `409 conflict` |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/comments/{thread}/replies` | `comment_on_artifact` | `{"body", "reply_to"?}`: a remark in the thread, answering the thread or one remark. A thread at 500 remarks is `409 conflict` |
| `PATCH /artifacts/{id}/comments/{thread}/remarks/{remark}` | `edit_artifact_comment` | `{"body"}`: what one of the caller's own remarks says now; somebody else's is `403 forbidden` |
| `DELETE /artifacts/{id}/comments/{thread}/remarks/{remark}` | `remove_artifact_comment` | Take one remark's words down; it keeps its place, marked removed. The author's, or an administrator's moderating |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/comments/{thread}/resolve` | `resolve_artifact_comment` | `{"version"?}`: resolve the thread citing the version that addressed it, from the version it was made on to the head (absent, the head) |
| `POST /artifacts/{id}/comments/{thread}/reopen` | `resolve_artifact_comment` | Reopen a resolved thread |
| `PUT /artifacts/{id}/folder` | `move_artifact` on the artifact and `artifacts.folder.file` on the folder | `{"folder": "<id>"}` files it in a folder, `{"folder": ""}` at the top level. See [Folders](#folders) |
| `POST /artifacts/folder-moves` | as `PUT /artifacts/{id}/folder`, for each item alone | `{"items": [{"artifact", "folder"}]}`, at most 25, answered `200` with `{"results": [{"artifact", "outcome", "message"?}]}`. See [Folders](#folders) |

**A share that reaches nobody is surfaced, not dropped.** An earlier grant rule let a share name a login as a seat (`seat:token:maya`), which no seat matches, so it grants nothing. The engine neither deletes nor sweeps such a share: it is authorisation data its owner wrote, and removing it silently would rewrite who was meant to have access. Instead `artifact_access` marks it `invalid: true`, the share dialog lists it with why ("token:maya is a sign-in, not a seat. Remove it and share with their seat.") and offers Remove as its one action, and the listing never counts it toward the login's Shared section.

Every write but the transfer carries an `Idempotency-Key`, from which every record id is derived, so a retry under the same key is the same operation (`400 op_id_invalid` without one). A write answers `200` with its `outcome`, `202` for one durable and not yet applied on this node, and `503` with `outcome: unknown` and the `op_id` for one nobody could account for: send it again under the same key, never a fresh one. The transfer needs no key: the upload claims each file before a byte is read, and a second put of it is refused `409 upload_consumed`. A node that runs no upload pipeline (no object store, or no coordination store to reserve the bytes in) answers every route that checks or publishes (create, check, publish, assets and transfer) `503 unavailable` with **no** `Retry-After`: the pipeline is built once per process, so no wait changes the answer; why is in the node's log.

### Linking to a work item

`POST /artifacts/{id}/work-items` puts an existing artifact on a Worklet item's Artifacts panel, as a create or publish carrying `work_item` does for what it makes. It records one `link_work_item` row in the artifact's history, filed under the item, and changes nothing else.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"work_item": "ENG-12"}' \
  "http://localhost:8000/artifacts/$ID/work-items"
```

- **The artifact is decided as a read** (`get_artifact`): any role, viewer and above. A caller with no relation is `404 not_found` like any artifact route; an administrator with none is admitted on the admin path, recorded as an elevated read first.
- **The item is decided as a write** (`update_work_item`), by the rule `PATCH /worklet/items/{key}` takes: a caller who does not use Worklet is `403 unauthorized`.
- **The item must be live.** `work_item` is a key or an item id, at most 64 bytes of visible ASCII; one Worklet does not hold or holds removed is `422 invalid`, as is a company whose work items another tracker keeps. A node not yet handed a company answers `503 no_active_revision`. A trashed artifact is `409 artifact_trashed`.
- **A link sent right after the item was filed names its create.** On a fleet the link can reach a node that has not applied the create yet.
